va-ts051.x: Last year the regional grocery chain Fernway replaced the self-checkout kiosks in its twelve largest stores with staffed checkout lanes. In the following six months, average weekly sales in those twelve stores rose by 9 percent, while sales in Fernway's other stores, which kept their kiosks, were essentially flat. Fernway's management concludes that shoppers prefer staffed lanes and that converting the remaining stores would raise sales there by a similar amount.

va-ts052.x: To reduce traffic deaths, the city of Marlow lowered the speed limit on its residential streets from 40 to 30 kilometers per hour. Critics argue that drivers simply ignore posted limits, so the change will have no effect. City planners respond that even a small drop in average speed sharply reduces the chance that a pedestrian struck by a car is killed, and they predict that pedestrian deaths on residential streets will fall.

va-ts053.x: In a two-year field study, researchers studying a population of desert lizards in southern Morocco found that individuals with darker skin spent, on average, 20 minutes less each morning basking in the sun before beginning to forage than lighter-skinned individuals did. Because darker skin absorbs heat faster, the researchers concluded that dark coloration gives these lizards an advantage: more time each day for finding food.

va-ts054.x: A large national health survey, repeated every year, found that the share of adults who reported getting at least the recommended amount of weekly exercise rose from 41 percent to 48 percent over a decade. During the same decade, however, the share of adults classified as obese also rose, and average daily calorie intake per person, as measured by food purchase records, changed very little.

va-ts055.x: Historians have long held that the medieval town of Veldt declined because a new trade route bypassed it. ⟦Yet tax records show that Veldt's population began to fall two decades before the new route opened.⟧ This timing does not by itself refute the trade-route account, since merchants may have anticipated the route and moved early. But letters from Veldt's council in those years complain repeatedly of flooding and say nothing about trade. ⟦The best explanation, then, is that the decline began with environmental damage and was only later accelerated by the change in trade.⟧

va-ts056.x: A furniture factory installed a camera system that inspects every glued joint on its chairs and tables before they are packed. In the year after the system was installed, the number of products returned by customers because of loose or broken joints fell by 30 percent. The factory's production director concludes that the cameras were responsible for most of this reduction and recommends buying a more advanced version of the system.

va-ts057.x: At Corlan Furniture, every product sold online is also sold in at least one of the company's showrooms. Some products sold in showrooms are made to order and take more than eight weeks to deliver. No product that takes more than eight weeks to deliver is eligible for the company's free-return guarantee. All products sold online, however, are eligible for the free-return guarantee.

va-ts058.x: The province of Tessaly plans to give a tax credit to farmers who plant strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields. Supporters say the strips will attract wild bees and other pollinators, and that higher pollinator numbers will raise the yields of nearby crops such as apples and canola enough to more than repay farmers for the land the strips take out of production.

va-ts059.x: A study followed 3,000 call-center employees at large firms for five years, checking in with each of them every six months. Those who used standing desks for at least half of their working day reported back pain far less often than those who sat all day. The study's authors conclude that standing for part of the day prevents back pain and recommend that employers provide standing desks to all of their staff.

va-ts060.x: A science journalist, writing about a large survey of how often published papers are cited, argues: "Research papers whose findings are later contradicted by other studies receive, on average, more citations than papers whose findings hold up. Clearly, then, scientists are more interested in sensational claims than in reliable ones, and the citation system, which shapes hiring and funding decisions, rewards bad science."

va-ts061.x: Three years ago the port city of Halvik began requiring cruise ships docked in its harbor during the summer season to plug into the city's electricity supply instead of running their diesel engines. Since then, air-quality monitors in the harbor district record a 15 percent drop in summer fine-particle pollution. The port authority concludes that the rule is the main reason for the improvement and argues that applying the same rule to cruise ships docked in winter would produce a comparable improvement in winter air.

va-ts062.x: Ashcombe, a maker of kitchen appliances, reviewed ten years of sales data and found that customers who registered their products online were twice as likely as other customers to buy a second Ashcombe product within two years. Ashcombe's marketing director therefore proposes offering a small gift card to every customer who registers, reasoning that a higher registration rate will bring a corresponding increase in repeat purchases.

va-ts063.x: When Harwick University replaced the lighting in its classroom buildings with LED lamps, which use about half as much electricity to produce the same amount of light, administrators expected the electricity bill for lighting those buildings to fall substantially. Two years after the replacement was completed, however, the bill was only slightly lower than before, even though electricity prices had not risen and the buildings had not been enlarged.

va-ts064.x: Historians have generally attributed the rapid spread of printing workshops in sixteenth-century Brabant to the growing wealth of the region's merchants, who bought books in large numbers. One historian argues instead that the decisive factor was the founding of several universities in the region, whose students and teachers created a steady demand for printed textbooks, and that merchant wealth mattered much less than has been claimed.

va-ts065.x: Some ecologists have proposed releasing a parasitic wasp to control the beetle that is killing ash trees in Lindor Forest. ⟦In laboratory trials, the wasp killed nearly all of the beetle larvae it was given.⟧ Opponents warn that the wasp might also attack native beetles. That risk appears small, since the wasp in trials ignored every native species offered to it. But laboratory success does not guarantee success outdoors: ⟦the beetle larvae in Lindor Forest live deep under thick bark, where the wasp, whose egg-laying organ is short, may be unable to reach most of them.⟧ The release should therefore be preceded by a field trial.

va-ts066.x: In a clinical trial, patients recovering from knee surgery were randomly assigned either to a standard physical therapy program or to the same program plus daily sessions with a new motion-tracking app that gives feedback on exercise form. After twelve weeks, the app group had regained significantly more range of motion. The app's developer concludes that the feedback on form is what produced the better recovery.

va-ts067.x: A survey of a coral reef found that every colony of the coral species Acropora velata that had bleached during the previous summer's heat wave was located in water shallower than four meters. Not every colony in water shallower than four meters bleached, however. All colonies of the species that host the alga strain Type D, which is known to tolerate heat, were found in water deeper than four meters.

va-ts068.x: Over the past five years, the share of new cars sold in the country of Vellmark that are electric has risen from 4 percent to 31 percent, and the number of public charging stations has more than quadrupled. Yet over the same period, the average revenue that a Vellmark gas station earns from selling fuel has fallen by only about 3 percent, while total spending on fuel nationwide has fallen far more.

va-ts069.x: To reduce evictions, the city of Rosendal plans to give tenants who receive an eviction notice free access to a lawyer. Officials note that, in the city's housing court, tenants who had a lawyer were evicted less than half as often as tenants who represented themselves. They conclude that providing lawyers to all tenants facing eviction will substantially reduce evictions in the city.

va-ts070.x: A city's library system installed self-service kiosks that let patrons borrow and return books without help from staff. In the year after installation, the number of books borrowed rose by 12 percent. The library director argues that the kiosks, by shortening waiting times at the desk, encouraged people to borrow more, and recommends installing kiosks in the system's remaining branches, which currently have none.

va-ts071.x: Engineers at a battery manufacturer have found that lithium cells charged at room temperature and then stored for a year lose about 8 percent of their capacity, whereas identical cells charged in a cold room lose about 15 percent. The engineers hypothesize that charging in the cold causes a thin layer of lithium metal to form on the cell's electrode, and that this layer, rather than the cold itself, is what permanently reduces capacity.

va-ts072.x: Analysts predicted that Quillon's decision to sell its budget smartphones only online would hurt its sales, since many budget buyers like to handle a phone in a store before buying. ⟦In the first year, Quillon's budget-phone sales did fall by 6 percent.⟧ But this figure is misleading. The entire budget-phone market shrank by 14 percent that year, so Quillon's share of the market actually grew. ⟦The online-only strategy, far from hurting Quillon, appears to have helped it,⟧ largely by allowing the company to cut prices with the money it saved on store displays.

va-ts073.x: Hospitals in the region of Aldmoor introduced a new screening program that identifies patients at high risk of developing sepsis, a dangerous response to infection, so that they can be treated early. Since the program began, the number of patients in Aldmoor's hospitals recorded as having sepsis has risen by 40 percent, yet the number of deaths from sepsis has fallen slightly.

va-ts074.x: In a new study of industrial life, a historian argues that the nineteenth-century textile workers of Lowenfeld were generally content with their working conditions. As evidence, she points out that the archive of the city's largest mill contains hundreds of letters written by workers to the mill's owners, and that the great majority of these letters express gratitude for the owners' generosity, while only a handful contain complaints about wages, hours, or the conditions in the workrooms.

va-ts075.x: A university study of 400 psychology experiments published over the past fifteen years in leading journals found that those whose data were shared publicly were much less likely than others to contain statistical errors. The study's authors conclude that the expectation of outside scrutiny leads researchers to check their analyses more carefully, and they argue that journals should require all authors to share their data.

va-ts076.x: Nutrition researchers measured how much vitamin D a group of volunteers absorbed from a supplement taken either with a high-fat breakfast or with a low-fat breakfast. Absorption was about 30 percent higher with the high-fat meal. The researchers conclude that people who take vitamin D supplements in order to maintain healthy blood levels of the vitamin should take them with their highest-fat meal of the day.

va-ts077.x: A national chain of coffee shops tested a loyalty app, which awards points toward free drinks, in twenty of its shops. Over six months, customers in those shops who used the app visited 35 percent more often than customers who did not. The chain's executives concluded that the app increases how often customers visit and decided to introduce it in all of the chain's shops.

va-ts078.x: At Velsen University, a student qualifies for the national merit scholarship only if his or her grades are in the top tenth of the class. Every student who holds the merit scholarship is also eligible for a guaranteed room in the university's new residence hall. Last year, some students who were eligible for a guaranteed room did not receive one, although every eligible student who applied for a room by the deadline received one.

va-ts079.x: A team of zoologists hypothesizes that the bright tail stripes of a species of forest frog serve to warn predators that the frog's skin is toxic. Critics suggest that the stripes might instead help males attract mates, since in many frog species bright markings play that role. The zoologists point out that in this species, females' stripes are just as bright as males' stripes.

va-ts080.x: Records from the port of Tremona show that in the decade after the city's harbor was deepened in 1702, allowing much larger ships to dock, the total weight of goods passing through the port nearly doubled. Over the same decade, however, the number of dockworkers employed at the port fell by about a fifth, even though the port's handling methods, which relied entirely on manual labor, did not change.

va-ts081.x: Five years ago the state of Dravia began paying a cash bonus to teachers who agreed to work in rural schools that had struggled to fill vacancies. Since then, the number of unfilled teaching positions in those schools has fallen by half. State officials argue that the bonus has solved the rural staffing problem and that the program can be ended next year without causing vacancies to rise again.

va-ts082.x: A company that makes wireless home security cameras, which most customers mount outdoors, plans to replace the cameras' rechargeable batteries with small solar panels. The company's engineers argue that the change will reduce customer complaints, most of which concern batteries that run down and must be recharged, and that it will not increase the number of camera failures, because the solar panels proved highly reliable in testing.

va-ts083.x: Scholars once believed that the ancient city of Kesh was abandoned suddenly, perhaps after an invasion. Recent excavations, however, found that the houses of Kesh contained almost no valuable objects such as tools, jewelry, or cooking pots, although such objects are plentiful in the city's rubbish heaps from earlier periods. The excavators conclude that the residents left gradually, taking their possessions with them, rather than fleeing in haste.

va-ts084.x: A popular view holds that adults need less sleep as they age. ⟦Surveys consistently find that people over sixty-five sleep, on average, about an hour less each night than middle-aged adults do.⟧ Yet older adults also report far more daytime drowsiness and are more likely to nap. This pattern suggests that they are not choosing less sleep because they need less, but are unable to get the sleep they need. ⟦Older adults, in other words, may need just as much sleep as younger ones,⟧ and the problem worth addressing is the disruption of their sleep.

va-ts085.x: Torvald Bikes, which sells bicycles through independent shops, has seen its share of the market fall for three straight years. Its chief executive attributes the decline to the company's failure to offer electric bicycles, which now make up a quarter of all bicycle sales. Some board members argue instead that the problem is poor service at the independent shops, which customers increasingly complain about.

va-ts086.x: In a mountain lake, the population of a small fish species that feeds on insect larvae fell sharply after anglers illegally introduced a larger predatory fish. Biologists then removed nearly all of the predators. Over the next four years, however, the small fish recovered only slightly, even though the lake's water quality and temperature remained much as they had been before the predators arrived, and no new predators or diseases were detected.

va-ts087.x: Researchers compared hospital records from two neighboring regions. In Region A, where a public campaign urged people with chest pain to call an ambulance at once, the death rate among heart-attack patients admitted to hospital was 9 percent. In Region B, which had no such campaign, it was 6 percent. A commentator concludes that the campaign has done more harm than good, perhaps by causing hospitals to be overcrowded with false alarms.

va-ts088.x: At Hallam Consulting, every employee who leads a client project has completed the firm's management course. Some employees who have completed the management course have also earned the firm's advanced analytics certificate. No employee who has been with the firm for less than two years is permitted to enroll in the management course. Priyanka Rao joined Hallam fourteen months ago as a senior analyst in its London office.

va-ts089.x: A city transit agency plans to replace paper tickets with a smartphone app on which riders can buy fares. The agency argues that the change will cut fare evasion, because inspectors checking app tickets can instantly confirm that a ticket is valid, whereas paper tickets can be forged. The agency also expects to save money by no longer printing and distributing paper tickets.

va-ts090.x: To reduce flooding in low-lying neighborhoods, the city of Breckford plans to require that new buildings include rooftop gardens, which absorb rainwater that would otherwise run into storm drains. Critics argue that the plan will do little, because new buildings each year make up only a tiny fraction of the city's rooftops. Planners reply that the plan will be effective because most of the city's new construction is concentrated in the small area of hillside neighborhoods that drain directly into the low-lying districts.

va-ts091.x: Many technology analysts argue that companies should move their computing work from their own servers to rented cloud services, since cloud providers can run servers more cheaply. ⟦For firms whose computing needs rise and fall unpredictably, this advice is sound.⟧ But for a firm whose computing load is large and steady, renting can cost more over time than owning, because the firm pays continuously for capacity it would otherwise have bought once. ⟦Such a firm, then, should keep its core work on its own servers and rent cloud capacity only to handle occasional peaks.⟧

va-ts092.x: A historian argues that the decline of the guilds in the city of Tolven during the 1700s was caused by the arrival of large workshops that employed unskilled laborers. As evidence, she notes that the number of guild members in Tolven fell by half between 1740 and 1780, the same period in which the number of large workshops in the city tripled, and that the guilds repeatedly petitioned the city council to restrict such workshops.

va-ts093.x: The country of Elbria offers a tax deduction to families who save for their children's university education in special accounts. A government report found that, since the deduction began, the total amount held in such accounts has tripled. Yet the share of Elbrian families who save anything at all for their children's education is no higher now than it was before the deduction was introduced.

va-ts094.x: A large employer introduced a program offering free sessions with a counselor to employees who report high levels of work stress. Among employees who used the program, the number of sick days taken fell by an average of four per year compared with the year before. The employer's human resources director argues that the program pays for itself, since the wages saved through fewer sick days exceed what the counseling costs.

va-ts095.x: A study of grant applications to a national science foundation found that proposals reviewed by panels whose members did not know the applicants' names received higher scores, on average, when submitted by researchers at less prestigious universities than proposals from such researchers received from panels that knew the applicants' names. The study's authors conclude that when reviewers know who the applicants are, they tend to favor researchers from prestigious institutions.

va-ts096.x: Pellam Airlines began charging passengers a fee for each checked bag two years ago. Since then, the average time its planes spend at the gate between flights has fallen by eight minutes, allowing the airline to schedule more flights each day. Pellam's managers conclude that the fee, by encouraging passengers to bring fewer bags, has shortened loading times, and they plan to raise the fee further to shorten turnaround times still more.

va-ts097.x: Astronomers have found that stars in a certain cluster that host large, close-orbiting planets rotate, on average, faster than otherwise similar stars in the cluster that have no such planets. Because the stars all formed at about the same time, the astronomers conclude that the planets are speeding up their host stars, probably through tidal forces, rather than simply forming more often around stars that were already fast rotators.

va-ts098.x: Records from the medieval abbey of Saint-Aurel list every manuscript copied in its scriptorium between 1150 and 1200. Every manuscript on the list that was copied for another monastery was written on parchment from the abbey's own flocks. None of the manuscripts on the list that were copied for wealthy laypeople used the abbey's own parchment; the abbey bought parchment from town merchants for these. Every manuscript that the abbey sold, rather than gave away, was copied for a layperson.

va-ts099.x: A city installed sensors at its busiest intersections that adjust the timing of traffic lights according to the flow of cars. In the year after installation, the average time drivers took to cross the city center at rush hour fell by 12 percent. City engineers attribute the improvement to the sensors and propose installing them at every signaled intersection in the city, predicting a similar reduction in travel times across the whole road network.

va-ts100.x: Members of the Haldor dairy cooperative switched their herds to a new feed last spring, and over the following six months the volume of milk produced per cow rose by 10 percent. The number of cows in the cooperative's herds did not change, and the price that dairies pay per liter of standard milk stayed the same. Yet the cooperative's income from milk sales fell during the same six months.

va-ps011.x: In a yearly survey, a town's health department noticed that residents who drank coffee every day reported fewer headaches than residents who drank no coffee. A local café owner concludes that coffee prevents headaches and has begun advertising her coffee as a headache remedy. She points out that the survey asked more than a thousand residents about their habits and their health.

va-ps012.x: The owner of a bookstore believes that adding a small café inside the store will increase book sales, because customers who stay in the store longer will have more time to browse and will therefore buy more books. Her business partner doubts that a café will make any difference to how many books customers buy, and he would rather spend the money on more shelves.

va-ps013.x: A large school district plans to give every high school student a laptop computer to use at school and at home. District officials argue that this will improve students' writing, since students will be able to revise their essays more easily on a computer than by hand. They expect that within two years the average score on the district's annual writing test will rise noticeably.

va-ps014.x: Biologists studying a species of songbird found that birds living in noisy city parks sing at a higher pitch than birds of the same species living in quiet forests. Higher-pitched songs are harder for the birds to produce and require more energy. Nevertheless, city birds that sing at a higher pitch raise more young, on average, than city birds of the same species that sing at a lower pitch.

va-ps015.x: Three years ago the city of Dunmore began offering free bus travel to residents over sixty-five. Since then, the number of trips taken on city buses by people over sixty-five has risen by 70 percent. City council members conclude that the program has greatly increased older residents' mobility and plan to extend free travel to residents under eighteen, expecting a similar rise in trips by young people.

va-ps016.x: According to records kept in the city archives of Venlo, every merchant who held a seat on the town council between 1600 and 1650 also belonged to the cloth guild. Some members of the cloth guild during that period were also members of the silversmiths' guild. No member of the silversmiths' guild was permitted to hold a seat on the town council during those years.

va-ps017.x: Medical researchers studying heart health have proposed that a diet rich in fiber lowers the risk of heart disease partly by feeding gut bacteria that produce substances which reduce inflammation in blood vessels. Skeptics argue that the benefit of fiber may come entirely from other effects, such as lowering the level of cholesterol in the blood, and that gut bacteria play no important role.

va-ps018.x: When Ferro Tools moved its customer-service center overseas, many observers expected its customer satisfaction scores to fall. ⟦In fact, Ferro's scores rose in each of the following two years.⟧ Some analysts credit the new center's staff, but this explanation is doubtful, since the overseas center hired mostly inexperienced workers. ⟦A more likely explanation is that Ferro introduced an online repair guide at the same time, which allowed most customers to solve problems without contacting the center at all,⟧ leaving the center to handle a much smaller number of calls.

va-ps019.x: The region of Orvala plans to cut the number of serious injuries on its rural roads by lowering the legal blood-alcohol limit for drivers. Officials point out that, in regions that have lowered the limit, the number of drivers arrested for drunk driving fell by about a third within two years, and they conclude that a lower limit in Orvala would produce a substantial drop in serious injuries on its rural roads.

va-ps020.x: A commentator on scientific research writes: "Studies funded by companies that make a product are more likely to report favorable results about that product than studies funded by governments or charities. This shows that company-funded researchers distort their findings to please their sponsors. Journals should therefore refuse to publish any study funded by a company with a financial interest in its results."

va-ts001.x: Last spring the Harmon City public library extended its opening hours on Saturdays and Sundays. Over the following six months, the number of visits to the library rose by 20 percent compared with the same months a year earlier. The library's director concludes that the longer weekend hours were responsible for the increase, and she recommends extending weekday hours as well in order to attract still more visitors.

va-ts002.x: Researchers followed 2,000 office workers for one year. The workers who took a short walk after lunch on at least four days a week reported far fewer afternoon headaches than the workers who rarely walked after lunch. Both groups worked in the same buildings and held similar jobs. The researchers conclude that a short walk after lunch helps to prevent afternoon headaches.

va-ts003.x: The owners of Lindqvist Bakery plan to stop printing paper receipts and to offer receipts by email instead. They argue that the change will lower the bakery's costs, because the bakery now spends a noticeable sum each month on receipt paper and printer ink, while sending an email costs almost nothing. They also expect customers to welcome the change, since it will reduce paper waste.

va-ts004.x: After the town of Ostrava Falls installed much brighter LED streetlights on its main roads, the number of nighttime traffic accidents on those roads fell, as officials had hoped. During the same period, however, the number of nighttime accidents on the town's side streets, where the older and dimmer lights remained, rose noticeably. The amount of nighttime traffic on the side streets did not change.

va-ts005.x: For many years, historians held that the coastal town of Merovar was abandoned because violent storms in the 1290s filled its harbor with silt. Dr. Amara Okafor rejects this view. She points out that tax records show the town's population falling sharply in the 1250s, decades before the storms, and she concludes that the condition of the harbor played no part in the town's abandonment.

va-ts006.x: Many analysts predicted that Fernhill Motors' new electric scooter would sell poorly, because its price is higher than the prices of rival models. ⟦In its first year on the market, however, the scooter outsold every rival in its class.⟧ The main reason is probably its battery, which lasts nearly twice as long as the batteries of competing scooters: ⟦buyers who ride long distances every day have been willing to pay more to avoid recharging during the day.⟧

va-ts007.x: A survey covered 400 laboratories in universities, hospitals, and private companies. Every laboratory that had adopted a shared electronic notebook system reported losing fewer data files than in the previous year. None of the laboratories that reported losing fewer data files had reduced its staff during the year. Some of the laboratories that reduced staff, however, reported spending more time on record keeping.

va-ts008.x: The city of Vale Rosa plans to charge drivers a fee for entering the old city center during weekday business hours. Officials argue that the fee will reduce traffic congestion in the center, because many drivers will choose to take the bus or the tram rather than pay. Money raised by the fee would be spent on repairing the center's narrow streets.

va-ts009.x: A software company found that its programmers who used a new code-checking tool made 40 percent fewer errors per month than the programmers who did not use it. Use of the tool had been voluntary, and each programmer decided whether to try it. The company's managers concluded that the tool reduces programming errors, and they decided to require every programmer to use it.

va-ts010.x: Pottery fragments found at a site in the Ardena Valley are decorated with a spiral pattern otherwise known only from the coastal settlement of Thalos, more than 200 kilometers away. The fragments date from the same century as the earliest decorated pottery at Thalos. The archaeologist Chen Wei argues that the people of the valley traded with Thalos rather than developing the pattern on their own.

va-ts011.x: A hospital in Porto Verde began sending text-message reminders to patients on the day before their appointments. In the following year, the share of patients who missed their appointments fell from 18 percent to 11 percent. The hospital's administrator credits the reminders with the improvement and plans to begin sending the same reminders to patients of the hospital's dental clinic, expecting a similar drop in missed appointments there.

va-ts012.x: Last year, the bookstore chain Sundara Books cut the price of every paperback it sells by 15 percent. Over the following year, the number of paperbacks the chain sold rose by 30 percent, more than enough to make up for the lower price. Nevertheless, the chain's total profit from book sales fell during the year, even though its costs for rent and staff did not change.

va-ts013.x: In a recent study, older mice that were fed a diet containing a blueberry extract found their way through a maze faster than older mice that were fed an ordinary diet. The two groups were otherwise treated identically. On the basis of this study, a health magazine advises older adults to eat a cup of fresh blueberries every day in order to improve their memory.

va-ts014.x: Some city council members argue that the city should stop paying for its free summer concerts, since the money could be spent on road repairs instead. ⟦This proposal is shortsighted.⟧ A survey of local businesses found that restaurants and shops near the concert park take in nearly a third more money on concert evenings than on other summer evenings, and ⟦the extra sales tax they collect brings the city more money than the concerts cost.⟧

va-ts015.x: Over the past five years, the share of households in Kestrel County with high-speed internet access rose from 40 percent to 75 percent. Over the same period, the county's unemployment rate fell by half. A county official concludes that the spread of high-speed internet access was the main reason for the fall in unemployment and urges neighboring counties to expand access as well.

va-ts016.x: The hotel chain Grünwald Hotels found that guests who booked their rooms through the chain's own website rated their stays more highly than guests who booked through travel agencies. The chain's marketing director concludes that the pleasant booking experience on the website puts guests in a better frame of mind, and she proposes spending heavily to improve the website further.

va-ts017.x: Records from the port of Saldanha show that in 1820 every ship that arrived from the north carried timber, salt, or both. Every ship that carried salt that year paid a harbor tax, while ships that carried only timber paid none. Ships from other directions carried a wide variety of goods. The port's accounts show that the Albatros, which arrived from the north in 1820, paid no harbor tax.

va-ts018.x: Engineers at a power company propose covering parts of the company's reservoirs with floating solar panels. Water from the reservoirs is used both for drinking and for cooling the company's power plants. The engineers argue that, in addition to producing electricity, the panels would reduce the amount of water the reservoirs lose to evaporation, because the panels would shade the water from direct sunlight.

va-ts019.x: A team of ecologists counted songbirds in a forest before and after a highway was built along one edge of it. After the highway opened, the number of songbirds nesting within 300 meters of the road fell by half, while the number nesting deeper in the forest did not change. The team concludes that traffic noise drives songbirds away from nesting sites near busy roads.

va-ts020.x: When the city of Brennick raised the fine for parking illegally downtown from $30 to $80, officials expected the number of parking tickets issued downtown to fall, since fewer drivers would risk the higher fine. Instead, over the following year the number of tickets issued downtown rose by 25 percent. The number of parking spaces downtown and the amount of traffic there stayed about the same.

va-ts021.x: Two years ago, the grocery chain Okonkwo Markets began offering free delivery on all online orders over $50. Since then, the chain's online sales have tripled, while sales in its stores have fallen only slightly. The chain's finance director argues that offering free delivery has been profitable for the company, because the increase in online sales is far larger than the decline in store sales.

va-ts022.x: In Lunari Province, the rate of hip fractures among people over 70 fell by 20 percent in the decade after doctors began routinely prescribing vitamin D supplements to older patients. Health officials conclude that the supplements caused the decline. Critics point out that the number of people over 70 in the province grew during the decade, but because the figure the officials cite is a rate rather than a total, that growth does not affect their comparison.

va-ts023.x: Astronomers at a mountain observatory report that the sharpness of their images has improved steadily over the past decade. During the same decade, light from the growing town in the valley below has made the night sky above the observatory noticeably brighter, and a brighter sky normally makes astronomical images worse. The observatory has used the same telescope throughout the decade.

va-ts024.x: The city of Marisol plans to plant 10,000 street trees in its poorer neighborhoods, which have few trees. City officials argue that the trees will lower summer temperatures in those neighborhoods and so reduce the number of residents who need hospital treatment for heat illness. Critics object that a newly planted tree provides little shade for at least a decade, so the plan will do nothing for residents in the near future.

va-ts025.x: ⟦Sales of printed maps have fallen by more than half over the past decade⟧, and some publishers have concluded that the printed map has no future. This conclusion is premature. ⟦Sales of printed maps for hiking and cycling have risen during the same period⟧, and because such maps are used in places where phone batteries run down and signals fail, they meet a need that digital maps cannot easily fill. Publishers who specialize in these maps are therefore likely to prosper.

va-ts026.x: Last year the city of Ardmore replaced the paper timetables at its bus stops with a smartphone app that shows the location of every bus in real time. Records show that the buses ran no more punctually in the year after the change than in the year before. Yet complaints about late buses fell by 60 percent. The transit authority concludes that riders who can see when their bus will arrive are much less bothered by delays.

va-ts027.x: A transport survey of 600 households in the town of Kerava found that 450 of the households own at least one car and 300 own at least one bicycle. Every household that owns a bicycle but no car lives within two kilometers of the town center. Households that own neither a car nor a bicycle were asked how their members travel to work. The town council will use the survey to plan new bicycle lanes.

va-ts028.x: A museum has displayed a portrait as the work of the eighteenth-century painter Ilse Brandt for more than a century. A curator now argues that it is a later copy. Her evidence is that the canvas was woven on a type of mechanical loom that, according to the manufacturer's records, did not come into use until 1810, twelve years after Brandt's death.

va-ts029.x: Arcelia Airlines plans to remove two rows of seats from each of its planes in order to give passengers more legroom. Although each flight will then carry fewer passengers, the airline's managers argue that the change will increase its revenue, because a survey of 2,000 recent passengers found that most of them would be willing to pay a higher fare for the extra space.

va-ts030.x: Over the past twenty years, the number of frogs living in and around Lake Varna has fallen sharply. During the same period, a pesticide used on nearby farms has been detected in the lake's water at steadily rising levels. A biologist concludes that the pesticide is the main cause of the frogs' decline and urges the regional government to ban its use near the lake.

va-ts031.x: Last autumn the town of Belmira opened a walk-in clinic that offers free flu vaccinations, and the number of residents vaccinated against flu rose by a third compared with the year before. The vaccine was well matched to the strains that circulated that winter. Yet the number of flu cases recorded by health workers in Belmira that winter was the highest in a decade.

va-ts032.x: The historian Kofi Mensah argues that cheap printed almanacs increased literacy among farmers in the province of Ostland during the eighteenth century. His evidence is that the share of farmers who signed marriage registers with their names, rather than with a mark, rose from 20 percent to 45 percent between 1720 and 1780, the period in which almanac sellers began traveling regularly through the province.

va-ts033.x: Two years ago, the province of Talvora began requiring restaurants to display their official hygiene ratings on their front doors. Since then, the number of food poisoning cases traced to restaurants in the province has fallen by 30 percent. Officials conclude that public ratings have pushed restaurants to improve their hygiene, and they propose requiring food trucks to display ratings as well.

va-ts034.x: ⟦Many engineers have assumed that self-driving delivery robots will first succeed in dense city centers, where customers live closest together.⟧ But city centers are also where sidewalks are most crowded and where theft and vandalism are most common, and both problems slow the robots down and raise their operating costs. Quiet suburbs, by contrast, have wide sidewalks and few pedestrians. ⟦It is therefore in the suburbs, not the city centers, that delivery robots are likely to prove profitable first.⟧

va-ts035.x: A business magazine surveyed the 50 most profitable companies in the country and found that 46 of them allow employees to work from home at least two days a week. A management consultant quoted in the magazine concludes that allowing employees to work from home makes companies more profitable, and she advises every company to adopt such a policy. The magazine did not survey any other companies.

va-ts036.x: A video-streaming company plans to lower its costs by reducing the picture quality of videos sent to subscribers' phones, which would cut the amount of data it must transmit. The company's engineers argue that the change will not cost the company any subscribers, because on a phone's small screen most viewers cannot tell the difference between the current picture quality and the lower one.

va-ts037.x: The guild records of the medieval city of Corvenna list nearly three times as many weavers in 1400 as in 1350. The historian Sofia Marchetti concludes that the amount of cloth produced in and around Corvenna rose greatly during that half century, and she argues that this growth explains why the city built a large new cloth hall in 1405.

va-ts038.x: At Halvorsen Electronics, every product launched in the past five years was tested by a panel of customers before its launch. Every product that the panel rated favorably sold more than 100,000 units in its first year, although some products that the panel rated unfavorably also sold more than 100,000 units. None of the products that sold fewer than 50,000 units in their first year is still being made.

va-ts039.x: In the Sarnia River delta, a species of wading bird that feeds only on mudflats has become steadily more numerous over the past fifteen years. During the same period, rising sea levels have permanently flooded about a quarter of the delta's mudflats. The birds have not begun feeding anywhere else, and the number of birds that arrive from other regions has not changed.

va-ts040.x: To reduce costs, the school board of Nordhaven is considering a four-day school week. Opponents argue that a shorter week will harm students' learning. Supporters reply that each of the four school days would be made longer, so that students would spend the same total number of hours in class each week as they do now, and they conclude that learning will not suffer.

va-ts041.x: A ten-year study of 5,000 adults found that those who reported drinking at least three cups of green tea a day were 30 percent less likely to develop high blood pressure during the study than those who drank no green tea. A tea company now cites the study in advertisements that claim green tea protects drinkers against high blood pressure.

va-ts042.x: Battery makers are racing to build cells that store more energy per kilogram, and ⟦the lightest batteries will probably win the market for electric aircraft.⟧ For electric delivery vans, however, weight matters far less than price and lifespan. ⟦A heavier battery that lasts through twice as many charging cycles would cost a van operator less over the life of the van⟧, so makers who focus only on lighter batteries may lose the much larger van market to their rivals.

va-ts043.x: The council of the seaside town of Esk Harbor plans to build a large new car park near its beach. Council members argue that a shortage of parking keeps visitors away from the town in summer, and that the extra visitors drawn by the new car park would bring more business to the town's shops and cafés. They point out that the beach's existing car parks hold only 200 cars.

va-ts044.x: Fossil teeth of a prehistoric horse species from 8 million years ago have much taller crowns than teeth of the same species from 10 million years ago. Tall crowns allow teeth to withstand heavy wear, and grasses are far more gritty and wearing than the leaves of shrubs. Paleontologists conclude that grasslands spread through the region between 10 million and 8 million years ago.

va-ts045.x: Juniper Phones cut the price of its basic model by 20 percent, and in the following quarter sales of that model rose by 50 percent. The company's head of sales concludes that Juniper's customers are highly sensitive to price, and she recommends cutting the price of the company's premium model as well, expecting a similar rise in its sales. The basic model's features were not changed during the quarter.

va-ts046.x: In the 1880s the port city of Valdora built a railway linking its harbor to the mining towns of the interior, expecting the amount of cargo passing through the harbor to grow. Over the following decade, the total tonnage of cargo shipped through the harbor did increase sharply. Yet the number of ships calling at the harbor each year fell during the same decade.

va-ts047.x: A university's computer science department replaced the lectures in its introductory programming course with short online videos that students watch at home, and it now uses class time for supervised programming practice. In the first year of the new format, the share of students who passed the course's final exam rose from 68 percent to 81 percent. The head of the department argues that the new format improves students' learning.

va-ts048.x: In the country of Meridia, every household with a yearly income below 30,000 dollars qualifies for a heating subsidy, and every qualifying household is sent an application form. The subsidy, worth about 600 dollars a year, is paid only to households that return the form. Last winter, only half of the households that were sent the form returned it. Officials found that the households that returned it had, on average, the lowest incomes.

va-ts049.x: Researchers at a coastal laboratory found that a strain of bacteria broke down plastic bottles twice as fast in seawater samples kept at 30°C as in samples kept at 15°C. Before testing, the samples were filtered to remove sand and other particles. The researchers propose releasing the bacteria into tropical seas, where the surface water is about 30°C, to clean up the plastic floating there.

va-ts050.x: Clinic director: Patients who visit our clinic's nutrition counselor lose more weight over the following six months than patients who do not. Last year, though, only 10 percent of our patients chose to visit the counselor. If we required every patient to see the counselor, the average weight loss among all our patients would rise substantially. Our counselor has years of experience, and patients who see her rate her very highly.

va-ps001.x: Last month, Brightline Logistics installed a new filter that blocks unwanted email before it reaches employees' inboxes. Since then, employees have reported receiving 70 percent fewer unwanted messages. The company's IT manager concludes that the filter is saving employees a large amount of working time, since they no longer have to read and delete so many unwanted messages each day.

va-ps002.x: A city health department found that neighborhoods in which fresh fruit stands opened had lower rates of childhood obesity five years later than similar neighborhoods without fruit stands. The department now plans to pay for more fruit stands in other neighborhoods, arguing that the stands improve children's diets and so help to prevent obesity. The stands sell fruit at about the same prices as local supermarkets do.

va-ps003.x: Letters written by the composer Anton Vasek mention a symphony that he finished in 1832, but no copy of its score has ever been found. A music historian claims that an unsigned score recently discovered in an archive in Prague is that lost symphony, because it is written on paper made in 1832 by the mill that supplied the paper for all of Vasek's other known scores.

va-ps004.x: Over the past three years, the number of customers using self-checkout machines at Petrov Supermarkets has doubled, and the chain has cut the number of cashiers it employs by more than a third. Yet over the same three years, the chain's total spending on store staff has risen, even though the number of its stores and their opening hours have not changed.

va-ps005.x: ⟦Some astronomers have proposed that the unusual dimming of the star KX-14 is caused by a vast swarm of comets passing in front of it.⟧ If comets were responsible, however, the dimming would repeat in a regular pattern that followed the comets' orbits, and twenty years of observations show no such pattern. ⟦A more likely cause is dust from a recent collision between two planets⟧, since such dust spreads unevenly and would block the star's light at irregular intervals.

va-ps006.x: Five years ago, Gallen City began requiring every new office building to include secure bicycle parking and showers for employees. Since then, the share of downtown workers who cycle to work has risen from 4 percent to 9 percent. The city's planning office credits the building rule with most of this increase and recommends extending it to new apartment buildings as well.

va-ps007.x: Nakamura Consulting offers a leadership course to employees who wish to move into management. Every employee who was promoted at the firm last year had completed the course. Half of the employees who completed the course, however, were not promoted. The firm admits to the course only employees who have worked there for at least three years. Promotions at the firm are decided once a year by a committee of partners.

va-ps008.x: For decades, browsing elk in Halden National Park ate nearly every young aspen along the park's streams. In the twelve years since wolves were reintroduced, aspen saplings there have rebounded sharply. Ecologists attribute the recovery less to the wolves' killing of elk than to a change in elk behavior: wary of ambush, the elk now avoid lingering on stream banks where approaching predators are hard to see.

va-ps009.x: In a large five-year trial, patients were randomly assigned either a new cholesterol drug or the standard one. The new drug lowered blood cholesterol considerably more than the standard drug did, and high cholesterol is a well-established cause of heart attacks. Nevertheless, patients taking the new drug suffered heart attacks at the same rate as those taking the standard drug, and both groups took their medication equally faithfully.

va-ps010.x: Officials in Corvania plan to replace the toll booths on the country's highways with an electronic system that photographs each vehicle's license plate and mails a bill to its registered owner. Critics warn that many drivers will simply ignore the bills. The officials dismiss this worry: any unpaid tolls, they say, will be added to the fee that a vehicle's owner must pay to renew the vehicle's Corvanian registration each year.

vl-ts021.x:
Banded iron formations, the striped rocks in which layers rich in iron oxide alternate with layers of chert, were deposited in ancient oceans for more than a billion years and then largely ceased to form. For decades geologists treated them as a straightforward record of early photosynthesis: oxygen released by cyanobacteria, the argument ran, reacted with dissolved ferrous iron, and the insoluble oxides that resulted rained down onto the seafloor. On this reading, the abundance of the formations measured the rising productivity of oxygen-producing microbes, and their disappearance marked the moment when the oceans had been swept clean of dissolved iron.

The tidiness of this account has not survived closer scrutiny. Laboratory cultures have shown that certain bacteria can oxidize iron without producing any oxygen at all, using light to strip electrons directly from ferrous iron. If such organisms flourished in the early oceans, the formations could have accumulated in waters that were entirely anoxic, and their presence would say nothing about when oxygen-producing photosynthesis began. A third camp has proposed that ultraviolet radiation, unfiltered by an ozone layer that did not yet exist, could have oxidized surface iron with no biological help, though experiments simulating realistic seawater chemistry suggest that this process would have been too slow to account for the thickest deposits.

It would be premature, however, to conclude that the formations are uninformative. Iron isotopes fractionate differently depending on the pathway by which iron is oxidized, and several research groups now argue that the isotopic signatures of particular layers can discriminate among the competing mechanisms. The difficulty is that diagenesis, the slow chemical alteration that sediments undergo after burial, can shift those signatures in ways that are themselves poorly constrained. The rocks, in other words, may contain the answer, but only in a script whose grammar has been partly rewritten by time. What seems clear is that the formations cannot be read as a single uniform archive; different deposits, laid down in different basins and epochs, may record different processes, and the older habit of generalizing from one well-studied sequence to the entire record now looks less like parsimony than like wishful simplification.

vl-ts022.x:
Economic historians long regarded the craft guilds of late medieval Europe as brakes on innovation. By fixing prices, restricting entry and dictating the methods by which goods could be made, guilds supposedly protected their members' incomes at the expense of consumers and inventors alike. Adam Smith's hostility to such corporations gave this view an intellectual pedigree, and it fitted comfortably into a narrative in which economic growth began only when markets were freed from corporate privilege.

A revisionist literature has complicated this picture without wholly overturning it. Its proponents point out that the apprenticeship system, which guilds regulated, was the principal means by which tacit technical knowledge passed between generations in an age with few written manuals. Because a guild could enforce the obligations of both master and apprentice, it made long training contracts credible: masters could expect years of cheap labor in return for instruction, and apprentices could expect that the instruction would actually be given. Moreover, journeymen who traveled from town to town before settling, a practice many guilds encouraged or required, carried techniques across regions and may have done more to diffuse innovations than any patent system of the period.

Critics of the revisionists concede the importance of apprenticeship but question whether guilds were necessary to sustain it. Training contracts were also enforced by municipal courts and by families with reputations to protect, and in several prosperous towns apprenticeship flourished where guilds were weak. The critics further note that the documentary record is skewed: guild statutes survive in abundance precisely because guilds were record-keeping bodies, while informal arrangements left few traces, so a historian reading the archive may mistake the visibility of guild regulation for its indispensability.

The disagreement thus turns less on what guilds did than on what would have happened in their absence, a counterfactual that no archive can directly answer. Both sides would probably accept that guilds were neither uniformly obstructive nor uniformly beneficial, and that their effects varied with the trade, the town and the century in question.

vl-ts023.x:
The epistolary novel, which tells its story entirely through letters, enjoyed a vogue in eighteenth-century Europe that critics have often explained by appeal to its apparent immediacy. Because each letter is written, or purports to be written, in the heat of the moment, the form seems to offer unmediated access to a character's feelings as they arise, before retrospection has had a chance to tidy them. Readers of the period, so the argument goes, prized this effect of sincerity, and novelists cultivated it by insisting in their prefaces that they were merely the editors of a genuine correspondence.

This account captures something real, but it neglects a feature of the form that its most accomplished practitioners exploited with evident relish: the letter is never addressed to no one. Every letter is shaped by its writer's sense of a particular recipient, and a character who confides in a friend will present events differently from the way she presents them to a parent or a suitor. Far from guaranteeing sincerity, the form therefore invites the reader to compare versions, to notice what is emphasized for one correspondent and suppressed for another, and to infer a truth that no single letter states. The immediacy the form promises is, on this view, precisely what it teaches the reader to distrust.

One need not conclude that eighteenth-century readers were naive in taking the letters at face value, for the evidence of their responses is mixed. Some contemporary readers wrote to authors in distress over the fates of characters, as though the correspondence were genuine; others, in reviews and private notes, remarked with amusement on the self-serving rhetoric of particular letter writers. What the mixed evidence suggests is not that one reading was correct and the other mistaken, but that the form sustained both at once. A novel in letters could be consumed as a sequence of sincere outpourings and, simultaneously or on a second reading, as a study in the strategic management of sincerity. That doubleness, rather than immediacy alone, may best account for the form's appeal, and for its decline once novelists found other means, such as the free indirect style, of letting readers glimpse a gap between what characters say and what they mean.

vl-ts024.x:
Botanists have reported for some years that certain plants appear to treat their relatives differently from strangers. In a frequently cited greenhouse study, seedlings of a beach-dwelling annual grew fewer fine roots when potted with siblings than when potted with unrelated plants of the same species, as though competing less vigorously against kin. Subsequent work has described similar effects in several other species, and some researchers now speak of kin recognition in plants as an established phenomenon, attributing it to chemical cues released by roots.

Skeptics have raised two objections, one methodological and one conceptual. The methodological objection concerns how root allocation is measured. Plants potted with siblings are, by definition, more similar to one another in size and growth rate than plants potted with strangers, and size asymmetries alone can alter how much a plant invests in roots. Unless an experiment controls for such asymmetries, a difference attributed to recognition may simply reflect the fact that evenly matched neighbors compete differently from mismatched ones. Several reanalyses that adjusted for plant size found that the apparent kin effect shrank, and in some cases vanished.

The conceptual objection is subtler. To say that a plant recognizes kin is to imply that it detects relatedness as such, rather than responding to some correlate of relatedness, such as genetic similarity at a few loci that happen to govern root exudates. Defenders reply, reasonably enough, that recognition in animals is also mediated by correlates, since no organism perceives genealogy directly; a ground squirrel that distinguishes siblings by odor is responding to chemistry, not to pedigree. If the term is acceptable for the squirrel, they ask, why not for the sunflower?

The reply has force, but it does not settle the matter, because the animal cases are persuasive for reasons that go beyond the existence of a cue. In those cases, discrimination has been shown to produce behavior that benefits relatives at some cost to the actor, which is what evolutionary theory predicts kin recognition should do. For most plant studies, that demonstration is still missing: a plant that grows fewer roots near siblings may be conserving resources for itself rather than ceding them to kin. Until such costs and benefits are measured, the more cautious description, that plants respond differently to neighbors of differing relatedness, seems the one the evidence supports.

vl-ts025.x:
That workers in large cities earn more than otherwise similar workers in small towns is one of the most robust findings in urban economics. The difference is usually attributed to agglomeration economies: when many firms and workers cluster together, they share suppliers, draw on a deep pool of specialized labor and learn from one another, and these advantages raise productivity enough to pay for the higher wages and rents that dense places impose. On this interpretation, the urban wage premium is a measure of something that cities create.

A persistent difficulty is that the workers who move to cities are not a random sample of the population. If more able or more ambitious workers sort into large cities, part of the wage premium reflects who lives there rather than what the city does for them. Economists have tried to separate these effects by following individual workers as they move. Studies of this kind generally find that a worker who moves to a large city does not receive the full premium at once; instead, her wage rises gradually over the following years and, strikingly, much of the gain persists if she later moves back to a smaller place.

This pattern has been read in two ways. Some take it as evidence that cities foster the accumulation of skills, so that the premium reflects learning that workers carry with them. Others caution that the workers who move to a city, stay for several years and then leave may differ systematically from those who never move or who stay permanently, and that the persistence of their gains could reflect selection operating at a second stage. The first reading treats the city as a school; the second warns that we may be observing only the school's most promising pupils.

The choice between these readings matters for policy. If the premium arises mainly from learning, then subsidizing access to large cities, for instance by easing the housing restrictions that keep rents high, could raise the productivity of workers who would otherwise never benefit. If the premium is largely a matter of sorting, such measures would chiefly reshuffle where productive workers live without making anyone more productive. Current evidence leans toward a substantial role for learning, but the second-stage selection problem has not been convincingly ruled out.

vl-ts026.x:
For much of the twentieth century, art historians approached Dutch still-life painting of the seventeenth century as a repository of hidden meanings. A peeled lemon, a guttering candle, a watch lying open beside a half-eaten pie: each object, it was argued, belonged to a vocabulary of moral emblems familiar to contemporary viewers, who would have recognized in such arrangements a meditation on the transience of earthly pleasure. Scholars who adopted this approach, often called iconographic, assembled impressive evidence from emblem books of the period, in which images of everyday things were paired with verses drawing exactly such lessons.

Beginning in the 1980s, a number of scholars objected that the iconographic method had become self-confirming. Almost any object could be matched with some emblem, and once a painting was assumed to carry a message, the absence of explicit cues could be explained away as subtlety. The critics proposed instead that the paintings be understood in relation to the commercial culture that produced them: as luxury goods made for an expanding market of urban buyers, who valued them for their dazzling imitation of textures and for the costly imported objects they depicted. A Chinese porcelain bowl, on this account, signaled the reach of Dutch trade rather than the fragility of life.

It is tempting to treat these as rival interpretations between which one must choose, but the opposition may be less stark than either camp has supposed. The emblem books themselves were commercial products, sold to the same urban public that bought paintings, and their popularity suggests that buyers enjoyed precisely the oscillation between delight in things and reflection on their vanity. A painting that rendered a silver goblet with astonishing skill could at once flatter its owner's taste and remind him, if he cared to be reminded, that such possessions would not outlast him. To insist that the painting meant only one of these things is to impose a coherence that the culture may not have demanded.

This reconciliation has its own risk, of course. If every painting can be read both ways, the claim becomes difficult to test. The more productive course may be to ask, of particular works, which reading the specific choices of the painter make more probable.

vl-ts027.x:
The discovery in the 1990s of gas giant planets orbiting their stars in a matter of days posed an immediate puzzle. Theories of planet formation, built largely to explain our own solar system, held that giant planets could assemble only far from their stars, beyond the so-called snow line, where ices are abundant enough to build massive solid cores quickly. A Jupiter-sized planet circling its star at a small fraction of Mercury's distance therefore seemed to require that the planet had formed farther out and then moved inward.

Two migration mechanisms have been proposed. In disk migration, a young planet exchanges angular momentum with the gas disk from which it formed and spirals gradually inward, a process that would leave its orbit nearly circular and aligned with the star's equator. In high-eccentricity migration, gravitational interactions with other planets or with a companion star fling the planet onto an elongated orbit whose closest approach brings it near the star, where tidal forces then shrink and circularize the orbit over hundreds of millions of years. Because this second process begins with a violent perturbation, it would often leave the orbit tilted relative to the star's spin.

Measurements of that tilt have accordingly been treated as a test between the mechanisms. Many hot Jupiters do turn out to have strongly misaligned orbits, a result initially welcomed as support for high-eccentricity migration. Yet the inference is less secure than it first appeared. The star's spin axis may itself be tilted relative to the disk, through processes unrelated to the planet, so that even a planet that migrated smoothly through the disk could end up misaligned with its star. Conversely, tides raised by a massive planet might, around some kinds of stars, gradually realign an orbit that had begun tilted.

Meanwhile, a once-neglected alternative has gained ground: that some hot Jupiters formed where we find them. Simulations suggest that, under certain conditions, solids could drift inward and accumulate close to the star rapidly enough to build a core before the gas disk dissipates. No one claims that this possibility explains every case. Its advocates argue more modestly that the population of hot Jupiters may be heterogeneous, the product of several pathways, and that searching for a single mechanism may have been a mistake from the start.

vl-ts028.x:
Creole languages, which arise when speakers of different languages are brought together in circumstances that demand a new common tongue, have long attracted linguists interested in how grammar emerges. Two broad accounts have dominated the debate. Substrate theorists hold that a creole's grammar is inherited largely from the languages its first speakers already knew: although most of the vocabulary may come from the socially dominant language, the underlying structures, such as how tense is marked or how questions are formed, are carried over from the speakers' native languages. Universalists counter that creoles across the world share features, such as preverbal markers of tense and aspect, that cannot be traced to any single set of source languages, and that these shared features reveal a default grammar that human beings produce when inherited models are unavailable.

Each position faces difficulties. The universalist argument depends on the claim that the similarities among creoles exceed what common sources would explain, yet many well-studied creoles drew on related source languages, so that resemblances between them may reflect shared inheritance after all. The substrate argument, for its part, struggles with cases in which a creole possesses a construction found in none of the languages known to have contributed to it. Substrate theorists can reply that our knowledge of which languages were present is often incomplete, but this reply, however plausible in particular cases, risks becoming an all-purpose escape.

More recent work has tended to dissolve the dichotomy rather than resolve it. Researchers who examine the social history of particular colonies have found that the demographic conditions under which creoles formed varied enormously, from settings in which a few source languages were spoken by large, stable groups to settings in which constant turnover prevented any group from transmitting its grammar. On this view, the relative weight of inheritance and invention is not a constant to be discovered but a variable that depends on such conditions. Creoles that emerged where a single substrate predominated should show more substrate influence; those that emerged amid extreme linguistic diversity might show more of the features universalists emphasize. Whether the evidence bears out these predictions is still being examined, but the reframing has at least made the question empirically tractable.

vl-ts029.x:
The movement known as historically informed performance, which seeks to play older music on the instruments and in the styles of its own era, began in the mid-twentieth century as a marginal enterprise and has since become something close to an orthodoxy in the performance of Baroque repertory. Its early advocates presented it as a corrective to a romanticized tradition that had smothered the music of Bach and Handel under massed strings and sentimental tempos. By recovering gut strings, period wind instruments and the evidence of contemporary treatises, they claimed, performers could hear the music as its composers had intended.

The most searching criticism of the movement has come not from defenders of the older style but from scholars sympathetic to its results. They have pointed out that the treatises on which performers rely are fragmentary, often contradictory and frequently prescriptive rather than descriptive: a writer who complains that singers ornament too lavishly tells us what he disliked, not necessarily what was usual. More fundamentally, the critics argue that the goal of reproducing the composer's intentions is incoherent, since even a perfect reconstruction of an eighteenth-century performance would be heard by listeners whose ears have been shaped by two further centuries of music. The sound might be authentic; the experience could not be.

The sharpest of these critics went further, contending that historically informed performance was less a recovery of the past than an expression of modern taste. The lean textures, brisk tempos and rhythmic clarity that its practitioners favored, they observed, bore a suspicious resemblance to the aesthetic of twentieth-century modernism, with its distrust of romantic excess. The movement, on this reading, had not escaped the habit of remaking old music in the image of the present; it had merely exchanged one present for another.

That argument is more illuminating than its tone sometimes suggested. It need not imply that the movement's achievements are spurious. Performers who have learned to play period instruments have discovered sonorities and balances that no amount of reading could have revealed, and many listeners find the resulting performances more vivid than what preceded them. What the criticism undermines is not the value of these performances but the claim of authority that once accompanied them: they are persuasive interpretations, not recoveries of a single correct sound.

vl-ts030.x:
The idea that predators at the top of a food web can reshape entire ecosystems, a phenomenon ecologists call a trophic cascade, gained wide currency through studies of rocky shores and lakes in the 1960s and 1970s. Removing a predatory starfish from a stretch of shoreline, for instance, allowed mussels to monopolize the rock and crowd out dozens of other species. Such experiments were persuasive in part because the systems were small and the interventions could be replicated and reversed.

Extending the concept to large terrestrial landscapes has proved more contentious. When a top predator returns to a region from which it had long been absent, ecologists often report changes at lower levels of the web: herbivores become warier, browsing declines in certain areas, and plants long suppressed begin to recover. It is natural to read these changes as a cascade set in motion by the predator. Yet in such landscapes the predator's return rarely occurs in isolation. Herbivore populations may also be shrinking because of hunting by people, competition from other grazers or a run of severe winters; rainfall and stream flow may be shifting; and plant recovery may lag years behind any of these causes, making it hard to say which one it is following.

The disagreement is not merely about data but about what would count as adequate evidence. Proponents of a strong cascade argue that convergent patterns across many sites, each imperfect on its own, make the predator's role the most economical explanation. Skeptics reply that convergence is only as informative as the independence of the sites, and that many of the landscapes studied share climate trends and management histories that could produce similar patterns without any predator effect at all. They favor approaches, such as fencing plots to exclude herbivores, that isolate one causal link at a time, even though such experiments cannot capture the indirect effects of fear that cascade theorists consider important.

Neither side, it seems fair to say, has a monopoly on rigor. Small-scale exclusion experiments establish mechanisms cleanly but may misrepresent how those mechanisms operate across a landscape; broad comparisons capture the landscape but blur the mechanisms. The most defensible conclusions so far are likely to be modest ones: predators can contribute to vegetation recovery, but the magnitude of their contribution probably varies from place to place.

vl-ts031.x:
Why people in several parts of the world began to cultivate plants, a practice that at first seems to have demanded more labor for less nutrition than foraging, remains one of archaeology's enduring questions. For much of the twentieth century the dominant answers invoked necessity: a warming climate, a growing population or the depletion of large game, it was argued, pressed communities to intensify their use of plants until cultivation became unavoidable. Such accounts had the virtue of explaining why a costly innovation was adopted, but they predicted that the earliest farmers should show signs of nutritional stress, and in several regions the skeletal evidence has proved equivocal.

An alternative proposal, sometimes called the feasting hypothesis, shifts attention from subsistence to social life. On this view, ambitious individuals in relatively prosperous foraging societies sponsored communal feasts in order to accumulate prestige and obligations, and the demand for foods suitable for feasting, especially grains that could be brewed into beer, encouraged the deliberate tending of particular plants. Cultivation would thus have begun not as a response to scarcity but as a by-product of competition for status under conditions of relative abundance. Excavations at some early sites have uncovered large stone vessels and the remains of what appear to be communal gatherings, which proponents cite in support.

The hypothesis has attracted interest partly because it explains a puzzle that necessity-based accounts leave untouched: why the first cultivated plants in some regions were not the most calorie-efficient ones available. Yet its evidential basis is thinner than its explanatory appeal. Residues that would confirm brewing are difficult to distinguish from those left by other forms of food preparation, and large gatherings could have served purposes, such as ritual or the exchange of marriage partners, that had nothing to do with competitive display. Moreover, the hypothesis requires that feasting precede cultivation at the sites in question, and the dating of the relevant layers is often too coarse to establish the order.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of the debate is that the transition need not have had a single cause. Social motives may have initiated the tending of certain plants in some places, while climatic and demographic pressures later turned a marginal practice into a way of life.

vl-ts032.x:
Thought experiments occupy an awkward place in accounts of scientific knowledge. A physicist who imagines riding alongside a beam of light, or a philosopher who asks what would follow if a person's memories were transferred to another body, performs no measurement and gathers no new data. Yet such imagined scenarios have, by the testimony of scientists themselves, sometimes reshaped entire fields. The question is how reasoning about situations that never occur can teach us anything about the world.

One influential answer holds that thought experiments are simply arguments in picturesque dress. On this deflationary view, any genuine conclusion a thought experiment yields can be reconstructed as an explicit argument from stated premises, and the imagined scenario contributes nothing beyond making the argument vivid and memorable. Whatever we learn, we learn because the premises were already known, perhaps tacitly, and the reasoning from them is valid. The view has the merit of demystifying the practice: it requires no special faculty of insight, only ordinary inference.

Critics object that the deflationary view misdescribes how thought experiments actually function. They point out that a well-constructed scenario often reveals a tension among beliefs that the thinker did not realize were in conflict, and that the premises needed to reconstruct the argument become visible only after the scenario has done its work. A reconstruction may thus be possible in retrospect without capturing how the knowledge was acquired.
