The two views need not exclude each other. A guild could guarantee quality and restrict competition at once, and the balance between these functions probably shifted from town to town and century to century.

vr-ts027.x: Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it, which is one reason glaciers can persist in places where summer air temperatures rise above freezing. When the surface darkens, it absorbs more energy and melts faster. Soot from distant fires and industry has long been recognized as one darkening agent, but field studies on the Greenland ice sheet have drawn attention to another: pigmented algae that bloom on bare, wet ice during the melt season. The algae produce dark compounds that protect them from intense radiation, and in doing so they lower the reflectivity of the ice around them. Because more melting creates more of the wet surface the algae need, the process can feed on itself. Researchers caution, however, that the size of this effect varies widely between seasons and regions, and current climate models do not yet represent it.

vr-ts028.x: Many Victorian novels first reached readers not as books but in installments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more. Critics have often treated this mode of publication as a commercial constraint that authors endured, blaming it for sprawling plots and contrived cliffhangers. Yet serialization also shaped the novels in ways that were not merely defects. Because readers lived with a story for many months, characters could age and change at something like the pace of ordinary life. Authors, moreover, could watch sales and letters from readers and adjust a plot while it was still unfinished, so that the novel became in part a conversation with its audience. To read such a work in a single volume, in a few sittings, is therefore to experience something its first readers never did.

vr-ts029.x: Creole languages arise when speakers of different languages, brought together under conditions such as plantation labor or long-distance trade, develop a shared means of communication that children then acquire as a first language. Because creoles form quickly, they have attracted linguists interested in how grammar emerges. One influential hypothesis held that creoles around the world share structural features, such as marking tense with separate particles rather than word endings, because children who acquire an unstable input fall back on an innate default grammar. Critics have replied that many of these shared features can be traced to the languages the original speakers brought with them, and that the similarities among creoles have been overstated by comparing only a few well-studied cases. The debate matters beyond creoles themselves, since it bears on how much of grammar is learned and how much is given.

vr-ts030.x: Many migratory birds can orient using Earth's magnetic field, but how they sense it has long been uncertain. One proposal locates the sensor in tiny iron-oxide particles that would act like compass needles. Another, now favored by many researchers, holds that the sense depends on light-triggered chemical reactions in the eye. In this account, a protein called cryptochrome, when struck by blue light, forms pairs of molecules whose subsequent reactions depend subtly on the orientation of the magnetic field. Two observations support it. Caged robins orient correctly under blue or green light but become disoriented in red light, which does not activate cryptochrome. And weak radio-frequency noise, too feeble to move an iron particle but capable of disturbing the chemical reaction, disrupts their orientation. Neither observation proves the hypothesis, but together they are hard to explain by magnetic particles alone.

vr-ts031.x: The flying buttress is often presented as the engineering key to Gothic architecture: by carrying the outward thrust of a high vault across open air to a pier standing away from the wall, it allowed walls to be thinned and filled with glass. That account is correct as far as it goes, but it can suggest that builders first wanted luminous interiors and then invented a device to obtain them. The surviving evidence points to a messier process. Early buttresses were often added to existing churches whose walls had begun to lean, and only later were they planned from the start. Builders learned what the device could do partly by repairing failures. The soaring, glass-filled interior was thus as much a consequence of accumulated structural experience as the realization of a prior aesthetic program.

vr-ts032.x: Microfinance lenders in many developing economies have often lent to small groups of borrowers, each of whom is responsible in part for the others' loans. Such joint liability was thought to solve two problems that make lending to poor households costly: lenders cannot easily tell reliable borrowers from unreliable ones, and they cannot cheaply monitor how loans are used. Neighbors, by contrast, know one another's habits and can apply social pressure. Field experiments, however, have complicated this picture. In several programs, converting groups from joint to individual liability did not noticeably raise default rates, while it did attract more borrowers, some of whom had disliked being held responsible for others' debts. Regular group meetings, which continued under both arrangements, may have done more to sustain repayment than the shared obligation itself.

vr-ts033.x: Reef-building corals depend on single-celled algae living in their tissues, which supply most of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. When water grows unusually warm, the partnership breaks down and the coral expels its algae, turning white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals can recover if conditions improve, but repeated episodes often kill them. Some corals, however, host more than one type of alga, and certain types tolerate heat better than others. After a bleaching event, such corals sometimes recover with a larger share of the tolerant type, which makes them less likely to bleach in the next warm spell. This flexibility has encouraged hope that reefs might adapt to warming seas. The hope should be tempered: heat-tolerant algae often supply less energy, so corals that host them may grow more slowly, and not every coral species can take up new partners.

vr-ts034.x: Scholars once assumed that a long poem could be composed only by an author who wrote it down or memorized a fixed text. Fieldwork among singers in the Balkans in the twentieth century challenged that assumption. The singers performed epics thousands of lines long without a written text, yet no two performances of the same song were identical. They worked with a stock of traditional phrases, each fitted to a particular place in the metrical line, along with familiar scenes such as arming for battle or a feast. Using these resources, a skilled singer recomposed the song as he performed it. Applied to ancient epics, this finding suggested that repeated epithets, long thought to be padding, were the working tools of composition. It also unsettled the very idea of an original version, since each performance was as authentic as any other.

vr-ts035.x: For a long time historians credited the printing press with transforming European intellectual life almost by itself: cheap, identical copies were said to have spread new ideas rapidly and fixed texts in stable form. More recent work has qualified both claims. Early printed books were often riddled with errors, and printers freely altered texts from one edition to the next, so print did not at once produce the stability attributed to it. Nor did manuscripts disappear; scribes continued to copy works for which demand was too small to justify a print run, and manuscript newsletters circulated alongside printed ones well into the eighteenth century. Revisionists do not deny that print mattered. They argue rather that its effects depended on the people who used it, and that they unfolded over generations rather than years.

vr-ts036.x: When the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed in the early twentieth century that the continents had drifted apart, most geologists rejected the idea. His evidence, which included the matching coastlines of Africa and South America and similar fossils on widely separated continents, was suggestive, but he could offer no plausible force strong enough to push continents through the solid ocean floor. The idea revived in the 1960s for reasons Wegener could not have anticipated. Surveys of the seafloor revealed stripes of rock magnetized in alternating directions, recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field, and the stripes formed mirror images on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern made sense only if new crust formed at the ridges and spread outward. Continents, it turned out, did not plow through the ocean floor; they rode along with it.

vr-ts037.x: When photography became commercially available in the 1840s, many observers predicted the end of portrait painting. For the middle classes, at least, the prediction proved partly accurate: miniature painters, who had supplied small, affordable likenesses, lost much of their trade within a generation, and some of them became photographers or hand-colored photographic prints. Yet painted portraits of the wealthy did not decline, and in some respects their prestige rose. A photograph could record a face, but it could not easily flatter, and it was cheap enough that owning one no longer distinguished its owner. A commissioned painting, by contrast, signaled both expense and the attention of a named artist. Photography thus divided the market it had been expected to destroy, absorbing the modest likeness while leaving the luxury portrait more exclusive than before.

vr-ts038.x: Economists have long argued that charging drivers a fee to enter crowded city centers at peak hours would reduce traffic more efficiently than building new roads. New roads, they note, tend to fill up again as drivers who had avoided the congested route return to it, whereas a price makes each driver weigh the delay his or her trip imposes on others. The few cities that have adopted such charges have generally seen traffic fall and travel times improve. Public opinion has followed a curious pattern in these places. Support is often weak before a charge is introduced and grows after residents have experienced its effects, a shift that suggests the main obstacle is not the policy's performance but the difficulty of imagining its benefits in advance.

vr-ts039.x: Until the late 1970s, biologists assumed that nearly all life on Earth depended, directly or indirectly, on energy from sunlight. The discovery of dense animal communities around hydrothermal vents on the deep seafloor overturned that assumption. Far below the reach of light, giant tubeworms, clams and shrimp flourish around openings that release hot, mineral-laden water. The base of this food web consists of microbes that obtain energy by oxidizing hydrogen sulfide and other chemicals in the vent fluid, a process known as chemosynthesis. The tubeworms lack mouths and guts altogether; they house such microbes in a specialized organ and absorb the compounds the microbes produce. Even here, however, sunlight is not wholly absent from the story, since the oxygen many vent microbes use to oxidize sulfide is itself a product of photosynthesis at the surface.

vr-ts040.x: Translators of literature have long disagreed about how visible the foreignness of a text should be. One approach aims at a version that reads as though it had been written in the reader's language, smoothing away unfamiliar idioms, customs and rhythms. Its defenders argue that a translation should give readers the experience the original gave its first audience, who did not find their own language strange. Critics reply that this fluency comes at a cost: by making every foreign work sound familiar, it conceals what is distinctive about other cultures and quietly reinforces the reader's sense that his or her own conventions are natural. They favor translations that preserve some strangeness, even at the price of ease. Neither camp, it should be said, can claim complete fidelity, since every translation must choose which features of the original to sacrifice.

vr-ps004.x: A honeybee that finds a rich source of nectar returns to the hive and performs a movement known as the waggle dance. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The direction of the straight run, measured against the vertical surface of the comb, tells other bees the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run, the farther away the food. Bees that follow the dancer then leave the hive and search in the indicated area. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a dancer adjusts the angle of its run over time, so that the information it gives remains accurate.

vr-ps005.x: When employers in several countries changed their retirement savings plans so that new workers were enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out, participation rose sharply, often from under half of new employees to well over three quarters. Since the workers remained free to leave the plan at no cost, standard economic models, which assume that people choose the option they prefer, predict little change. The gap between prediction and result has been attributed to several causes. Deciding how much to save is tedious, and many people postpone tedious decisions indefinitely. Some workers may also read the default as a recommendation from an employer who presumably knows more than they do. The same research, however, found a drawback: many automatically enrolled workers stayed at the low contribution rate the plan had set, saving less than they might have chosen on their own.

vr-ps006.x: Painters of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries returned again and again to ruined abbeys and broken columns, and the fashion is usually explained as nostalgia for a vanished past. That reading is not wrong, but it is incomplete. A ruin is not simply what remains of a building; it is a building in the act of becoming landscape, as ivy, weather and collapse dissolve the boundary between human design and natural process. Many of these painters were less interested in the past the ruin recalled than in this ongoing transformation, which allowed them to depict time itself rather than a moment in it. The ruin's appeal, on this account, lay not in what it had lost but in what it was still undergoing. Nostalgia looks backward; these canvases often seem instead to contemplate a process that has no end.

vr-ts041.x: For two decades, popular accounts have described forests as cooperative communities in which trees use underground fungal networks to feed struggling neighbors. The underlying observations are real: the threads of mycorrhizal fungi do connect the roots of different trees, and isotope-labeled carbon released by one tree has been detected in another. Yet several ecologists now argue that the interpretation has outrun the evidence. The quantities of carbon transferred in field studies are usually small, and it is rarely clear whether the carbon reached the neighbor's shoots or merely remained in fungal tissue inside its roots. Moreover, the fungi are not neutral pipes; they are organisms pursuing their own interests, and a transfer that looks like generosity between trees may simply reflect the fungus moving resources toward wherever it is itself growing fastest. None of this shows that the networks are unimportant, only that the language of altruism is premature.

vr-ts042.x: Readers who open a thirteenth-century psalter are sometimes startled to find, in the margins beside solemn texts, rabbits jousting with knights, snails battling armored men, and monkeys playing bagpipes. Earlier scholars tended to treat such images as idle doodles, the scribe's relief from tedious copying. That explanation has grown hard to sustain. Marginal images were often planned before the text was written, since space was left for them, and they were usually painted by specialist illuminators rather than by the scribes themselves. Many also respond to particular words on the page, punning on a phrase or inverting its meaning. Some historians therefore read the margins as a deliberate commentary, a space where the ordered world of the central text could be playfully turned upside down. Whatever their precise purpose, the images were clearly part of the book's design, not an afterthought.

vr-ts043.x: In negotiations over salary, the first number spoken aloud exerts a pull that is out of proportion to its informational value. Experiments in which participants bargain over a hypothetical job find that final agreements cluster near whichever figure was offered first, even when participants are told that the opening offer was chosen at random. Psychologists call this anchoring: people adjust away from an initial value, but typically not far enough. The practical advice that follows, to make the first offer and make it ambitious, is not without risk, however. An opening demand perceived as unreasonable can end a negotiation before any adjustment begins, and the effect appears weakest when the other party has precise knowledge of market rates. Anchors, in other words, work best where uncertainty is greatest.

vr-ts044.x: Tardigrades, microscopic animals found in moss and leaf litter, can survive the loss of nearly all their body water by entering a dormant state called a tun. For years, researchers assumed that tardigrades protected themselves the way many desiccation-tolerant organisms do, by filling their cells with the sugar trehalose, which forms a glassy solid that holds delicate molecules in place. Yet many tardigrade species produce little or no trehalose. The puzzle was partly resolved by the discovery of proteins found only in tardigrades that remain unfolded in water but, as cells dry, appear to form a gel-like matrix serving much the same function as the sugar glass. When the genes for these proteins were inserted into yeast and bacteria, those organisms became markedly more tolerant of drying, suggesting that the proteins are not merely present during desiccation but actively contribute to survival.

vr-ts045.x: In much Baroque music, the composer wrote out only a bass line, sometimes with small numerals indicating the harmonies above it; the keyboard or lute player was expected to improvise the rest. This practice, known as basso continuo, presents modern performers with a dilemma. Printed editions of the twentieth century often supplied a fully written-out accompaniment, and many players still perform from these realizations note for note. Such fidelity, however, is fidelity to the editor rather than to the composer, for the written part freezes into one version what was meant to change from performance to performance. Some ensembles have accordingly begun training their continuo players to improvise again, accepting occasional roughness as the price of a texture that responds to the singers and to the room. The results are uneven, but at their best they restore a quality that no edition can capture.

vr-ts046.x: Between the late twelfth and early fourteenth centuries, the fairs held in a handful of towns in the county of Champagne became the principal meeting place for merchants from Italy and Flanders. Historians once credited this success chiefly to geography, since the towns lay along routes connecting the two regions. Geography alone, however, cannot explain why these towns and not others along the same routes prospered. A more persuasive account emphasizes institutions. The counts of Champagne guaranteed safe conduct to merchants traveling to the fairs, maintained courts that settled disputes quickly, and enforced contracts even against their own subjects. Such guarantees reduced the risk of trading with strangers. Tellingly, the fairs began to decline after the county was absorbed into the French kingdom, when royal policies came to favor local interests over those of foreign traders.

vr-ts047.x: Many migratory songbirds can orient themselves using Earth's magnetic field, but how they sense the field has long been uncertain. One leading hypothesis locates the compass in the eye. According to this view, light striking certain retinal proteins called cryptochromes produces pairs of molecules whose chemical behavior depends on their alignment with the magnetic field, so that the bird may literally see the field as a pattern overlaid on its vision. The hypothesis explains a curious finding: in experiments, robins lose their magnetic orientation under some wavelengths of light but not others. It also accounts for reports that very weak radio-frequency noise, far too feeble to heat tissue, disrupts orientation, since such noise could interfere with a delicate chemical reaction. A competing hypothesis, involving iron-rich particles in the beak, has fared less well since the supposed receptor cells proved to be immune cells.

vr-ts048.x: It is a commonplace of art history that Japanese woodblock prints, arriving in Paris in quantity after the 1850s, transformed French painting: their flat areas of color, asymmetrical compositions and high viewpoints are said to have liberated artists such as Degas and Monet from academic convention. The account is not wrong, but it is often told as if the prints supplied ideas the French could not have reached alone. In fact, several of the features attributed to Japanese influence were already being explored, in the cropped frames of photography and in popular French illustration. What the prints offered may have been less a revelation than a confirmation, an example from a respected tradition that lent authority to experiments already under way. Influence, on this view, is not a one-way transfer but a meeting between what an artist finds and what the artist is already looking for.

vr-ts049.x: Creole languages arise when speakers of different languages, brought together by trade or labor, develop a shared tongue that children then acquire as their first language. Linguists have long noticed that creoles separated by oceans often share grammatical features, such as marking tense with separate words placed before the verb rather than with endings. One influential explanation held that these similarities reveal an innate grammar that children fall back on when the language around them is fragmentary. Critics reply that the resemblance may be less striking than it seems once the languages that contributed to each creole are taken into account; many creoles drew on related West African or European sources, which could account for shared features without any appeal to innate structure. The debate matters beyond creole studies, because creoles offer one of the few natural settings in which the emergence of a grammar can be observed.

vr-ts050.x: The Venus flytrap faces a problem of discrimination. Its leaves snap shut on insects, but closing is costly, consuming energy and taking hours to reverse, so a trap that closed on every falling raindrop or blown seed would soon exhaust the plant. The solution lies in a set of sensitive hairs on the inner surface of each leaf. A single touch to one hair produces an electrical signal but does not close the trap. Only if a second touch follows within about half a minute does the leaf snap shut. Struggling prey then triggers further signals, and after several more the plant begins producing digestive enzymes. In effect, the plant counts, and each threshold guards a more expensive commitment. Debris rarely touches the hairs twice in quick succession; a live insect exploring the leaf almost always does.

vr-ts051.x: Long oral poems, recited by singers who could not read, pose an obvious question: how could anyone hold thousands of lines in memory? Fieldwork among traditional singers in the twentieth century suggested that the question was misframed. The singers did not memorize fixed texts at all. Instead they commanded a stock of formulas, ready-made phrases that fit the meter, along with recurring scenes such as the arming of a hero or the arrival of a guest. With these resources a skilled singer recomposed the poem in each performance, so that no two renditions were identical, even when the singer sincerely insisted that he had performed the song exactly as before. The finding changed how scholars read ancient epics that survive in writing. Repeated epithets that once seemed padding came to look like traces of a technique, evidence that the written poems grew out of such performance.

vr-ts052.x: When employers began enrolling new workers in retirement savings plans automatically, while allowing anyone to opt out, participation rose sharply, in some firms from under half of new hires to nearly all of them. Standard economic models had predicted little effect, because the choice itself was unchanged: a worker who wished to save could always have enrolled, and one who did not could still leave. Behavioral economists offered several reasons the default mattered. Enrolling requires effort and attention that people tend to postpone; a default may be read as an implicit recommendation; and staying put avoids the discomfort of making an active decision. Yet the same studies revealed a less welcome result. Many automatically enrolled workers remained at the default contribution rate, which was often set low, and some saved less than they would have chosen to save on their own.

vr-ts053.x: On cliffs and boulders in arid regions, a thin dark coating known as desert varnish forms over thousands of years. The coating is rich in manganese, often concentrated to levels many times higher than in the surrounding dust and rock, and explaining this enrichment has long divided geologists. Some favor a purely chemical account in which slight changes in acidity, as dew forms and evaporates, cause manganese to precipitate. Others argue that microbes living on rock surfaces concentrate the metal, pointing to bacteria that can oxidize manganese in the laboratory. The biological account faces a difficulty, however: such bacteria are scarce in varnish itself. A more recent proposal tries to reconcile the views, suggesting that microbes use manganese to protect themselves from the intense sunlight of deserts and that the metal remains on the rock after they die.

vr-ts054.x: The flying buttresses of Gothic cathedrals are usually explained as engineering: by carrying the outward thrust of high stone vaults down to piers outside the building, they allowed walls to be thinned and opened up for vast windows. Structural analyses broadly confirm this function. Yet the buttresses were not merely solutions to a problem builders happened to face. Medieval patrons sought height and light because they prized both as marks of splendor and civic prestige, and the buttress was the means by which these aims could be pursued further than earlier construction allowed. Seen this way, the engineering served an aesthetic program rather than determining it. The point is not that function is irrelevant to Gothic form, but that the problem the buttresses solved was itself chosen. Builders content with lower, darker churches would have had no need of them.

vr-ts055.x: Anthropologists studying societies in which goods circulate largely as gifts have observed that a gift is rarely free. Accepting one creates an obligation to reciprocate, and the return gift is often expected not immediately but after a delay, sometimes of months. The delay is not incidental. An immediate return of equal value would cancel the debt and, with it, the relationship; it would resemble a purchase. By leaving a balance outstanding, the parties keep a tie alive, each anticipating the next exchange. For the same reason, returning exactly what was received can give offense, signaling a wish to be quits. Market transactions, by contrast, are designed to end cleanly, leaving buyer and seller with no further claim on each other. The difference lies less in the goods than in what the exchange is meant to do.

vr-ts056.x: Most known planets outside our solar system were found by one of two methods. The transit method watches for the slight dimming of a star as a planet passes in front of it; the radial-velocity method detects the faint wobble that a planet's gravity induces in its star. Both methods favor certain kinds of planets. A transit is seen only if the planet's orbit is aligned nearly edge-on to our line of sight, an alignment far more likely for planets orbiting close to their stars, and close-in planets also transit more often, giving observers more chances to catch them. Radial-velocity signals, meanwhile, are strongest for massive planets in tight orbits. As a result, early catalogs were crowded with giant planets orbiting closer to their stars than Mercury does to the Sun. Astronomers caution that this abundance tells us as much about the instruments as about the galaxy.

vr-ts057.x: Eighteenth-century novels told entirely in letters offered readers an illusion of immediacy: events seemed to unfold as the characters wrote, with no narrator standing between them and the reader. The form also imposed constraints that its best practitioners turned to advantage. Because each letter reflects only what its writer knows and is willing to say, the reader often understands more than any single correspondent. A heroine may describe a suitor's attentions with innocent pleasure in one letter while, a few pages later, the suitor's own letter to a friend reveals his calculating motives. The gap between the two accounts produces an irony that no character perceives. Critics who dismissed the form as clumsy, pointing to characters who improbably write long letters in moments of crisis, overlooked how much of its interest lies precisely in what each writer cannot see.

vr-ts058.x: Roman amphorae, the clay jars in which wine, olive oil and fish sauce were shipped across the Mediterranean, are among the most abundant finds at ancient sites. Because many were stamped with the names of producers or estates, and because their shapes changed in datable ways, archaeologists have used them to reconstruct patterns of trade, tracing for instance how oil from southern Spain reached military camps on the Rhine. The method has limits that its users acknowledge. Amphorae were often reused, refilled with goods other than those for which they were made, so a jar's origin does not always reveal its last contents. And goods shipped in barrels or sacks, which rot, leave far fainter traces than goods shipped in clay. A map of trade drawn from amphorae is therefore a map of what traveled in amphorae, which may not be the same thing.

vr-ts059.x: Cuttlefish are masters of camouflage, matching the color and texture of their surroundings within a fraction of a second. Yet behavioral tests indicate that most species are colorblind: their eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive pigment, which ordinarily allows an animal to distinguish brightness but not hue. How an animal that cannot see color matches it so well remains unresolved. One possibility is that matching brightness and pattern is enough, since many predators of cuttlefish are themselves poor at distinguishing colors. Another proposal concerns the cuttlefish's oddly shaped pupil, curved like the letter W. Such a pupil could allow different wavelengths of light to come into focus at slightly different depths in the eye, so that the animal might infer color from blur. The idea is ingenious but has yet to be tested directly in living animals.

vr-ts060.x: Early photographs of city streets are strangely empty. Exposures in the 1840s could last several minutes, so anything that moved, whether carriages or pedestrians, left no trace, while buildings, lampposts and an occasional figure standing still for a shoeshine were recorded in sharp detail. Contemporary viewers were less troubled by this absence than we might expect. Many valued the new medium chiefly for its fidelity to fixed things: architecture, monuments, the texture of stone. Painters, meanwhile, drew a different lesson. If the camera could not capture motion, then the depiction of movement, of crowds and weather and the passing moment, remained the painter's territory, and some artists embraced it with new determination. Only as exposure times shortened did photography begin to claim that territory as well, prompting painters to look elsewhere once more.

vr-ps007.x: Economists have long puzzled over why firms in the same industry crowd together in particular cities when land and labor are cheaper elsewhere. Three advantages are usually cited. Clustered firms can share specialized suppliers that no single firm could support; they draw on a deep pool of workers with the relevant skills, which lowers the risk of hiring for both sides; and ideas spread more readily among people who meet, change jobs and talk shop. The last of these is the hardest to measure, since knowledge leaves no receipts. One ingenious approach examines patents, which must cite earlier inventions: citations turn out to come disproportionately from inventors in the same metropolitan area as the cited patent, even after accounting for the existing concentration of the industry there. Proximity, it seems, still matters in an age of instant communication.

vr-ps008.x: During dry nights, the roots of some deep-rooted plants do something that seems, at first, self-defeating. Water drawn from moist soil far below moves up through the roots and leaks out into the parched upper layers, a phenomenon called hydraulic lift. With the leaf pores closed, the plant is not losing water to the air, and the movement is passive, following the gradient from wet soil to dry. Why would natural selection tolerate such leakage? Several benefits have been proposed. Moistened surface soil keeps the fine roots there alive and able to absorb nutrients, which are concentrated near the surface but become unavailable when it dries out. The water released at night is also largely reabsorbed the next day, so the soil acts as a temporary reservoir. Less flattering to the plant, neighbors with shallow roots sometimes take up a share of the lifted water.

vr-ts061.x: Populations of white-crowned sparrows separated by only a few kilometers often sing recognizably different song dialects, and for decades the variation was taken as evidence that song is learned and transmitted culturally, much as regional accents are. Yet geographic variation alone cannot distinguish cultural transmission from genetic divergence, since neighboring populations that rarely interbreed could drift apart in inherited song templates as readily as in learned ones. The decisive evidence came instead from cross-fostering: nestlings raised by tutors from a distant dialect reliably acquire the tutors' song rather than that of their biological parents. Even this result, however, establishes only that learning is sufficient to produce dialects, not that it explains their persistence in the wild. Dialect boundaries might be maintained because females prefer local songs, because young males settle near the tutors they heard, or because both pressures operate together, possibilities that cross-fostering experiments, conducted in captivity, are not designed to separate.

vr-ts062.x: The grotesque creatures, armored snails and acrobatic rabbits that crowd the margins of many thirteenth-century manuscripts have long embarrassed interpreters who assume that every element of a sacred book must serve a devotional end. One school of thought treats the images as the idle play of bored illuminators, tolerated because margins were thought to lie outside the text proper. A second reads them as deliberate commentary, parodying the very passages they adjoin. Neither account is fully satisfying. The idleness thesis cannot explain why patrons who paid dearly for these books evidently requested such images, nor why particular motifs recur across workshops that had no contact with one another. The parody thesis, for its part, founders on the many margins whose images bear no discernible relation to the adjacent text. A more promising view holds that the images served memory: vivid, incongruous pictures were a recognized aid to recalling one's place in a long text, and their very absurdity was the point.

vr-ts063.x: Students placed among high-achieving classmates often earn better grades, but economists have struggled to show that the classmates are the cause. Families who value achievement tend to choose the same schools, so a correlation between a student's performance and that of her peers may simply reflect shared advantages that predate any interaction. To escape this difficulty, researchers have turned to settings in which assignment is effectively random, such as university dormitories that place first-year roommates by lottery. These studies typically find peer effects that are real but modest, far smaller than the raw correlations suggest. Some scholars caution, however, that the remedy introduces a problem of its own. A randomly assigned roommate is a single peer encountered at an unusual moment, whereas the peer groups that concern policymakers are entire classrooms sustained over years. Effects measured cleanly in the first setting may therefore understate, or simply fail to describe, those operating in the second.

vr-ts064.x: Around 700 million years ago, glacial deposits formed at what were then tropical latitudes, and directly atop them lie thick layers of carbonate rock of a kind that ordinarily precipitates in warm seas. Proponents of the 'Snowball Earth' hypothesis read this abrupt juxtaposition as the signature of a planet frozen nearly from pole to pole. With the oceans sealed beneath ice, they argue, volcanic carbon dioxide would have accumulated in the atmosphere for millions of years, unchecked by the weathering of rock that normally removes it, until a runaway greenhouse melted the ice and the excess carbon was rapidly deposited as carbonate. Critics accept the deposits but not the inference. A 'slushball' planet, with open water near the equator, could also have hosted low-latitude glaciers, and some carbonate layers appear to have accumulated over intervals longer than a sudden post-glacial pulse would allow. The dispute thus turns less on what the rocks contain than on how quickly they formed.

vr-ts065.x: Modern performers of Baroque music who play with little or no vibrato often justify the practice by citing eighteenth-century treatises that describe vibrato as an ornament, to be applied sparingly to particular notes. The argument is less conclusive than it appears. Treatises are prescriptive documents, and writers rarely trouble to forbid what nobody does; repeated warnings against excessive vibrato might indicate that many players used it liberally. Moreover, the treatises disagree among themselves, and their authors were often teachers addressing students rather than describing the habits of celebrated soloists. None of this proves that continuous vibrato was the norm. It suggests rather that the written record underdetermines the sound of the past, and that the austere tone now associated with 'authentic' performance owes something to modern taste. Historical evidence has constrained the revival of early music, but it has not dictated its every choice.

vr-ts066.x: The Dutch tulip craze of the 1630s, in which single bulbs reportedly changed hands for the price of a canal house, has become a byword for collective irrationality. Recent archival work complicates the legend. Most of the extravagant prices were recorded not in completed sales but in contracts for future delivery, traded in taverns during a winter when no bulbs could be lifted from the ground, and many of these contracts were later settled for a small fraction of their face value or not at all. Few traders appear to have been ruined, and the wider Dutch economy shows no sign of the distress that the story's moralists described. None of this means that prices behaved sensibly; a brief speculative frenzy evidently occurred. But a market in which promises were cheap to make and easy to abandon may tell us less about the folly of crowds than about how prices form when commitments carry little cost.

vr-ts067.x: Fungal threads that link the roots of neighboring trees have been celebrated as a 'wood wide web' through which mature trees nourish their shaded seedlings and warn neighbors of insect attack. The underlying observations are genuine: labeled carbon fed to one tree has been detected in another, and many seedlings grow better when connected to a fungal network. What remains doubtful is the interpretation. Carbon detected in a neighbor may have traveled through soil rather than through fungal threads, and in most experiments the amounts transferred were too small to matter to the recipient's growth. Improved seedling growth, likewise, could reflect the fungi's own contribution, such as better access to soil nutrients, rather than any subsidy from adult trees. The fungi, moreover, are organisms with interests of their own; a network that moves resources may be serving its fungal members rather than performing a service on behalf of the forest.

vr-ts068.x: Novelists of the nineteenth century refined a technique, now called free indirect discourse, in which a narrator's sentences take on the vocabulary and judgments of a character without the signal of quotation marks or a phrase such as 'she thought.' A sentence like 'How tiresome the vicar was, with his endless parables!' may belong to the narrator, to the heroine, or ambiguously to both. Critics once praised the technique chiefly for its psychological intimacy, the sense it gives of overhearing a mind. More recent readers have stressed instead its capacity for irony: because the narrator never formally disowns the character's view, the reader must decide how far to share it, and the pleasure of the method lies partly in the discovery that one has been sharing it too readily. On this account the technique does not merely represent consciousness; it implicates the reader in the very errors of judgment the novel exposes.

vr-ts069.x: Anthropologists once expected kinship terminologies to mirror social arrangements closely. If a language uses one word for both one's father and one's father's brother, the reasoning went, then the two men must occupy similar roles, perhaps sharing authority over the children of the household. Field studies have repeatedly strained this expectation. Communities with nearly identical terminologies organize inheritance, residence and marriage quite differently, and terminologies sometimes persist for generations after the arrangements they supposedly encoded have disappeared. Some linguists now argue that terminologies are better understood as compact classification systems, shaped partly by the cognitive economy of using few terms and partly by descent from ancestral languages. The social interpretation has not been abandoned, however. Its defenders contend that a terminology may preserve the imprint of past arrangements, much as the layout of a city's streets records the boundaries of fields that were long ago built over.

vr-ts070.x: Because nearly all the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere is produced by photosynthesis, astronomers have long regarded abundant oxygen in the atmosphere of a distant planet as one of the strongest possible signs of life. Laboratory and modeling studies have weakened that confidence. On a planet that has lost most of its water, ultraviolet light can split the remaining water vapor, and when the light hydrogen escapes to space, oxygen may accumulate without any biological help. Planets orbiting small, active stars may be especially prone to such buildup. Few researchers conclude that oxygen is therefore useless as a biosignature. The emerging view is that it must be read in context: oxygen found together with methane, which reacts with oxygen and would soon disappear unless something kept replenishing it, is far harder to explain without life than oxygen found alone.

vr-ts071.x: The flying buttress is often presented as a triumph of structural reasoning: by carrying the outward thrust of a high vault across open air to a pier standing clear of the wall, it freed Gothic builders to replace masonry with vast windows. The account is not wrong, but it is incomplete. Medieval builders possessed no theory of forces in the modern sense; their knowledge was a body of proportional rules, refined through trial and, on occasion, through collapse. Several early buttresses were placed too high to meet the thrust they were meant to resist, and they appear to have survived because the walls behind them were thicker than strictly necessary. Nor was the device chosen for utility alone. Once established, buttresses were multiplied and elaborated with pinnacles and tracery well beyond structural need, becoming part of the visual vocabulary by which a church announced its ambition.

vr-ts072.x: Few findings in behavioral economics are cited as often as loss aversion, the tendency to weigh a loss more heavily than a gain of the same size. Early experiments, in which participants declined coin-flip bets offering equal chances of winning and losing modest sums unless the potential gain was roughly twice the potential loss, seemed to reveal a stable feature of human psychology. Later work has made the picture less tidy. When stakes are very small, many people accept such bets readily, and the asymmetry shrinks or vanishes when participants regard the money as already belonging to a budget for gambling. Some researchers conclude that loss aversion is an artifact of experimental framing. Others hold that it is real but conditional, emerging when an outcome is perceived as a departure from what one already has or expects. The second view has the merit of explaining both the original results and their exceptions, though at the cost of making predictions depend on expectations that are difficult to measure.

vr-ts073.x: Reports of steep declines in insect abundance have alarmed ecologists, but the evidence is uneven in ways that complicate any global estimate. Most long-term records come from a handful of well-studied regions, chiefly in Europe and North America, where intensive agriculture and habitat loss are already known to be severe. Many series also begin in years that happen to have been unusually productive, so that later counts look low partly by comparison with an exceptional baseline. Skeptics sometimes conclude that the declines have been exaggerated. That inference does not follow. Biases in where and when sampling began make the size of the decline uncertain, but uncertainty runs in both directions: the regions least studied include tropical forests, where clearing has been rapid and where losses could exceed anything yet recorded. What the record supports is not complacency but a recognition that the global picture remains largely unmeasured.

vr-ts074.x: Seventeenth-century Dutch still lifes, with their half-peeled lemons, overturned goblets and guttering candles, are routinely read as vanitas images, sermons in paint on the brevity of earthly pleasure. The interpretation has textual support: emblem books of the period attached moralizing verses to similar objects. Yet it sits awkwardly with how the paintings were made and sold. Many were produced on speculation for an open market, by specialists who repeated profitable compositions with small variations, and inventories show them hanging in dining rooms beside maps and portraits rather than in places of private devotion. A buyer might well have relished the painted oysters and imported porcelain as displays of skill and of the abundance that trade had brought. The two readings need not be exclusive. A painting could flatter its owner's prosperity while gently reminding him of its impermanence, and the ambiguity may have been part of what made such pictures sell.

vr-ts075.x: Death rates in many European cities fell substantially in the late nineteenth century, and historians have long disagreed about why. One influential argument held that medicine deserved little credit, since mortality from several major diseases began declining before effective treatments existed; improved nutrition, made possible by rising incomes, was proposed instead. Critics have pointed out that this argument proceeds largely by elimination: having set aside medical treatment, it assigns the remainder of the decline to diet without measuring diet directly. They emphasize municipal investments in filtered water and sewers, which coincided closely with falls in waterborne disease in city after city. The coincidence is suggestive rather than conclusive, since cities that built waterworks were often also growing wealthier. Yet the timing in several cases is sharp enough, with deaths falling within a few years of a new supply, that income, which rose gradually, seems an unlikely explanation for the abrupt changes.

vr-ts076.x: Bats and toothed whales independently evolved echolocation, and in the early 2010s several studies reported that the two groups had also converged at the molecular level, with the same amino-acid substitutions appearing in genes involved in hearing. The finding was striking because convergence in form is common, whereas convergence in genetic sequence had been thought rare enough to serve as a reliable sign of shared ancestry. Subsequent analyses tempered the excitement. When researchers compared the number of shared substitutions in echolocating lineages with the number shared, purely by chance, between pairs of lineages that do not echolocate, much of the apparent signal disappeared across the genome as a whole. A few hearing genes still showed more convergence than chance would predict. The episode illustrates a general hazard: in a dataset large enough, striking coincidences are guaranteed, and their significance can be judged only against an explicit estimate of how often they would arise anyway.

vr-ts077.x: Translators have long been described as choosing between two strategies. A domesticating translation smooths a foreign text into idiomatic prose, so that a reader may forget it was ever written in another language; a foreignizing translation preserves unfamiliar syntax, customs and allusions, reminding the reader of the distance the text has traveled. Advocates of the second approach have often presented it as the more respectful, even the more ethical, choice, since domestication can quietly erase what is distinctive in a source culture. The dichotomy is useful but can mislead. What strikes one audience as foreign depends on that audience's habits, so the same rendering may seem exotic in one decade and ordinary in the next. Moreover, a translator who preserves every unfamiliar construction may produce prose that seems clumsy rather than foreign, and readers may attribute the clumsiness to the original author, a distortion no less serious than the one foreignization was meant to avoid.

vr-ts078.x: The abandonment of many lowland Maya cities in the ninth century has often been attributed to drought, and lake sediments from the region do record several severe dry periods at about that time. Yet the decline did not unfold as a single event. Some cities in the southern lowlands were emptied decades before the driest intervals, while others in the north, where rainfall was lower to begin with, flourished during them. Such a pattern is awkward for a purely climatic account. Many archaeologists now describe drought as a stress that acted on societies already strained by warfare among rival dynasties and by heavy demands on farmland. On this view, the crucial question is not whether the climate changed but why some states could absorb the shock while others could not. Answering it requires evidence of political organization that sediment cores cannot supply.

vr-ts079.x: Reef-building corals depend on algae living within their tissues, and when water grows too warm the partnership breaks down: the coral expels its algae and, if conditions do not improve, starves. Some corals, however, host several types of algae that differ in heat tolerance, and after a bleaching event they may recover with a community dominated by the hardier type. This 'shuffling' has been hailed as a way reefs might adapt to warming without waiting for slow genetic change in the corals themselves. The hope rests on a trade-off that is easy to overlook. Heat-tolerant algae typically supply their hosts with less food, so corals that shuffle may grow more slowly and reproduce less. Moreover, in several monitored reefs the hardier algae were gradually replaced by the original types once temperatures returned to normal, suggesting that the protection lasts only as long as the stress that produced it.

vr-ts080.x: Portraits from the first decades of photography show sitters who rarely smile, and the solemnity is often explained by the long exposures early processes required: a grin held for half a minute becomes a grimace, and a blurred one besides. The technical explanation is true as far as it goes, but exposure times had shortened to a few seconds by the 1860s, and unsmiling faces remained the convention for decades afterward. Some historians therefore look to older traditions of painted portraiture, in which an open smile was associated with drunkenness, foolishness or the stage. A portrait was meant to record a person's settled character, not a passing mood, and the earliest photographers inherited this expectation along with many of the painters' poses and props. On this view technology did not create the solemn photographic face; it merely failed, for a time, to challenge a convention that predated it.

vr-ps009.x: In the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, London's coffeehouses multiplied rapidly, and historians have often described them as the birthplace of a new kind of public life. For the price of a cup, a customer could read newspapers, hear the latest commercial and political rumors, and argue with strangers of different ranks. Some coffeehouses became associated with particular trades: merchants interested in shipping gathered in one, while booksellers and writers favored another. Admirers of this history stress the openness of these spaces, yet the openness had limits. Women rarely took part as customers, and the cost of leisure time, if not of coffee, kept many laborers away. The coffeehouse may therefore be better understood as widening the circle of public discussion than as opening it to everyone.

vr-ps010.x: That sleep strengthens memory is supported by many experiments: people who sleep after learning a list of word pairs typically recall more of them the next day than people who spend the same hours awake. What sleep contributes, however, remains disputed. One hypothesis holds that sleep actively consolidates memories, replaying the day's experiences so that fragile traces become durable. A rival hypothesis holds that sleep helps chiefly by protection: a sleeper encounters no new information that could interfere with what was just learned. The two accounts make different predictions. If sleep merely shelters memories, a quiet period of wakefulness with little new input should help nearly as much; if sleep consolidates, it should outperform even such quiet wakefulness. Results so far are mixed, partly because 'quiet' wakefulness is hard to arrange; people left alone in a dim room still think, and their thoughts are themselves new information.

vr-ts001.x: Lichens are not single organisms but partnerships between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga. The fungus provides structure and shelter, while the alga produces sugars through photosynthesis. Because lichens have no roots and no protective outer layer, they absorb water and minerals directly from the air and rain. This habit makes them unusually sensitive to air quality. Sulfur dioxide, a common industrial pollutant, damages the algal partner and causes many lichen species to disappear from affected areas. Ecologists have therefore used lichens as living monitors: by recording which species grow on trees and stones in a region, they can estimate pollution levels without expensive instruments. Some cities that reduced industrial emissions in recent decades have seen sensitive lichens gradually return, a recovery that researchers regard as evidence that the air has improved.

vr-ts002.x: Dutch still-life paintings of the seventeenth century often look like simple celebrations of abundance. Tables overflow with lemons, oysters, silver cups and delicate glassware, all rendered with astonishing precision. Yet many of these works carry a second message. A half-peeled lemon, bright on the outside but sour within, could suggest that pleasant appearances deceive. A watch, a guttering candle or a skull reminded viewers that time passes and possessions cannot last. Art historians call such paintings vanitas images, after a Latin word for emptiness. The genre thus allowed wealthy buyers to enjoy pictures of luxury while also feeling that they were reflecting on serious moral questions. Not every still life was meant to be read this way, however, and scholars disagree about how far ordinary viewers noticed the symbols at all.

vr-ts003.x: Traditional economic models assume that people weigh the costs and benefits of every choice. Studies of workplace retirement plans suggest a more complicated picture. When employees must actively sign up for a savings plan, many never do, even though the plan offers matching contributions that amount to free money. When the same employers enroll workers automatically and allow them to leave the plan at any time, participation rises sharply, and most workers keep the contribution rate that was set for them. The financial incentives are identical in both arrangements; only the starting point differs. Behavioral economists interpret this pattern as evidence that inertia and the effort of making a decision shape behavior far more than standard models predict. The finding has influenced policy, but it also raises a question: if defaults are so powerful, who should decide what the default will be?

vr-ts004.x: For most of the twentieth century, biologists assumed that nearly all life on Earth depended, directly or indirectly, on energy from sunlight. The discovery of hydrothermal vents on the deep ocean floor in 1977 challenged that belief. Around these vents, where mineral-rich water heated by volcanic activity pours from the seabed, researchers found dense communities of giant tube worms, clams and shrimp living in total darkness. The base of this food web is not plants but bacteria that obtain energy from chemical compounds, such as hydrogen sulfide, dissolved in the vent water. This process, called chemosynthesis, allows the bacteria to build organic matter without light. Tube worms have no mouth or gut; instead, they house the bacteria inside their bodies and absorb the nutrients the bacteria produce.

vr-ts005.x: Readers who meet ancient epic poetry for the first time are often struck by its repetitions. Heroes are described with the same fixed phrases again and again, and entire scenes, such as the arming of a warrior or the preparing of a feast, recur in nearly identical words. In the early twentieth century, scholars studying living traditions of oral poetry in the Balkans proposed an explanation. Singers who performed long poems without writing did not memorize a fixed text. Instead, they drew on a large stock of ready-made phrases that fit the poem's meter, which let them compose fluently while performing. On this view, the repetitions are not signs of a careless or limited poet but the tools of a skilled craft. Many scholars now read the ancient epics as products of a similar oral tradition, though the exact role of writing in their final form is still debated.

vr-ts006.x: In many medieval European towns, craftsmen who practiced the same trade organized themselves into guilds. A guild set standards for the materials its members used, inspected finished goods and punished members who sold shoddy work. It also controlled entry to the trade: a boy typically served for years as an apprentice, then worked for wages as a journeyman, and only later, after producing a piece judged worthy by senior members, became a master entitled to open a shop. Historians have long debated whether these arrangements helped or harmed consumers. Defenders point out that buyers could not easily judge quality themselves and that guild inspection protected them from fraud. Critics reply that by limiting the number of masters, guilds kept prices high and discouraged new methods that might have threatened established workshops.

vr-ts007.x: Many migratory birds travel thousands of kilometers and return to the same breeding sites year after year. How they find their way has puzzled scientists for centuries. Experiments have shown that birds use several cues, including the position of the sun, the pattern of stars and familiar landmarks. Yet birds can also orient themselves under overcast night skies, when none of these cues is available. This ability led researchers to suspect that birds sense Earth's magnetic field. In one kind of test, caged birds that were restless to migrate tended to hop toward the direction they would normally fly; when scientists altered the magnetic field around the cages with electric coils, the birds shifted their hopping accordingly. How the birds detect the field remains uncertain, but one leading hypothesis points to light-sensitive molecules in the eye.

vr-ts008.x: After Japan opened its ports to Western trade in the 1850s, Japanese woodblock prints began to reach Paris in large numbers. French painters who collected them were struck by features that European academic art discouraged. The prints used flat areas of bright color instead of careful shading, cut figures off abruptly at the edges of the picture and viewed scenes from unusual angles, such as from high above. Artists including Edgar Degas and Mary Cassatt borrowed these devices, and Vincent van Gogh copied several prints in oil paint. The fashion came to be called Japonisme. The exchange was not a simple case of copying, however. European painters adapted what suited their own aims, often with little understanding of the place the prints had held in Japanese popular culture.

vr-ts009.x: Bilingual speakers often move between their two languages within a single conversation, or even within a single sentence. Linguists call this practice code-switching. It was once widely taken as a sign that speakers had not fully mastered either language and were filling gaps in their vocabulary. Research since the 1970s has largely overturned that view. Studies of bilingual communities have found that switching follows regular grammatical patterns: speakers tend to switch at points where the structures of the two languages fit together, and they rarely switch where the result would break the rules of either. Switching also serves social purposes. A speaker may change languages to quote someone, to show closeness to a listener or to mark a shift from casual to serious talk. Far from revealing a deficit, then, code-switching often reflects skill in both languages.

vr-ts010.x: Volcanic eruptions can bury fields under ash, yet the land around many volcanoes is among the most densely farmed in the world. The reason lies in the soil. Volcanic ash and weathered lava are rich in minerals such as potassium, calcium and phosphorus, which plants need to grow. Fresh ash, however, is not immediately fertile. It must first break down through weathering, a process that can take years or decades depending on the climate. In warm, wet regions, weathering is fast, and productive soils may form within a generation. In cold or dry regions, the same process can take much longer. Volcanic soils also tend to hold water well, which helps crops survive dry spells. These advantages explain why farmers have long been willing to accept the risks of living near an active volcano.

vr-ts011.x: The instrument we call the piano was first known as the gravicembalo col piano e forte, a harpsichord with soft and loud. Its inventor, Bartolomeo Cristofori, built the first examples in Florence around 1700. The name pointed to the instrument's chief novelty. On a harpsichord, a key plucks the string with the same force no matter how the player presses it, so a performer cannot make a single note louder or softer by touch. Cristofori's mechanism instead struck the string with a small hammer that rebounded at once, and the harder the player pressed the key, the louder the tone. Early pianos were quiet by modern standards and attracted few composers at first. Over the following century, however, builders strengthened the frame and enlarged the hammers, and composers began writing music that depended on gradual swells and sudden contrasts of volume.

vr-ts012.x: In many societies studied by anthropologists, gifts are not free in the way the word suggests. Accepting a gift creates an obligation to give something in return, and refusing a gift can be taken as an insult or a rejection of friendship. The return gift is usually not expected at once; a delay shows that the exchange is part of a continuing relationship rather than a trade that settles a debt. An exact return of equal value can even be considered rude, since it suggests that the giver wishes to end the relationship. Seen this way, gift giving is less about the objects than about the ties it creates and maintains. Some anthropologists have argued that similar expectations shape modern customs, such as the exchange of holiday presents or the habit of taking turns paying for meals among friends.

vr-ts013.x: Beneath most forests lies a network that is easy to overlook. The fine threads of certain soil fungi wrap around or enter the roots of trees, forming partnerships called mycorrhizae. The fungus extends far beyond the reach of the roots and gathers water and nutrients, especially phosphorus, which it passes to the tree. In return, the tree supplies the fungus with sugars made by photosynthesis. Because a single fungus can connect to several trees at once, researchers have suggested that these networks may also carry materials between trees. Some experiments with labeled carbon have detected transfers from large trees to nearby seedlings. Other scientists caution that such transfers are often small and that their importance in natural forests has not been established. The popular image of trees deliberately sharing food through the soil, they argue, goes beyond the evidence.

vr-ts014.x: The great cathedrals built in northern France from the twelfth century onward appear to defy the weight of stone. Their walls rise to remarkable heights and are pierced by enormous windows of colored glass. Earlier churches in the Romanesque style had needed thick walls with small openings, because the walls themselves carried the outward push of the heavy stone vaults above. Gothic builders solved this problem with the flying buttress, an arm of masonry that leaps from the upper wall to a pillar standing outside the building. The buttress receives much of the vault's outward thrust and carries it down to the ground. Freed from this load, the wall could become thinner and be opened up with glass. What looks like delicate decoration from inside is thus made possible by heavy structure placed outside.

vr-ts015.x: Most products lose nothing when other people buy them; a loaf of bread is just as useful whether or not the neighbors own one. The telephone was different. A single telephone was worthless, and each new subscriber made the service more valuable to everyone already connected, since there was one more person to call. Economists call this a network effect. It helps explain a pattern seen in many communication technologies: slow early adoption followed by rapid growth once enough people have joined. Network effects can also make markets hard to enter. A new company offering a better service may still fail if customers are unwilling to leave a larger network where their contacts already are. For this reason, early telephone companies competed fiercely to sign up subscribers, sometimes charging very low prices to build their networks.

vr-ts016.x: Where did the Moon come from? The explanation most widely accepted today is the giant-impact hypothesis. According to this idea, early in the solar system's history a body roughly the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision threw an enormous amount of material into orbit, and that debris gradually gathered to form the Moon. Several observations support the hypothesis. The Moon has a small iron core compared with Earth, which fits a model in which the Moon formed mostly from rocky outer layers. Rock samples returned by the Apollo missions are also strikingly similar to Earth's mantle in their chemical makeup. Yet this similarity is itself a puzzle, because computer simulations suggest that much of the Moon should have come from the impacting body, which would likely have had a different composition.

vr-ts017.x: Many of the best-known novels of the nineteenth century first reached readers not as complete books but in installments. A novel might appear a chapter or two at a time in a monthly magazine, or in separate paper-covered parts sold for a small price, over a year or more. This method of publication shaped the novels themselves. Writers needed each installment to end in a way that made readers eager to buy the next, so cliffhangers and sudden revelations became common. Because authors often wrote while publication was under way, they could respond to readers' reactions, expanding a popular character or changing the direction of a plot. Serial publication also made long novels affordable to readers who could not pay for an expensive bound volume all at once, widening the audience for fiction.

vr-ts018.x: Students preparing for an examination often study a topic intensively in a single long session. Research in psychology suggests that this habit is less efficient than it feels. In a typical experiment, two groups study the same material for the same total time. One group studies it in one block; the other spreads the study over several shorter sessions separated by days. On a test given weeks later, the second group usually remembers considerably more. This finding, known as the spacing effect, has been observed with many kinds of material, from foreign vocabulary to mathematics. One reason massed study remains popular is that it produces quick improvement during the session itself, which gives learners a misleading sense of mastery. Spaced study feels harder, because some forgetting occurs between sessions, but the effort of recalling the material appears to strengthen memory.

vr-ts019.x: Few animals change their surroundings as thoroughly as beavers. By cutting trees and piling branches, mud and stones across streams, beavers build dams that flood the land behind them and create ponds. The ponds protect the beavers' lodges from predators, but their effects reach far beyond the beavers themselves. Slower, deeper water allows fine sediment to settle, and the wet ground around a pond supports plants that cannot grow beside a fast stream. Frogs, ducks, insects and fish find new habitat. Because ponds store water and release it slowly, streams with beaver dams may keep flowing during dry seasons. Ecologists therefore describe beavers as ecosystem engineers. In some regions, land managers have begun returning beavers to streams where they had disappeared, hoping the animals will restore wetlands at little cost.

vr-ts020.x: Jazz musicians of the mid-twentieth century often improvised on a shared body of popular songs known as standards. A performance usually began with a statement of the melody, after which each player took a turn inventing new lines over the song's repeating sequence of chords. Because listeners and fellow musicians knew the originals well, they could appreciate how far a soloist departed from the tune while still following its harmonic plan. Familiarity, in other words, made invention audible. Some musicians wrote new melodies over the chords of well-known songs, a practice that allowed them to perform their own compositions while relying on structures other players already knew. Critics who dismiss jazz improvisation as unplanned miss this point: the freedom of the soloist rests on a framework that everyone in the room understands.

vr-ps001.x: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction in special organs near the end of the abdomen. A compound called luciferin reacts with oxygen with the help of an enzyme, and the energy released is given off almost entirely as light rather than heat. For many species, these flashes are a form of courtship. Males fly through the dark emitting a pattern of flashes that is particular to their species, differing in length, number and timing. A female of the same species, usually waiting on low vegetation, answers with a flash of her own after a characteristic delay, and the pair continue the exchange as the male approaches. Because each species has its own code, the signals help fireflies avoid mating with the wrong species. Bright artificial lighting at night can interfere with this exchange, and researchers are studying whether it contributes to declines in some firefly populations.

vr-ps002.x: Until the later nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, setting clocks so that noon fell when the sun stood highest overhead. Because the sun reaches that point at different moments in different places, a town a few dozen kilometers to the east kept time several minutes ahead of its neighbor. For travelers on foot or horseback, such small differences hardly mattered. Railways changed that. A train crossing a region passed through dozens of local times, and timetables that listed each one invited confusion and missed connections. Railway companies responded by adopting standard times of their own, and in many countries these were later made official for everyone. The change was not universally welcomed. Some critics complained that clocks no longer matched the sun, and a few towns kept their local time for years after the railways had abandoned it.

vr-ps003.x: Translators have long been pulled between two ideals. One holds that a translation should read as if it had been written in the reader's own language, smoothing away unfamiliar idioms and customs so that nothing interrupts the reader's absorption. The other holds that a translation should let the reader feel the foreignness of the original, preserving odd turns of phrase and references that require effort to understand. Advocates of the second approach argue that fluent translation, however pleasant, quietly erases the differences that make a foreign text worth reading; the reader encounters only a familiar voice. Their opponents reply that a deliberately awkward translation misrepresents the original, which was presumably not awkward to its first readers. Neither position is as tidy as its slogans. Every translation domesticates some features and preserves others, and the interesting question is less which ideal a translator serves than which differences the translator judges worth keeping.

questions.e: The director assumes the website causes the higher ratings. If website bookers are mostly returning guests who already liked the hotels, the higher ratings reflect who books online, not the booking experience. (D) would matter only if website bookings were concentrated in summer, and the passage gives no reason to think so.
o: Booking through travel agencies costs the chain a fee for each reservation that is made.
The chain's website was last redesigned two years ago.
Some guests who book through travel agencies visit the chain's website first in order to compare prices.
Ratings of hotel stays tend to be higher in summer than in winter.
Most guests who book on the chain's website are returning guests who already liked its hotels.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
questions.e: Any ship carrying salt paid the tax, so the Albatros, which paid none, carried no salt. Since every northern ship carried timber, salt, or both, the Albatros must have carried timber. (C) is the trap: a ship carrying both timber and salt would have paid the tax, so timber ships did not all go untaxed.
o: Every ship that paid no harbor tax in 1820 had arrived from the north.
The Albatros carried timber but no salt.
No ship that carried timber paid a harbor tax in 1820.
The Albatros made more than one voyage to Saldanha in 1820.
Most of the ships that arrived at Saldanha in 1820 carried salt.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the engineers' argument?
questions.e: The argument's key claim is that shade cuts evaporation. A direct test showing that shaded water evaporates much less than unshaded water in the same conditions supports that claim. (C) mentions evaporation but names a second cause the panels are not said to affect, so it does nothing to support the engineers.
o: Floating solar panels cost more to install than panels of the same size mounted on land.
Some of the reservoirs already have small areas covered by floating water plants.
Wind blowing across a reservoir's surface also adds considerably to the amount of water that evaporates from it.
In tests, shaded tanks of water lost far less to evaporation than unshaded tanks in the same weather.
The company's reservoirs supply drinking water to several large towns.

questions.s: The team's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: If construction had cleared much of the habitat near the road, the birds may have left because their nesting sites were gone, not because of noise. The conclusion therefore requires that the habitat largely survived. (D) is not required, and in fact the unchanged numbers deeper in the forest suggest the birds did not simply move there.
o: Building the highway did not destroy much of the nesting habitat within 300 meters of the road.
Songbirds are more common in the forest than any other kind of bird.
Traffic on the highway is heavier during the day than it is at night.
The songbirds that left the area near the road moved to nesting sites deeper in the forest.
Traffic noise affects all kinds of forest birds in the same way.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the number of tickets rose?
questions.e: The number of tickets depends not only on how many drivers park illegally but also on how many are caught. More patrol officers could catch a larger share of a smaller number of offenders, so tickets could rise even if illegal parking fell. (E) points the wrong way: fewer drivers downtown should mean fewer tickets.
o: Most drivers who receive parking tickets in Brennick pay them on time.
The fine for parking illegally in other parts of the city did not change.
When the fine was raised, the city also hired more officers to patrol downtown for illegal parking.
Illegally parked cars in the downtown area make it harder for delivery trucks to stop and unload their goods.
