Some drivers who used to park downtown now take the bus instead.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the finance director's argument?
questions.e: The director treats a rise in sales as proof of profit, but sales are not profit. If each delivery costs more than the chain earns on the order, every extra online sale loses money, so free delivery could be unprofitable however much sales grow. (E) is the trap: a modest national rise does not explain a tripling, and in any case it concerns the cause of the growth, not whether the growth made money.
o: Online orders at the chain are, on average, somewhat larger than purchases made in its stores.
Some of the customers who now order online also continue to shop in the chain's stores every week or so.
The chain's store sales had been falling slightly for several years before free delivery was offered.
Delivering a typical online order costs the chain more than the profit it makes on the goods in that order.
Online grocery sales across the country rose by about 10 percent over the same two years.

questions.s: The health officials' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: A prescription can lower fractures only if patients take the pills. If almost none of them did, the supplements could not have caused the decline, so the officials must assume many patients took them. (D) is the trap: the passage itself explains that population growth does not matter for a rate, so the argument does not need it. (C) concerns safety, which is irrelevant to whether the supplements worked.
o: A substantial share of the older patients who were prescribed the supplements actually took them.
Hip fractures among people over 70 were already more common in Lunari than in any neighboring province.
Vitamin D supplements cause no harmful side effects in people over the age of 70.
The number of people over 70 living in Lunari did not grow during the decade.
Most hip fractures among older people are the result of falls that happen at home.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox described above?
questions.e: The images became sharper even though one factor, sky brightness, got worse. If the observatory removed a larger source of blur, atmospheric distortion, the gain could outweigh the loss from the brighter sky. (A) is tempting, but the passage states that the sky did become brighter, so less polluting lights cannot explain why the images still improved.
o: Most of the town's newer street lighting points downward and is switched off after midnight.
Observatories at several other sites have also reported brighter night skies over the past decade.
The observatory now shares its images with universities in several other countries.
The population of the town in the valley has grown by about a third during the decade.
The observatory added a system that corrects blurring by the atmosphere, formerly the main limit on its images.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' argument against the critics' objection?
questions.e: The critics assume that trees cool a street only through shade. If young trees cool the air by releasing water within a few years, the plan can help long before the trees are large, which answers the objection directly. (E) describes when heat illness occurs but says nothing about how soon the trees could make a difference.
o: Heat illness is more common among older residents of Marisol than among younger residents.
Many residents of the poorer neighborhoods have said that they would prefer new parks to street trees.
Young trees cool the air around them by releasing water from their leaves, within two or three years of planting.
Trees planted along streets sometimes damage the pavement with their roots as they grow larger.
Most hospital visits for heat illness in Marisol take place during a few very hot weeks in the middle of each summer.

questions.s: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The overall fall in sales is the basis for some publishers' view that printed maps have no future, a view the argument calls premature. The rise in hiking and cycling maps is the argument's own evidence for its conclusion that specialist publishers will prosper. (C) reverses the roles: the argument does not use the overall decline to support its own position.
o: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered against that conclusion.
The first is evidence offered for a conclusion the argument rejects; the second is evidence the argument uses to support its own conclusion.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its own conclusion; the second is a consideration that the argument concedes weighs against that conclusion.
The first is a judgment that the argument accepts; the second is a prediction that the argument goes on to reject.
The first and the second are both evidence offered in support of the view that the printed map has no future.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the transit authority's conclusion?
questions.e: The authority reads fewer complaints as a sign that riders mind delays less. If complaining became much harder at the same time, the drop could reflect the new process rather than any change in riders' feelings. (E) does not help the critic: if anything, a rise in other complaints suggests riders were still able to complain.
o: Some riders do not own smartphones and still rely on printed notices posted at the bus stops.
Riders who use the app check it an average of three times during each journey.
Since the change, complaints can be made only through a feedback page in the app that many riders cannot find.
Bus delays in Ardmore are caused mainly by heavy traffic in the city center during the morning and evening rush hours.
Complaints from riders about crowded buses rose slightly over the same year.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
questions.e: There are only 600 households, so 450 car owners and 300 bicycle owners must overlap by at least 450 + 300 − 600 = 150. (C) is the trap: the question to households owning neither does not show that any exist, since 300 car-only, 150 both and 150 bicycle-only households would fill all 600. (B) fails because households owning both a car and a bicycle may live anywhere.
o: Most of the households in the survey that own a bicycle live within two kilometers of the town center.
No surveyed household that lives more than two kilometers from the town center owns a bicycle.
Some of the households in the survey own neither a car nor a bicycle.
Households that own a car are less likely to own a bicycle than other households are.
At least 150 of the surveyed households own both a car and a bicycle.

questions.s: Which of the following would it be most useful to establish in order to evaluate the curator's argument?
questions.e: The curator dates the painting by its canvas. Restorers sometimes transfer an old paint layer to a new canvas; if that happened here, the canvas could date from after 1810 while the paint is Brandt's, and the argument would collapse. (E) is the trap: students working in Brandt's lifetime would have used canvas made before 1810, so their existence does not bear on the canvas evidence.
o: Whether the paint could have been moved from an older canvas onto a newer one during a restoration
Whether Brandt's other paintings sold for high prices during her lifetime
How many visitors have viewed the portrait since the museum acquired it
Whether the company that made the loom also produced looms of several other types
Whether Brandt had students who painted portraits in a style very close to her own during her lifetime

questions.s: The managers' argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: Revenue rises only if what the airline gains from higher fares outweighs what it loses by having fewer seats to sell, so the managers must assume that the gain is larger. (C) is a trap: if planes often fly with empty seats, removing seats loses even less revenue, so the argument does not need full planes. (B) is not required either, since revenue could rise even if rivals copied the change.
o: Most of Arcelia's passengers travel for business purposes rather than for pleasure.
Rival airlines will not also remove seats from their planes in order to offer more legroom.
Arcelia's planes are full, or nearly full, on most of the routes that the airline flies.
The higher fares on the remaining seats will bring in more than the removed seats would have.
Passengers have complained more about Arcelia's legroom than about any other feature of its service.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the biologist's conclusion?
questions.e: If frogs declined equally where the pesticide is absent, some other cause is at work, and that cause may explain the decline at Lake Varna too. (A) is weaker: it names a possible cause but gives no evidence that the disease is present near the lake. (C) actually supports the biologist.
o: A fungal disease that kills frogs has been reported in several regions of the world.
Frog numbers have fallen just as sharply in mountain lakes far from farms, where the pesticide has never been found.
In one year when farmers near the lake used less of the pesticide than usual, the number of frogs in the lake rose slightly.
The pesticide breaks down more slowly in cold water than it does in warm water.
Several farms near the lake have switched to growing crops that need less water.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?
questions.e: More vaccinations should mean fewer cases, so the record count is puzzling. If the clinic also tests people and records mild cases that used to go uncounted, the number of recorded cases can rise even if actual infections fell. (C) only deepens the puzzle, and the passage rules out a mismatched vaccine, so (E) explains nothing about this winter.
o: The clinic also tests people with flu-like symptoms, so many mild cases that once went unrecorded are now counted.
Most of the residents who were vaccinated at the new clinic were more than 65 years old.
Neighboring towns without such a clinic recorded fewer flu cases per resident that winter than Belmira did.
Some residents vaccinated at the clinic had been vaccinated by their own doctors in previous years.
Flu vaccinations are recommended every year because the strains that circulate change from one season to the next.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens Mensah's argument?
questions.e: Mensah's evidence is only that literacy rose while almanacs spread. If literacy stayed flat where almanacs rarely reached, the rise is tied to the almanacs rather than to some province-wide change. (C) is the trap: more schools offer a rival explanation and so weaken the argument, and (B) questions whether signatures measure reading ability at all.
o: Almanacs of the period contained weather forecasts, planting advice, and short stories.
Signing one's name requires much less skill than reading a whole page of printed text.
The number of village schools in Ostland doubled between 1720 and 1780, mostly in the farming districts.
In Ostland districts that almanac sellers rarely visited, the share of farmers signing their names barely changed.
Almanacs were also popular among merchants and craftsmen in Ostland's towns.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' conclusion?
questions.e: The officials count cases traced to restaurants. If fewer staff now trace cases, fewer cases will be linked to restaurants even if restaurant hygiene has not changed, so the drop may be a product of weaker investigation. (D) is a weaker challenge: a slight fall in home cases does not account for a 30 percent drop. (A) and (C) tend to support the officials.
o: Some restaurants that received low ratings have closed since the rule took effect.
Food trucks in Talvora serve fewer meals each day than most of its restaurants do.
Many diners say that they check a restaurant's rating before deciding whether to eat there.
Food poisoning cases traced to meals cooked at home in Talvora also fell slightly over the same two years.
Since the rule began, the province has cut the staff who trace food poisoning cases to their source.

questions.s: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The argument introduces the engineers' assumption only to challenge it with the problems of crowded city sidewalks. The second portion, introduced by "therefore," is what all the evidence supports, so it is the main conclusion. (D) is the trap: the first role is right, but the second portion is the conclusion drawn from the evidence, not a piece of the evidence itself.
o: The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its conclusion; the second is that conclusion.
The first is a view that the argument opposes; the second is the argument's main conclusion.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is a consequence said to follow from that conclusion.
The first is a view that the argument opposes; the second is evidence offered against that view.
The first is an assumption on which the argument relies; the second is a prediction that the argument rejects.

questions.s: The consultant's reasoning is flawed because it
questions.e: The survey looks only at highly profitable companies. If most less profitable companies also let employees work from home, the policy is simply common and says nothing about profit; without that comparison the conclusion is unsupported. (A) is the trap: the survey covers all 50 companies it describes, so its size is not the problem.
o: relies on a survey of too few companies to support any conclusion about them
assumes without evidence that most employees prefer to work from home
ignores whether less profitable companies are just as likely to allow work from home
confuses the profitability of a company with the number of people it employs
treats a policy that applies two days a week as though it applied every working day

questions.s: The engineers' argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The argument relies on the small screen hiding the change. If many subscribers sent phone video to large television screens, they would see the poorer picture, and the claim that no subscribers will be lost would fail; so the engineers must assume few do this. (A) is not required: the argument is only about phone viewers, however many or few there are.
o: Most of the company's subscribers watch its videos on phones rather than on televisions.
The company's main rivals will not also lower the picture quality of the videos that they send to their subscribers' phones.
Sending less data will reduce the company's costs more than any other measure it could take.
Viewers who watch on phones care more about the subscription price than about picture quality.
Few subscribers send video from their phones to television screens, where the lower quality would show.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens Marchetti's conclusion?
questions.e: Marchetti treats a rise in registered weavers as a rise in production. If village weavers who were already working simply began to be counted after 1360, the records could triple with little change in the cloth actually made in and around the city. (B) is the trap: a population recovery is consistent with real growth in weaving, so it does not undermine the conclusion.
o: Cloth made in Corvenna was sold in markets throughout the region by 1400.
The population of Corvenna fell sharply in the late 1340s and had largely recovered by the year 1400.
In 1360 the guild began requiring weavers in nearby villages, who had never registered, to join.
Guild records from 1350 are kept in the same city archive as those from 1400.
The price of raw wool in Corvenna rose steadily between 1350 and 1400.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true of the products launched in the past five years?
questions.e: A favorable rating guarantees more than 100,000 first-year sales, so a product that sold fewer than 50,000 cannot have been rated favorably; it was rated unfavorably. (B) contradicts the passage, which says some unfavorably rated products sold more than 100,000. (C) and (D) may or may not be true, since the passage does not say which products are still made apart from the low sellers.
o: Any of them that sold fewer than 50,000 units in its first year was rated unfavorably by the panel.
Every one that the panel rated unfavorably sold fewer than 100,000 units in its first year on the market.
Every one that is still being made was rated favorably by the panel.
Some that the panel rated favorably are no longer being made.
Those rated unfavorably are less likely than the others to be made today.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the increase in the number of wading birds?
questions.e: The birds have less feeding ground, so they should be fewer, unless the food available to them has grown. If each square meter of the remaining mudflat now holds several times as many worms, the total food supply can rise even as the area shrinks. (A) describes protection that has been in place for fifty years, so it cannot explain a change over the last fifteen.
o: The wading birds have been protected by law from hunting throughout the region for more than fifty years.
On the remaining mudflats, the worms the birds eat have become several times more plentiful per square meter.
The mudflats that remain in the delta are covered by the tide twice each day.
Several other species of wading bird in the delta have declined over the same fifteen years.
Scientists expect the sea level in the delta to keep rising for several more decades.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the supporters' conclusion?
questions.e: The supporters claim that the same hours spread over fewer days will not harm learning. Evidence that comparable districts saw no change in test scores after making the switch supports exactly that claim. (A) is the trap: it supports the case for saving money, but the conclusion at issue is about learning. (C) suggests longer days could hurt learning, so it weakens.
o: A four-day week would save the school board a large sum each year on heating and on school buses.
Most teachers in Nordhaven have said that they would prefer to work four longer days.
Students tend to be more tired near the end of a long school day than near its beginning.
Districts that moved to four longer days saw no change in test scores relative to similar districts.
Some parents would need to find child care for their children on the fifth weekday.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the claim made in the advertisements?
questions.e: The study shows only that tea drinkers had less high blood pressure. If the same people also exercised more and ate less salt, those habits could explain the difference, so the claim that the tea itself protects them is undermined. (E) points to imprecise measurement, but loose measurement makes a real link harder to detect rather than creating a false one.
o: The tea company also sells black tea, a drink that the study did not examine.
Some of the people in the study who drank no green tea drank black tea instead.
High blood pressure becomes more common as people grow older.
The daily green tea drinkers in the study also exercised more and ate less salt than the others.
The study asked participants about their tea drinking only once, at the very start of the ten-year period.

questions.s: In the argument, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The argument grants that light batteries will probably win in aircraft, then turns to vans, where it says other factors matter more. The second portion gives the reason makers focused only on weight may lose the van market, which is the main conclusion. (C) is the trap: the argument never rejects the aircraft prediction; it simply limits its scope, and the second portion is not the conclusion, which rules out (D) and (E).
o: The first is a claim the argument accepts about one market; the second supports the argument's conclusion about another market.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is evidence that the argument offers in support of that conclusion.
The first is a prediction that the argument goes on to reject; the second is evidence that the argument offers against that prediction.
The first is evidence that supports the second; the second is the main conclusion that the argument draws.
The first is a consideration the argument raises against its own conclusion; the second is the argument's main conclusion.

questions.s: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the council's argument?
questions.e: The argument depends on the claim that a lack of parking keeps visitors away. If the existing 200 spaces are seldom full, parking is not what limits visitor numbers, and a new car park would bring few extra customers. (D) is the trap: cost bears on whether the project is worth paying for, but not on whether it would bring more business, which is what the council argues.
o: Whether the town's cafés serve fish caught by local boats
How many residents of Esk Harbor walk to the beach from their homes
Whether nearby towns have more beaches than Esk Harbor has
How much the new car park would cost compared with the town's yearly budget
Whether the beach's existing car parks are often full during the summer

questions.s: The paleontologists' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The reasoning runs from taller crowns to heavier wear, and from heavier wear to a diet of grass. If the wear came mainly from dust on the same shrub leaves, the horses' teeth could have changed without any spread of grasslands, so the conclusion needs this possibility ruled out. (A) is too strong: grasslands could have spread even if the horses still ate some leaves.
o: The horses of the region ate grass and no other kind of plant at all from 8 million years ago onward, in every season.
Tall-crowned teeth appeared in every grazing species in the region at the same time.
The extra wear on the horses' teeth was not caused mainly by dust settling on the leaves they already ate.
Grasslands today cover a larger share of the region than they did 8 million years ago.
Fossil teeth are more often preserved than other parts of horse skeletons.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the head of sales' conclusion that customers are highly sensitive to price?
questions.e: If the main competing phone disappeared from shops that quarter, many buyers may have chosen Juniper because their first choice was unavailable, not because of the lower price. (E) is the trap: a slow existing rise cannot account for a sudden 50 percent jump. (C) concerns profit, which says nothing about how customers respond to price.
o: The basic model still costs more than several rival phones with similar features.
In the same quarter, the leading rival basic phone was withdrawn from sale because of a battery defect.
Juniper's profit on each basic phone sold fell after the price was cut.
The premium model already sells more units than any rival company's premium model.
Sales of the basic model had already been rising slowly for a full year before its price was cut by Juniper.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy?
questions.e: More cargo carried by fewer ships is puzzling only if each ship carries about the same load. If small sailing ships were replaced by much larger steamships, each visit moved far more cargo, so total tonnage could rise while the number of ships fell. (B) explains why cargo increased, but not why fewer ships came.
o: The railway carried passengers as well as cargo between the harbor and the mining towns.
The mining towns produced considerably more ore in the 1890s than they had in the 1880s.
During that decade, shipping companies replaced many small sailing ships with far larger steamships.
Some of the goods from the mining towns were still carried down to the coast by road rather than by rail.
Several other harbors along the same coast also built railways to the interior in the 1880s.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the department head's argument?
questions.e: A higher pass rate could come from an easier exam or stronger students rather than better learning. Ruling out both of those explanations leaves the new format as the most likely cause. (A) is the trap: enjoying a course is not the same as learning more from it.
o: Students in the course said in surveys that they enjoyed the new format more than lectures.
Several other universities have replaced lectures with online videos in some of their courses.
The videos can be watched at any time of day and as often as a student wishes.
More students enrolled in the course in the first year of the new format than in the year before.
The exam was as hard as in past years, and the new students had similar entry grades to earlier ones.

questions.s: Which of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?
questions.e: Every household sent the form qualified, the subsidy goes only to households that return it, and half did not return it, so some qualifying households went without the subsidy. (C) is a possible reason for the low return rate, but nothing in the passage establishes it, and (B) reads a motive into the pattern that the facts do not support.
o: Most households in Meridia have yearly incomes below 30,000 dollars.
Households with incomes just below 30,000 dollars have no real need for the subsidy.
The application form is too complicated for many households to complete.
Some households that qualified for the subsidy last winter did not receive it.
Meridia spends more on heating subsidies than on any other kind of public assistance.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, casts the most serious doubt on the likely success of the researchers' proposal?
questions.e: The laboratory results come from filtered water, which lacked the small animals found in the open sea. If those animals quickly eat the bacteria, the bacteria will not survive long enough to break down much plastic, so the plan is unlikely to work. (B) is the trap: the proposal targets floating plastic, so plastic that sinks lies outside it.
o: In the open sea, the bacteria are quickly eaten by tiny animals that the filtering had removed.
Some kinds of plastic sink below the sea's surface into water that is much colder than 30°C.
The bacteria break down plastic bottles more slowly than they break down plastic bags.
Plastic floating in tropical seas is often carried long distances by ocean currents.
The laboratory also tested the bacteria at 22°C and found a rate of breakdown between the other two.

questions.s: The director's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
questions.e: The patients who saw the counselor chose to go, so they may have been unusually motivated, and their motivation, not the counseling, may explain their greater weight loss. Patients forced to attend might gain little. (A) is a weaker objection: a single year of data can still be informative, and it does not address the real gap in the reasoning.
o: relies on figures from only a single year at a single clinic
overlooks that patients who choose to see the counselor may be more eager than others to lose weight
assumes that weight loss is the only sign of good health that matters to patients
fails to state how much each visit to the counselor would cost the clinic
confuses the number of patients who see the counselor with the number of separate visits that each patient makes

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens management's conclusion?
questions.e: The argument credits the staffed lanes for the 9 percent rise. If a competitor closed stores near most of the converted locations, its former customers offer an alternative cause for the jump, and that cause would not repeat at the other stores. Choice (A) concerns costs, not whether sales rise. Choice (E) is tempting, but a higher starting level does not explain why sales grew only in the converted stores.
o: Staffed checkout lanes cost Fernway more to operate per transaction than self-checkout kiosks do.
Several of Fernway's smaller stores are located in towns where no competing grocery store operates.
During the same six months, a rival chain closed stores near nine of the twelve converted Fernway stores but near none of Fernway's other stores.
Some shoppers at the converted stores have asked Fernway to bring back at least a few self-checkout kiosks.
Fernway's twelve largest stores had higher average weekly sales than its other stores even before the conversion, and they also carry a much wider range of fresh and prepared foods.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the planners' prediction?
questions.e: The planners need average speeds to drop at least a little, despite the critics' claim that drivers ignore the limit. Evidence that average speeds fell elsewhere even while many drivers broke the limit answers the critics directly. Choice (C) shows support for the policy, but approval does not show that anyone drives more slowly. Choice (B) suggests the policy targets a small share of deaths, which does not support the prediction.
o: Measurements taken in other cities after similar changes found that average speeds on residential streets fell by several kilometers per hour even though many drivers still exceeded the new limit.

Most traffic deaths in Marlow occur on highways and major roads rather than on residential streets, so the new limit, which does not cover those roads, addresses only a minority of the city's traffic deaths.
Marlow's residents were surveyed and a majority said they supported the lower speed limit.
Drivers who ignore speed limits are also more likely than other drivers to ignore stop signs.
The cost of replacing the speed limit signs on Marlow's residential streets was paid from the city's road maintenance budget.

questions.s: The researchers' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The conclusion is that darker lizards gain foraging time. That follows only if the 20 minutes saved in the morning is not lost later, for example by having to retreat from the heat sooner. If darker lizards overheat earlier and stop foraging earlier, the advantage disappears, so the argument assumes this does not happen. Choice (B) would point to a cost of dark skin, but the conclusion concerns only foraging time, so the argument does not need to rule it out.
o: Lighter-skinned lizards are more common in the population than darker-skinned lizards.
Darker-skinned lizards are more easily seen by predators than lighter-skinned lizards are, especially on the pale sand where most of the population's foraging takes place.
Basking in the sun is the only way these lizards can raise their body temperature.
The lizards studied belong to a species that has been observed in several different deserts.
Darker-skinned lizards do not have to stop foraging correspondingly earlier in the day, for instance because they overheat sooner.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
questions.e: The puzzle is that exercise apparently rose while obesity also rose and calorie intake held steady. If the rise in reported exercise reflects growing overstatement rather than real activity, actual exercise may not have increased, and rising obesity is no longer surprising. Choice (E) questions the calorie data, but nothing suggests restaurant eating changed over the decade, so it does not explain the trend. Choice (D) notes a method change without saying how it would bias the results.
o: Obesity rates rose faster among adults over sixty than among younger adults.
Over the decade, people became more likely to overstate how much they exercise when answering survey questions, because exercise had become more widely seen as a social virtue.
Many adults who exercise regularly also try to limit the amount of sugar they eat.
The survey was conducted by telephone at the start of the decade and online at the end, and the online version asked about exercise using somewhat different wording.
Food purchase records do not capture food eaten in restaurants.

questions.s: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The first portion, the early population decline, is evidence that challenges the historians' trade-route view. The argument then concedes this evidence is not decisive, adds the council letters, and concludes with the second portion, which keeps trade as a later factor but puts environmental damage first. Choice (B) is tempting, but the argument never rejects the tax-record evidence; it relies on it. Choice (E) fails because the argument says the timing is not decisive.
o: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered in support of that conclusion.
The first is a claim the argument rejects; the second is the position the argument defends.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support a rival account; the second is that rival account, which the argument goes on to accept only in part.
The first is evidence that casts doubt on a traditional account; the second is the argument's main conclusion, which revises that account.
The first is a consideration the argument concedes is decisive; the second is an objection to that consideration.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the director's conclusion?
questions.e: The director attributes the drop in returns to the cameras. If the factory introduced far fewer new designs that year, and new designs are where most joint failures arise, there were simply fewer weak points to fail, which explains the drop without the cameras. Choice (B) bears on whether to buy the upgrade but not on what caused the reduction. Choice (D) rules out one alternative explanation, a change in how returns were made, so it slightly supports the director.
o: In the same year, the factory introduced far fewer new furniture designs than usual, and in earlier years most joint failures had occurred in newly introduced designs.
The more advanced version of the camera system costs roughly three times as much as the version the factory now uses.
Some workers at the factory disliked the system at first because it flagged many sound joints as faulty, which slowed production and led a few teams to switch it off for several weeks.
Customers returned products through the same online form and under the same return policy both before and after the system was installed.
Other furniture makers that installed similar camera systems have generally continued to use them for several years afterward.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
questions.e: Some showroom products take more than eight weeks, so those products are not eligible for the guarantee. Every online product is eligible, so those slow showroom products cannot be sold online; therefore some showroom products are not sold online. Choice (A) contradicts this. Choice (B) is the reverse of what follows: nothing says online products are made to order, and the slow made-to-order items are excluded from online sales. Choice (E) goes beyond the statements, which say only that some made-to-order products take more than eight weeks.
o: Every product sold in Corlan's showrooms is also sold online.
Some products sold online are made to order.
Most of Corlan's showroom products are eligible for the free-return guarantee.
Some products sold in Corlan's showrooms are not sold online.
No made-to-order product at Corlan can be delivered in less than eight weeks, whether it is bought in a showroom or online.

questions.s: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the supporters' claim?
questions.e: The claim is that more pollinators will raise yields enough to repay the lost land. That chain works only if yields are now held back by too few pollinators; if crops are already fully pollinated, extra bees add nothing. Choice (E) concerns the cost to the province, not whether farmers' gains exceed their losses. Choice (A) might matter for ecology, but the claim does not depend on whether the flowers are native.
o: Whether the wildflower species proposed for the strips are native to Tessaly
Whether farmers in Tessaly have received tax credits for other conservation practices in the past
Whether the yields of apples and canola in Tessaly are currently limited by a shortage of pollinators
Whether wildflower strips are more attractive to look at than the grass borders they would replace
Whether the tax credit would cost the province more than it collects each year from taxes on farmland in the regions where most apples and canola are grown

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, casts the most doubt on the authors' conclusion?
questions.e: The authors infer that standing prevents back pain from the fact that standers reported less of it. If people with existing back trouble chose not to stand, the sitters' group started out with more back pain, so the difference may reflect who chose each desk rather than any effect of standing. Choice (C) shows that some sitters avoided back pain, but that is compatible with standing still helping on average. Choice (A) concerns the recommendation's cost, not the causal claim.
o: Standing desks are more expensive than ordinary desks, though their prices have fallen in recent years.
Workers who stood for most of the day were about as likely to report foot pain as those who sat all day.

Some of the workers who sat all day exercised regularly outside of work, and most of these regular exercisers reported little or no back pain at any of the check-ins during the five years of the study.
The study included workers in several countries, and the rates of back pain differed somewhat from one country to another.
Workers who already had back problems at the start of the study were much more likely than other workers to avoid standing desks because standing aggravated their pain.

questions.s: The journalist's reasoning is most vulnerable to which of the following criticisms?
questions.e: The journalist takes high citation counts as a sign that scientists favor sensational claims. But checking and disputing a finding also requires citing it, so a contradicted paper may gather citations precisely because others challenged it, which is not a reward. Choice (D) is tempting, yet the journalist's point is about what citations reveal about interest, not a claim that they measure quality precisely. Choice (C) misdescribes the argument, which never mentions dishonesty.
o: It relies on the opinions of journalists rather than on the views of practicing scientists.
It overlooks the possibility that many of the citations a contradicted paper receives come from the very studies that test and dispute its findings.
It assumes that a paper whose findings are contradicted must have been dishonestly produced.
It treats the number of citations a paper receives as though it were a precise measure of the paper's scientific quality, rather than one rough indicator among several.
It fails to consider that some fields of science produce many more papers each year than other fields do.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the authority's argument that a winter rule would produce a comparable improvement?
questions.e: The argument predicts that the same rule would bring the same benefit in winter, which assumes that winter pollution, like summer pollution, comes largely from docked cruise ships. If few ships dock in winter and wood stoves produce most winter particles, the rule would touch little of the problem. Choice (C) is the attractive trap: more winter visits mean more winter ship pollution, which if anything gives a winter rule more to remove, so it does not undercut the prediction. Choice (B) offers another cause of improvement, but the ferries run all year, so they do not explain a summer-only effect.
o: Before the rule was introduced, summer pollution in the harbor district was worse than pollution anywhere else in Halvik.
Fees paid by ships for the city's electricity have been used to buy cleaner ferries that serve the harbor all year round.
Some cruise lines that formerly docked in Halvik in summer now schedule more of their visits for the winter months, when the rule does not apply, so winter cruise visits have risen noticeably.
Few cruise ships dock in Halvik in winter, and most of the harbor district's winter fine-particle pollution comes from wood-burning stoves in its older apartment buildings.
Fine-particle pollution in nearby ports that have no such rule has stayed roughly constant over the past three years.

questions.s: The marketing director's reasoning relies on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The director moves from a correlation (registrants buy again more often) to a prediction that inducing more registrations will raise repeat buying. That works only if registration itself, for example through follow-up offers, contributes to repeat buying, rather than both simply reflecting existing loyalty. Choice (A) is tempting, but the reasoning concludes only that repeat purchases will increase, not that the plan is profitable. Choice (D) offers one reason people fail to register, but the plan could work whatever the reason.
o: The cost of the gift cards, together with the cost of handling the extra registrations, will be lower than the profit Ashcombe earns on the additional repeat purchases.
Registering a product, rather than some prior attachment to the brand that also makes customers likely to register, is at least partly what makes those customers more likely to buy again.
Customers who receive a gift card will be more likely than other customers to spend the card on a Ashcombe product.
Most customers who do not now register their products are unaware that registration is possible, even though instructions are printed on every box.
Ashcombe's competitors do not already offer gift cards or other rewards to customers who register their products.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the lighting bill did not fall as much as administrators expected?
questions.e: The expectation assumed the university would buy the same amount of light at half the power. If it instead installed more lamps and kept many lit all night, it used much of the efficiency gain to produce more light, so total consumption fell only a little. Choice (A) concerns maintenance, not the electricity bill. Choice (C) deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it, and (D) concerns total use, while the bill in question is for lighting alone.
o: LED lamps last several times longer than the lamps they replaced, which has reduced the university's spending on maintenance staff.
Some instructors complained that the light from the new lamps appeared harsher and bluer than the old light, and the university responded by fitting diffusing covers to the lamps in many classrooms.
Several other universities that installed LED lighting in the same years reported much larger savings than Harwick did.
Lighting accounts for only a small part of the university's total electricity consumption.
Because the new lamps were cheap to run, the university installed more of them than before and kept corridors and study rooms lit through the night.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the historian's argument?
questions.e: The historian's claim is comparative: universities, not merchant wealth, drove the spread. Evidence that workshops followed universities even where merchants were few, and failed to appear in rich towns without universities, separates the two factors and favors the historian. Choice (C) is tempting because it explains why universities created demand, but it does nothing to show that merchant wealth mattered less. Choice (B) suggests merchants also bought books from elsewhere, which only weakly bears on local workshops.
o: Surviving inventories show that workshops opened mainly in university towns, including some with few wealthy merchants, but not in rich trading towns lacking a university.
Wealthy merchants in sixteenth-century Brabant often owned private libraries that included books printed in other regions.
Universities in sixteenth-century Brabant required students to buy their own copies of assigned texts, and many students could not afford the copies sold by booksellers from other regions.
The number of printing workshops in neighboring regions also increased during the sixteenth century.
Some printers in Brabant produced both textbooks and decorative books intended for wealthy households.

questions.s: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The first portion is the laboratory evidence behind the proposal to release the wasp. The second portion explains why that evidence may not carry over to the forest, which supports the actual conclusion that a field trial should come first. Choice (E) is the attractive trap: the second portion raises a doubt, but about reaching the target beetles, not about harm to native species, which the argument judges a small risk. Choice (B) fails because the conclusion is the call for a field trial, and the first portion does not support that call directly.
o: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is a consideration that the argument rejects.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its conclusion; the second is a qualification of that conclusion.
The first is evidence offered in support of a proposal; the second is a consideration that the argument uses to show that this evidence does not settle whether the proposal would work.
The first is a finding that opponents of the proposal use against it; the second is evidence that the argument offers in support of the proposal.
The first is a claim that the argument disputes; the second is evidence that the argument cites in support of the opponents' warning that the wasp might also attack the forest's native beetles.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the developer's conclusion?
questions.e: Random assignment makes the groups comparable, so the app probably did cause better recovery; the question is which feature of it did. If app users simply exercised much more, the extra practice, perhaps prompted by reminders, could explain the gains without any help from feedback on form. Choice (A) is the attractive trap, but the age difference is small and not significant, which randomization is expected to produce. Choices (C) and (E) concern cost and how recovery is measured, not the cause of the measured improvement.
o: Patients in the app group were, on average, slightly younger than patients in the standard group, although the difference was not statistically significant.
Records from the app show that patients in the app group completed far more exercise repetitions each week than patients in the standard group did.
The motion-tracking app is considerably more expensive than a standard course of physical therapy, so many insurers may decline to pay for it.
Some patients in the app group reported that the app's feedback was occasionally inaccurate when they exercised in poorly lit rooms.
Range of motion is only one of several measures that physical therapists use to judge how well a patient is recovering from knee surgery.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true of Acropora velata colonies on the reef?
questions.e: Every bleached colony was in shallow water, and every Type D colony was in deep water, so no Type D colony can have been among the bleached ones. Choice (B) is tempting because Type D is heat-tolerant, but the statements establish only where colonies are, not why they bleached; that causal claim does not follow. Choice (A) fails because shallow colonies that did not bleach cannot host Type D, and (D) contradicts the first statement.
o: Every colony that did not bleach hosts the alga strain Type D.
Colonies in water shallower than four meters bleach because they lack the alga strain Type D.
Most colonies in water deeper than four meters host the alga strain Type D.
Some colonies in water deeper than four meters bleached during the heat wave.
None of the colonies hosting the alga strain Type D bleached.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy above?
questions.e: The puzzle is that national fuel spending fell far more than the average station's fuel revenue. If many stations closed and their customers moved to the survivors, the national total could fall sharply while the shrinking number of stations each kept nearly the same revenue. Choice (E) is the trap; it explains why fuel spending has not collapsed, but it applies equally to the national total and so cannot explain the gap between the two figures. Choice (D) concerns non-fuel income, which is outside the revenue being compared.
o: Over the five years, hundreds of small gas stations closed, and many of their former customers now buy fuel at the gas stations that remain.
Electric cars in Vellmark are driven, on average, slightly fewer kilometers per year than gasoline cars are.
The price of fuel in Vellmark rose sharply during the first two of the five years and then fell back to about its original level.
Many of Vellmark's gas stations now earn a growing share of their income from selling snacks, coffee, and car-washing services rather than from selling fuel.
Because most cars remain in use for well over a decade, electric cars still make up only a small share of all the cars on Vellmark's roads.

questions.s: The officials' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The officials infer from past outcomes that lawyers cause lower eviction rates. If the tenants who hired lawyers had mostly stronger cases, for example because lawyers took only winnable ones, the lower rate reflects case strength, and giving lawyers to everyone would help much less. The argument must assume this was not the case. Choice (A) helps explain why the program is needed but the conclusion would stand even if some tenants could afford lawyers. Choice (C) concerns a possible side effect on rents, while the conclusion is only about evictions.
o: Most tenants who receive an eviction notice in Rosendal cannot afford to hire a lawyer at current market rates.
The program will not cost the city more than it currently spends on emergency shelter for evicted households.
Landlords in Rosendal will not respond to the program by raising rents for all tenants.
The tenants who hired lawyers in the past did not, for the most part, have stronger cases than tenants who represented themselves.
Tenants who represent themselves in housing court are usually unfamiliar with the court's rules and procedures.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the director's argument?
questions.e: If borrowing rose by about the same amount in nearby systems without any change to their checkout methods, a wider trend probably accounts for the rise, and the kiosks need not have caused it. Choice (C) is relevant but, if anything, fits the director's story, since the patrons who disliked queues are the ones who borrowed more. Choice (D) shows only that some patrons do not use kiosks, which is compatible with kiosks raising borrowing overall.
o: Staff at the branches with kiosks now spend more of their time helping patrons find books and use the library's computers, rather than checking books in and out.
Kiosks require periodic software updates, during which patrons must again borrow books at the staffed desk.
At the branches with kiosks, borrowing rose most sharply among patrons who had previously borrowed only a few books each year and who had often complained about queues at the desk.
Some patrons, especially older ones, still prefer to borrow books at the staffed desk even where kiosks are available.
The number of books borrowed rose by a similar percentage at the library systems of several nearby cities during the same year.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the engineers' hypothesis?
questions.e: The hypothesis separates two candidate causes: the cold and the lithium layer. If cells charged in the cold without forming the layer lose no extra capacity, the cold alone does no harm and the layer is implicated, which is exactly what the engineers claim. Choice (B) shows the layer can form in other conditions but not that it reduces capacity. Choice (A) concerns storage temperature, not charging, and (D) does not distinguish the layer from the cold.
o: Cells that are stored, rather than charged, in a cold room lose capacity more slowly than cells stored at room temperature, a finding that the company has used in its advice to customers.
Lithium metal layers have been observed on electrodes of cells that were charged very rapidly at room temperature.
Cells charged slowly in the cold, a method known to prevent lithium metal from forming, lose no more capacity over a year than cells charged at room temperature.
Customers in cold climates report shorter battery life than customers in warm climates.
The company's newest cells use an electrode material that is less sensitive to temperature than the material used in older cells.

questions.s: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The first portion, the 6 percent fall, appears to bear out the analysts' prediction, and the argument says it is misleading in context. The second portion is the conclusion the argument reaches using the market data: the strategy helped, not hurt. Choice (B) is wrong because the fall in sales is not evidence for that conclusion; the argument has to explain it away. Choice (E) misreads the second portion, which is the conclusion itself, while the price cuts are offered as its explanation.
o: The first is a finding that seems to confirm the analysts' prediction; the second is the argument's main conclusion, which opposes that prediction.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its main conclusion; the second is that conclusion.
The first is the analysts' prediction; the second is a finding that the argument offers against that prediction.
The first is a finding that the argument rejects as false; the second is a position that the argument attributes to the analysts and then criticizes as unsupported.
The first is a finding that the argument accepts as accurate but irrelevant; the second is a consideration offered in support of the argument's main conclusion about pricing.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the facts described above?
questions.e: Recorded cases rose sharply while deaths fell. If screening uncovers many mild cases that were previously missed, the count of cases grows even if no more people actually develop sepsis, and since such cases rarely kill, deaths need not rise; earlier treatment can then reduce them. Choice (A) explains a slow rise in true cases at most, not a 40 percent jump alongside falling deaths. Choice (C) suggests some other cause of fewer deaths, but it leaves the rise in recorded cases unexplained.
o: Sepsis is more common among elderly patients, and the share of Aldmoor's hospital patients who are over seventy has grown slowly but steadily over the past decade as the region's population has aged.
The screening program has led doctors to diagnose many mild cases of sepsis that previously would have gone unrecorded, and such cases rarely end in death.
Several hospitals outside Aldmoor that did not adopt the program have also seen a slight fall in deaths from sepsis.
Treating sepsis early requires powerful antibiotics, which can cause side effects in some patients.
Before the program began, Aldmoor's hospitals had a higher rate of deaths from sepsis than the national average.

questions.s: The historian's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
questions.e: The letters were written to the owners and kept in the owners' archive. Workers addressing their employers had strong reasons to sound grateful, and owners could have discarded unflattering letters, so the sample is likely biased toward praise. Choice (C) is tempting because it also raises representativeness, but illiteracy alone gives no reason to think nonwriters were less content; the problem is the direction of the bias, which (D) identifies. Choice (B) is vague: different politeness norms do not show that the expressed gratitude was false.
o: assumes without justification that the city's largest mill employed more workers than any other mill in Lowenfeld during the nineteenth century
relies on letters written in the nineteenth century, when standards of politeness in correspondence were very different from today's standards, particularly in letters between workers and employers
fails to consider that some workers may have been unable to write letters at all
overlooks the possibility that workers had reason not to complain in writing to their employers, and that the owners chose which letters to keep
takes for granted that working conditions in Lowenfeld were similar to working conditions in the textile mills of other European cities

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the authors' conclusion?
questions.e: The authors claim that expected scrutiny causes more careful checking. If careful researchers are the ones who choose to share, and they were equally careful when not sharing, the lower error rate reflects who shares rather than any effect of sharing. Choice (D) is tempting, since it suggests errors in some studies were not yet found, but it applies to shared and unshared studies alike unless we assume otherwise. Choice (A) raises a cost of the recommendation without touching the causal claim.
o: Sharing data publicly can take researchers a considerable amount of time, especially for large studies with many variables, and this burden may discourage some from submitting to journals that require it.
Some journals already require authors to share their data, while others merely encourage it.
Researchers who choose to share their data tend to be those who already check their analyses carefully, and they were just as careful in earlier work they did not share.
Some statistical errors in published experiments are discovered only years after publication, when other researchers attempt to repeat the experiments.
Most of the experiments in the study were conducted at universities in North America and Europe.

questions.s: The researchers' conclusion relies on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The study tested only breakfasts, but the advice concerns whichever meal of the day is highest in fat. The researchers therefore assume that fat increases absorption at other meals as well, not only in the morning. Choice (A) is tempting, but the advice works even for people whose fattiest meal is modest; it says only to use the highest-fat one. Choice (C) would undercut the advice if true, so the argument certainly does not assume it, and (D) is not required because the conclusion depends on the fat content, not on the breakfasts being typical.
o: Most people who take vitamin D supplements eat at least one high-fat meal each day.
Vitamin D is also obtained from exposure to sunlight, which varies greatly with the season.
High-fat meals have health risks that outweigh any benefit from improved absorption of vitamin D, at least for people who already eat a diet high in fat.
The volunteers in the study ate breakfasts typical of the diets of people who take vitamin D supplements.
The greater absorption seen with high-fat breakfasts would also occur when the supplement is taken with a high-fat meal at other times of the day.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the executives' conclusion?
questions.e: The executives treat the higher visit rate of app users as an effect of the app. If the users were mostly regulars who already visited that often before the trial, the difference reflects who adopted the app, not any change it caused. Choice (C) concerns spending per visit, which is relevant to whether the app pays off but not to whether it increases visits. Choice (D) actually supports the generalization from the test shops to the whole chain.
o: The chain's competitors have begun to offer loyalty apps of their own, some of which give larger discounts.
During the trial, the app was promoted mainly by staff to customers they already recognized as regulars, and these customers had visited about as often before the trial began.
Customers who used the app spent slightly less per visit, on average, than customers who did not.
The twenty shops in the test were chosen to represent the full range of locations in which the chain operates, from city centers to suburban shopping malls.

Some customers who downloaded the app during the trial stopped using it after a few weeks because they found it confusing to redeem rewards, and they returned to paying in the usual way for the rest of the trial.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
questions.e: Some eligible students did not receive a room, yet every eligible student who applied by the deadline did receive one. So those who went without cannot have applied by the deadline. Choice (E) is the trap: the passage says holding the scholarship is sufficient for eligibility, not that it is the only route, so other students might be eligible too. Choice (B) confuses receiving a room with receiving the scholarship, about which the passage says nothing.
o: Every student at Velsen whose grades were in the top tenth of the class applied for a room last year.
Some students at Velsen who qualified for the merit scholarship did not receive the scholarship last year.
Most students who received a guaranteed room in the new residence hall last year held the merit scholarship.
Some students who were eligible for a guaranteed room did not apply for one by the deadline last year.
Only students whose grades are in the top tenth of the class are eligible for a guaranteed room.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the zoologists' hypothesis over the critics' alternative?
questions.e: If the stripes served only in courtship, frogs too young to breed would gain nothing from them. Finding the stripes on toxic juveniles, together with evidence that predators learn to avoid striped frogs, fits the warning role and is hard to explain on the mate-attraction view. Choice (C) confirms that the frog is toxic, which both sides could accept, but it does not link the stripes to that toxicity. Choice (B) supports the critics, and (E) weakens the warning hypothesis.
o: Young frogs of both sexes, which are too immature to breed, have the bright stripes and are toxic, and birds that once tasted one avoid striped frogs afterward.
In several related species, males with brighter markings are chosen more often by females during the breeding season.

The skin of this frog contains a toxin that is chemically similar to the toxins found in several other species of frog that live in the same forest, and the toxin is strong enough to sicken a snake or bird that swallows the frog.
The bright stripes of this frog become slightly duller when the frog is kept in captivity for long periods.
Some predators of this frog hunt mainly at night, when the frog's stripes are difficult to see even at close range.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
questions.e: With trade doubling and methods unchanged, one would expect more workers, not fewer. If large ships formerly had to unload offshore, every cargo was handled twice, by boatmen and by dockworkers; deepening the harbor removed that extra step, so much more cargo could move with less labor. Choice (B) is the attractive trap: it explains why workers left, but with handling still entirely manual it leaves unexplained how the port handled twice the goods with fewer of them. Choice (D) helps only a little, since heavier crates still require handling, and (A) explains the rise in trade, not the fall in jobs.
o: Shipowners began building larger ships after the harbor was deepened, because larger ships could carry more cargo at a lower cost per ton.

Many dockworkers left Tremona during the decade to work in the city's growing shipbuilding yards, which paid higher wages and offered steadier work throughout the year than loading and unloading ships did.
Before the harbor was deepened, large ships had to anchor offshore while their cargo was rowed to the docks in small boats, which required many extra workers to load and unload each cargo twice.
The goods passing through Tremona after 1702 were, on average, heavier per crate than the goods that had passed through it earlier.
Several neighboring ports were deepened during the same decade and experienced similar increases in the weight of goods handled.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' argument?
questions.e: The officials grant that the bonus filled the posts but claim the gains will last after it ends. If most recruits are obliged to stay only while the bonus is paid, many may leave once it stops, and vacancies would return. Choice (C) is the attractive trap: it offers another possible cause of the improvement, but the officials' prediction is about what happens when the bonus ends, and (C) does not suggest vacancies will rise then. Choice (D) concerns cost, not staffing.
o: Most of the teachers who took rural positions under the program are bound by contracts that require them to stay only as long as they continue to receive the bonus.
The number of unfilled teaching positions in Dravia's urban schools has also fallen over the past five years, though less sharply than in its rural schools.
Some of the rural schools in the program have also received new funding for building repairs and classroom equipment during the past five years.

The program has cost the state considerably more than officials originally estimated, largely because more teachers applied for the bonus than expected, and the legislature has asked for a full review of its spending.
Teachers in rural schools in neighboring states, which offer no bonus, earn salaries similar to those of teachers in Dravia's rural schools.

questions.s: Which of the following would be most useful to establish in evaluating the engineers' argument?
questions.e: The engineers rely on test results to predict that the panels will work well in the field. If the panels were tested in full sun but customers mount cameras in shade, the panels might fail to keep cameras powered, causing both failures and complaints. Choice (D) is relevant to reliability in general, but those components are unchanged by the plan, so their reliability cannot make the switch increase failures. Choice (C) concerns price, which the argument does not address.
o: Whether the company's competitors have received a similar number of complaints about their cameras' batteries
Whether customers who complain about batteries are more likely than other customers to buy a second camera from the company
Whether the solar panels would add to the price that customers pay for each camera
Whether the cameras' other components, such as lenses and wireless transmitters, are as reliable in outdoor use as the solar panels proved to be in the company's tests
Whether the solar panels were tested in positions like those in which customers usually mount the cameras, such as under eaves and in shaded doorways

questions.s: The excavators' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The excavators infer from empty houses that the residents took their things with them. That inference fails if someone else, such as invaders or later scavengers, stripped the houses after a sudden flight, so the argument must assume this did not happen. Choice (D) is tempting because it touches the rubbish-heap evidence, but that evidence only shows such objects were common earlier; the conclusion does not depend on why they were discarded. Choice (A) is not needed, since the objects, not the buildings, are the evidence.
o: The houses of Kesh were built of materials that would have survived for many centuries after the city was abandoned.
Kesh was not the only city in its region whose residents eventually left it.
The valuable objects missing from the houses were not removed by looters or invaders after the residents had gone.
Residents of Kesh did not throw valuable objects onto rubbish heaps, except when the objects were broken or worn out.
No other ancient city in the region was invaded during the period when Kesh was abandoned.

questions.s: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The survey finding that older adults sleep less is the natural basis for the popular view that they need less sleep. The argument accepts the finding but reinterprets it, and the second portion is its conclusion that older adults may need as much sleep as anyone, contrary to the popular view. Choice (D) is the trap: the argument never says the survey finding is mistaken, only that the inference drawn from it is. Choice (E) fails because the second portion rejects the popular view rather than qualifying it.
o: The first is evidence that the argument uses to support its main conclusion; the second is a position that the argument rejects.
The first is evidence that has been taken to support a view the argument opposes; the second is a conclusion the argument draws in opposition to that view.
The first is a claim that the argument disputes; the second is evidence offered in support of that claim.
The first is a finding that the argument says is mistaken; the second is the explanation the argument offers for why that finding is mistaken.

The first is a consideration offered in support of the popular view; the second is a qualification that the argument adds to that popular view in light of the evidence about naps and daytime drowsiness.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the chief executive's explanation rather than the board members' explanation?
questions.e: If Torvald has kept pace in conventional bikes, where the market is flat, its share loss must come from the growing segment it does not serve: electric bikes. Poor service would presumably hurt conventional sales too, so steady conventional sales count against the board members. Choice (B) is relevant to the service complaints, but knowing what customers complain about does not show whether those complaints cost Torvald sales. Choice (E) shows competitors use the same kind of shops, which helps a little, but it says nothing about whether their service is as poor.
o: Many independent bicycle shops have begun offering repair services for electric bicycles as well as conventional ones.
Customers who complain about service at independent bicycle shops most often mention long waits for repairs rather than problems at the time of purchase.
Electric bicycles generally earn retailers a higher profit per sale than conventional bicycles do.
Over the three years, Torvald's sales of conventional bicycles have held steady, while sales of conventional bicycles across the market have also been flat.
Torvald's main competitors, which do sell electric bicycles, also sell most of their products through independent shops.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the slow recovery of the small fish?
questions.e: With predators gone and conditions unchanged, quick recovery would be expected unless something else now limits the small fish. A competing beetle that grew numerous during the small fish's decline and now eats most of their food supply would hold the population down. Choice (D) makes the slow recovery more puzzling rather than explaining it. Choice (A) is relevant to the predator's effects on the lake, but it does not explain why the small fish stay scarce now that the predator is gone.
o: The predatory fish had fed on a wide variety of prey, including frogs and other fish species, and not only on the small fish.
Before the predators were introduced, the small fish had been one of the most abundant fish species in the lake.
Anglers who visit the lake have been informed that introducing fish is illegal and can harm the lake's native species, and a sign explaining this has been posted at the trailhead.
Small fish species in other mountain lakes have recovered rapidly after predators were removed.
While the predators were present, a species of beetle that also feeds on insect larvae multiplied greatly, and it now consumes most of the larvae on which the small fish depend.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the commentator's conclusion?
questions.e: The comparison covers only patients admitted to hospital. If, without the campaign, the most critical patients in Region B died before admission, Region B's hospital death rate looks lower simply because its sickest patients were never counted, while Region A's campaign brought such patients in alive. Choice (A) is the attractive trap: it shows the false alarms the commentator mentions really occur, which if anything supports the commentator's suggested mechanism. Choice (B) deepens the puzzle of Region A's higher rate rather than explaining it away.
o: Most of the people who called an ambulance in Region A because of chest pain turned out not to be having a heart attack.
Hospitals in Region A have more cardiologists per patient than hospitals in Region B, and they also have shorter average waiting times in their emergency departments.
In Region B, many heart-attack patients who would have survived only with rapid treatment died before reaching a hospital, and so were never counted among admitted patients.
The campaign in Region A was paid for by a charitable foundation rather than by the regional government.
Heart-attack death rates in both regions have fallen gradually over the past twenty years as treatments have improved and fewer people smoke.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
questions.e: Rao has been at the firm for less than two years, so she cannot have enrolled in, and thus completed, the management course; and every project leader has completed it, so she cannot lead a project. Choice (B) is the trap: nothing says the analytics certificate requires the management course, so she might hold it. Choice (C) does not follow, because the employees with the certificate need not be project leaders, and (E) assumes she will be eligible and will seek to enroll, which the statements do not establish.
o: Priyanka Rao does not lead a client project at Hallam.
Priyanka Rao has not earned the advanced analytics certificate.
Some employees who lead client projects at Hallam have earned the advanced analytics certificate.
Every employee at Hallam who has been with the firm for more than two years has completed the management course.
Priyanka Rao will be permitted to enroll in the management course within the next year.

questions.s: The agency's argument that the change will cut fare evasion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The agency's mechanism is that app tickets cannot be forged. That cuts evasion only if forgery is a real part of the problem; if evaders simply ride without any ticket, an unforgeable ticket changes nothing. Choice (A) matters for whether the plan is practical, but the claim about evasion could hold among app users even if some riders keep using other options. Choice (B) concerns the separate claim about saving money, and (C) is not required because the argument depends on faster verification, not on checking more riders.
o: Most of the agency's riders already own smartphones on which they could install the app.
The savings from no longer printing paper tickets will exceed the cost of developing and maintaining the app.
Inspectors currently check a smaller share of riders than they would be able to check if all tickets were on the app.
Forged paper tickets account for a meaningful share of fare evasion, rather than evasion consisting almost entirely of riders who have no ticket at all.
Riders who buy fares on the app will be less likely than other riders to lose their tickets or to forget to bring them, since few people leave home without their phones.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners' reply to the critics?
questions.e: The planners concede that new buildings are few but argue that their location matters. Evidence that the flood water mostly comes from the hillside neighborhoods, where the gardens would be built, shows that even a few roofs there could cut a large share of the problem. Choice (E) confirms that flooding is worsening but gives no reason to think the gardens would help. Choice (D) is weak, since no results from the other cities are available.
o: Rooftop gardens also reduce the amount of energy that buildings use for cooling during the summer.
Studies of past floods show that most of the storm water that overwhelms drains in the low-lying districts comes from the hillside neighborhoods during brief, intense rainfalls.
Rooftop gardens add considerably to the cost of constructing a new building, and developers have lobbied against the requirement.

Several other cities have adopted similar requirements for new buildings in recent years, and planners in those cities describe the programs as popular, although none has yet published data on their effects.
The low-lying neighborhoods have flooded more often in the past decade than in any earlier decade for which records exist.

questions.s: In the argument above, the two portions in brackets play which of the following roles?
questions.e: The argument endorses the analysts' advice, but only for firms with unpredictable needs; that is the first portion. It then reasons about firms with steady loads, which lie outside that scope, and concludes in the second portion that such firms should mostly own their servers. Choice (B) is the trap: the argument does not reject the analysts' advice, it limits it. Choice (A) fails because the first portion is not the main conclusion, which concerns steady-load firms.
o: The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is a consideration that has been offered against that conclusion.
