The first is a position that the argument rejects; the second is a conclusion that the argument draws in opposition to that position.
The first is evidence that the argument uses to support the analysts' view; the second is that view.
The first is a judgment the argument accepts within a limited scope; the second is the argument's conclusion about cases outside that scope.
The first is a prediction that the argument says has been confirmed; the second is a recommendation that the argument says follows from that prediction.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?
questions.e: The historian rests her causal claim on the overlap between the workshops' rise and the guilds' decline. If the decline started earlier, after a steep rise in entry fees, and was well under way before most workshops opened, the timing points to another cause. Choice (A) is the attractive trap: members moving to the workshops actually fits the historian's view that the workshops drew people away. Choice (E) explains how workshops could compete, which supports her, and (D) is irrelevant to the cause in Tolven.
o: Some guild members in Tolven left their guilds to become owners or managers of the large workshops, and several of these former members later signed the petitions against further workshops.
Guild membership began to fall sharply around 1730, after the guilds steeply raised their entry fees, and most of the large workshops opened only after 1760.
Guild records from Tolven are incomplete for several years in the 1760s because a fire destroyed part of the guild hall.
Guilds in several other cities also petitioned their governments to restrict large workshops during the 1700s.
The large workshops in Tolven generally produced cheaper goods than guild members did, though the goods were of lower quality.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?
questions.e: Account balances tripled, yet no more families save. If the growth came mainly from families who were already saving and simply shifted money into the tax-favored accounts, balances could soar without any new families beginning to save. Choice (D) is tempting because it explains why few new families joined, but it does not explain where the large increase in balances came from. Choice (E) makes the puzzle harder, since heavy advertising would be expected to draw in new savers.
o: Most of the money now in the special accounts was moved there from other savings by families who were already saving for education.
The cost of a university education in Elbria has risen considerably faster than the general rate of inflation since the deduction was introduced.
Families who save in the special accounts must use the money for education or else pay a penalty when they withdraw it.
Surveys show that many Elbrian families do not know that the tax deduction exists or how to open one of the special accounts at their bank.

In recent years Elbrian banks have heavily advertised the special accounts, often offering small cash bonuses to customers who open one, and the number of banks offering the accounts has doubled since the deduction began.

questions.s: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the director's argument?
questions.e: The director compares participants with their own previous year. If people tended to join right after an unusually stressful year with many sick days, their sick days would likely fall afterward anyway, so the savings could be overstated. Choice (E) is the attractive trap: comparing users with non-users sounds rigorous, but the groups may differ for many reasons, and the argument's comparison is with the same employees' past. Choice (B) concerns satisfaction rather than the cost savings at issue.
o: Whether the counselors who work in the program have training in treating workplace stress specifically
Whether employees who used the program reported greater satisfaction with their jobs afterward
Whether employees' sick days typically decline after an unusually bad year even without any intervention, and whether many joined the program just after such a year
Whether other large employers in the same industry offer similar counseling programs, and whether those programs have reduced the number of sick days their employees take
Whether employees who did not use the program took more sick days, on average, than employees who did

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the authors' conclusion?
questions.e: Random assignment means the two sets of proposals from less prestigious universities should be similar in quality, so the score gap points to the effect of knowing names. And if prestigious applicants scored the same either way, the difference arises specifically for less prestigious ones, fitting the claim of favoritism. Choice (D) is the attractive trap: guessing would make the blind panels less blind, which works against finding any difference, so if anything it suggests the true effect is understated, but it adds no evidence that the gap reflects favoritism. Choice (B) is a self-report that cannot rule out unconscious bias.
o: Researchers at prestigious universities submit a larger number of grant proposals each year than researchers at less prestigious universities do.
Reviewers on panels that knew applicants' names reported that they tried to judge each proposal only on its scientific merit.
Proposals from researchers at less prestigious universities are, on average, shorter than proposals from researchers at more prestigious institutions.
Some reviewers on the blind panels said afterward that they could often guess which university a proposal came from by its writing style, its equipment, or the work it cited.
The proposals were assigned to blind or named panels at random, and proposals from prestigious universities received similar scores from both kinds of panel.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' plan to shorten turnaround times by raising the fee?
questions.e: The plan assumes that a higher fee will keep shortening turnarounds. If the bottleneck is now cabin boarding slowed by carry-on bags, a higher fee would push still more bags into the cabin and lengthen turnaround times. Choice (E) is the attractive trap: it offers another cause of the past improvement and so weakens the claim about the fee's effect, but it does not show that raising the fee would fail. Choice (A) suggests the fee works similarly elsewhere, which fits the managers' view.
o: Several of Pellam's competitors introduced checked-bag fees during the same two years, and their turnaround times also fell, by amounts similar to Pellam's, over the same period of time.
Since the fee was introduced, Pellam's revenue from checked-bag fees has exceeded the airline's original estimates.
Since the fee began, far more passengers carry bags into the cabin, and boarding is now held up chiefly by passengers searching for overhead space, a delay that a higher checked-bag fee would worsen.
Some passengers have switched from Pellam to rival airlines that do not charge for checked bags, especially on long-distance routes where most travelers carry more luggage.
Two years ago Pellam also began using larger baggage carts that allow ground crews to load and unload the hold faster than before, even when planes carry a full load of checked bags.

questions.s: The astronomers' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
questions.e: The astronomers explicitly reject the alternative that planets form more often around fast rotators, and their reasoning needs that alternative to be false: if fast young stars were more likely to acquire close giant planets, the correlation would be explained without any spin-up. Choice (E) is the trap: if planet hosts lost speed at a different rate, that might be precisely the tidal effect the astronomers propose, so the argument does not need (E); indeed, its final clause conflicts with the conclusion. Choice (C) is a detail about the probable mechanism, which the conclusion does not depend on.
o: Stars that rotate fast when young are not, for that reason, more likely than slower stars to end up with large planets in close orbits.
Most stars in the cluster have at least one planet, although the planets of many of them are too small or too distant to detect.
Tidal forces between a star and a close-orbiting planet are stronger the more massive the planet is.
Stars in other clusters that host large, close-orbiting planets also rotate faster than similar stars without such planets.
The stars in the cluster all lose rotation speed with age at the same rate, regardless of their size, temperature, or composition, and regardless of whether they host planets.

questions.s: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true of the manuscripts on the abbey's list?
questions.e: A manuscript for a monastery used the abbey's own parchment, and no manuscript for a layperson did, so no manuscript was copied for both. Every sold manuscript was for a layperson, so none of the monastery copies can have been sold. Choice (A) reverses the last statement: being sold requires a lay buyer, but a lay manuscript need not have been sold, and the remark about paying merchants does not change that. Choice (C) is tempting, but the statements never establish that any manuscripts for monasteries exist, and (D) contradicts the statements.
o: Every manuscript copied for a layperson was sold rather than given away, since the abbey had to pay merchants for the parchment.
None of the manuscripts copied for other monasteries were sold.
Some of the manuscripts that the abbey gave away were copied for other monasteries.
Some of the manuscripts written on parchment from the abbey's own flocks were sold to wealthy laypeople.
Most of the manuscripts copied in the scriptorium were copied for laypeople rather than for other monasteries.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the engineers' prediction?
questions.e: Even if the sensors caused the improvement downtown, the prediction requires that other intersections would benefit similarly. If those intersections carry light, steady traffic that fixed timings already handle almost optimally, adaptive sensors have little to improve there. Choice (B) is the attractive trap: it seems to offer another cause of the downtown improvement, but since the rail line drew few former drivers, it does little to explain shorter driving times. Choice (C) describes the earlier trend and, if anything, makes the recent drop more impressive.
o: The sensors cost less to install than the engineers had expected, because the city was able to use its existing traffic-light wiring and poles, and the engineers expect the same savings at the remaining intersections.
During the year after installation, the city also opened a new rail line to the center, although surveys found that few of its riders had previously driven there at rush hour.
Average rush-hour travel times in the city center had been rising slowly for a decade before the sensors were installed.
Most of the city's other signaled intersections carry light, steady traffic, for which fixed light timings are already close to the most efficient possible.
Drivers surveyed after the installation said they had noticed shorter waits at red lights in the city center, especially in the evening rush hour.

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the fall in the cooperative's milk income?
questions.e: More milk at an unchanged price should raise income, unless the cooperative is not simply paid by volume. If payment depends on butterfat and the new feed dilutes it, the cooperative may deliver more liters yet earn less. Choice (A) is the attractive trap: higher feed costs reduce profit, but the passage concerns income from milk sales, which costs do not affect. Choice (C) concerns how much feed is eaten, which again bears on costs rather than income.
o: The new feed costs more per ton than the feed the cooperative's members used before, so the members' total spending on feed has risen.
Several other dairy cooperatives in the region began using the same feed last year and also report higher volumes of milk per cow.
Cows given the new feed eat slightly less of it each day than they ate of the old feed, although they produce more milk.
Demand for milk in the region has been stable for several years, while demand for cheese and yogurt has grown slowly.
The dairies pay the cooperative according to the butterfat content of its milk, and the new feed sharply lowers the butterfat in each liter.

questions.s: The forecast had called for (i) _____ skies all weekend, so the hikers were caught unprepared when a (ii) _____ storm drove them off the mountain on Saturday afternoon.
questions.e: Being 'caught unprepared' means the forecast promised good weather, clear skies. The storm surprised them, so it was sudden. 'Predicted' contradicts the hikers' surprise, and a 'gentle' storm would not drive anyone off a mountain.

questions.s: The teacher's explanations were so (i) _____ that even students who had struggled with the topic for weeks finally understood it, and several thanked her afterward for the (ii) _____ with which she went over the material again and again.
questions.e: Explanations that finally made a hard topic understood are lucid, clear and easy to follow. Going over the material 'again and again' for struggling students shows patience. 'Confusing' reverses the result, and neither 'severity' (strictness) nor 'indifference' fits a teacher who kept repeating the material until it was understood.

questions.s: Sea otters may look (i) _____ as they float on their backs, but they are fierce predators whose appetite for sea urchins helps (ii) _____ kelp forests from being stripped bare.
questions.e: 'But they are fierce predators' requires that otters look the opposite, harmless. Sea urchins strip kelp, so otters that eat urchins help save the forests. 'Dangerous' gives no contrast with 'fierce', and 'remove' kelp forests from being stripped makes no sense.

questions.s: Paper money was at first (i) _____ by merchants accustomed to gold and silver coins, but once they saw how much easier it was to carry, its use became (ii) _____.
questions.e: 'At first' and 'but once they saw' its convenience signal a change of attitude, so merchants first distrusted paper money. After the change, its use became widespread. 'Welcomed' leaves no change for 'but' to mark, and 'rare' contradicts the merchants' new view.

questions.s: Ballet can look (i) _____, as if the dancers were floating through the air. In fact it demands enormous (ii) _____, and many dancers train for years before they can make the hardest steps appear (iii) _____.
questions.e: 'As if the dancers were floating' describes something that looks effortless. 'In fact' reveals the hidden reality: ballet demands strength. Years of training let dancers make hard steps appear easy, matching the first sentence. 'Difficult' is the trap: dancers train to hide difficulty, not to show it.

questions.s: The researcher's findings were at first (i) _____ because they came from a single small study; only after three independent teams obtained (ii) _____ results did the field begin to accept them.
questions.e: A single small study is weak evidence, and 'only after' implies early doubt, so the findings were discounted, given little weight. Acceptance came when other teams obtained consistent results, matching the original ones. 'Retracted' findings would not later be accepted, and 'contradictory' results would deepen the doubt.

questions.s: Silent-film actors relied on (i) _____ gestures and expressions, since they could not use their voices; when sound arrived, this style quickly came to seem (ii) _____, and actors had to learn a subtler manner.
questions.e: Without voices, actors had to show feeling through exaggerated gestures. Once sound arrived and a 'subtler manner' was needed, the old style seemed overwrought, too intense and overdone. 'Restrained' and 'understated' are a trap pair: they describe the subtler manner that replaced silent acting, not silent acting itself.

questions.s: Early translation software produced sentences that were grammatically (i) _____ yet often absurd in meaning, because it matched words one by one without grasping (ii) _____; a sentence could be correct in every part and nonsensical as a whole.
questions.e: 'Yet often absurd' and 'correct in every part' show the grammar itself was flawless. Matching words one by one ignores how surrounding words shape meaning, which is context. 'Syntax' (sentence structure) is the trap: the sentences were grammatically correct, so syntax was not the problem.

questions.s: The fossil was initially classified as a (i) _____ of a known species, since it differed only slightly from earlier specimens. A closer examination, however, revealed features so (ii) _____ that researchers now place it in a new genus, and its discovery has (iii) _____ debate about how the group evolved, since it fits none of the existing family trees.
questions.e: Differing 'only slightly' from known specimens makes it a variant, a slightly different form, of the species. 'However' and a new genus show the features were distinctive. A fossil that 'fits none of the existing family trees' reignited debate. 'Settled' is tempting for an important find, but a misfit fossil raises questions rather than answering them.

questions.s: When the suspension bridge opened, many engineers considered its slender deck dangerously (i) _____. The designer, however, had tested models in wind tunnels and was (ii) _____ that the deck would hold, and a century of (iii) _____ service has proved him right.
questions.e: A 'slender' deck that worried engineers was considered flimsy, too weak. 'However' and wind-tunnel testing show the designer was confident. Proof that he was right is a century of uneventful service, free of problems. 'Turbulent' service would support the engineers' worry, not the designer's judgment.

questions.s: The essayist's style is (i) _____, circling a subject from many angles and wandering through anecdotes before settling on a claim, and readers who prefer (ii) _____ argument, proceeding step by step from premise to conclusion, find her maddening.
questions.e: Circling a subject and wandering through anecdotes define a discursive style, one that moves from topic to topic. Readers frustrated by it want the opposite, linear argument, which the sentence glosses as 'step by step from premise to conclusion'. 'Meandering' is the trap: it describes the essayist, so readers who prefer it would enjoy her, and 'terse' (brief and blunt) contradicts the wandering.

questions.s: The observatory's director was (i) _____ about announcing the unusual signal, insisting that her team first rule out every mundane explanation. Her (ii) _____ proved wise: the signal was eventually traced to a microwave oven in the staff kitchen, an outcome that would have been (iii) _____ had the discovery already been trumpeted to the press.
questions.e: Insisting on ruling out every ordinary cause before speaking shows she was circumspect, cautious and wary. 'Her ... proved wise' refers to that same quality, restraint. A kitchen appliance revealed after a public announcement would have been mortifying, deeply embarrassing. 'Precipitate' (hasty) and 'alacrity' (eager speed) describe the opposite of her behavior, and 'inconsequential' ignores how damaging the false announcement would have been.

questions.s: The academy's apparent (i) _____, its willingness to admit any qualified painter, masked a subtler exclusivity: the entrance examinations were so (ii) _____ and costly that only the children of existing members could realistically prepare for them, so that the academy's celebrated (iii) _____ was more rhetorical than real.
questions.e: 'Willingness to admit any qualified painter' defines openness, and 'masked a subtler exclusivity' shows it was only apparent. Exams that only insiders could prepare for were onerous, heavily burdensome; 'perfunctory' (done as a mere formality) would let anyone through. The celebrated but unreal quality is the same claim to openness, egalitarianism, belief in equal access. 'Parochialism' (narrowness) describes the reality the academy hid, not the image it celebrated.

questions.s: Fungi were long treated as (i) _____ organisms, mere decomposers of dead matter. It is now clear that many are indispensable partners of living plants, trading nutrients through root networks so (ii) _____ that some forests could not persist without them; the old view, in retrospect, was not merely incomplete but (iii) _____.
questions.e: 'Mere decomposers' casts fungi as peripheral, of minor importance; 'pivotal' is the newer view. Networks on which whole forests depend must be intricate, richly interconnected, not sparse. 'Not merely incomplete but' calls for a stronger fault, misguided, wrong in its basic direction. 'Prescient' (showing foresight) would praise the old view the sentence criticizes.

questions.s: The playwright's dialogue seems at first (i) _____, a string of banal remarks about the weather and dinner; only gradually does the audience realize that each platitude is (ii) _____ with menace, and that what the characters leave unsaid is more (iii) _____ than anything they say.
questions.e: Banal remarks about weather and dinner seem innocuous, harmless; 'sinister' is what the audience discovers 'only gradually', not the first impression. A platitude that hides menace is freighted with it, loaded with a heavy hidden meaning. The unsaid speaks louder than speech, so silence is more eloquent, expressive. 'Embellished' suggests open decoration, but the menace here is concealed, and 'trivial' contradicts the turn toward hidden meaning.

questions.s: The museum's new wing was meant to (i) _____ larger crowds, but its confusing layout left many visitors (ii) _____, wandering the same hallways in search of the exit.
questions.e: A new wing is built to “accommodate” (make room for) more visitors; “confuse” cannot be its purpose, since “but” introduces the confusion as an unwanted result. People wandering in search of the exit are “lost”. “Delighted” and “rested” do not match a confusing layout.

questions.s: Although the hiking trail looked (i) _____ on the map, it turned out to be steep and rocky, and even experienced walkers found it (ii) _____.
questions.e: “Although” sets the map against reality: the trail looked “gentle” but was steep and rocky. A steep, rocky trail that troubles even experienced walkers is “exhausting”. “Treacherous” in blank (i) removes the contrast, since the trail really was difficult, and “effortless” contradicts “even experienced walkers”.

questions.s: The scientist was (i) _____ about her results, refusing to announce them until other labs had repeated the experiment; her rivals, by contrast, were quick to (ii) _____ their own findings.
questions.e: Refusing to announce results until they are confirmed is “guarded”, careful and reserved; “boastful” is the opposite. “By contrast” means the rivals did what she would not: they were quick to “publicize” their findings. “Conceal” would make the rivals just like her.

questions.s: Because the bakery's bread was so (i) _____, it usually sold out by noon, and customers who arrived late often found the shelves (ii) _____.
questions.e: Bread that sells out by noon must be “popular”; “stale” or “expensive” bread would not sell out so fast. After it sells out, late customers find the shelves “empty”. “Stocked” contradicts “sold out”.

questions.s: The city's old harbor was once (i) _____, crowded with ships and workers. When trade moved to a larger port, the area fell (ii) _____, and its warehouses stood empty for years. Today, converted into shops and apartments, it is (iii) _____ once more.
questions.e: “Crowded with ships and workers” defines “bustling”, full of activity. When trade left and warehouses emptied, the area fell “silent”; “prosperous” contradicts the empty warehouses. “Once more” means it has returned to its first state, so it is “lively” again. “Abandoned” describes the middle period, not the revival.

questions.s: The historian's account of the dock strike is admirably (i) _____, giving equal weight to the owners' and the workers' views; readers looking for a (ii) _____ will be disappointed.
questions.e: Giving equal weight to both sides is “evenhanded”, fair; “partisan” (favoring one side) is the opposite. Readers who would be disappointed by fairness want a “polemic”, a strong attack on one side. “Chronicle” and “summary” are the trap: an evenhanded account could easily be either, so those readers would not be disappointed.

questions.s: The tree frog was thought to be (i) _____ until a small population was found in a remote valley, a discovery that (ii) _____ conservationists' hopes of protecting it.
questions.e: Finding a population matters only if the frog was thought to be gone, so it was believed “extinct”. Discovering survivors “rekindled” (revived) hopes of protecting it. “Abundant” makes the discovery unremarkable, and “dashed” reverses the good news.

questions.s: The software company's early growth was (i) _____: it doubled its users every few months. That pace proved difficult to (ii) _____, and as competitors copied its features, the company's growth slowed to a (iii) _____.
questions.e: Doubling every few months is “meteoric”, extremely fast; “steady” is too mild and “sluggish” is the opposite. Such a pace is hard to “sustain” (keep up) for long. Growth that “slowed” ends at a “crawl”; “gallop” and “surge” are fast, which contradicts “slowed”.

questions.s: The chef's menu was resolutely (i) _____: rather than chasing culinary trends, she cooked the dishes of her grandmother's village, using recipes that had changed (ii) _____ in a century.
questions.e: Rejecting trends in favor of a grandmother's dishes makes the menu “traditional”; “fashionable” is what she avoided. Old village recipes that she preserves have changed “scarcely”, hardly at all, over the years. “Eclectic” (drawing from many sources) is the trap: her menu comes from one village, and “drastically” or “frequently” changed recipes would not be traditional.

questions.s: The novelist's first book was praised for its (i) _____ portrait of a fishing town, rendered with an insider's eye for detail. Her second, set in a city she had visited only briefly, struck reviewers as (ii) _____ by comparison, and several wondered whether she should (iii) _____ to familiar ground.
questions.e: An “insider's eye for detail” produces an “intimate” portrait, one based on close knowledge. A city she barely knew yields a book that seems “thin” by comparison; “rich” and “authentic” reverse the comparison. Reviewers wondered whether she should “return” to familiar ground, the kind of place she knew. “Superficial” in blank (i) is the second book's problem, not the first book's praise.

questions.s: Uniformitarian geologists held that the processes shaping the earth today—erosion, sedimentation, the slow rise of mountains—were (i) _____ with those of the distant past, operating at the same (ii) _____ rates. The view was a needed corrective to earlier appeals to sudden catastrophe, though its strictest form proved too (iii) _____, since the rock record does preserve some genuinely abrupt events.
questions.e: The examples and “the same ... rates” show that today's processes were thought “continuous” with past ones; “incommensurable” (impossible to compare) and “unconnected” deny that link. Erosion and the slow rise of mountains work at “leisurely”, unhurried, rates. A strict form that ignores real abrupt events is too “doctrinaire”, rigidly committed to a theory. “Tentative” is the opposite problem, and “catastrophist” names the earlier view the theory corrected.

questions.s: The firm's code of conduct was more (i) _____ than practical: its lofty language about integrity offered employees little (ii) _____ when they faced actual dilemmas.
questions.e: “Lofty language” that urges good behavior without practical detail is “hortatory”, exhorting or encouraging. “Pragmatic” cannot be set against “practical”, since the two mean nearly the same. Inspiring words without specifics give employees little “guidance” in real dilemmas. “Temptation” and “resentment” do not describe what a code of conduct is meant to supply.

questions.s: The director's adaptation is scrupulously (i) _____ to the novel's plot, yet it feels oddly (ii) _____: by reproducing every event, it leaves no room for the narrator's (iii) _____, the sly asides that made the book memorable.
questions.e: Reproducing every event means the film is scrupulously “faithful” to the plot. “Yet” introduces a flaw: crammed with events and lacking the narrator's voice, the film feels “airless”, stifling and lifeless. “Sly asides” restate blank (iii): the narrator's “irony”. “Solemnity” is the opposite of sly asides, and “verbosity” would be a fault, not what made the book memorable.

questions.s: Hyperinflation is often blamed on the (i) _____ printing of money, and rightly so; but governments rarely print recklessly by choice. More often they are (ii) _____ by debts they cannot otherwise pay, so that the printing press becomes less a policy than a (iii) _____.
questions.e: “Print recklessly” restates blank (i): the printing is “profligate”, wildly wasteful. “But ... rarely by choice” shows that governments are forced into it, “cornered” by debts they cannot pay. A measure taken because nothing else is left is a “last resort”. “Emboldened” implies choice, which the sentence denies, and “panacea” (cure-all) is far too positive for a cause of hyperinflation.

questions.s: Kitsch is often defined as art that (i) _____ emotion rather than earning it, offering the viewer a ready-made sentiment in place of genuine experience. Its appeal lies precisely in this (ii) _____: it asks nothing of us, and its pleasures are therefore (iii) _____ and soon forgotten.
questions.e: A “ready-made sentiment in place of genuine experience” is a fake feeling, so kitsch “counterfeits” emotion. “Evokes” is the trap: all art evokes emotion, so it cannot be what distinguishes kitsch, and it does not contrast with “earning it”. Art that “asks nothing of us” appeals through “effortlessness”. Pleasures that are “soon forgotten” are “fleeting”; “profound” and “enduring” contradict that phrase.

questions.s: Early telescopes were so (i) _____ that astronomers often mistook a pair of close stars for a single blurred point of light; only when lens makers achieved far greater precision did such pairs become (ii) _____.
questions.e: The blur and the later contrast with 'far greater precision' show that the first telescopes were crude, that is, roughly made. Better lenses then made the two stars distinguishable, able to be told apart. 'Powerful' contradicts the blur, and 'invisible' reverses the improvement that precise lenses brought.

questions.s: Critics, fearing that owners would cut staff to cover higher payrolls, warned that raising the minimum wage would (i) _____ employment in small restaurants, but the data collected afterward showed job numbers essentially (ii) _____.
questions.e: Owners cutting staff means the critics predicted the wage rise would reduce employment. 'But' signals that the prediction failed, so the job numbers stayed unchanged. 'Halved' would confirm the warning rather than contrast with it, and 'unrecorded' makes no sense for data that 'showed' the numbers.

questions.s: Unlike most languages of the region, which borrow freely from their neighbors, the island's language has remained remarkably (i) _____, keeping nearly all of its native vocabulary; linguists attribute this (ii) _____ partly to centuries of geographic isolation.
questions.e: 'Unlike' sets the island's language against languages that borrow freely, so it stayed unmixed, keeping its own words. The second blank names that same quality: conservatism, here the tendency of a language to keep old forms. 'Hybrid' describes the borrowing languages, and 'innovation' is the opposite of keeping native vocabulary.

questions.s: The painter's early canvases are (i) _____, crowded with figures and bright color, whereas her late works are so (ii) _____ that some contain little more than a single line on a pale ground.
questions.e: 'Crowded with figures and bright color' defines exuberant, full of energy and abundance. 'Whereas' then contrasts the late works, which are spare, meaning bare and minimal, as a single line on a pale ground shows. 'Austere' is the trap for the first blank: it fits the late works, not the early ones.

questions.s: Because wolves keep deer from lingering along riverbanks, the wolves' return to the park allowed streamside willows to (i) _____, which in turn (ii) _____ the beavers that depend on those trees.
questions.e: With fewer deer browsing at the water's edge, the willows could recover. Beavers that depend on willows would then be benefited by the healthier trees. 'Wither' reverses the cause and effect, and 'endangered' would only follow if the willows had declined.

questions.s: Though the composer was celebrated in his lifetime, his music fell into (i) _____ soon after his death, and it was not until a century later that a few devoted performers (ii) _____ it.
questions.e: 'Though ... celebrated' signals a reversal, so after his death the music fell into obscurity, being forgotten. 'Not until a century later' points to devoted performers who revived it, bringing it back into use. 'Fashion' repeats his lifetime fame instead of contrasting with it, and performers cannot have 'composed' music that already existed.

questions.s: The judge's ruling was deliberately (i) _____, addressing only the narrow question before the court, so legal scholars cautioned against reading it as a (ii) _____ statement about privacy rights in general.
questions.e: 'Addressing only the narrow question' restates a limited ruling. Because it was narrow, scholars warned against treating it as a broad statement about privacy 'in general'. 'Sweeping' contradicts the narrow scope, and nobody would need to be warned against reading a narrow ruling as 'tentative'.

questions.s: Critics initially dismissed the glass library as (i) _____, a building more concerned with looking striking than with serving its readers; yet librarians report that its abundant daylight has made it unusually (ii) _____ to work in.
questions.e: 'More concerned with looking striking than with serving its readers' defines showy. 'Yet' introduces a point in the building's favor, and abundant daylight makes it pleasant to work in. 'Functional' is the opposite of the critics' complaint, and 'dim' contradicts 'abundant daylight'.

questions.s: The canyon's rock layers record a slow, (i) _____ process: each band of sediment took thousands of years to settle, so the full sequence represents an almost (ii) _____ span of time.
questions.e: 'Slow' and 'thousands of years' for each band point to a gradual process. Many bands, each taking thousands of years, add up to a vast span of time. 'Sudden' clashes with 'slow', and 'brief' ignores that the layers multiply the time.

questions.s: The company's founder was famously (i) _____ with money, reusing envelopes and refusing first-class travel, so employees were startled when she (ii) _____ millions on a new research campus.
questions.e: Reusing envelopes and refusing first-class travel describe someone frugal, careful not to waste money. Employees were 'startled' only because the new action broke this habit, so she lavished, or spent generously, millions. If she had been 'extravagant' or 'careless' with money, a large expense would not have surprised anyone.

questions.s: Participants who were told the puzzle was easy grew (i) _____ when they failed to solve it quickly, whereas those warned of its difficulty remained (ii) _____ and kept working.
questions.e: Expecting an easy puzzle and then failing quickly would leave people discouraged. 'Whereas' contrasts the second group, who 'kept working', so they remained persistent. 'Determined' belongs to the second group, not the first, and 'frustrated' would not explain why they kept going.

questions.s: The novelist's prose is so (i) _____ that readers can finish a chapter in minutes, but this ease is (ii) _____: beneath the simple sentences lie layers of irony that reward rereading.
questions.e: Reading a chapter in minutes shows the prose is accessible, easy to understand. 'But' and the hidden 'layers of irony' show that the ease is deceptive, misleading about how simple the book really is. 'Dense' contradicts the fast reading, and 'genuine' ignores the contrast that follows the colon.

questions.s: Most cacti store water in thick stems, an adaptation that lets them (i) _____ long droughts; when rain finally comes, their shallow, widespread roots (ii) _____ moisture within hours.
questions.e: Stored water lets a plant endure, or survive, a long dry period; a plant rooted in place cannot 'avoid' a drought. When rain falls, the roots absorb moisture to refill the stems. 'Release' reverses the roots' job, which is to take water in.

questions.s: Planners had hoped the new tram line would (i) _____ traffic in the old city center, but because the trams ran only twice an hour, few drivers found them a (ii) _____ alternative to their cars.
questions.e: Planners 'hoped' for a good result, so the tram was meant to ease traffic. The reason given, trams 'only twice an hour', is about convenience, so drivers did not find them a practical alternative. 'Costly' and 'noisy' are possible complaints, but neither follows from the infrequent service the sentence names.

questions.s: Although the chemist's theory was (i) _____ by most of her colleagues when she first proposed it, later experiments (ii) _____ it so thoroughly that it now appears in every introductory textbook.
questions.e: A theory that 'now appears in every introductory textbook' was confirmed by later experiments. 'Although' requires the colleagues' first reaction to contrast with that success, so they rejected it. 'Praised' gives no contrast, and 'refuted' could not lead to a place in every textbook.

questions.s: The villagers' hospitality was (i) _____: strangers were offered food and shelter without question, and turning away a guest was considered a serious (ii) _____.
questions.e: Offering food and shelter 'without question' means the hospitality was unconditional, given with no conditions attached. In such a culture, turning a guest away would be a serious offense. 'Grudging' contradicts the willing welcome, and calling a refusal an 'honor' reverses the custom.

questions.s: Deep-sea vents were once thought to be (i) _____ places, too hot and dark to support life. Explorers who reached them found them instead (ii) _____ with tube worms, clams and bacteria, a discovery that forced biologists to (iii) _____ their assumptions about where life can exist.
questions.e: 'Too hot and dark to support life' describes barren places, lifeless ones. 'Instead' reverses that belief, so the vents were teeming, full of living things. A surprise like this forced biologists to revise their assumptions; 'confirm' would mean the old belief had been right, which the discovery disproved.

questions.s: The director is known for her (i) _____ approach to casting: she often hires people with no acting experience at all. Some critics find the resulting performances (ii) _____, but admirers argue that this roughness gives her films an (iii) _____ that polished acting could not achieve.
questions.e: Hiring people with no acting experience is an unconventional approach. 'This roughness' in the next clause refers back to the critics' view, so they found the performances awkward. Admirers value roughness for what polish cannot give, a sense of authenticity, of being real; 'elegance' is exactly what polished acting would supply.

questions.s: For generations, farmers in the valley relied on a single crop, a practice that left them (i) _____ to disease. After a blight destroyed several harvests, many began to (ii) _____ their plantings, and today the region's farms are far more (iii) _____.
questions.e: A single crop can be wiped out by one disease, so the farmers were vulnerable. The lesson of the blight was to diversify, planting several crops, which makes the farms resilient, able to recover from setbacks. 'Uniform' describes the old single-crop system, not the improved one.

questions.s: A good translator must be (i) _____ to the original text, yet a word-for-word rendering is often (ii) _____ in the new language. The best translations therefore strike a (iii) _____ between accuracy and natural expression.
questions.e: The 'accuracy' in the last sentence shows that a translator must be faithful, true, to the original. 'Yet' introduces the drawback of extreme accuracy: word-for-word versions are clumsy. Weighing these two demands means striking a balance; 'elegant' fails because it would be no drawback at all.

questions.s: The comet's appearance had been predicted so (i) _____ that observers knew the very hour it would rise above the horizon; its brightness, however, proved far less (ii) _____, flaring and fading in ways no model had anticipated.
questions.e: Knowing 'the very hour' shows the timing was predicted precisely. 'However' contrasts the brightness, which behaved 'in ways no model had anticipated', so it was far less predictable. 'Spectacular' and 'visible' are tempting, but flaring is not less spectacular, and the clue is about what the models expected, not about how much could be seen.

questions.s: Although ride-hailing work is often praised for the (i) _____ it offers drivers, who can choose their own hours, many drivers report that the platforms' shifting pay rates make their incomes so (ii) _____ that planning even a month ahead is difficult.
questions.e: 'Who can choose their own hours' restates flexibility. 'Although' then sets up a drawback: shifting pay makes income erratic, irregular and unpredictable, which is why planning is hard. 'Security' is the trap; the sentence's point is that this work lacks it, and 'transparent' pay would make planning easier, not harder.

questions.s: Prescriptive grammarians tend to treat new usages as (i) _____ of the language, but descriptive linguists regard such changes as neither good nor bad, viewing them simply as evidence that a living language is always in (ii) _____.
questions.e: 'But' contrasts the grammarians with linguists who judge change 'neither good nor bad', so the grammarians must judge it bad: they see new usages as corruptions. The linguists see them only as signs that language is always in flux, constant change. 'Decline' is the trap: it carries the very negative judgment the linguists refuse to make.

questions.s: Far from being the (i) _____ genius of popular legend, working alone in a garret, the sculptor ran a large workshop and (ii) _____ much of the carving to assistants, reserving for himself only the final finishing.
questions.e: 'Working alone in a garret' defines the solitary genius of legend, and 'far from' says the real sculptor was the opposite. Running a workshop and keeping only the finishing for himself means he delegated, handed over, the carving to assistants. 'Taught' is tempting, but teaching carving would not explain why he did only the final stage himself.

questions.s: Invasive species are not always (i) _____; in some degraded wetlands, introduced reeds actually (ii) _____ the soil that native plants need, so removing them can do more harm than good.
questions.e: Removing the reeds 'can do more harm than good', so the reeds help: they stabilize, or hold in place, the soil. This exception shows invasive species are not always detrimental, meaning harmful. 'Erode' and 'contaminate' would make the reeds damaging, contradicting the claim that removal is the harmful act.

questions.s: Jazz improvisation can seem entirely (i) _____ to new listeners, but musicians know that even the freest solo is (ii) _____ by the underlying chord progression, which limits which notes will sound right.
questions.e: Improvisation seems spontaneous, made up on the spot, to newcomers. 'But' and 'limits which notes will sound right' show that the solo is actually constrained, restricted, by the chords. 'Liberated' reverses the limiting role of the progression, and 'rehearsed' is not how improvisation seems to a new listener.

questions.s: Contract law generally (i) _____ agreements made under duress, on the principle that a promise extracted by threat does not reflect the (ii) _____ consent of the party who made it.
questions.e: A promise 'extracted by threat' lacks genuine, freely given, consent, which is why the law invalidates such agreements. 'Enforces' would contradict the principle stated after 'on the principle that'. 'Coerced' is the trap: the promise is coerced, so saying it does not reflect coerced consent turns the logic upside down. Duress means pressure by threats.

questions.s: The architect's (i) _____ local materials was not mere sentiment: stone quarried a few miles away needed no long-distance transport, which made her buildings both cheaper and more (ii) _____ than those of rivals who imported steel.
questions.e: The colon explains a practical reason for using nearby stone, so the architect showed an insistence on local materials. Avoiding long-distance transport lowers cost and environmental impact, making the buildings more sustainable. 'Ornate' and 'fragile' have nothing to do with transport, and 'disdain for' contradicts her use of the quarried stone.

questions.s: Historians once portrayed medieval guilds as (i) _____ institutions that stifled innovation, but recent archival work suggests a more (ii) _____ picture: some guilds actively spread new techniques among their members.
questions.e: Institutions that 'stifled innovation' are hidebound, rigidly attached to old ways. 'But' and the evidence that some guilds spread new techniques show the new picture is more nuanced, mixed rather than wholly negative. 'Damning' is the trap: it would agree with the old portrayal instead of qualifying it.

questions.s: Contrary to the popular belief that multitasking boosts efficiency, studies show that switching between tasks (i) _____ performance on each, because the brain must repeatedly (ii) _____ itself to new demands.
questions.e: 'Contrary to the popular belief' that multitasking helps, the studies show switching degrades, or worsens, performance. The cause is the cost of each switch: the brain must reorient, readjust, itself to the new task. 'Enhances' simply restates the belief the sentence rejects.

questions.s: The physicist was notoriously (i) _____ in print, hedging every claim with qualifications, yet in private letters she stated her conclusions with a (ii) _____ that startled her correspondents.
questions.e: 'Hedging every claim with qualifications' defines being cautious. 'Yet' signals that her letters were the opposite, and what startled correspondents was her bluntness, plain and direct statement. 'Reticence' and 'modesty' would continue the cautious manner rather than contrast with it, and 'dogmatic' contradicts the hedging.

questions.s: Because the central bank's announcements had become so (i) _____, investors learned to ignore them, and when the bank finally issued a clear warning, the markets were slow to (ii) _____.
questions.e: 'Finally issued a clear warning' implies earlier announcements were not clear: they were equivocal, open to more than one reading. Having learned to ignore the bank, investors were slow to react. 'Candid' would give investors a reason to listen, and 'recover' makes no sense before any fall has been described.

questions.s: Coffee first reached many European cities not as a beverage of pleasure but as a supposed (i) _____, sold by apothecaries for headaches; within a century, however, it had become so (ii) _____ that few drinkers gave any thought to its medicinal reputation.
questions.e: Being sold by apothecaries for headaches marks coffee as a supposed remedy, a cure. 'However' shows that its medical image faded as it became commonplace, an ordinary part of life. 'Luxury' is the trap: the sentence explicitly says coffee did not arrive as a 'beverage of pleasure'.

questions.s: The memoir's appeal lies in its (i) _____: the author neither excuses her youthful mistakes nor dwells on them for sympathy, recounting them with a (ii) _____ that some readers find almost clinical.
questions.e: Neither excusing nor milking her mistakes means she tells them honestly, so the appeal is her candor, frankness. A tone 'almost clinical' is detachment, emotional distance. 'Warmth' and 'bitterness' are both emotional tones, the opposite of clinical, and 'sentimentality' is ruled out by her refusal to dwell for sympathy.

questions.s: Octopuses were long considered (i) _____ creatures, capable only of simple reflexes, but experiments showing them unscrewing jars and escaping from tanks have made that view seem (ii) _____.
questions.e: 'Capable only of simple reflexes' defines a primitive creature. Clever feats such as unscrewing jars contradict that view, making it untenable, impossible to defend. 'Prescient' (showing foresight) would mean the experiments confirmed the old view, and 'ingenious' belongs to the new picture, not the old one.

questions.s: Rather than publicly (i) _____ the rival firm's product, as its combative chief executive had done with earlier competitors, the company quietly studied it and released a version that (ii) _____ its strengths while fixing its weaknesses.
questions.e: A 'combative' leader's usual response would be to attack, so the company was expected to be publicly denouncing the rival. Studying the product and fixing its weaknesses means the new version incorporated its strengths. 'Ignoring' is tempting because 'quietly studied' contrasts with it, but nothing combative or public is involved in ignoring.

questions.s: The surgeon's insistence on washing her hands between patients was at first (i) _____ by colleagues as a needless ritual; only when her ward's infection rate fell far below theirs did they begin to (ii) _____ the practice.
questions.e: Calling the practice 'a needless ritual' shows colleagues derided, or mocked, it. 'Only when' her results proved better did they begin to emulate, or copy, her. 'Adopted' is the trap: it belongs to the later stage, not the first reaction, and 'question' would not be a change of attitude.

questions.s: Children acquiring a language often (i) _____ its rules, saying 'goed' instead of 'went'; such errors, far from showing confusion, reveal that the child has (ii) _____ a general pattern and is simply applying it too widely.
questions.e: 'Applying it too widely' restates overgeneralize, to stretch a rule beyond where it belongs. Such an error shows the child has internalized, truly absorbed, the pattern for forming the past tense. 'Memorize' is the trap: a child who memorized forms would say 'went', and 'ignore' contradicts applying the rule.

questions.s: Coral reefs occupy a (i) _____ fraction of the ocean floor, less than one percent, yet they shelter a (ii) _____ share of marine species, perhaps a quarter of the total.
questions.e: 'Less than one percent' is a minuscule, extremely small, fraction. 'Yet' contrasts this with a quarter of all species, a disproportionate share, far larger than the area would suggest. 'Negligible' would echo the first blank rather than contrast with it.

questions.s: The conductor's interpretations were (i) _____ rather than reverent; she would change tempos and cut repeats whenever she felt a score dragged, and purists accused her of treating great works with (ii) _____.
questions.e: Changing tempos and cutting repeats are bold liberties, so her interpretations were audacious, daring, rather than reverent. Purists would complain of irreverence, a lack of respect. 'Piety' repeats the 'reverent' quality she lacked, and 'indifference' does not fit a conductor who cared enough to reshape the works.

questions.s: Far from settling the dispute, the statute's wording proved so (i) _____ that two courts reading the same sentence reached opposite conclusions, and the legislature was eventually obliged to (ii) _____ the provision in an amendment.
questions.e: Two courts reading one sentence in opposite ways shows the wording was ambiguous, open to more than one meaning. The fix for ambiguity is to clarify the provision. 'Explicit' would have settled the dispute, and 'enforce' is the courts' role, not something an amendment does to unclear wording.

questions.s: The excavation team was careful not to (i) _____ the significance of the single coin they found, since one object could easily have been dropped by a later traveler and offered only (ii) _____ evidence that the site had been a trading post.
questions.e: The reason given, that one coin might have been dropped by anyone, is a reason for caution, so the team avoided overstating its importance. A single object offers only tenuous, weak, evidence. 'Understate' is the trap: the doubt about the coin is a reason to claim less, not a warning against claiming too little.

questions.s: Restorers today favor (i) _____ interventions, removing grime but adding as little new paint as possible, in contrast to their predecessors, who (ii) _____ repainted damaged passages to suit the taste of their own era.
questions.e: 'Adding as little new paint as possible' defines minimal interventions. 'In contrast to' means the predecessors did the opposite and freely repainted passages to their own taste. 'Reluctantly' and 'rarely' would make the predecessors similar to today's restorers, removing the contrast.

questions.s: The neighborhood's transformation was less (i) _____ than residents had feared: rents rose, but slowly enough that most long-time tenants were able to stay, and many came to regard the new shops as a (ii) _____ addition.
questions.e: Tenants were able to stay, so the change was less disruptive than feared. The positive tone continues: many saw the shops as a beneficial addition. 'Gradual' is the trap, since the change was in fact slow, so calling it 'less gradual than feared' reverses the meaning; 'intrusive' clashes with the relief the sentence describes.

questions.s: For decades the planet's rings were assumed to be as old as the planet itself. Recent measurements of their brightness, however, suggest that they are (i) _____, perhaps only a few hundred million years old, since ancient rings would long ago have been (ii) _____ by infalling dust. If this estimate holds, astronomers today are (iii) _____ to be observing a feature that may not last.
questions.e: 'However' and 'only a few hundred million years old' show the rings are young compared with the planet. Their brightness is the evidence, so old rings would have been darkened by dust. Living during a passing feature makes astronomers fortunate. 'Primordial' (existing from the beginning) is the old assumption, and 'unlikely' contradicts the fact that they are already observing the rings.

questions.s: Economists distinguish unemployment that is (i) _____, lasting only while workers move between jobs, from unemployment that is structural, arising when workers' skills no longer (ii) _____ what employers need. The first is a normal feature of a healthy economy; the second is far more (iii) _____, since retraining a workforce can take years.
questions.e: 'Lasting only while workers move between jobs' defines transitory, short-lived. Structural unemployment arises when skills no longer match employers' needs. Because retraining takes years, it is intractable, hard to solve. 'Benign' (harmless) is the trap: it describes the first kind, which the passage calls 'normal'; 'chronic' would describe the second kind, not the first.

questions.s: The dialect was long dismissed as a (i) _____ form of the standard language, riddled with errors. Linguists who studied it closely found instead that it was (ii) _____, governed by consistent rules of its own, and their work helped (iii) _____ its speakers, who had been taught to be ashamed of how they talked.
questions.e: 'Riddled with errors' shows the dialect was dismissed as debased, a corrupted version. 'Instead' and 'consistent rules' show it is systematic. Work proving the dialect rule-governed would vindicate, or clear of blame, speakers taught to feel ashamed. 'Archaic' (old-fashioned) does not match the charge of errors, and 'embarrass' reverses the effect of the research.

questions.s: The movement's painters rejected the (i) _____ finish prized by the academies, leaving brushstrokes visible and edges rough. Critics at first took this as a sign of (ii) _____, as if the artists simply lacked skill; only later was the roughness understood as (iii) _____, a means of capturing fleeting light.
questions.e: Rejecting the academies' finish in favor of visible strokes means the academies prized a polished one. 'As if the artists simply lacked skill' restates incompetence. 'Only later' brings the corrected view: the roughness was purposeful, a chosen means to an end. 'Arrogance' is not lack of skill, and 'accidental' would repeat the critics' mistake.

questions.s: Foresters once believed that wildfires were (i) _____ to every ecosystem and should always be suppressed. Decades of suppression, however, allowed dead wood to pile up, so that when fires did occur they were far more (ii) _____. Many managers now set small controlled burns, accepting minor damage in order to (iii) _____ catastrophe.
questions.e: A belief that fires 'should always be suppressed' means fire was seen as inimical, harmful, to ecosystems. Piled-up dead wood is fuel, so later fires were more destructive, the 'catastrophe' managers now try to forestall, or prevent in advance. 'Frequent' is tempting, but extra fuel makes fires bigger, not more common, and 'invite' reverses the purpose of controlled burns.

questions.s: The symphony's premiere was a (i) _____: the audience whistled and walked out, and reviewers called it noise. Yet within a generation the work had become a (ii) _____ of the concert repertoire, and the very dissonances that once (iii) _____ listeners are now taught as models of orchestral color.
questions.e: Whistling, walkouts and reviews calling it noise mark the premiere as a fiasco, a complete failure. 'Yet' turns to later success: the work became a staple, a standard item, of the repertoire. The dissonances 'once' affronted, or offended, listeners. 'Footnote' would mean the work stayed minor, and 'bored' does not match an audience angry enough to walk out.

questions.s: The defendant's lawyer did not (i) _____ the facts; instead she argued that the law under which her client was charged was so vague that no citizen could know what it forbade. The court, though ordinarily (ii) _____ to strike down a statute, agreed that this one failed the basic test of (iii) _____.
questions.e: 'Instead' shows the lawyer argued about the law rather than disputing, or contesting, the facts. 'Though' requires the court's usual attitude to contrast with its agreement, so it is ordinarily reluctant to strike down laws. A law too vague to understand fails the test of clarity. 'Severity' is tempting, but the complaint is vagueness, not harshness.

questions.s: Brutalist buildings, with their raw concrete and massive forms, were for years (i) _____ as cold and forbidding, and many were demolished. Recently, however, a younger generation has come to admire their (ii) _____, praising the honesty with which they display their materials, and preservation groups now campaign to (iii) _____ the survivors.
questions.e: Being called 'cold and forbidding' and torn down means the buildings were reviled, intensely disliked. 'Praising the honesty with which they display their materials' restates frankness. Preservation groups campaign to protect what remains. 'Ornament' is wrong for bare concrete, and 'disguise' would hide the very materials admirers praise.

questions.s: Memories feel like (i) _____ recordings of the past, but research shows that they are (ii) _____: each time we recall an event we rebuild it, and details can shift without our noticing. Eyewitness testimony, however (iii) _____ the witness may be, should therefore be treated with caution.
questions.e: 'But research shows' contrasts the feeling with the fact, so memories feel accurate. Being rebuilt each time and shifting unnoticed means they are malleable, easily reshaped. 'However ... may be' introduces a quality that would normally earn trust, so the witness may be sincere and still wrong. 'Unreliable' fails because a concession needs a point in the witness's favor.

questions.s: Tariffs are often defended as a way to (i) _____ young domestic industries from foreign competition. Yet the protection can prove (ii) _____: sheltered firms, facing little pressure to improve, may grow so (iii) _____ that they cannot compete once the tariffs are removed.
questions.e: 'Protection' and 'sheltered firms' show tariffs are meant to shield industries. 'Yet' introduces a drawback: firms with no pressure grow complacent, self-satisfied and unwilling to improve, so the protection proves counterproductive, defeating its own aim. 'Temporary' does not explain why the firms end up unable to compete, and 'efficient' reverses the effect.

questions.s: Some orchids attract pollinators through (i) _____ rather than reward: their flowers mimic the scent of a female wasp, so that males arrive expecting a mate and leave (ii) _____, having received no nectar. Because the trick works only if wasps cannot easily tell the difference, the orchids' mimicry must be remarkably (iii) _____.
questions.e: Mimicking a female wasp is a trick, so the orchids rely on deception rather than reward. Males who get 'no nectar' leave unrewarded. A trick that fails if wasps can 'tell the difference' must be convincing. 'Satiated' (fully fed) contradicts 'no nectar', and 'crude' mimicry would be easy to detect.

questions.s: Early printed books were designed to look as much like manuscripts as possible, and printers (i) _____ the conventions of scribes, even copying their abbreviations. Only gradually did printers (ii) _____ these habits and develop a typography suited to the new technology, one that exploited the press's capacity to produce thousands of (iii) _____ copies.
questions.e: Making books look like manuscripts and 'even copying their abbreviations' means printers imitated scribes. 'Only gradually' marks a change, so printers later shed those habits. The press's distinctive capacity is producing identical copies; hand-decorated, or 'illuminated', pages belong to the manuscript tradition, and thousands of 'unique' copies is a contradiction.

questions.s: Biologists had assumed that the songbirds navigated by the stars, but birds raised under (i) _____ skies found their way just as well, suggesting that the stars were (ii) _____ to their navigation. Further experiments pointed to a magnetic sense, though how the birds (iii) _____ the earth's field remains unclear.
questions.e: 'But' signals that the test undermined the star theory, so the birds must have been raised without a view of the stars, under overcast skies. Navigating 'just as well' without stars shows the stars were incidental, not necessary. A magnetic sense requires that birds detect the field. 'Essential' is the old assumption the experiment disproved.

questions.s: The poet's (i) _____ was legendary; she published only two slim volumes in fifty years, revising each poem dozens of times. Admirers saw this as (ii) _____, a refusal to release anything less than perfect, while detractors called it (iii) _____, a fear of judgment dressed up as principle.
questions.e: Revising each poem dozens of times shows fastidiousness, extreme care over details; 'prolificacy' contradicts two slim volumes in fifty years. 'A refusal to release anything less than perfect' is the admirers' positive reading, integrity. 'A fear of judgment' is the detractors' negative reading, timidity. 'Vanity' is negative, so it cannot be the admirers' view.

questions.s: Seismologists can say with some confidence where large earthquakes are likely, but not when; forecasts of timing remain so (i) _____ that public agencies tend to (ii) _____ them, focusing instead on building codes that make structures (iii) _____ to shaking whenever it comes.
questions.e: Being unable to say 'when' means timing forecasts are unreliable. Agencies therefore disregard them, 'focusing instead' on building codes, whose purpose is to make buildings resistant to shaking. 'Publicize' would contradict 'instead', and 'vulnerable' reverses the purpose of a building code.

questions.s: Start-ups often (i) _____ larger rivals not because they have more resources but because they have fewer: without layers of management, they can (ii) _____ quickly when customers' needs change. As they grow, however, many acquire the very (iii) _____ that once slowed their competitors.
questions.e: The sentence explains an advantage, so start-ups outmaneuver, outwit through quicker movement, larger rivals. Without management layers they adapt quickly. 'However' introduces the irony of growth: they gain the bureaucracy that slowed rivals. 'Agility' is the trap: it is what the start-ups had, not what slowed the competitors.

questions.s: The critic's praise was so (i) _____ that artists learned to discount it; a reviewer who called every exhibition 'remarkable' offered readers no (ii) _____ by which to tell genuine achievement from mere competence.
questions.e: Calling every exhibition 'remarkable' is praise that is indiscriminate, given without distinguishing between cases. Such praise supplies no criterion, a standard for judging, that separates real achievement from competence. 'Incisive' (sharply perceptive) is the trap: perceptive praise would be worth trusting, and 'grudging' praise would not be handed to every show.

questions.s: Far from being (i) _____, the theory's predictions were hedged so carefully that almost any experimental outcome could be reconciled with them, a pliancy that its critics regarded not as a strength but as a symptom of its (ii) _____.
questions.e: A theory that can be reconciled with 'almost any' outcome cannot be proved wrong, so 'far from being' points to falsifiable, capable of being tested and refuted. Critics see this pliancy as a sign of vacuity, emptiness: a theory compatible with everything says nothing. 'Robustness' is the defenders' reading, the 'strength' the critics reject, and 'ambiguous' agrees with the hedging instead of contrasting with it.

questions.s: Although the pianist's technique was (i) _____, her playing was faulted for a certain (ii) _____: every note was in place, yet listeners came away unmoved, as if they had heard an exercise rather than a performance.
questions.e: 'Every note was in place' shows her technique was impeccable, flawless. 'Although' sets up a fault despite this: listeners were unmoved, so her playing had aridity, a dry lack of feeling. 'Gaucheness' (awkwardness) is a fault, but a technical one that contradicts the flawless technique; 'effervescence' (bubbly liveliness) would move listeners rather than leave them cold.

questions.s: The chronicler's account, once (i) _____ as the most reliable source for the reign, has lately come under suspicion; scholars note that it was written for the king's grandson and is (ii) _____ in its praise of the dynasty, passing over every defeat in silence.
questions.e: 'Once' and 'has lately come under suspicion' show a fall in reputation, so the account was once prized as reliable; 'impugned' (attacked as false) describes the present view, not the past one. Written for the king's grandson and silent on every defeat, the praise is fulsome: excessive and flattering. 'Measured' would make the account more trustworthy, not suspect.

questions.s: The ecologist's warnings were neither (i) _____ nor equivocal: she conceded every uncertainty in her data, yet she refused to let uncertainty become an excuse for (ii) _____, since waiting for proof would mean waiting until the wetland was gone.
questions.e: The colon explains the two denials in order. Conceding every uncertainty shows she was not dogmatic, asserting views as beyond doubt. Refusing to let doubt justify delay shows she was not equivocal; the excuse she rejects is for inaction, since waiting would cost the wetland. 'Tentative' and 'diffident' (lacking confidence) are near-synonyms of equivocal, and conceding uncertainty would not rule them out.

questions.s: Loanwords seldom keep their original meanings intact: a term borrowed for some (i) _____ purpose, such as naming a single dish or a legal procedure, often broadens until it is so thoroughly (ii) _____ that speakers no longer sense anything foreign about it.
questions.e: Naming 'a single dish or a legal procedure' is a narrow, specialized purpose, and the word then 'broadens', which only makes sense if it began narrow; 'general' reverses this. A word whose foreignness speakers no longer sense is naturalized, fully absorbed into the borrowing language. 'Exotic' is the opposite, and 'obsolete' words are not used enough to broaden.

questions.s: The astronomer's notebooks reveal a mind far less (i) _____ than his published papers suggest. In print he presented each discovery as the inevitable result of method; in private he recorded false starts, (ii) _____ hunches and long stretches of bafflement, a record that makes his eventual success seem less (iii) _____ and more hard-won.
questions.e: The papers present discoveries as 'the inevitable result of method', so the notebooks show him less methodical than that. Alongside false starts and bafflement, the hunches were inchoate, only partly formed. The private record makes success seem less foreordained, settled in advance, echoing 'inevitable'. 'Unerring' hunches would fit the published image, and 'laborious' means much the same as 'hard-won', so it cannot be its contrast.

questions.s: Advocates of the four-day work week insist that its benefits are not merely (i) _____, a matter of happier staff, but tangible for employers, citing trials in which output held steady. Skeptics counter that such trials are (ii) _____, since the firms that volunteer are presumably those best suited to the change, and that results from so (iii) _____ a sample cannot be generalized.
questions.e: 'Not merely ... but tangible' needs a contrast with tangible, and 'happier staff' describes a benefit that is intangible, hard to measure. Firms that volunteer because they suit the change make the trials skewed, biased in one direction. Such a self-selected group is an unrepresentative sample. 'Premature' is a possible criticism, but the reason the skeptics give is about who takes part, not about timing; a 'randomized' sample is exactly what these trials lack.

questions.s: Because the painter destroyed most of her sketches, scholars must (i) _____ her working methods from the finished canvases alone, a task made more (ii) _____ by her habit of painting over earlier compositions. X-ray studies have begun to (iii) _____ this difficulty, revealing abandoned figures beneath the visible surface.
questions.e: Without sketches, scholars must infer, reason out, her methods from indirect evidence; 'document' would require direct records, which were destroyed. Painting over earlier work hides evidence, so the task is more fraught, full of difficulty. X-rays that reveal hidden figures attenuate, or lessen, the problem. 'Compound' (make worse) reverses the effect of a technique that uncovers what was hidden.

questions.s: The island's flora is famously (i) _____: most of its species occur nowhere else. This uniqueness, however, carries a (ii) _____ cost, since species confined to a single small range have no populations elsewhere from which to recover, and conservationists thus regard the island's botanical richness as at once a treasure and a (iii) _____.
questions.e: Species that 'occur nowhere else' are endemic, native to and restricted to one place; 'cosmopolitan' species occur worldwide. The danger is hidden until a disaster strikes, so the cost is latent, present but not yet visible. 'At once a treasure and' calls for a contrasting negative: a liability, a source of risk. 'Negligible' contradicts the warning, and nothing in the sentence concerns money.

questions.s: The composer's late quartets baffled his contemporaries, who heard in their abrupt shifts of mood only (i) _____, the incoherence of a mind in decline. Later listeners discerned a (ii) _____ logic beneath the apparent disorder, and the works once dismissed as (iii) _____ are now ranked among his most profound.
questions.e: Abrupt shifts heard as 'incoherence' amount to caprice, sudden unpredictable change. The logic later found lay 'beneath the apparent disorder', so it was recondite, hidden and hard to grasp; a 'transparent' logic would have been obvious to contemporaries. Works blamed on a declining mind were dismissed as aberrations, departures from his normal standard. 'Pastiches' (imitations of others' styles) does not fit a charge of incoherence.

questions.s: The new regulation was meant to be (i) _____, applying only until the agency could study the problem; yet, as often happens with stopgap rules, it proved remarkably (ii) _____, and two decades later it remains in force, its (iii) _____ origins largely forgotten.
questions.e: 'Applying only until the agency could study the problem' defines provisional, temporary. 'Yet' and 'remains in force' two decades later show the rule was tenacious, persistently long-lasting; 'ephemeral' (short-lived) is what it was meant to be. Its forgotten beginnings were expedient, chosen for convenience as a quick fix. 'Venerable' (respected for age) describes what it has become, not how it began.

questions.s: Dictionaries were once regarded as (i) _____ authorities whose rulings settled disputes about usage. Modern lexicographers disclaim this role, describing their work as (ii) _____ rather than prescriptive; yet readers persist in consulting dictionaries as arbiters, and the lexicographers' (iii) _____ has done little to change the habit.
questions.e: Authorities whose rulings 'settled disputes' were seen as magisterial, speaking with commanding authority. 'Rather than prescriptive' calls for its contrast, descriptive, recording usage rather than ruling on it; 'normative' means much the same as prescriptive. 'Disclaim this role' is restated by disavowal, a denial of responsibility. 'Imprimatur' (an official stamp of approval) is the authority they reject.

questions.s: The cathedral's builders knew they would not live to see it finished, since construction took more than two centuries; their (i) _____ is all the more striking given how (ii) _____ the project seemed to contemporaries, many of whom mocked it as a folly. Today the structure stands as a monument less to any single architect than to collective (iii) _____.
questions.e: Working for generations on a building they would never see shows tenacity, persistent determination. A project mocked as a folly seemed quixotic, idealistic and impractical. The monument honors the shared virtue that kept work going, steadfastness. 'Prudent' contradicts the mockery, and 'extravagance', though a charge critics might make, does not explain why the builders deserve a monument.

questions.s: The therapist's approach was (i) _____: rather than offering interpretations, she asked questions and let clients reach their own conclusions. Colleagues who favored more (ii) _____ methods considered her passive, but she argued that insights clients arrived at themselves were less likely to be (iii) _____ once therapy ended.
questions.e: Guiding people by questions so that they reach their own conclusions is a Socratic approach; 'didactic' (instructive, lecturing) is its opposite. Colleagues who found her passive preferred directive methods, in which the therapist steers. Her argument is that self-found insight lasts, so it is less likely to be discarded afterward. 'Internalized' and 'cherished' reverse her claim, since she wants these outcomes to be more likely.

questions.s: The botanist was (i) _____ in the field, tramping through swamps in all weathers to collect specimens, but (ii) _____ at home: her herbarium was a jumble of unlabeled sheets, and only after her death did a curator, sorting patiently through the (iii) _____, discover several species new to science.
questions.e: Tramping through swamps 'in all weathers' shows she was indefatigable, tireless. 'But' contrasts this with her home habits: a jumble of unlabeled sheets is slapdash, careless and hasty work. The curator sorted through that clutter. 'Meticulous' contradicts the jumble, 'careless' in the field would leave no contrast with her home habits, and a 'catalog' is what the collection lacked.

questions.s: Satire depends on a shared standard: the satirist mocks what an audience already recognizes as (i) _____. When a society's values are too (ii) _____ for any such consensus to exist, satire loses its target, and what was meant as ridicule may be read as (iii) _____.
questions.e: Mockery works when the audience already sees its target as risible, deserving laughter. Without consensus, values must be fragmented, broken into separate camps; 'uniform' or 'stable' values would make consensus easy. Ridicule that misses its mark may then be taken as its opposite, endorsement, approval. 'Parody' is itself a form of ridicule, so it gives no misreading.

questions.s: Glass appears (i) _____, yet its molecules lack the orderly lattice of a crystal; this (ii) _____ structure once fed the popular claim that old windowpanes flow like a very slow liquid, a notion physicists have since (iii) _____, calculating that any such flow would take far longer than the age of the universe.
questions.e: 'Yet' requires a contrast with lacking a crystal's lattice, so glass looks rigid, like an ordered solid; 'translucent' sets up no such contrast. A structure without an orderly lattice is amorphous, lacking definite form, and 'crystalline' contradicts the clause before it. Showing the flow would take longer than the universe's age means physicists debunked the claim; 'corroborated' reverses their finding.

questions.s: The ethnographer's early reports cast the community's gift exchanges as purely (i) _____, acts of generosity that expected nothing in return. Later fieldwork revealed an intricate (ii) _____: every gift created an obligation, and failure to repay was a source of lasting shame. The earlier account, in short, had mistaken a (iii) _____ system for spontaneous kindness.
questions.e: 'Generosity that expected nothing in return' defines altruistic. Gifts that create obligations to repay form a system of reciprocity, mutual exchange. A system enforced by shame is binding, not 'spontaneous'. 'Voluntary' is the trap: it repeats the early, mistaken view, and 'hierarchy' is never mentioned in the evidence about repayment.

questions.s: The hypothesis was at first greeted with (i) _____, for it required the existence of matter that no telescope had detected.
