As observations accumulated that no rival theory could explain, however, resistance gave way first to grudging tolerance and then to open (ii) _____, until the once (iii) _____ idea had become the field's orthodoxy.
questions.e: Requiring unseen matter would draw skepticism, and the later word 'resistance' confirms it. The sequence moves from resistance toward acceptance, so after grudging tolerance comes open advocacy, active support. An idea that became orthodoxy must once have been heterodox, contrary to accepted views. 'Canonical' describes where the idea ended, not where it began, and 'repudiation' runs backward along the sequence.

questions.s: Glaciologists once assumed that ice sheets respond to warming only (i) _____, over many centuries; recent observations of sudden collapses suggest that their behavior can be far more (ii) _____.
questions.e: “Over many centuries” restates blank (i): ice sheets were thought to respond “ponderously”, slowly and heavily. “Sudden collapses” point the other way, so their behavior can be far more “precipitous”, sudden and steep. “Glacial” is the trap: it sounds right in a sentence about ice, but it means very slow, which repeats the old assumption. “Abruptly” in blank (i) contradicts “over many centuries”.

questions.s: Critics who had dismissed the director's early films as (i) _____ exercises in style were forced to reconsider when her later work revealed that the stylistic flourishes had always served a (ii) _____ purpose.
questions.e: “Dismissed” signals a negative judgment, so the early films were seen as “hollow” exercises in style, empty of meaning. The critics reconsidered because the style turned out to serve a real, “substantive” purpose. “Profound” and “rigorous” are praise, not dismissal; “decorative” and “frivolous” would confirm the critics' first view instead of forcing them to reconsider.

questions.s: Economists had long assumed that the region's farmers were (i) _____ new technology, but a closer look at the data suggested that their hesitation was (ii) _____: the new seeds required irrigation that most farms simply lacked. What looked like stubbornness was, in fact, a (iii) _____ response to real constraints.
questions.e: The farmers' “hesitation” and the word “stubbornness” show that economists thought them “averse to” new technology. The colon then gives a good reason for the hesitation (no irrigation), so it was “warranted”, not “capricious” (driven by whim). A sensible reaction to real limits is “prudent”. “Feigned” fails because nothing suggests the hesitation was pretended, and “reckless” reverses the point.

questions.s: The first stethoscopes were simple wooden tubes, and many physicians (i) _____ them as a gimmick, preferring to press an ear directly to the patient's chest; but the instrument's ability to reveal faint sounds soon made it (ii) _____ in clinical practice.
questions.e: Calling the tubes a “gimmick” and preferring the old method shows that physicians “disparaged” (belittled) them. “But” turns to the instrument's success: its usefulness soon made it “ubiquitous”, found everywhere. “Embraced” contradicts “gimmick”, and “obsolete” reverses the success the second clause describes.

questions.s: The poet's late style is marked by (i) _____: where her early verse sprawled across pages of ornate imagery, the final collection contains poems of only a few lines, each word chosen with (ii) _____ care.
questions.e: The colon explains the late style: short poems instead of sprawling ones, so the style is marked by “concision”, brevity. Words in such poems are chosen with “scrupulous” (extremely careful) care. “Extravagance” describes the early verse, not the late; “perfunctory” (done without real interest) and “haphazard” contradict the idea of carefully chosen words.

questions.s: The planners' proposal to widen the avenue was meant to (i) _____ congestion, yet traffic studies from other cities suggest that new lanes tend to (ii) _____ additional drivers, so that within a few years the roads are as crowded as before. Critics therefore regard the plan as (iii) _____.
questions.e: Widening a road is meant to “alleviate” (ease) congestion. “Yet” introduces a problem: roads end up as crowded as before, which happens only if new lanes “lure” more drivers. A plan that cannot achieve its goal is “futile”. “Discourage” would make the roads emptier, contradicting the result, and “visionary” is praise that critics would not give a self-defeating plan.

questions.s: Far from being a (i) _____ curiosity, the strange behavior of superconductors has proved (ii) _____ to technologies as varied as medical imaging and particle accelerators.
questions.e: “Far from being” sets up a reversal: the behavior was thought a “trivial” curiosity, but in fact it is “integral” (essential) to major technologies. “Fundamental” fails in blank (i) because the sentence denies it, and it makes no sense to deny the importance the second half asserts. “Irrelevant” repeats the rejected view, and “detrimental” (harmful) does not fit technologies that rely on the effect.

questions.s: The philosopher's critics accused her of (i) _____, noting that she had defended both positions in different books; she replied that changing one's mind in light of better arguments is not inconsistency but intellectual (ii) _____.
questions.e: Defending both positions in different books is the evidence for “inconstancy”, a failure to hold one view; her reply even names it as “inconsistency”. She reframes the change as a virtue, “integrity”. “Dogmatism” is the opposite fault (refusing to change); “timidity” and “arrogance” are faults, so they cannot be the positive word her defense needs.

questions.s: The ice core was expected to yield only a (i) _____ record, a few thousand years at most, so the discovery that its lowest layers were nearly a million years old was nothing short of (ii) _____. Even the normally (iii) _____ lead researcher allowed herself a public celebration.
questions.e: “Only” and “a few thousand years at most” show that the team expected a “meager” record. Finding a million years of ice against such expectations is “astonishing”. “Even” in the last sentence means the leader does not usually celebrate in public, so she is normally “reserved”. “Exuberant” reverses that clue: an exuberant person celebrating would not be worth an “even”.

questions.s: Because the dialect was spoken by only a few elderly villagers, linguists worked with some (i) _____ to record it before it became (ii) _____.
questions.e: A language with only a few elderly speakers is about to disappear, so linguists worked with “dispatch” (speed) before it became “defunct” (no longer existing or in use). “Nonchalance” (casual unconcern) and “diffidence” (shyness) ignore the urgency. “Codified” is a trap: recording a dialect may codify it, but that is not a danger to race against.

questions.s: The pianist's recordings are (i) _____ for their tempos, so slow that some listeners find them almost (ii) _____; admirers counter that the slowness reveals inner voices that brisker performances (iii) _____.
questions.e: Tempos that provoke complaints and defenses are unusual, so the recordings are “singular”, one of a kind; “conventional” and “typical” would give no one anything to argue about. Very slow playing can seem “soporific”, sleep-inducing; “frenetic” contradicts “slow”. The admirers' point is that faster performances “blur” the inner voices that slowness reveals. “Illuminate” is the trap: it gives the credit to the brisk performances instead of the slow ones.

questions.s: The biologist cautioned that the drug's success in mice was (i) _____ evidence at best, since many compounds that work in rodents prove (ii) _____ in human trials.
questions.e: “Cautioned” and “at best” mark the evidence as weak, so it is “tentative”. The reason given is that rodent results often fail to carry over, so such compounds prove “ineffectual” in people. “Spurious” (false) is the trap: the biologist doubts how far the result generalizes, not whether it is genuine. “Potent” and “benign” would not justify caution.

questions.s: The investor was (i) _____ by temperament, slow to commit and quick to sell at the first sign of trouble; it is all the more surprising, then, that her most celebrated decision was an (ii) _____ bet on an unproven startup.
questions.e: Being slow to commit and quick to sell shows a “circumspect” (wary, cautious) temperament; “impetuous” (rash) reverses it. “All the more surprising” signals behavior against type, so her famous decision was an “audacious”, daring, bet. “Overcautious” fits her temperament but removes the surprise, and an “inconsequential” bet would not be her most celebrated decision.

questions.s: Birdwatchers long treated the sightings of a rare warbler in the valley as (i) _____ events, unrelated to one another. Only when an ornithologist noticed that the sightings clustered in the same two weeks each spring did anyone suspect that the birds were (ii) _____ visitors, passing through on an (iii) _____ migration route.
questions.e: “Unrelated to one another” restates blank (i): the sightings were treated as “discrete”, separate events. Sightings at the same time every spring mean the birds are “seasonal” visitors following an “established” route. “Vagrant” is the trap: it means a bird that has strayed off course, which is the old view, not the new insight. “Resident” birds would be seen all year, and an “improvised” route would not repeat.

questions.s: Readers who expect the novel's narrator to be a (i) _____ guide will be disappointed: he misremembers dates, contradicts himself, and conceals his own role in the events he describes, making him one of fiction's most (ii) _____ storytellers.
questions.e: The narrator misremembers, contradicts himself and hides things, so readers expecting a “trustworthy” guide will be disappointed, and he is one of fiction's most “unreliable” storytellers. “Deceitful” in blank (i) would make the expectation already negative, so there would be no disappointment. “Garrulous” and “verbose” (talkative, wordy) describe length, which the evidence never mentions.

questions.s: Although the painter insisted that her canvases were purely (i) _____, with no hidden meaning, scholars have found it difficult to resist (ii) _____ them as coded autobiography.
questions.e: “With no hidden meaning” restates blank (i): the painter called her work purely “decorative”. “Although” sets the scholars against her claim, so they cannot resist “construing” (interpreting) the canvases as coded autobiography. “Allegorical” is the trap: an allegory has a hidden meaning, which is exactly what the painter denies. “Dismissing” would agree with the painter rather than resist her.

questions.s: Planetary scientists once regarded the moon as a (i) _____ world, geologically dead for billions of years. Images from a recent probe have (ii) _____ that view, revealing fresh fault lines and young lava flows which suggest that the surface is still being (iii) _____.
questions.e: “Geologically dead” restates blank (i): the moon was seen as a “static” world. Fresh faults and young lava flows have “upended” (overturned) that view; “corroborated” would confirm it. Such features show the surface is still being “reshaped”. “Preserved” is the trap: it fits the old view of an unchanging world, not the new evidence. “Volcanic” in blank (i) contradicts “dead”.

questions.s: The sociologist's survey was hardly (i) _____: it drew its respondents from a single affluent suburb, so its sweeping claims about the nation's habits rest on a (ii) _____ foundation.
questions.e: A sample from one affluent suburb cannot stand for the whole nation, so the survey was hardly “representative”. Sweeping national claims built on such a narrow sample rest on a “precarious” (unstable, risky) foundation. “Solid” and “broad” contradict the criticism, and “expensive” or “anonymous” have nothing to do with the problem the colon describes.

questions.s: Rather than being (i) _____ by the reaction, the catalyst emerges from it (ii) _____, ready to be used again.
questions.e: “Ready to be used again” tells us the catalyst survives the reaction. “Rather than” contrasts that with being “consumed” (used up), and the catalyst emerges “intact”. “Diminished” and “altered” would only make sense if the catalyst were partly used up, which the last phrase denies; “accelerated by the reaction” reverses what a catalyst does.

questions.s: The designer's kitchen tools (i) _____ decoration entirely: no colors, no patterns, nothing but brushed steel. Admirers praise this (ii) _____ as honesty about function; detractors find the results (iii) _____, about as cozy as a hospital ward.
questions.e: The colon lists what is missing, so the tools “eschew” (deliberately avoid) decoration. Bare steel with no color reflects “austerity”, severe plainness; “opulence” (luxury) and “eclecticism” (mixing styles) contradict the description. “About as cozy as a hospital ward” is sarcastic, so detractors find the tools “clinical”, cold and impersonal. “Inviting” takes the sarcasm literally.

questions.s: Early travelers described the herding societies of the steppe as (i) _____, wandering at random in search of grass; later anthropologists showed that their movements followed routes so (ii) _____ that families returned to the same campsites year after year.
questions.e: “Wandering at random” restates blank (i): the travelers thought the herders “aimless”. The anthropologists corrected this; returning to the same campsites every year shows routes that were “invariable”, never changing. “Sedentary” (staying in one place) contradicts “wandering”, and “improvised” would support the travelers' mistaken view instead of correcting it.

questions.s: The proof was so (i) _____ that only a handful of specialists could follow it at first; it took a decade of patient commentary before its ideas became (ii) _____ to ordinary mathematicians.
questions.e: If only a few specialists could follow it, the proof was “abstruse”, hard to understand. Years of explanation then made its ideas “accessible”. “Elegant” is the trap: elegance is a compliment and does not explain why so few could follow. “Alien” reverses the effect of the commentary.

questions.s: Introduced to control beetles in the sugar fields, the toads proved (i) _____ at that task, ignoring the beetles almost entirely. Worse, they multiplied (ii) _____, and their poison has since (iii) _____ native predators that try to eat them.
questions.e: Toads that ignored the beetles were “inept” at controlling them; “adept” reverses this. “Worse” introduces more bad news, so they multiplied “prodigiously”, in huge numbers. Their poison has “decimated” (killed large numbers of) predators that eat them. “Harmlessly” fails because it cancels the “Worse”, and “nourished” makes no sense for a poison.

questions.s: The painter's canvases are deceptively (i) _____: at first glance they show only a few flat bands of color, but sustained looking reveals a (ii) _____ web of tones layered beneath the surface.
questions.e: “Only a few flat bands of color” makes the canvases look “artless”, simple and unsophisticated; “deceptively” warns that the simplicity hides something. Beneath lies a “labyrinthine” (maze-like, intricate) web of tones. “Florid” (elaborately ornate) contradicts the plain first impression, and “transparent” cancels the contrast that “but” sets up.

questions.s: Volunteers deprived of sleep rated their own performance as barely (i) _____, even as their scores on the test plummeted, which suggests that fatigue impairs not only skill but also the capacity to (ii) _____ that impairment.
questions.e: “Even as their scores plummeted” shows a gap between self-rating and reality: the volunteers thought their performance barely “diminished”. So fatigue also weakens the ability to “discern” (notice) the impairment. “Exceptional” is too strong for “barely”, and “exaggerate” reverses the finding, since the volunteers underrated rather than overrated their decline.

questions.s: The pesticide was expected to (i) _____ the harvest by eliminating the beetles that ravaged the crop. In practice it proved (ii) _____: by also killing the wasps that preyed on a second pest, it allowed that pest to multiply, and the resulting damage (iii) _____ whatever the spraying had saved.
questions.e: Killing the beetles was meant to “safeguard” the harvest. “In practice” signals the plan failed: the second pest's damage “negated” (cancelled) the savings, so the spraying was “self-defeating”, working against its own aim. “Irrelevant” is too weak, because the pesticide actively caused new damage, and “amplified” would mean the damage increased the savings.

questions.s: Early photographers were often accused of merely (i) _____ nature, as if pointing a camera required no judgment; the best of them answered by producing images whose composition was as (ii) _____ as any painter's.
questions.e: The charge was that photography takes no judgment, so photographers were “merely transcribing” (copying) nature. The answer to that charge is composition as “deliberate”, carefully chosen, as a painter's. “Idealizing” is the trap: improving on nature would require judgment, the opposite of the accusation. “Accidental” and “crude” would support the critics.

questions.s: Weather forecasting was long regarded as (i) _____ guesswork, but advances in computing have made week-ahead forecasts so (ii) _____ that farmers and airlines now plan around them.
questions.e: “But” contrasts the old view with the new one. Forecasting was seen as “crude” guesswork; now forecasts are so “dependable” that businesses plan around them. “Scientific guesswork” is self-contradictory and removes the contrast. “Tentative” and “ambiguous” forecasts would not be something farmers and airlines rely on.

questions.s: A curator mounting an exhibition of fragile manuscripts faces a (i) _____ choice: display the originals and risk damage from light, or show facsimiles and (ii) _____ visitors of the encounter with the real object. Most curators accept that some (iii) _____ is inevitable and rotate the originals for brief periods.
questions.e: Either option costs something, so the choice is “stark”, harsh and unavoidable; “trivial” and “welcome” ignore the losses on both sides. Showing copies would “deprive” visitors of seeing the real thing; “spare” wrongly treats that loss as a favor. Rotating originals for short periods is a “compromise” between the two risks. “Negligence” fails because the curators act deliberately and carefully.

questions.s: The update was so (i) _____ that most users never noticed it had been installed; a less careful team might have left the program feeling (ii) _____, with familiar buttons suddenly moved and menus renamed.
questions.e: If users never noticed the change, the update was “seamless”, smooth and without visible joins. A careless team would have moved buttons and renamed menus, leaving the program “disjointed”, its parts no longer fitting together. “Ostentatious” (showy) and “hurried” contradict an unnoticed update. “Intuitive” and “immaculate” describe the good result, not what careless work would produce.

questions.s: When the surgeon first proposed operating under anesthesia, many colleagues were (i) _____, fearing that patients would never wake. The first public demonstrations, however, went so smoothly that skepticism quickly (ii) _____, and within a few years operating on a conscious patient seemed not merely old-fashioned but (iii) _____.
questions.e: Colleagues “fearing that patients would never wake” were “apprehensive”; “sanguine” (optimistic) reverses this. Smooth demonstrations made skepticism “evaporate”. “Not merely old-fashioned but” calls for a stronger negative word, and surgery on a conscious patient came to seem “barbaric”, cruel. “Prudent” is positive and “commonplace” is weaker than “old-fashioned”, not stronger.

questions.s: Newspaper writers of the era favored a (i) _____ style, piling clause upon clause; when the telegraph made every transmitted word expensive, reporters learned to write in a more (ii) _____ manner.
questions.e: “Piling clause upon clause” defines a “prolix” style, long-winded and wordy; “terse” is the opposite. Paying for each word pushed reporters toward a “clipped” manner, short and abrupt. “Ornate” and “leisurely” describe the old style that cost too much, not the change the telegraph forced.

questions.s: Socratic questioning is often mistaken for mere (i) _____, a way of scoring points against an opponent. Its aim, however, is (ii) _____ rather than victory: by exposing contradictions in what we believe, it clears the ground for (iii) _____ understanding.
questions.e: “Scoring points” describes “sophistry”, clever but misleading argument meant to win. “However” corrects that view: the aim is “inquiry”, a search for truth, rather than victory. Clearing away contradictions prepares the way for “sounder” understanding. “Conquest” and “rhetoric” (the art of persuading) are both kinds of winning, the very thing the sentence sets aside.

questions.s: Medieval maps were often less concerned with geographic (i) _____ than with meaning: the mapmaker's own city might sit at the center, drawn far larger than its neighbors, reflecting its (ii) _____ in his eyes rather than its actual size.
questions.e: Placing one's own city at the center and drawing it oversized ignores real geography, so the maps cared less about “accuracy” than meaning. The large drawing reflects the city's “prominence”, its importance, in the mapmaker's eyes. “Symbolism” is the trap for blank (i): it is the “meaning” the maps did care about. “Proximity” would explain the central position but not the exaggerated size.

questions.s: Desert soils can appear (i) _____, mere sand and rock, yet many are bound together by a thin crust of mosses, lichens and bacteria. This living skin is surprisingly (ii) _____: a single footstep can crush it, and it may take decades to (iii) _____.
questions.e: “Mere sand and rock” restates blank (i): the soils look “lifeless”, while “yet” reveals the living crust. A crust that one footstep can crush is “fragile”; “resilient” reverses the colon's evidence. Damage that lasts decades means the crust is slow to “regenerate”, grow back. “Erode” is the trap: the crust is already crushed, so what takes decades is recovery, not further loss.

questions.s: The biographer's account is (i) _____ rather than critical: she quotes her subject's letters at length but rarely questions them, so the book reads less like history than like (ii) _____.
questions.e: A biographer who never questions her subject's letters is “reverential”, full of deep respect, rather than critical. Such a book reads like “hagiography”, writing that treats its subject as a saint. “Dispassionate” is the trap: it means neutral and objective, which would fit a critical historian, not an uncritical admirer. “Exposé” and “satire” attack their subjects.

questions.s: Park managers initially treated the spread of the vine as a (i) _____ problem that would fade once a dry summer arrived. When the vine instead (ii) _____, they were forced to clear entire hillsides by hand, a remedy far more (iii) _____ than the early action they had declined to take.
questions.e: A problem expected to “fade” is “passing”, temporary; “chronic” (long-lasting) reverses the managers' belief. “Instead” overturns that expectation, so the vine “proliferated”, spread rapidly; “withered” is what they had hoped. Clearing whole hillsides by hand is far more “arduous” (laborious, exhausting) than early action. “Palatable” and “modest” contradict the scale of the work.

questions.s: Though the slime mold is a single-celled organism, about as (i) _____ as life gets, it finds the shortest route through a maze with a (ii) _____ that has astonished researchers.
questions.e: “Single-celled” and “about as ... as life gets” call for a word meaning simple: “rudimentary”, at the most basic stage. “Though” sets that simplicity against a clever feat, so the mold shows “resourcefulness”. “Predatory” and “colorful” do not contrast with problem-solving, and “lethargy” (sluggishness) would not astonish anyone.

questions.s: Preservationists argued that the old market hall was (i) _____ to the neighborhood's identity and that demolishing it would be (ii) _____. The developers, however, dismissed such objections as (iii) _____, insisting that a building should be judged by its usefulness, not by the memories attached to it.
questions.e: Preservationists defend the hall, so they call it “central” to the neighborhood's identity and its loss “irrevocable”, impossible to undo. The developers reply that memories do not matter, which means they dismiss the objections as “sentimental”, based on feeling. “Pragmatic” is the developers' own stance on usefulness, not their label for the other side; “legalistic” has no support.

questions.s: Free verse is sometimes thought to require less skill than metered poetry, but its apparent (i) _____ is misleading: without the support of a regular beat, the poet must create rhythm through (ii) _____ attention to the sound of every phrase.
questions.e: Free verse is thought to need less skill, so its apparent “laxity” (looseness, lack of strictness) is what misleads. Without a fixed beat, the poet must pay “unremitting” (never easing) attention to sound. “Rigor” reverses the common view described in the first clause, and “casual” or “occasional” attention would confirm that view instead of correcting it.

questions.s: The utilitarian's principle looks (i) _____ in the abstract: who could object to maximizing happiness? Its difficulties emerge only in particular cases, where the calculus seems to (ii) _____ acts that ordinary moral sense finds abhorrent, so that what began as a self-evident principle ends in conclusions many find (iii) _____.
questions.e: The rhetorical question shows the principle seems harmless at first: “innocuous”. The trouble is that the calculation can “sanction” (approve) acts most people find abhorrent; “prohibit” would remove the difficulty. Approving abhorrent acts leads to “repugnant” (deeply offensive) conclusions. “Sinister” in blank (i) jumps ahead to the problem the sentence says appears only later, and “banal” is too mild for conclusions about abhorrent acts.

questions.s: The grandmaster's style was often called (i) _____, since she seldom attacked and seemed content to shuffle her pieces while opponents overreached. Yet this apparent (ii) _____ concealed a strategy of considerable (iii) _____: she was inviting errors she had foreseen many moves in advance.
questions.e: Seldom attacking and shuffling pieces looks “passive”; “pugnacious” (eager to fight) is the opposite. “Apparent” and “concealed” show that the look of “inertia” (inactivity) hid something. Luring opponents into errors foreseen far ahead takes “guile”, sly cunning. “Virtuosity” is the trap for blank (ii): it describes the hidden skill, not the misleading surface. “Transparency” contradicts “concealed”.

questions.s: To call the region's recovery (i) _____ would be premature; the gains, though real, are concentrated in a single industry whose fortunes have historically been anything but (ii) _____.
questions.e: “Premature” means the label is too optimistic for now, so the speaker will not yet call the recovery “assured”. “Precarious” is the hurried reader's choice, but it is the speaker's actual worry, not a claim that would be premature. “Chimerical” (imaginary) is ruled out by “though real”. The double negative “anything but” means the industry has been unstable, so its fortunes have been anything but “steady”; “mercurial” (changeable) reverses the meaning once negated.

questions.s: The recommendation letter was (i) _____: it praised the candidate's punctuality and neat handwriting while saying nothing about her research. Committee members fluent in the genre read it as a (ii) _____ warning, all the more (iii) _____ for being dressed as praise.
questions.e: Praising trivial habits while staying silent about research is “equivocal”, open to two readings; “unstinting” (generous, without reservation) ignores the telling silence. Only readers who know the genre notice the warning, so it is “veiled”, not “blatant”. Disguised as praise, it becomes even more “barbed”, sharply hurtful. “Innocuous” (harmless) reverses “all the more”.

questions.s: Plate tectonics met fierce resistance when first proposed, chiefly because its advocates could not identify a (i) _____ mechanism by which continents might move. The idea was not so much refuted as (ii) _____ for decades, until evidence from the seafloor made it impossible to (iii) _____.
questions.e: Resistance arose because no believable cause was known, so advocates lacked a “plausible” mechanism. “Not so much refuted as” points to a milder fate: the idea was “shelved”, set aside unresolved. Seafloor evidence eventually made it impossible to “gainsay” (deny). “Vindicated” describes the ending, not the decades of neglect, and “corroborate” reverses the logic: the evidence made the idea easy, not impossible, to confirm.

questions.s: Proponents of miasma theory were not simply (i) _____; their belief that disease spread through foul air led them to drain swamps and clean streets, measures that were (ii) _____ effective even though the reasoning behind them was (iii) _____.
questions.e: The semicolon introduces evidence that these thinkers achieved something useful, so they were not simply “benighted”, ignorant and unenlightened. Their measures worked “even though” the reasoning behind them was “erroneous”, so the success was “serendipitous”, a lucky accident. “Prescient” (seeing the future) is the trap for blank (i): the sentence defends them against a charge, and prescience is not a charge. “Predictably” clashes with “even though”.

questions.s: Classical models portrayed consumers as (i) _____ calculators who weigh every option before buying. Behavioral economists find this portrait (ii) _____: real shoppers rely on habit and rules of thumb, and their choices can be swayed by details as (iii) _____ as the order in which products appear on a shelf.
questions.e: Calculators who weigh every option are “dispassionate”, free of emotion. Behavioral economists reject the portrait as “fanciful”, unrealistic, because real shoppers use habits. The order of products on a shelf is an example of an “inconsequential” (unimportant) detail that still sways choices. “Impulsive” describes the real shoppers, not the classical model, and “compelling” contradicts the evidence after the colon.

questions.s: The skeptic's challenge is notoriously difficult to (i) _____: any argument offered against it must rely on the very faculties of reason whose reliability the skeptic has called into question, so every reply seems (ii) _____.
questions.e: The colon explains why the challenge is hard to “rebut” (argue against successfully). A reply that uses reason to defend reason assumes what it is trying to prove, so it seems “circular”. “Redundant” is the trap: it means unnecessary repetition, but the flaw described is assuming the conclusion, not repeating it. “Articulate” fails because the difficulty concerns answering the challenge, not stating it.

questions.s: The documentary's (i) _____ style—long, static shots, no narration, no music—struck some viewers as tedious. Others found that its very refusal to (ii) _____ the audience's responses gave them room to think, and they praised the director's (iii) _____ in letting images speak for themselves.
questions.e: No narration and no music describe an “ascetic” (severely self-denying) style; “frenetic” (wildly fast) contradicts “long, static shots”. Leaving room to think means the film refuses to “dictate” how viewers respond. Holding back and letting images speak is “forbearance”, patient restraint. “Didactic” (aiming to teach or preach) is the trap: a preachy film would dictate responses. “Temerity” (reckless boldness) does not describe restraint.

questions.s: For decades physicists regarded the luminiferous ether as (i) _____: light was a wave, and a wave, they reasoned, must travel through some medium. When increasingly precise experiments failed to detect it, the ether was not abandoned at once but (ii) _____ with ever more elaborate hypotheses, until it seemed less a physical substance than a (iii) _____ invoked to save appearances.
questions.e: The colon gives reasoning that made the ether seem self-evidently necessary, so it was “axiomatic”. “Not abandoned at once but” means it was kept alive, “propped up” with new hypotheses; “supplanted” (replaced) is what “not abandoned” rules out. Something invented only to save appearances is a “contrivance”, an artificial device. “Dubious” in blank (i) is how it came to look later, not how it was regarded for decades.

questions.s: The sculptor's late works, once dismissed as the (i) _____ efforts of an artist past his prime, are now seen as deliberate experiments, their roughness not a sign of failing skill but a (ii) _____ rejection of polish.
questions.e: “Past his prime” and “failing skill” show the old view: the works were “enfeebled” efforts, weakened by age. The new view calls them deliberate, so their roughness is a “willful” (intentional) rejection of polish. “Audacious” would be praise, not dismissal; “negligent” (careless) brings back the old view of failing skill, and “grudging” clashes with deliberate experiment.

questions.s: Mid-century planners, convinced that the mixed, crowded streets of old neighborhoods were (i) _____, replaced them with orderly towers set in open lawns. The new districts proved strangely (ii) _____: with shops and homes separated, the sidewalks emptied, and the casual surveillance of passersby that had once kept streets safe (iii) _____.
questions.e: Planners who tore the old streets down thought them “pathological”, diseased and harmful; “vibrant” and “picturesque” are praise that would not motivate demolition. Empty sidewalks make the new districts “desolate”. With fewer passersby, the informal watching that kept streets safe “dwindled”. “Endured” is the trap: it ignores that the watchers themselves had gone.

questions.s: Far from being an (i) _____, the conductor was known for consulting the orchestra's principal players before settling on an interpretation, a practice that some colleagues regarded as an (ii) _____ of authority.
questions.e: Consulting the players is the opposite of ruling alone, so “far from being” rejects the label “autocrat”, a ruler with absolute power. Critical colleagues would see sharing decisions as an “abdication”, a giving up, of authority. “Usurpation” is the trap: it means seizing power wrongly, which reverses what consulting others does. “Assertion” likewise reverses the practice.

questions.s: Purists who regard every performance of a Baroque work on modern instruments as a (i) _____ forget that the composers themselves were (ii) _____ about such matters, rewriting their pieces freely for whatever players happened to be available. Insistence on a single “authentic” version is thus itself somewhat (iii) _____.
questions.e: Purists see modern-instrument performances as a “desecration”, a violation of something sacred. The composers rewrote pieces for whatever players were at hand, so they were “pragmatic”, practical, about instruments; “fastidious” (very particular) is what the purists are. Demanding one fixed version imposes a later idea on the past, so it is “anachronistic”, out of keeping with the period. “Authoritative” would support the purists, whom the sentence criticizes.

questions.s: The auction house's estimates are rarely (i) _____: a painting expected to fetch a modest sum may spark a bidding war, while a celebrated canvas can fail to sell at all. This (ii) _____ reflects the fact that prices depend less on any intrinsic quality than on the (iii) _____ of the particular collectors in the room.
questions.e: The examples show estimates going badly wrong, so they are rarely “infallible”, never mistaken. Prices that swing unexpectedly show “volatility”. If prices do not follow quality, they follow the “whims” (sudden fancies) of the bidders present. “Conservative” is the trap: it explains only the bidding war, not the celebrated canvas that fails to sell. “Unanimity” contradicts bidding wars.

questions.s: The new diagnostic test is (i) _____ to a fault: it flags nearly every patient who has the disease but also so many who do not that its positive results are (ii) _____ without confirmation.
questions.e: A test that catches nearly every true case but also many false ones is “sensitive” to a fault: it reacts too readily. Because many positives are wrong, a positive result is “inconclusive” on its own. “Selective” is the trap: a selective test would flag few patients, the opposite of the problem described. “Definitive” reverses the point of “without confirmation”.

questions.s: The novelist's first readers were (i) _____ by the book's fragmented structure and abandoned it in droves. Yet what baffled one generation (ii) _____ the next, and the techniques once condemned as (iii) _____ are now taught in writing courses as models of innovation.
questions.e: Readers who abandoned a baffling book were “nonplussed”, confused and unsure how to respond. “Yet” signals a reversal: the next generation was “captivated”. Techniques now praised as innovative were once condemned as “perverse”, deliberately contrary. “Conventional” and “derivative” fail because they would never be the complaint against techniques that baffled readers by their newness.

questions.s: The volcano's long (i) _____ lulled nearby residents into treating it as extinct, so when it finally erupted, evacuation plans proved woefully (ii) _____.
questions.e: Only a long period of inactivity, “quiescence”, would make people think a volcano was extinct; “turbulence” reverses this. Residents who expected no eruption would have weak plans, so they proved “inadequate”. “Premature” fails because plans cannot be too early for an eruption that has already happened.

questions.s: Medieval merchants trading across great distances could not rely on courts to enforce their contracts; instead, a merchant who cheated a partner found himself (i) _____ by the whole network of traders, who refused to deal with him. The threat of such (ii) _____ made honesty less a matter of virtue than of (iii) _____.
questions.e: Traders who refuse to deal with a cheat have “ostracized” him, shut him out of the group. That shared punishment is a “reprisal”, retaliation for a wrong. “Litigation” is the trap: the sentence says merchants could not rely on courts. If cheating costs a merchant his whole trade, honesty becomes a matter of “self-interest” rather than virtue; “happenstance” (chance) ignores the deliberate calculation.

questions.s: The second law of thermodynamics is sometimes invoked as a (i) _____ for pessimism, proof that everything tends toward decay. Yet the same law (ii) _____ the emergence of local order—snowflakes, living cells—provided that disorder increases elsewhere; it is thus less a decree of universal ruin than an (iii) _____ rule of accounting, balancing gains in one place against losses in another.
questions.e: “Proof that everything tends toward decay” restates blank (i): the law is cited as a “warrant” (justification) for pessimism. “Yet” and “provided that” show the law allows local order under a condition, so it “countenances” (permits) it; “mandates” (requires) goes too far, and “precludes” reverses it. A rule that simply balances gains against losses is “impartial”. “Optimistic” is the trap: rejecting pessimism does not make the law hopeful, only neutral.

questions.s: The fossil was hailed as a (i) _____ form linking dinosaurs and birds, but closer study revealed that its feathered tail had been glued onto an unrelated skeleton. The episode was a (ii) _____ reminder that the desire for a spectacular find can (iii) _____ even experienced researchers' judgment.
questions.e: Something “linking dinosaurs and birds” is a “transitional” form. “Spurious” (fake) is the trap: it is what the fossil turned out to be, but no one would hail a fossil as fake. A hoax that fooled experts is a “chastening” (humbling, corrective) reminder; “gratifying” reverses the tone. Eagerness for a great find can “cloud” judgment, not “sharpen” it.

questions.s: Her argument is (i) _____ but not sound: each step follows from the last, yet the premise from which it begins is false, so the conclusion, however rigorously derived, remains (ii) _____.
questions.e: In logic an argument whose steps follow correctly is “valid”; it is sound only if its premises are also true. Because the starting premise is false, the conclusion remains “suspect”, open to doubt. “Fallacious” contradicts “each step follows from the last”. “Inescapable” is the trap: rigorous derivation makes a conclusion inescapable only from true premises.

questions.s: Early animated features were dismissed by many critics as (i) _____ fare, fit only for children. Yet the studios' artists pursued their craft with (ii) _____ seriousness, studying the movement of animals frame by frame, and their technical discoveries were soon (iii) _____ by live-action filmmakers eager to borrow them.
questions.e: “Fit only for children” restates blank (i): critics called the films “juvenile”. “Yet” turns to the artists' real commitment: studying motion frame by frame shows “unflagging” (tireless) seriousness, not “intermittent” effort. Filmmakers “eager to borrow” the discoveries “appropriated” them, took them for their own use. “Disdained” contradicts “eager”.

questions.s: Inoculation with material from smallpox sores was a (i) _____ remedy: it usually produced a mild case that conferred lifelong immunity, but it occasionally triggered the very illness it was meant to prevent. Physicians therefore welcomed the cowpox vaccine, which offered the same protection without the (ii) _____ hazard, and within decades the older practice had been (iii) _____.
questions.e: A remedy that usually protects but sometimes causes the disease is “double-edged”, with both good and bad effects; “foolproof” ignores the risk. The new vaccine removed the “attendant” hazard, the danger that came with the old method. Once a safer option existed, the old practice was “proscribed” (forbidden). “Negligible” contradicts the reason physicians welcomed the vaccine, and “perfected” would keep the old practice in use.

questions.s: Decades of failed attempts had made decipherment of the ancient script seem (i) _____, so when a young linguist announced a solution, senior scholars greeted the claim with (ii) _____, an attitude that softened only when her readings of newly found tablets proved correct.
questions.e: After decades of failure, the project looked “chimerical”, as unrealistic as a fantasy. Scholars expecting failure greeted the claim with “incredulity”, disbelief, which “softened” once the readings were confirmed. “Imminent” and “routine” contradict decades of failure. “Indifference” is the trap: it is negative, but an attitude that changes when proof arrives is doubt, not lack of interest.

questions.s: The city's transit agency, long (i) _____ for its chronic delays, has lately become an unlikely model of reform. Its new director, rather than announcing grand plans, concentrated on (ii) _____ improvements—repainting stations, fixing signals, posting accurate timetables—whose cumulative effect has been anything but (iii) _____.
questions.e: Chronic delays make the agency “notorious”, famous for something bad; “lauded” (praised) contradicts the “unlikely model” turn. Unlike grand plans, fixing signals and repainting stations are “prosaic”, ordinary and unexciting, improvements; “visionary” is what the director avoided. Because the agency is now a model, the combined effect has been “anything but negligible”. “Substantial” is the trap: after “anything but” it would mean the effect was small.

questions.s: Because poets in the period depended on wealthy patrons, dedications were often (i) _____, heaping praise on figures the poet scarcely knew. Readers today may find such flattery (ii) _____, but to contemporaries it was a convention as (iii) _____ as the signature at the bottom of a letter.
questions.e: Heaping praise on patrons out of dependence is “obsequious”, servilely flattering. “Perfunctory” is the trap: praise for strangers might sound half-hearted, but “heaping praise” means it was lavish, not minimal. Modern readers find such flattery “cloying”, sickeningly sweet. “But” contrasts this with how contemporaries saw it: as a convention as “unremarkable” as a signature. “Scandalous” would agree with the modern reaction instead of contrasting with it.

questions.s: Admirers credit the reform with (i) _____ the city's finances, but the improvement is more apparent than real: the deficit shrank only because repairs to bridges and roads were deferred, a (ii) _____ that will make future budgets even tighter.
questions.e: Admirers give the reform credit, so they say it is “shoring up” (strengthening) the finances. The improvement is only apparent because it comes from postponing repairs, a “stopgap”, a temporary fix that stores up costs. “Panacea” (cure-all) and “windfall” (unexpected gain) are positive words that contradict “more apparent than real” and “even tighter”.

questions.s: The claim that some infinite sets are larger than others struck many nineteenth-century mathematicians as not merely (i) _____ but absurd, an offense against common sense. The proof, however, was (ii) _____: once its premises were granted, the conclusion followed with a rigor that left critics little choice except to (iii) _____ the premises themselves.
questions.e: “Not merely ... but absurd” needs a milder negative than absurd: “counterintuitive”, contrary to what seems natural. “However” turns to the proof's strength: it was “unassailable”, impossible to attack. If the reasoning cannot be faulted, critics can only “impugn” (challenge the truth of) the premises. “Embrace” fails because these are critics looking for a way out, and “slipshod” contradicts “rigor”.

questions.s: The choreographer's early works were (i) _____, packing every moment with leaps and spins until audiences felt almost battered. Her mature pieces, by contrast, are notable for their (ii) _____; a dancer may stand nearly motionless for minutes, and a single raised arm can carry the (iii) _____ of an entire climax.
questions.e: Leaps and spins at every moment are “frenetic”, wildly energetic; “languid” (slow, relaxed) describes the opposite. “By contrast” and near-motionless dancers point to “economy”, achieving much with few movements. “Virtuosity” is the trap: it means dazzling skill, which fits the early works, not the restrained later ones. A single gesture carrying the “import” (significance) of a climax completes the idea; “levity” would undercut a climax.

questions.s: Bronze Age smiths had no theory of alloys; their skill was (i) _____, passed from master to apprentice by demonstration, and it was no less (ii) _____ for lacking a scientific explanation.
questions.e: Knowledge passed on by demonstration rather than by written rules is “tacit”, understood without being stated. “Theoretical” contradicts “no theory”, and “codified” (written into a system) contradicts learning by demonstration. “No less ... for lacking” defends the skill, so it was no less “sophisticated”. “Rudimentary” is the trap: “no less rudimentary” would insult the skill the sentence defends.

questions.s: Demographers had predicted that the country's birth rate would (i) _____ only gradually as incomes rose, as it had elsewhere. Instead it fell with a (ii) _____ that surprised everyone, dropping by half in a single decade, a change so (iii) _____ that schools built for a growing population stood half empty within a few years.
questions.e: “Instead it fell” shows the prediction was also a decline, only slower, so the rate was expected to “subside” gradually; “surge” reverses the direction. Halving in a decade shows “celerity”, great speed. Half-empty schools prove the change was “drastic”, severe. “Imperceptible” contradicts the visible effect on schools, and “regularity” misses the surprise of the speed.

questions.s: Scientists like to describe their field as a (i) _____, in which ideas rise or fall on evidence alone. Historians of science paint a less (ii) _____ picture: reputations, funding and personal rivalries have often determined which theories received a hearing, and good ideas from (iii) _____ researchers have sometimes languished for decades.
questions.e: A field where ideas succeed “on evidence alone” is a “meritocracy”, a system that rewards merit. The historians' account, in which reputation and money matter, is less “flattering” to scientists. If reputation decides who gets a hearing, it is ideas from “obscure” (little-known) researchers that are neglected. “Cynical” is the trap: the historians' picture is the MORE cynical one, so “less cynical” reverses the contrast.

questions.s: The film's score is so (i) _____ that viewers rarely notice it, yet removing it, as one experiment showed, leaves the scenes curiously (ii) _____.
questions.e: Music that viewers rarely notice is “unobtrusive”, not drawing attention to itself. “Yet” shows the score still matters: without it the scenes feel “inert”, lifeless. “Bombastic” and “memorable” contradict “rarely notice”. “Suspenseful” fails because removing the music would weaken, not add, dramatic tension.

questions.s: Although the ground-based telescope's images are less (i) _____ than those from orbiting observatories, its enormous mirror gathers enough light to detect galaxies so (ii) _____ that no space telescope has yet recorded them; what it lacks in sharpness it more than (iii) _____ in reach.
questions.e: “What it lacks in sharpness” restates blank (i): the images are less “crisp”. Collecting more light matters for galaxies that are very “faint”; “luminous” (bright) galaxies would not need a giant mirror. Making up for a weakness with a strength is what “recoups” means. “Forfeits” (gives up) reverses the logic of “more than”.

questions.s: Prices, in the economist's view, are not arbitrary numbers but (i) _____ signals: a rising price for copper tells miners to dig more and manufacturers to economize, coordinating millions of decisions that no central planner could (ii) _____.
questions.e: The colon shows prices carrying rich information to many people at once, so they are “telling” signals, revealing and meaningful. “Capricious” (unpredictable) repeats the “arbitrary” view the sentence rejects, and “punitive” (punishing) misses the point that prices guide rather than penalize. Prices coordinate decisions that no planner could “orchestrate”, arrange in harmony. “Subvert” (undermine) makes no sense as something a planner would try to do with these decisions.

questions.s: The poem's surface is (i) _____, a sequence of plain statements about a garden; its power lies in what it (ii) _____, the longing the speaker never names but that presses on every line. Readers who mistake its restraint for (iii) _____ miss the point entirely.
questions.e: Plain statements about a garden make the surface “placid”, calm and untroubled; “turbulent” and “ornate” contradict “plain”. A longing that is “never named” is something the poem “withholds”, not “proclaims”. Readers who miss what lies beneath would mistake restraint for “vapidity”, emptiness of thought. “Profundity” is the trap: it is what the poem actually has, so mistaking restraint for it would not be missing the point.

questions.s: Bloodletting persisted for centuries not because physicians were (i) _____ but because the theory behind it was internally (ii) _____: if illness arose from an excess of blood, removing blood was the obvious cure. Only when careful trials compared treated and untreated patients did the practice's (iii) _____ become undeniable.
questions.e: “Not because ... but because” denies a charge against the physicians, so blank (i) needs a fault: “obtuse”, slow to understand. The colon shows the theory's logic hanging together, so it was internally “coherent”; “contradictory” reverses the colon. Trials comparing patients exposed the practice's “futility”, its uselessness. “Efficacy” is the trap: the sentence explains why a mistaken practice lasted, so the trials must have revealed failure.

questions.s: The spokesperson's statement was a model of (i) _____: it expressed regret without admitting fault and acknowledged concerns without promising action, leaving reporters with nothing they could (ii) _____.
questions.e: Saying something without committing to anything is “prevarication”, speaking evasively to avoid the plain truth. “Contrition” (sincere remorse) is the trap: the statement “expressed regret”, but without admitting fault, so the regret is a dodge rather than real contrition. A carefully empty statement gives reporters nothing to “seize on”, nothing to grab and use. “Overlook” reverses the point: the statement leaves everything to overlook.

questions.s: The corpuscular theory of light held sway for a century largely because of its author's (i) _____; few physicists dared contradict the man who had explained the motions of the planets. When experiments on interference finally (ii) _____ the rival wave theory, its champions met resistance less from evidence than from (iii) _____.
questions.e: Few dared contradict a famous author, so the theory survived on his “prestige”. Experiments that left the wave theory's champions facing only non-evidential resistance must have “vindicated” (proved right) it; “refuted” would give critics real evidence. The remaining resistance came from “deference”, respect for the great man's authority. “Data” contradicts “less from evidence”, and “apathy” ignores the reverence the first sentence describes.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage describes the crows' tools, the mix of inherited tendency, practice and possible copying behind them, and why they may reveal which ingredients of tool use are necessary. The second choice is too extreme, since captive crows with no models still poke sticks into crevices. The third overstates the evidence: many researchers 'prefer caution' about calling the styles culture.
o: Tool use remains a reliable mark that separates humans from all other animals.
New Caledonian crows learn to make their tools entirely by watching and copying their parents.
The local styles of crow tools have now been shown to be a genuine form of animal culture.
The crows' toolmaking draws on several capacities and may show what tool use truly requires.
The brains of crows are organized in much the same way as the brains of chimpanzees and other primates.

questions.s: According to the passage, young crows raised in captivity without seeing an adult use a tool
questions.e: The second paragraph says such crows 'will still pick up sticks and poke them into crevices,' which suggests an inherited tendency. The fourth choice reverses the passage, which calls early attempts clumsy, and the third assumes that captive birds could learn a local style with no one to copy.
o: never attempt to use any kind of tool
make leaf tools in the same local style as wild crows
make more skillful tools than wild juveniles do
learn at once to cut barbed probes from leaves

questions.s: The passage suggests that which of the following could explain why leaf tools differ in shape from one area to another? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The second paragraph offers learning by 'watching and copying,' and the third offers 'differences in the plants available' as an alternative the researchers cannot yet rule out. Different species are never mentioned; the passage treats all the birds as New Caledonian crows.
o: Young birds copy the designs used by adults nearby.
The plants available differ from one area to another.
The crows in different areas belong to different species.

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
questions.e: The first two paragraphs set the restorers' principle against the critics' objection, and the third says the critics' view prevailed but is 'harder to apply than to state.' The fourth choice reverses the guidelines, which discourage conjectural reconstruction. The third picks up a point the critics make in passing rather than the passage's purpose.
o: argue that nineteenth-century restorers should have rebuilt even more of the missing towers and carvings
describe a dispute over how to treat old buildings and the complications facing the view that prevailed
explain how medieval builders planned and constructed their churches over the course of centuries
criticize modern international guidelines for permitting reconstruction that is based on conjecture
show that visitors prefer old buildings that have never been restored in any way

questions.s: Select the sentence in the third paragraph that identifies a difficulty arising from the nature of repair work itself.
questions.e: The third sentence says every repair replaces some material, so repair and creative restoration shade into each other. The fourth and fifth sentences describe a different difficulty, one that arises from the history of the nineteenth-century restorations rather than from repair work as such; the second sentence announces a difficulty without identifying one.
o: The principle the critics championed eventually prevailed, and international guidelines for the care of monuments now generally discourage reconstruction based on conjecture.
Yet the principle is harder to apply than to state.
Every repair involves some replacement of material, and the line between necessary repair and creative restoration is not always clear.
Moreover, the restorations of the nineteenth century have themselves become historical.
Many visitors admire buildings whose most famous features are largely nineteenth-century work, and removing those features now would be to commit, in reverse, the very error the critics condemned.

questions.s: The author suggests that removing nineteenth-century additions from a medieval building today would
questions.e: The last sentence says removing such features would 'commit, in reverse, the very error the critics condemned,' that is, stripping away alterations that have become part of the building's history. The first choice is the trap: it applies the old restorers' reasoning, which the passage presents as mistaken. The fourth contradicts the statement that many visitors admire the nineteenth-century features.
o: return the building to the form its original designers had intended
be required by the international guidelines now in force
be acceptable as long as the work rested on careful research
please most visitors, who prefer authentic medieval work
repeat the restorers' mistake of erasing part of a building's history

questions.s: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage argues that the old dispute over numbers hid a deeper issue: income, health and other components of welfare need not move together, so the question needs specifying. The fifth choice is the most convincing trap, but the last paragraph says explicitly that the question was 'not meaningless,' only underspecified. The fourth confuses two kinds of evidence: heights fell while wages rose.
o: The pessimists were right that workers' material conditions declined during early industrialization.
Wage series are a more trustworthy guide than height records to how ordinary workers actually lived.
The debate over workers' welfare is complicated by the recognition that different measures of welfare can diverge.
Records of soldiers' heights show that real wages fell for workers born in the early nineteenth century.
Historians now agree that whether workers were better off is a question that cannot be meaningfully posed.

questions.s: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The first statement follows from the second paragraph: daily rates say nothing about days actually worked or the shifting earnings of women and children, so household income could fall while men's rates rose. The third restates the point that price-index assumptions 'can turn a modest gain into a modest loss.' The second is wrong because the author says the paradox 'need not mean that either kind of evidence is mistaken' and ranks neither above the other.
o: A wage series showing rising daily rates for adult men is compatible with a fall in total household income.
The author regards height records as a more accurate measure of welfare than wage data.
Assumptions about what working families bought can affect whether real earnings appear to rise or fall.

questions.s: The author's claim that the original question "was underspecified" most directly implies that the question
questions.e: The next sentence explains the term: 'better off' bundles income, health, security and working conditions, which need not move in tandem, so the question failed to say which was meant. The second choice treats underspecified as unanswerable, which the author rejects in saying the question was not meaningless. The fourth is tempting after the third paragraph, but the author presents heights as one measure among several, not a replacement.
o: did not make clear which aspects of welfare were to be assessed
could not be answered with any evidence available to historians
had been answered by both sides using falsified figures
should be settled by abandoning money-based measures in favor of heights
was resolved once records of heights became available to researchers

questions.s: The passage is mainly about
questions.e: The passage describes the waggle dance, explains how it encodes direction and distance, and tells how robotic-bee experiments settled whether bees use the dance. The robotic bees are only one part of that story, so the fourth choice is too narrow. The scientist is mentioned for his discovery, not his life.
o: how honeybees communicate the location of food and how researchers confirmed that they do so
why honeybees prefer flowers with strong scents
the life and career of an Austrian scientist
how researchers built small robotic bees and programmed them to perform dances on the honeycomb
the reasons honeybees build their combs vertically

questions.s:
According to the passage, which of the following information can a bee's waggle dance convey?

Select all that apply.
questions.e: The second paragraph says the direction of the run matches the direction of the food relative to the sun, and the length of the run is related to distance. The type of flower is not conveyed by the dance; the passage says bees use scent, carried by the forager, to find the exact flowers.
o: The direction of the food relative to the sun
How far away the food is
The type of flower that produced the food

questions.s: Why were the experiments with robotic bees important?
questions.e: The robots danced without carrying any scent, and bees still flew in the indicated direction, so the dance by itself could guide them. This answered critics who thought bees might only follow scent. The first choice goes too far: the last paragraph says bees do use scent to find the exact flowers.
o: They showed that bees cannot detect the scent of flowers.
They proved that real bees dance more accurately than robots.
They showed that bees could be guided by the dance alone, without any scent.
They revealed that bees ignore dances performed on vertical surfaces.
They showed that bees cannot find food that is more than several kilometers away from the hive, even with a dance.

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
questions.e: The passage explains why towns kept local time, how railways created the need for a common time, and then argues that the familiar story of imposition is incomplete because businesses and ordinary people adopted standard time before laws required it. The fourth choice reverses the passage: only some towns resisted, and the change spread anyway. The danger of single-track lines is a detail in the second paragraph.
o: argue that local time was more accurate than railway time
describe how the telegraph was invented
explain why trains on single-track lines were dangerous
show that most towns successfully resisted the adoption of railway time, even when the dispute reached the courts
explain how standard time came to be adopted and correct an oversimplified account of that process

questions.s: Select the sentence in the third paragraph that gives an example showing that standard time was adopted voluntarily before it was legally required.
questions.e: The sentence about businesses that relied on the telegraph gives a concrete example of voluntary adoption before any law. The last sentence is tempting because it states the same idea, but it is a general conclusion, not an example. The sentence about resisting towns supports the opposite side of the story.
o: It is often said that the railways imposed standard time on a reluctant public, and there is some truth in the claim.
Some towns resisted giving up their local noon, and in a few places the dispute reached the courts.
Many businesses, especially those that depended on the telegraph, found a common time convenient and adopted railway time well before any law required it.
The law, in these cases, confirmed a change that had largely taken place.

questions.s: According to the passage, why did many stations display two clocks for a time?
questions.e: The second paragraph says stations showed one clock with railway time and one with local time, and travelers had to keep both in mind. The third choice misuses a detail from the third paragraph: some disputes reached the courts, but the passage never says courts required two clocks.
o: Railway companies could not agree on which city's time to use.
Railway time and local time differed, and travelers needed to know both.
Courts required stations to show local time alongside railway time.
The telegraph sent two different time signals to every station.
Clocks of that period were unreliable, so a second clock served as a check.

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
questions.e: The passage presents the ethical case for foreignization, then argues that the foreignization-domestication opposition is unstable and that the ethical concern must be addressed through particular choices. The first choice is wrong because the author does not rank domestication above foreignization; the last paragraph says neither stylistic policy settles the question. The last choice contradicts the claim that what seems exotic to one generation may seem old-fashioned to the next.
o: argue that domesticating translations, because they read fluently in the reader's own language, are ethically superior to foreignizing ones
describe the history of literary translation from antiquity to the present
explain why translators should always preserve the syntax of the source text
examine an argument for one translation strategy and question the opposition on which it depends
show that readers of every generation respond to foreign constructions in the same way

questions.s:
The author suggests which of the following as problems for the claim that foreignization respects cultural difference?

Select all that apply.
questions.e: The third paragraph says preserved syntax may strike readers as clumsy prose, and that translators choose which features to preserve according to their own assumptions, which can yield a stylized image of otherness. The passage never discusses how many readers each kind of translation attracts, so the third option is out of scope.
o: Readers may perceive preserved foreign features as poor writing rather than as cultural difference.
The features a translator preserves may reflect the translator's own preconceptions about the source culture.
Foreignizing translations are usually read by fewer people than domesticating ones.

questions.s: The author's attitude toward the critics who champion foreignization is best described as
questions.e: The author credits the argument with being influential and useful and states that the ethical concern is not misguided, yet argues that it cannot be satisfied by a stylistic policy applied in advance. The second choice ignores the explicit statement that the concern is not misguided. The third choice misses the author's criticism of the dichotomy on which the critics rely.
o: sympathetic to their underlying concern but doubtful that their preferred strategy can meet it
dismissive of both their concern and their proposed remedy
fully persuaded by their argument and eager to extend it
indifferent, since the author regards translation as a purely technical matter
hostile, because the author believes that their ethical campaign has harmed the reputation of fluent translators and the readers who prefer them

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
questions.e: The passage presents the 'mother tree' account and then devotes two paragraphs to the critics' reasons for thinking it has outrun the evidence. The first choice is too extreme: the passage says fungal links have been shown repeatedly; the objection concerns what the links do. The third choice reverses the passage's skeptical stance, and the fifth describes only a detail from the first paragraph.
o: argue that the fungal threads said to connect neighboring trees have never actually been observed in real forests
describe a popular claim about forest networks and explain why some scientists find it insufficiently supported
defend the view that large trees deliberately nourish their own seedlings through the soil
compare the laboratory methods used by forest ecologists in the 1990s with the field methods they rely on today
explain how mycorrhizal fungi obtain the sugars they need from trees

questions.s: According to the passage, one reason critics doubt that the carbon-labeling studies show sharing between trees through fungi is that
questions.e: The second paragraph says many experiments 'could not rule out simpler routes,' such as carbon leaking into the soil and being absorbed by nearby roots. The second choice overstates the point: the passage says only that it was often unclear whether carbon left the fungus. The fifth choice contradicts the passage, which refers to field studies.
o: the isotopes used to label the carbon decayed before measurements could be made
fungi have been shown to consume all of the carbon they receive from trees
the carbon could have passed between trees through the soil rather than through fungal links
shaded seedlings were found to produce more sugar of their own than the large trees growing beside them
most of the studies were conducted in laboratories rather than in actual forests

questions.s: The author of the passage would most likely agree with which of the following statements? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The passage states that fungal links between trees have 'been shown repeatedly,' and the last paragraph allows that further work may 'confirm some of their bolder ideas.' The third statement is contradicted: the author says the critique does not mean the researchers were careless, and blames the hardening of the hypothesis on public discussion, not on deliberate exaggeration.
o: Fungi physically connect the roots of different trees.
Some of the bolder ideas about forest networks may eventually be confirmed.
The original researchers deliberately exaggerated their findings to attract public attention.

questions.s: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage moves from what logbooks were for, to the difficulties of using them, to the results they have produced for climate science. The second choice is half right: the passage notes the need for caution but never ranks logbooks below instruments or limits their use. The fourth choice contradicts the passage, which says terms differed between navies and were matched fleet by fleet.
o: Naval historians have long misread eighteenth-century logbooks because they ignored the weather information those books contain.
Ship logbooks are less reliable than instrument readings and should be used only when no other records exist.
Old ship logbooks, though kept for navigation, have become a valuable if demanding source for studying past climate.
Climate scientists have developed a single standard scale that converts all sailors' wind terms into numbers.
The oceans were poorly observed until weather satellites were introduced in the twentieth century.

questions.s: Select the sentence in the second paragraph that explains why some logbook records are given more weight than others.
questions.e: The last sentence of the paragraph says agreement among several nearby ships raises confidence, while a lone record is used 'more cautiously,' so records are weighted differently. The sentence about checking translations against instrument readings is tempting, but it concerns how wind terms are converted to speeds, not why one ship's record counts for more than another's.
o: Using the logbooks is not straightforward.
Sailors described the wind in words rather than numbers, and the meaning of a term such as "fresh breeze" could differ between navies or change over time.
Researchers have therefore compared the vocabulary of different fleets, matching each phrase to a likely range of wind speeds.
They have also checked their translations against periods and places for which instrument readings exist.
Where the descriptions of several ships sailing near one another agree, confidence in the reconstruction rises; where a single ship's record stands alone, it is used more cautiously.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage primarily serves to
questions.e: The sentence generalizes: records made for navigation answered unforeseen questions, so an archive's value is 'not fixed by the intentions' of its makers. The third choice goes too far, since the author compares logbooks with no other kind of document. The fourth reverses the paragraph, which reports that the reconstructions have proved useful.
o: draw a broader lesson about archives from the case of logbooks
criticize sailors for failing to record the weather in numerical form
suggest that records made for navigation are more valuable than most other historical documents
question whether climate reconstructions based on logbooks can be trusted
explain why naval historians first became interested in logbooks

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
questions.e: The first paragraph gives the textbook story, the second presents the conservators' findings that complicate it, and the third draws the revised conclusion. The first choice repeats the very claim the passage corrects: the Netherlandish achievement was 'not the invention of a material.' The fifth choice names a detail that supports the argument rather than the passage's purpose.
o: praise the Netherlandish painters for inventing an entirely new kind of paint
argue that egg tempera allowed painters to achieve finer detail than oil paint did
explain why patrons in Italy continued to prefer tempera long after oil was available
show how technical evidence has revised a traditional account of a change in painting
describe the chemical and microscopic methods that conservators use to examine samples taken from old panels

questions.s: In the context in which it appears, "uneven" most nearly means
questions.e: The sentences that follow explain that workshops changed in different ways and that one city might adopt oil 'decades before its neighbor,' so the change proceeded at different rates in different places. 'Rough in texture' is a common meaning of uneven that fits a painted surface but not a historical process, and nothing in the passage suggests the change was unfair or failed.

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following affected how quickly oil painting was adopted? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The third paragraph lists 'local habits, the cost of materials and the expectations of patrons' as influences on the pace of change. Guild rules are never mentioned; choosing them relies on outside knowledge about how workshops were organized, not on the passage.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the main idea of the passage?
questions.e: The passage explains why the giant-impact hypothesis replaced older ideas and then describes the isotope finding it has not yet fully explained. The first choice reverses the last paragraph, which says few scientists see the puzzle as a reason to abandon the hypothesis. The second choice is one of the older ideas the hypothesis replaced.
o: The giant-impact hypothesis has been abandoned because lunar rocks resemble Earth's rocks too closely.
The Moon was most likely captured by Earth's gravity after forming in a distant part of the solar system.
Rock samples from the Apollo missions showed that the Moon contains a large core of iron.
Computer models have proved more reliable than rock samples for explaining when and how the Moon formed from Earth.
A widely accepted account of the Moon's origin explains much of the evidence but still faces a puzzle.

questions.s: Select the sentence in the second paragraph that cites evidence that the Moon's material was once extremely hot.
questions.e: The third sentence says lunar rocks lack water and other substances that evaporate easily, 'as would be expected if the material had been intensely heated.' The sentence about iron is also evidence from the Apollo samples, but it concerns which layers of the colliding bodies formed the Moon, not heating.
o: The giant-impact hypothesis won acceptance largely because it explained facts the others could not.

Rock samples returned by the Apollo missions indicated that the Moon has very little iron at its center compared with Earth, which fits a scenario in which the Moon formed mostly from the outer, rocky layers of the colliding bodies rather than from their iron cores.
The samples also showed that lunar rocks contain almost no water or other substances that evaporate easily, as would be expected if the material had been intensely heated.
And computer models showed that an off-center collision could give the Earth-Moon system the large amount of spin it has today.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the near-identical isotopic makeup of lunar and terrestrial rocks is surprising chiefly because
questions.e: The third paragraph reasons that if the bulk of the Moon came from the impactor, and bodies from different regions differ in isotopes, the Moon should differ from Earth. The fourth choice confuses the giant-impact hypothesis with the older capture idea. The third choice is true but explains a different fact, the Moon's small core.
o: the Apollo samples were too small for isotopes to be measured accurately
simulations indicate that most of the Moon's material came from a body that formed elsewhere
the Moon has much less iron at its center than Earth has
the Moon is now widely thought to have been captured from some distant region of the solar system
Earth's surface rocks have changed greatly since the time the Moon formed

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
