questions.e: The second sentence gives the reason directly: creoles 'form quickly', so linguists can study grammar as it emerges. The last sentence is the trap; it explains why the debate about creoles matters to broader questions, not why creoles drew researchers in the first place.
o: Creole languages arise when speakers of different languages, brought together under conditions such as plantation labor or long-distance trade, develop a shared means of communication that children then acquire as a first language.
Because creoles form quickly, they have attracted linguists interested in how grammar emerges.

One influential hypothesis held that creoles around the world share structural features, such as marking tense with separate particles rather than word endings, because children who acquire an unstable input fall back on an innate default grammar.

Critics have replied that many of these shared features can be traced to the languages the original speakers brought with them, and that the similarities among creoles have been overstated by comparing only a few well-studied cases.
The debate matters beyond creoles themselves, since it bears on how much of grammar is learned and how much is given.

questions.s: The radio-frequency experiment is significant chiefly because the noise used in it
questions.e: The noise was 'too feeble to move an iron particle but capable of disturbing the chemical reaction', so its effect on orientation favors the chemical account over the particle account. The third choice overstates the result: the author says that 'neither observation proves the hypothesis.' The experiment says nothing about whether iron particles are present, only that they cannot explain this effect.
o: shows that robins can detect radio waves as well as magnetic fields
could disturb one proposed mechanism but not the other
proves that cryptochrome is located in the eyes of migratory birds
demonstrates that robins have no iron-oxide particles at all
makes robins disoriented only when they are kept under red light

questions.s: Select the sentence in which the author assesses how strongly the evidence supports the light-based hypothesis.
questions.e: Only the last sentence weighs the evidence: it is not proof, yet it is hard to explain by the rival account. 'Two observations support it' is the tempting choice, but it merely announces that support exists without judging its strength; the sentence about the hypothesis being 'now favored' reports other researchers' opinion rather than the author's assessment.
o: Many migratory birds can orient using Earth's magnetic field, but how they sense it has long been uncertain.
One proposal locates the sensor in tiny iron-oxide particles that would act like compass needles.
Another, now favored by many researchers, holds that the sense depends on light-triggered chemical reactions in the eye.
In this account, a protein called cryptochrome, when struck by blue light, forms pairs of molecules whose subsequent reactions depend subtly on the orientation of the magnetic field.
Caged robins orient correctly under blue or green light but become disoriented in red light, which does not activate cryptochrome.
And weak radio-frequency noise, too feeble to move an iron particle but capable of disturbing the chemical reaction, disrupts their orientation.
Neither observation proves the hypothesis, but together they are hard to explain by magnetic particles alone.

questions.s: The author's main objection to the usual account of the flying buttress is that it
questions.e: The author accepts the engineering account 'as far as it goes' but objects that it suggests builders first wanted bright interiors and then invented the device, whereas the evidence 'points to a messier process' of repair and learning. The first choice is the trap: the author never doubts that buttresses carried the vault's thrust, only the story of why they were developed.
o: exaggerates the part the buttress played in carrying the thrust of Gothic vaults
ignores the importance of stained glass in Gothic churches
implies a tidier sequence of goal and invention than the evidence shows
attributes the device to builders of a later century
treats the buttress as a decorative rather than a structural element

questions.s: The author mentions churches “whose walls had begun to lean” most likely in order to
questions.e: The leaning walls show that early buttresses were 'added to existing churches' as repairs and 'only later' planned from the start, which supports the author's account of learning by fixing failures. The third choice reverses the point: the passage implies the buttresses worked well enough that builders came to plan them. Nothing in the passage judges the builders unskilled.
o: show that Gothic builders lacked basic engineering skill
explain why windows in later churches were made smaller
suggest that flying buttresses often failed to stop walls from moving
illustrate that buttresses were first used to correct existing problems
contrast early Gothic churches with the churches that preceded them

questions.s: The passage indicates that joint liability was expected to do which of the following? Select all that apply.
questions.e: Joint liability was meant to make use of the fact that neighbors 'know one another's habits and can apply social pressure', solving the lender's problems of selection and monitoring. Meetings 'continued under both arrangements', so ending them was never the aim. Attracting more borrowers is what individual liability did in the experiments, the opposite of the expectation.
o: Allow lenders to stop holding regular group meetings
Attract more borrowers than individual liability would
Let lenders benefit from what borrowers know about one another

questions.s: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the suggestion made in the final sentence of the passage?
questions.e: The final sentence suggests that meetings, not shared obligation, sustained repayment. If repayment fell when meetings stopped even though joint liability remained, the meetings would appear to be the active ingredient. The first choice repeats a fact already in the passage about why borrowers liked individual liability; it says nothing about what sustained repayment.
o: Some borrowers left joint-liability groups because they disliked having to cover the debts of other members.
Default rates in the programs studied were higher in rural areas than in towns.
Lenders that adopted individual liability also raised their interest rates.
Most borrowers in the programs had known one another for many years.
In programs that stopped holding meetings, repayment fell even where joint liability was kept.

questions.s: According to the passage, a coral that recovers from bleaching with a larger share of heat-tolerant algae is likely to
questions.e: The passage says the larger share of tolerant algae 'makes them less likely to bleach in the next warm spell.' The fourth choice reverses a detail: tolerant algae 'often supply less energy', so such corals may grow more slowly, not faster. Nothing suggests that the algae spread to other species; the passage notes that some species cannot take up new partners at all.
o: stop depending on algae for most of its energy
lose the ability to host more than one type of alga
be less prone to bleaching during the next warm period
grow faster than corals that host other types of algae
pass the tolerant algae on to other coral species on its reef

questions.s: The author's attitude toward the hope that reefs might adapt to warming seas is best described as
questions.e: The author says the hope 'should be tempered' and gives two limits: slower growth and the fact that not every species can change partners. Tempering a hope is not rejecting it, so 'dismissive' is too strong; the author still presents the flexibility as real. 'Guarded' captures cautious, qualified support.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the repeated epithets in ancient epics were once regarded as
questions.e: The epithets were 'long thought to be padding', that is, filler that contributes little. The fieldwork recast them as 'working tools of composition.' The second choice is tempting because repetition can mark style, but the passage describes the epithets as shared traditional phrases, not one author's signature.
o: evidence that the poems had been written down
signs of a single author's distinctive style
the most authentic parts of the original versions
words that added little to the poems' meaning
phrases borrowed from the songs of later singers

questions.s: Select the sentence that reports the observation most directly at odds with the assumption described in the first sentence.
questions.e: The assumption was that long poems need writing or a memorized fixed text. The third sentence reports singers performing very long epics with no written text and no fixed version, since performances differed. The second sentence is the trap: it says the fieldwork challenged the assumption but does not report what was observed.
o: Scholars once assumed that a long poem could be composed only by an author who wrote it down or memorized a fixed text.
Fieldwork among singers in the Balkans in the twentieth century challenged that assumption.
The singers performed epics thousands of lines long without a written text, yet no two performances of the same song were identical.
They worked with a stock of traditional phrases, each fitted to a particular place in the metrical line, along with familiar scenes such as arming for battle or a feast.
Using these resources, a skilled singer recomposed the song as he performed it.
Applied to ancient epics, this finding suggested that repeated epithets, long thought to be padding, were the working tools of composition.
It also unsettled the very idea of an original version, since each performance was as authentic as any other.

questions.s: The passage is primarily concerned with
questions.e: The passage outlines the older view of print as transformative 'almost by itself' and then the revisionist qualifications. The first choice is the trap: the revisionists 'do not deny that print mattered', they only slow and complicate its effects. Scribes are mentioned as continuing to work, not as resisting printing.
o: arguing that the printing press had little effect on European thought
explaining why scribes resisted the introduction of printing
describing how printers corrected the errors in early editions
comparing the cost of printed books with that of manuscripts
describing how historians have revised a once-dominant view

questions.s: Which of the following does the passage present as evidence against the claim that print quickly fixed texts in stable form? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The errors and the alterations between editions are given with the conclusion that 'print did not at once produce the stability attributed to it.' The scribes' copying answers a different claim, that print quickly replaced manuscripts, and the revisionists' acceptance that print mattered is a concession, not evidence about textual stability.
o: Scribes kept copying works for which demand was small.
Printers often altered texts from one edition to the next.
Revisionists accept that print mattered to European life.

questions.s: According to the passage, a major reason that geologists rejected Wegener's proposal was that
questions.e: The passage calls his evidence 'suggestive' but says he 'could offer no plausible force strong enough' to move continents through the ocean floor. The last choice is true of the period but is not given as a reason for rejection; the stripes became important only later. The seafloor surveys came in the 1960s and supported the idea, so the fourth choice reverses their role.
o: the coastlines of Africa and South America do not in fact match
he could not explain what force would move the continents
the fossils he cited had been wrongly identified
seafloor surveys had already contradicted his evidence
magnetic reversals had not yet been discovered by geologists

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to
questions.e: Wegener's problem was imagining continents pushed 'through the solid ocean floor'; the last sentence shows that, with seafloor spreading, continents need not plow through anything because they move with the floor. It grants the critics one point, that plowing was implausible, but not that they were right 'in every respect', since the continents did move. The mirror-image stripes are explained in the sentence before.
o: concede that Wegener's critics had been right about his evidence in every respect
introduce evidence that contradicts the account of seafloor spreading
explain why the magnetic stripes form mirror images of each other
suggest that the continents have now stopped moving
show how the new findings removed the objection Wegener faced

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
questions.e: The passage opens with the prediction that photography would end portrait painting, says it 'proved partly accurate' for miniatures, then shows that it missed the rise in prestige of painted portraits for the wealthy. The second choice is too strong, since the prediction is only partly wrong, and the passage does give causes (flattery, cost, the artist's name), so the fourth choice fails.
o: A prediction is stated, partly confirmed, and then shown to be incomplete.
A theory is presented and then rejected on the basis of new evidence.
Two competing explanations are described, and one is shown to be superior.
A historical change is described, and its causes are said to be unknown.
A general claim is supported by a series of examples drawn from several different countries.

questions.s: The passage suggests which of the following about photographs in the nineteenth century? Select all that apply.
questions.e: A photograph 'could not easily flatter', and it was 'cheap enough that owning one no longer distinguished its owner', which supports the first two. Miniature painters 'lost much of their trade' to photography, and the last sentence says photography absorbed 'the modest likeness', which supports the third. A reader looking for a single effect may stop too early; the passage names all three.
o: They were less able than paintings to present a sitter flatteringly.
Their low cost reduced their value as a sign of social standing.
They took over much of the trade once served by miniature painters.

questions.s: According to the passage, building new roads is often less effective than the economists' preferred policy because
questions.e: New roads 'tend to fill up again as drivers who had avoided the congested route return to it', so the gain in capacity is used up. The last choice borrows the passage's explanation for weak support for congestion charges and wrongly applies it to roads. Maintenance costs are never mentioned.
o: new roads cost more to maintain over time than they cost to build
drivers generally prefer to use routes on which they are not charged any fee
the added capacity draws back drivers who had avoided the route
public opinion usually turns against road building over time
residents cannot imagine the benefits of new roads in advance

questions.s: Select the sentence that offers an interpretation of a change in residents' attitudes.
questions.e: The last sentence both describes the shift in support and interprets it ('a shift that suggests' the obstacle is imagining benefits in advance). The sentence 'Public opinion has followed a curious pattern' is the trap: it signals that a change occurred but neither describes it nor explains it.
o: Economists have long argued that charging drivers a fee to enter crowded city centers at peak hours would reduce traffic more efficiently than building new roads.
New roads, they note, tend to fill up again as drivers who had avoided the congested route return to it, whereas a price makes each driver weigh the delay his or her trip imposes on others.
The few cities that have adopted such charges have generally seen traffic fall and travel times improve.
Public opinion has followed a curious pattern in these places.

Support is often weak before a charge is introduced and grows after residents have experienced its effects, a shift that suggests the main obstacle is not the policy's performance but the difficulty of imagining its benefits in advance.

questions.s: It can be inferred from the passage that the tubeworms described do which of the following? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The tubeworms absorb compounds made by microbes that draw energy from chemicals in the vent fluid, so they depend on those chemicals indirectly. Having no mouths or guts, they cannot swallow food, and the communities live 'far below the reach of light.' Each statement follows from a different sentence, so all three are supported.
o: depend, at least indirectly, on chemicals in the vent fluid for nourishment
obtain nourishment without swallowing food in the usual way
live in a habitat that sunlight does not directly reach

questions.s: The last sentence of the passage functions primarily to
questions.e: After presenting vent life as running on chemical energy, the author adds that the oxygen many vent microbes use comes from photosynthesis, so the independence from sunlight is not complete. The last choice overstates this: the original assumption was 'overturned', and the final sentence only limits how far, rather than restoring the old view.
o: reject the claim that vent communities depend on chemosynthesis
explain how tubeworms absorb the compounds that microbes produce
argue that vent communities first formed near the ocean surface
qualify the extent to which vent life is independent of sunlight
show that the assumption held by biologists before the late 1970s was correct

questions.s: The critics mentioned in the passage object to fluent translations chiefly because such translations
questions.e: The critics say fluency 'conceals what is distinctive about other cultures' by making every work sound familiar. The last choice reverses the issue: fluent translations remove unfamiliar idioms rather than rely on them. Difficulty for readers is the cost the critics accept for their own preferred approach, not their complaint about fluent ones.
o: are harder for ordinary readers to enjoy
hide what is distinctive about foreign works
were never read by the original work's first audience
sacrifice fewer features of the original than other translations do
rely on idioms that most readers find unfamiliar

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage implies which of the following? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The sentence says every translation 'must choose which features of the original to sacrifice', so some loss is unavoidable. It denies complete fidelity to 'neither camp' and so does not rank one approach above the other, which rules out the statement that preserving strangeness is more faithful. Saying that both sides fall short is not the same as saying the debate should end.
o: Translations that preserve strangeness are more faithful than fluent ones.
Translators should stop debating how visible foreignness should be.
Every translation gives up some features of the original.

questions.s: The primary purpose of the passage is to
questions.e: The passage accepts the observations but says 'the interpretation has outrun the evidence' and ends by calling the language of altruism premature, so its aim is to caution. Choice B is too extreme: the last sentence explicitly denies that the networks are unimportant. Choices D and E pick up details (isotope labeling, the fungi's interests) that serve the argument rather than being its purpose.
o: celebrate the discovery that trees share carbon through fungal networks
argue that fungal networks play no meaningful role in forest ecology
caution against a popular interpretation of findings about fungal networks
explain the chemical methods used to trace carbon from one tree to another
compare the interests of fungi with the interests of the trees they connect

questions.s: Which of the following does the passage present as grounds for doubting that trees deliberately feed their neighbors? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The fourth sentence gives both the small quantities and the uncertainty about whether carbon reached the neighbor's shoots or stayed in fungal tissue, so the first and third choices are correct. The passage never discusses whether connected trees belong to the same or different species, so the second choice is out of scope.
o: The amount of carbon moved between trees in field studies is generally small.
Trees joined by fungal threads rarely belong to different species.
Carbon detected in a neighbor may have stayed in fungal tissue within its roots.

questions.s: The sentence beginning 'Marginal images were often planned' serves primarily to
questions.e: The sentence follows directly on 'That explanation has grown hard to sustain' and gives two facts (space was left for the images; specialists painted them) that contradict the idea of a scribe's idle doodles. The commentary view (D) comes two sentences later and rests on the images' response to particular words, not on their planning. The sentence concedes nothing to the doodle theory, so E reverses its function.
o: present evidence that undermines an earlier explanation of the images
describe the techniques that specialist illuminators used in their work
suggest that scribes resented the tedious work of copying sacred texts
introduce the view that the images were a commentary on the central text
concede that the doodle theory accounts for some of the images

questions.s: Select the sentence in which the author states a conclusion that holds however the scholarly debate about the images' meaning is settled.
questions.e: 'Whatever their precise purpose' signals that the claim does not depend on which interpretation is right: the images belonged to the design either way. The sentence about historians reading the margins as commentary is tempting, but it states one side of the debate rather than a conclusion independent of it. 'That explanation has grown hard to sustain' rejects only the doodle theory.
o: Readers who open a thirteenth-century psalter are sometimes startled to find, in the margins beside solemn texts, rabbits jousting with knights, snails battling armored men, and monkeys playing bagpipes.
Earlier scholars tended to treat such images as idle doodles, the scribe's relief from tedious copying.
That explanation has grown hard to sustain.
Marginal images were often planned before the text was written, since space was left for them, and they were usually painted by specialist illuminators rather than by the scribes themselves.
Many also respond to particular words on the page, punning on a phrase or inverting its meaning.
Some historians therefore read the margins as a deliberate commentary, a space where the ordered world of the central text could be playfully turned upside down.
Whatever their precise purpose, the images were clearly part of the book's design, not an afterthought.

questions.s: It can be inferred from the passage that an ambitious first offer would be least likely to shape the final agreement when the other party
questions.e: The passage says the effect 'appears weakest when the other party has precise knowledge of market rates' and sums up that anchors work best where uncertainty is greatest. Choice A is the trap: the experiments found anchoring even when participants were told the offer was random, so that knowledge does not weaken it. Nothing in the passage concerns immediate counteroffers or moderate figures.
o: has been told that the opening offer was chosen at random
is bargaining over a hypothetical rather than a real position
responds at once with a counteroffer of its own
knows precisely what comparable positions typically pay
regards the opening figure as only moderately high

questions.s: According to the passage, anchoring occurs because people
questions.e: The passage defines anchoring directly: 'people adjust away from an initial value, but typically not far enough.' Choice D reverses the experimental finding, since even random figures pulled agreements toward them. Choice C is not stated; the passage says the first number's pull exceeds its informational value, which suggests people need not believe it reflects the market.
o: trust the first figure they hear more than any later figure
fail to move far enough away from an initial value
assume that opening offers accurately reflect market rates
disregard any number they believe was chosen at random
would rather end a negotiation than bargain at length

questions.s: In the context in which it appears, 'resolved' most nearly means
questions.e: A puzzle that is 'partly resolved' by a discovery is partly explained: the proteins account for how species without trehalose survive drying. 'Determined' is the trap, drawn from the sense of resolving to do something (making a firm decision), which does not fit a puzzle. 'Dissolved' is a chemical sense of the word that has no place here.

questions.s: Which of the following does the passage offer as evidence that the tardigrade proteins actively help organisms survive drying? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The last sentence reports that both yeast and bacteria became more drought-tolerant with the genes and draws the conclusion that the proteins 'actively contribute to survival', so the first two choices are correct. The third choice describes a property of the proteins, not evidence that they aid survival; it is true but does not support that conclusion.
o: Yeast given the genes for the proteins became more tolerant of drying.
Bacteria given the genes for the proteins became more tolerant of drying.
The proteins remain unfolded while the cells contain ample water.

questions.s: The author's attitude toward ensembles that train their continuo players to improvise is best described as
questions.e: The author admits that 'the results are uneven' and accepts 'occasional roughness', but says that at their best these performances restore something no edition can capture: approval with a reservation. 'Unreserved enthusiasm' ignores the admitted unevenness, and skepticism or disapproval contradicts the author's clear preference for improvisation over note-for-note editions.

questions.s: The author would most likely agree that a continuo player who performs a twentieth-century edition note for note
questions.e: The author says such fidelity is 'to the editor rather than to the composer' because the written part 'freezes into one version what was meant to change from performance to performance'. Choice A reverses this claim. Choice E is too extreme: the author implies less responsiveness, not none, and D attributes roughness to the wrong group.
o: is more faithful to the composer's intentions than a player who improvises
ought to disregard the numerals that the composer wrote above the bass
replaces a part meant to vary with one fixed version
produces a rougher texture than an improvising player does
cannot respond to the singers or the room in any way

questions.s: The author mentions the absorption of the county into the French kingdom primarily in order to
questions.e: 'Tellingly' marks the decline as evidence: when the protective institutions gave way to policies favoring locals, the fairs faded even though their location had not changed, which supports the institutional account. Choice D is too broad, since the passage speaks only of policies that disadvantaged foreign traders. Choice B contradicts the passage, which says the guarantees reduced the risk of trading.
o: show that geography became less important to trade over time
suggest that the counts' guarantees had never been effective
explain why Italian merchants came to prefer trading in Flanders
argue that royal policies were harmful to every kind of commerce
lend support to an institutional explanation of the fairs' success

questions.s: Select the sentence that identifies a weakness in an earlier explanation.
questions.e: The earlier explanation is geography, and the third sentence names its weakness: other towns on the same routes did not prosper, so location cannot be the whole story. The second sentence only states the earlier explanation. The last sentence supports the new institutional account rather than pointing to a flaw in the old one.
o: Between the late twelfth and early fourteenth centuries, the fairs held in a handful of towns in the county of Champagne became the principal meeting place for merchants from Italy and Flanders.
Historians once credited this success chiefly to geography, since the towns lay along routes connecting the two regions.
Geography alone, however, cannot explain why these towns and not others along the same routes prospered.
A more persuasive account emphasizes institutions.
The counts of Champagne guaranteed safe conduct to merchants traveling to the fairs, maintained courts that settled disputes quickly, and enforced contracts even against their own subjects.
Such guarantees reduced the risk of trading with strangers.
Tellingly, the fairs began to decline after the county was absorbed into the French kingdom, when royal policies came to favor local interests over those of foreign traders.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the effect of weak radio-frequency noise on orientation is significant because the effect
questions.e: The passage says the noise is too weak to heat tissue but 'could interfere with the delicate chemical reaction', so the finding fits the cryptochrome hypothesis. Choice A reverses the point about heating. Choice C attaches the evidence to the competing hypothesis, which the passage says has fared less well.
o: indicates that the magnetic sense depends on heating of retinal tissue
shows that robins orient by light rather than by the magnetic field
confirms that iron-rich particles in the beak serve as receptors
demonstrates that cryptochromes occur only in migratory species
fits a compass that relies on a sensitive chemical reaction

questions.s: Which of the following findings, if true, would most clearly cast doubt on the hypothesis that the compass lies in the eye?
questions.e: If birds oriented normally without working cryptochromes, the proteins could not be the compass, which directly undercuts the hypothesis. Cryptochromes in nonmigratory birds (B) is compatible with the hypothesis, since the proteins may have other roles. Choices C and E restate findings the passage says the hypothesis explains, and D concerns the competing hypothesis.
o: Birds with disabled retinal cryptochromes still oriented normally.
Some birds that never migrate also possess cryptochromes in the retina.
Robins orient poorly when exposed to certain wavelengths of light.
Immune cells in the beaks of songbirds contain large amounts of iron.
Radio-frequency noise disrupts orientation in several songbird species.

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the 'commonplace' mentioned in the first sentence?
questions.e: The author says 'the account is not wrong' but objects that it is told as if the prints supplied ideas the French could not have reached alone, so the commonplace is right in outline yet overstates the prints' novelty. Choice A ignores the concession 'not wrong'. Choice D overreaches: photography is one place the features were already being explored, not the chief source of the style.
o: It is entirely mistaken and should be abandoned.
It is broadly right but exaggerates the novelty of the prints' ideas.
It underestimates how many prints reached Paris after the 1850s.
It correctly identifies photography as the chief source of the new style.
It neglects the influence of French painting on Japanese printmakers.

questions.s: The author's account of artistic influence implies which of the following? Select all that apply.
questions.e: All three follow. The last sentence calls influence 'a meeting between what an artist finds and what the artist is already looking for' (first choice). The prints 'lent authority to experiments already under way' (second choice). Calling the prints 'less a revelation than a confirmation' means they reinforced existing tendencies rather than creating them (third choice).
o: What an artist takes from a foreign source depends partly on what the artist already pursues.
A respected tradition can lend authority to experiments that have already begun.
A source can strengthen tendencies that were present in an artist's work before contact with it.

questions.s: The critics mentioned in the passage would most likely explain the shared features of two distant creoles by pointing to
questions.e: The critics argue that many creoles drew on related West African or European sources, which 'could account for shared features without any appeal to innate structure'. Choice A is the explanation the critics reject. Choice E is an example of a shared feature, not an explanation of why the features are shared.
o: the children's reliance on an innate grammar
the fragmentary language spoken around the children
similarities among the languages the creoles drew on
the conditions of trade under which the creoles arose
the placement of tense words before the verb

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage serves primarily to
questions.e: The sentence opens 'The debate matters beyond creole studies' and gives the reason: creoles are a rare natural setting for watching a grammar emerge. It takes no side, so A is wrong. Choice C reverses the claim, since the sentence says such emergence can be observed in creoles.
o: resolve the debate in favor of the critics
suggest that creoles are no longer emerging today
question whether a grammar can ever be seen emerging
explain why the debate has wider significance
introduce a further example of a creole language

questions.s: Based on the passage, which of the following is most likely to make a trap close without the plant then producing digestive enzymes?
questions.e: Two touches within about half a minute close the trap, but enzymes come only after several further signals from struggling prey; a seed that lies still supplies none. A single touch (B, C) or touches minutes apart (E) do not close the trap at all. Repeated struggling (D) is exactly what leads to enzyme production.
o: A seed that touches a hair twice in quick succession and then lies still
A single raindrop that strikes one of the sensitive hairs
An insect that brushes one hair once and then flies away
An insect that struggles repeatedly after the trap has closed
Two touches to the hairs that are separated by several minutes

questions.s: Select the sentence that states the general principle behind the plant's sequence of responses.
questions.e: 'In effect' introduces the generalization: the plant counts signals, and each higher count unlocks a costlier step (closing, then digesting). The first sentence names the problem rather than the principle behind the responses. The sentences about one touch, two touches and further signals describe individual steps, not the rule that links them.
o: The Venus flytrap faces a problem of discrimination.
Its leaves snap shut on insects, but closing is costly, consuming energy and taking hours to reverse, so a trap that closed on every falling raindrop or blown seed would soon exhaust the plant.
The solution lies in a set of sensitive hairs on the inner surface of each leaf.
A single touch to one hair produces an electrical signal but does not close the trap.
Only if a second touch follows within about half a minute does the leaf snap shut.
Struggling prey then triggers further signals, and after several more the plant begins producing digestive enzymes.
In effect, the plant counts, and each threshold guards a more expensive commitment.
Debris rarely touches the hairs twice in quick succession; a live insect exploring the leaf almost always does.

questions.s: The author mentions that singers 'sincerely insisted' they had performed a song exactly as before most likely in order to
questions.e: The renditions differed, yet the singers sincerely called them the same, so their idea of 'the same song' must rest on something other than identical words, such as the same story built from the same formulas and scenes. 'Sincerely' rules out deliberate deception (A). Choice C contradicts the statement that the singers 'did not memorize fixed texts at all'.
o: suggest that the singers were deliberately misleading the researchers who recorded them
imply that the singers judged sameness by something other than exact wording
indicate that some singers did in fact memorize fixed texts
explain why recurring scenes were popular with audiences
cast doubt on the reliability of the twentieth-century fieldwork

questions.s: The passage indicates which of the following about the formulas the singers used? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The passage defines formulas as 'ready-made phrases that fit the meter', so only the first choice is supported. 'Ready-made' contradicts the second choice: the poem was recomposed each time, but from existing formulas. The arming of a hero is given as an example of a recurring scene, a separate resource, not as the main place formulas appear.
o: They were phrases that fit the meter of the poem.
They were invented anew during each performance.
They were used mainly in scenes describing the arming of a hero.

questions.s: The 'less welcome result' mentioned in the passage is that automatic enrollment
questions.e: The final sentence explains the result: workers tended to stay at a low default rate, and some saved less than they would have chosen on their own. Choices A and C contradict the opening, which reports that participation rose to nearly all new hires in some firms. Choice B is wrong because workers could still opt out.
o: caused many workers to opt out of the plans entirely
made it more difficult for workers to leave the plans
failed to raise participation among most new hires
required more administrative effort than employers expected
led some workers to save less than they otherwise would have

questions.s: The passage suggests that standard economic models predicted little effect from automatic enrollment because the models assumed that
questions.e: The models predicted little effect 'because the choice itself was unchanged': the same options were open either way, so presentation should not matter. Choices A and B are among the behavioral economists' explanations of why the default did matter, which is the opposite of what the standard models assumed.
o: workers would read any default as an implicit recommendation
most workers prefer to postpone decisions about saving
choices depend on the options available, not on how they are framed
employers would tend to set default contribution rates too low
few new hires would wish to save for retirement at all

questions.s: The difficulty faced by the biological account would be most reduced if it were found that
questions.e: The difficulty is that manganese-concentrating bacteria are scarce in varnish. If such bacteria die and leave the metal behind, varnish could be biological in origin even though few living bacteria are found in it. Choice A supports the rival chemical account rather than rescuing the biological one, and the speed of laboratory bacteria (C) says nothing about their scarcity in the field.
o: manganese precipitates readily whenever dew evaporates
the dust around varnished rocks contains little manganese
laboratory bacteria oxidize manganese faster than wild ones
bacteria that concentrate manganese die but leave it behind
varnish forms over thousands rather than hundreds of years

questions.s: The passage is primarily concerned with
questions.e: The passage sets out the chemical account, the biological account, a difficulty for the latter and a proposal that tries to reconcile them, all about how varnish becomes rich in manganese. It does not side with the chemical view (B). Sun protection (C) appears only as part of the reconciling proposal, and D reverses the point that the laboratory bacteria are scarce in real varnish.
o: presenting competing explanations for a geological phenomenon
arguing that desert varnish is produced by chemistry alone
explaining how desert microbes shield themselves from sunlight
showing that a laboratory finding has been confirmed in the field
tracing the history of mining for manganese in arid regions

questions.s: The author's main point about flying buttresses is that they
questions.e: The author accepts the engineering account but argues that 'the problem the buttresses solved was itself chosen': patrons' desire for height and light created the need. Choice A contradicts the statement that structural analyses confirm the buttresses' function, and C ignores the author's insistence that function is not irrelevant. The buttresses carry thrust down to piers, so D misreads the mechanism.
o: were less important structurally than is usually claimed
solved a problem that arose from the builders' own ambitions
were added to cathedrals chiefly as decoration
made it possible to build high vaults without piers
were designed by patrons rather than by builders

questions.s: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The buttress let patrons pursue height and light 'further than earlier construction allowed', so earlier methods set limits (second choice). Because the engineering 'served an aesthetic program rather than determining it', the aim preceded the means (third choice). The first choice reverses the passage, which says structural analyses broadly confirm the buttresses' function.
o: Structural analyses have shown that the buttresses were largely unnecessary.
Earlier methods of construction limited how tall and bright churches could be.
The desire for height and light came before the means of achieving it on a grand scale.

questions.s: According to the passage, an immediate return gift of equal value would be undesirable because it would
questions.e: The passage says such a return 'would cancel the debt and, with it, the relationship'. Choice C reverses the point: it is the delayed return that leaves a balance outstanding. Choice D distorts the remark about returning exactly what was received, which gives offense because it signals a wish to be quits, not because of any rule about kinds of goods.
o: make the recipient seem unable to afford a larger gift
require the two parties to agree on a price in advance
leave a balance outstanding between the two parties
break a rule against exchanging goods of the same kind
cancel the obligation that keeps the relationship going

questions.s: Select the sentence that states the author's conclusion about what distinguishes gift exchange from market exchange.
questions.e: The last sentence names what separates the two kinds of exchange: not the goods but the purpose, keeping a tie alive versus ending cleanly. The sentence about market transactions is the tempting choice, but it describes only one side of the contrast and draws no conclusion about what the difference consists in.
o: Anthropologists studying societies in which goods circulate largely as gifts have observed that a gift is rarely free.
Accepting one creates an obligation to reciprocate, and the return gift is often expected not immediately but after a delay, sometimes of months.
An immediate return of equal value would cancel the debt and, with it, the relationship; it would resemble a purchase.
By leaving a balance outstanding, the parties keep a tie alive, each anticipating the next exchange.
For the same reason, returning exactly what was received can give offense, signaling a wish to be quits.
Market transactions, by contrast, are designed to end cleanly, leaving buyer and seller with no further claim on each other.
The difference lies less in the goods than in what the exchange is meant to do.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage suggests that the abundance of close-in giant planets in early catalogs
questions.e: Saying the abundance 'tells us as much about the instruments as about the galaxy' means the catalogs are skewed by what both methods favor: close-in and massive planets. Choice B is exactly the conclusion astronomers warn against. Nothing suggests measurement errors (E); the bias comes from methods working as designed.
o: partly reflects which planets the methods detect most easily
proves that such planets are the most common type in the galaxy
shows that the transit method is more reliable than the radial-velocity method
indicates that planets resembling Mercury are rare around other stars
resulted from errors in measuring the dimming of stars

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following make planets that orbit close to their stars easier to find by the transit method? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The passage gives two reasons for the transit method: the edge-on alignment is 'far more likely' for close-in planets, and such planets 'transit more often'. The wobble in the first choice belongs to the radial-velocity method, not to transits, so it does not answer the question even though close, massive planets do produce strong wobbles.
o: Their gravity produces a stronger wobble in the stars they orbit.
Their orbits are more likely to be aligned so that they pass in front of their stars as seen from Earth.
They pass in front of their stars more frequently than distant planets do.

questions.s: The author refers to the heroine and the suitor primarily in order to
questions.e: The example follows the claim that 'the reader often understands more than any single correspondent' and shows it at work: the reader sees both the heroine's innocence and the suitor's motives. Choices A and E turn one illustration into a generalization the author never makes. The example answers the critics rather than supporting them (B).
o: show that heroines in such novels were usually naive
support the critics' complaint that the form was clumsy
illustrate how readers can grasp more than any one correspondent
explain why characters write long letters during a crisis
argue that suitors in letter novels are typically calculating

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the critics mentioned in the last sentence?
questions.e: The author says the critics 'overlooked how much of its interest lies precisely in what each writer cannot see': they attended to an awkward convention and missed the form's main appeal. The author does not dispute how often the convention occurs (C), and the passage opens by crediting the form with an illusion of immediacy, so B reverses it.
o: They identified the form's central strength.
They were right that the form lacks immediacy.
They exaggerated how often characters write during a crisis.
They fixed on a flaw and missed what makes the form interesting.
They preferred novels told by a single narrator.

questions.s: The passage suggests that a map of trade based on amphorae might understate the trade in
questions.e: Goods shipped in barrels or sacks 'leave far fainter traces' because those containers rot, so an amphora-based map would miss much of that trade. Spanish oil, fish sauce and stamped wine all traveled in clay jars, which is exactly what the map records well. Choice E confuses a dating tool with a traded good.
o: olive oil shipped from southern Spain
goods that were carried in wooden barrels
fish sauce sent to military camps
wine produced on estates that stamped their jars
jars whose shapes changed over time

questions.s: The author mentions that amphorae were often reused primarily in order to
questions.e: The reuse point is the first of the method's acknowledged limits: a refilled jar's stamp shows where it was made, not what it last carried. Choice C is too extreme, since the author treats amphorae as useful evidence with limits, not as useless. Nothing in the passage connects reuse to the jars' abundance, forgery or careless labeling.
o: explain why amphorae are so abundant at ancient sites
suggest that the stamps on amphorae were frequently forged
argue that amphorae are useless as evidence of ancient trade
imply that Roman producers were careless about labeling
note why a jar's origin may not reveal its last contents

questions.s: The first possibility mentioned in the passage would be weakened most if it were found that the main predators of cuttlefish
questions.e: The first possibility holds that matching brightness and pattern suffices because predators are poor at seeing color. Predators that easily distinguish colors of equal brightness would see through such a match, undermining that reasoning. Choice D would support the possibility rather than weaken it, and a preference for movement (C) does not bear on whether color matching is needed.
o: readily tell apart colors of similar brightness
hunt mainly at night when little light is available
detect prey chiefly by movement rather than by pattern
have eyes with only one type of light-sensitive pigment
avoid prey that closely match their surroundings

questions.s: Select the sentence that explains how cuttlefish might perceive color despite having only one type of pigment.
questions.e: The sentence about wavelengths focusing at different depths gives a mechanism by which the animal 'might infer color from blur'. The sentence before it only names the W-shaped pupil without saying how it would help. The brightness-and-pattern sentence explains how cuttlefish might camouflage well without perceiving color at all, which is a different claim.
o: Cuttlefish are masters of camouflage, matching the color and texture of their surroundings within a fraction of a second.
Yet behavioral tests indicate that most species are colorblind: their eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive pigment, which ordinarily allows an animal to distinguish brightness but not hue.
How an animal that cannot see color matches it so well remains unresolved.
One possibility is that matching brightness and pattern is enough, since many predators of cuttlefish are themselves poor at distinguishing colors.
Another proposal concerns the cuttlefish's oddly shaped pupil, curved like the letter W.
Such a pupil could allow different wavelengths of light to come into focus at slightly different depths in the eye, so that the animal might infer color from blur.
The idea is ingenious but has yet to be tested directly in living animals.

questions.s: The passage implies that a figure standing for a shoeshine appears in an early street photograph because he
questions.e: Exposures lasted several minutes, so only things that kept still were recorded; a man having his shoes shined stands still for that long. The passage gives no hint of posing, payment or retouching (A, E). Distance and lighting (B, C) are not what separated recorded from unrecorded subjects; movement was.
o: was paid by the photographer to pose for the camera
stood closer to the camera than the pedestrians did
was lit more brightly than the passing carriages
stayed in place long enough to be recorded
was added to the image after the exposure was made

questions.s: The passage suggests which of the following? Select all that apply.
questions.e: As exposures shortened and photography began to capture motion, painters were prompted 'to look elsewhere once more', so technology shaped painters' choices (third choice). The first choice contradicts the statement that buildings were recorded in sharp detail. The second reverses the claim that contemporary viewers were less troubled by the absence than we might expect.
o: Early photographs were unable to record buildings in fine detail.
Most viewers in the 1840s regretted the absence of people from street photographs.
Changes in photographic technology influenced the subjects painters chose.

questions.s: The passage is primarily concerned with
questions.e: The passage says cross-fostering was 'decisive' in showing that learning can produce dialects, then argues that it cannot explain why dialects persist in the wild; the purpose is to show what the evidence settles and what it leaves open. The genetic-inheritance choice reverses the passage's conclusion. Female preference is only one of several possibilities the author lists, so presenting it as the author's proposal is too narrow and too strong.
o: arguing that the song dialects of sparrow populations are inherited genetically rather than acquired by learning
describing in detail the procedure by which cross-fostering experiments on songbirds are carried out
explaining why one kind of evidence settles a question about song dialects but leaves a related question open
criticizing researchers for having treated geographic variation as proof that birdsong is learned
proposing that female preference for local songs is the main force that maintains dialect boundaries

questions.s: Select the sentence in which the author objects that a pattern in the data is compatible with two different explanations.
questions.e: The second sentence says geographic variation 'cannot distinguish' cultural transmission from genetic divergence, because both could produce the same pattern. The fourth sentence also states a limitation, but it concerns what an experiment fails to explain (persistence), not a pattern fitting two rival explanations. The last sentence lists several possibilities but locates the problem in the design of captive experiments.
o: Populations of white-crowned sparrows separated by only a few kilometers often sing recognizably different song dialects, and for decades the variation was taken as evidence that song is learned and transmitted culturally, much as regional accents are.

Yet geographic variation alone cannot distinguish cultural transmission from genetic divergence, since neighboring populations that rarely interbreed could drift apart in inherited song templates as readily as in learned ones.
The decisive evidence came instead from cross-fostering: nestlings raised by tutors from a distant dialect reliably acquire the tutors' song rather than that of their biological parents.
Even this result, however, establishes only that learning is sufficient to produce dialects, not that it explains their persistence in the wild.

Dialect boundaries might be maintained because females prefer local songs, because young males settle near the tutors they heard, or because both pressures operate together, possibilities that cross-fostering experiments, conducted in captivity, are not designed to separate.

questions.s: The author mentions that patrons "paid dearly" for the manuscripts primarily in order to
questions.e: The idleness thesis says the images were 'tolerated'; the author answers that patrons who paid heavily for the books 'evidently requested' them, so they were wanted, not just put up with. The price choice misreads the detail: the point is what patrons asked for, not how the images affected value. The detail is offered against the idleness thesis, not in support of the parody thesis.
o: suggest that marginal images substantially raised the price that a manuscript could command
show that the illuminators who painted the margins were far less bored by their work than earlier scholars have assumed
support the claim that the marginal images were intended to parody the adjacent passages
explain why illuminators in different workshops seldom came into contact with one another
cast doubt on the view that the marginal images were merely tolerated rather than actually wanted

questions.s: Which of the following does the passage present as a difficulty for one of the two earlier accounts of marginal images? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The unrelated margins undermine the parody thesis, and the recurrence of motifs across unconnected workshops undermines the idleness thesis, since random play would not produce shared conventions. The memory aid is not a difficulty for either account; it is the evidence for the author's preferred third view.
o: Many marginal images have no apparent connection to the text beside them.
Similar motifs appear in manuscripts produced by workshops that were not in contact.
Incongruous pictures were a recognized aid to remembering one's place in a long text.

questions.s: According to the passage, studies of randomly assigned roommates are valuable chiefly because they
questions.e: The problem the passage describes is that peers may share advantages 'that predate any interaction'; lottery assignment removes that shared background, which is why such settings 'escape this difficulty.' The studies find effects smaller than raw correlations, so the 'larger' choice is reversed, and 'vanish entirely' is too extreme because the effects are 'real but modest.' Whole classrooms over years are exactly what the roommate studies do not measure.
o: reduce the chance that a student and her peers share advantages that existed before they met
show that peer effects are considerably larger than raw correlations between students suggest
measure the influence of whole classrooms whose membership is sustained over several years
allow researchers to observe directly how families choose among competing schools
demonstrate that peer effects vanish entirely once the selection of schools is controlled

questions.s: The scholars mentioned in the passage would most likely agree with which of the following statements?
questions.e: The scholars accept that the roommate effects are 'measured cleanly' but argue that a single roommate differs from the classroom peer groups policymakers care about, so a sound result may not describe the relevant setting. They do not question the reliability of random assignment, and random assignment rules out family selection as the source of roommate effects. The passage suggests the roommate studies may understate classroom effects, the opposite of the last choice.
o: Random assignment is in general a less reliable method than observational comparison for estimating the size of peer effects.
The peer effects found among roommates are probably artifacts of the way families select schools.
Policymakers should rely on raw correlations because these reflect real classroom conditions.
A finding can be methodologically sound and still bear only loosely on the question that motivated it.
Peer effects are certain to be larger among first-year university students than among schoolchildren.

questions.s: The passage suggests that the length of time over which the carbonate layers accumulated is significant because
questions.e: Snowball proponents predict that the excess carbon was 'rapidly deposited,' while critics point to layers that took longer than 'a sudden post-glacial pulse would allow'; hence the dispute 'turns on how quickly they formed.' The critics explicitly 'accept the deposits,' so they do not deny the layering. Nothing in the passage ties glacier extent to duration or says the slushball view needs cold-water carbonates.
o: the carbonate layers could have formed only after the equatorial oceans had frozen completely
rapid accumulation is predicted by one hypothesis, whereas slower accumulation fits more easily with its rival
the duration of a glaciation determines whether glaciers are able to reach tropical latitudes
the critics deny that the carbonate layers lie directly on top of the glacial deposits
the slushball hypothesis requires that the carbonates precipitated in cold rather than warm water

questions.s: According to the passage, proponents of the Snowball Earth hypothesis hold that which of the following occurred? Select all that apply.
questions.e: All three are steps in the proponents' account: with oceans sealed, volcanic carbon dioxide accumulated 'for millions of years, unchecked by the weathering of rock,' and after the greenhouse melted the ice the carbon 'was rapidly deposited as carbonate.' A tempting error is to reject the third statement because critics question rapid deposition, but the question asks what the proponents hold.
o: The weathering of rock that ordinarily removes carbon dioxide was largely suppressed.
Carbon dioxide released by volcanoes built up in the atmosphere over a long period.
The melting of the ice was followed by a rapid deposition of carbonate.

questions.s: The author's attitude toward the practice of playing Baroque music with little vibrato is best described as
questions.e: The author calls the argument 'less conclusive than it appears' yet says 'None of this proves that continuous vibrato was the norm,' so the stance is doubt about the evidence, not endorsement of the opposite. The 'dismissive' choice is too extreme for exactly that reason. The author notes that the treatises 'disagree among themselves,' which rules out 'consistently,' and the final sentence grants history a real constraining role.
o: dismissive, on the grounds that continuous vibrato was clearly the historical norm
skeptical of the evidence offered for it, without claiming that the opposite practice is correct
approving, because the treatises consistently describe vibrato as an occasional ornament
indifferent, since the author holds that historical documents about musical performance cannot be interpreted at all
ambivalent, because the author ranks modern taste above historical evidence in importance

questions.s: Select the sentence in which the author suggests that a body of evidence might point to the reverse of what it is usually taken to show.
questions.e: The third sentence argues that repeated warnings against excessive vibrato 'might indicate that many players used it liberally,' turning evidence cited for sparing vibrato into possible evidence of frequent vibrato. The sentence about disagreeing treatises weakens the evidence but does not reverse it, and the sentence on 'underdetermines' draws a general conclusion rather than reinterpreting a specific source.
o: Modern performers of Baroque music who play with little or no vibrato often justify the practice by citing eighteenth-century treatises that describe vibrato as an ornament, to be applied sparingly to particular notes.
The argument is less conclusive than it appears.
Treatises are prescriptive documents, and writers rarely trouble to forbid what nobody does; repeated warnings against excessive vibrato might indicate that many players used it liberally.
Moreover, the treatises disagree among themselves, and their authors were often teachers addressing students rather than describing the habits of celebrated soloists.
None of this proves that continuous vibrato was the norm.
It suggests rather that the written record underdetermines the sound of the past, and that the austere tone now associated with 'authentic' performance owes something to modern taste.
Historical evidence has constrained the revival of early music, but it has not dictated its every choice.

questions.s: The author's reference to "a winter when no bulbs could be lifted from the ground" serves mainly to
questions.e: The detail explains why the famous prices come from 'contracts for future delivery': in winter no bulb could actually be handed over, so what traded were promises. The passage says 'Few traders appear to have been ruined,' which rules out the last choice, and it says nothing about scarcity of supply, deception about quality, or the length of the frenzy.
o: explain why the supply of tulip bulbs was too small to satisfy the demand of Dutch buyers
suggest that traders were deceived about the quality of the bulbs that they had purchased
show that the speculative frenzy lasted considerably longer than the traditional legend claims
indicate that the recorded prices attached to promises of later delivery rather than to bulbs that changed hands
account for the eventual financial ruin of most of the traders who took part in the craze

questions.s: The passage suggests which of the following about the traditional account of the tulip craze? Select all that apply.
questions.e: The legend says bulbs 'changed hands' at extravagant prices, but those prices come from contracts often settled for a fraction of face value or not at all, so the account took promises for payments. It also described a 'distress' that the wider economy does not show. The traditional account is precisely a story of frenzy; it is the author who grants, against an overcorrection, that 'a brief speculative frenzy evidently occurred.'
o: It treated prices written into contracts as though they were prices actually paid.
It overstated the economic harm that the episode caused.
It denied that any speculative frenzy had taken place.

questions.s: The author raises which of the following as a possible alternative explanation for the detection of labeled carbon in a neighboring tree? Select all that apply.
questions.e: For the carbon finding, the author's alternative is that it 'may have traveled through soil rather than through fungal threads.' Better access to soil nutrients is offered as an alternative explanation for a different observation, improved seedling growth. Insects appear only in the popular claim about warnings; they are never proposed as carriers of carbon.
o: The carbon may have moved through the soil rather than through fungal threads.
The fungi may have helped the neighboring tree obtain nutrients from the soil.
The carbon may have been carried to the neighboring tree by insects.

questions.s: The final sentence of the passage functions primarily to
questions.e: The last sentence grants that the network 'may' move resources but proposes that it serves 'its fungal members' rather than the forest, so any transfer need not be read as trees helping trees. It does not deny that resources move, and it challenges rather than concedes the popular account. The small quantities were mentioned earlier and are not explained here.
o: suggest that the movement of resources through the network need not be understood as benefiting the trees
deny that fungal networks are capable of moving any resources between neighboring trees
explain why the quantities of carbon transferred in experiments were too small to matter
concede that the popular account of the network as a forest-wide service is essentially correct
introduce new evidence that fungal networks warn trees of approaching insect attack

questions.s: The passage is primarily concerned with
questions.e: After defining free indirect discourse, the passage sets the older emphasis on 'psychological intimacy' against the more recent emphasis on 'irony' and develops the second. It names no particular novelists, and the technique is defined by the absence of quotation marks. The passage elaborates the recent view rather than defending the earlier one, so the last choice reverses its direction.
o: tracing the origins of a narrative technique to a few nineteenth-century novelists
arguing that the intimacy readers feel with characters is produced by quotation marks
explaining why readers of nineteenth-century novels routinely misjudged their heroines
defending an earlier critical view of a narrative technique against recent objections
contrasting two emphases in critical accounts of a narrative technique

questions.s: It can be inferred that the "more recent readers" would regard which of the following as a characteristic effect of free indirect discourse?
questions.e: The recent readers say the pleasure of the method lies in 'the discovery that one has been sharing [the character's view] too readily,' that is, in recognizing belatedly that the view deserved doubt. The narrator 'never formally disowns the character's view,' so explicit correction is the opposite of the technique, and the voices are said to blur, not stay separate.
o: A reader is told directly by the narrator which of a character's judgments are mistaken.
A reader perceives the narrator and the character as two clearly separate voices throughout.
A reader who adopted a character's view comes to see that the novel invites doubt about it.
A reader loses interest in a character's inner life because the narrator's irony is so obvious.
A reader is able to identify the exact words that a character spoke aloud to others.

questions.s: Select the sentence in which supporters of a view reinterpret a finding that had been taken to count against that view.
questions.e: The last sentence takes the finding that terminologies 'persist for generations after the arrangements they supposedly encoded have disappeared' and reads it as the preserved 'imprint of past arrangements,' turning an objection into support for the social interpretation. The sentence 'The social interpretation has not been abandoned' announces that defenders exist but does not yet reinterpret anything, and the fourth sentence reports the counterevidence itself.
o: Anthropologists once expected kinship terminologies to mirror social arrangements closely.

If a language uses one word for both one's father and one's father's brother, the reasoning went, then the two men must occupy similar roles, perhaps sharing authority over the children of the household.
Field studies have repeatedly strained this expectation.

Communities with nearly identical terminologies organize inheritance, residence and marriage quite differently, and terminologies sometimes persist for generations after the arrangements they supposedly encoded have disappeared.

Some linguists now argue that terminologies are better understood as compact classification systems, shaped partly by the cognitive economy of using few terms and partly by descent from ancestral languages.
The social interpretation has not been abandoned, however.
Its defenders contend that a terminology may preserve the imprint of past arrangements, much as the layout of a city's streets records the boundaries of fields that were long ago built over.

questions.s: The author mentions "the cognitive economy of using few terms" as
questions.e: The phrase belongs to the linguists' alternative account, in which terminologies are 'compact classification systems' shaped by economy of terms and by linguistic descent rather than by social arrangements. It is not offered by defenders of the social interpretation, and the passage notes that terminologies often persist after arrangements change, so 'change rapidly' reverses the evidence.
o: evidence that a father and a father's brother occupy similar roles within a household
a reason why terminologies tend to change rapidly whenever social arrangements change
one influence that, according to some linguists, shapes terminologies apart from social roles
an explanation put forward by the defenders of the social interpretation of kinship terminologies
the principal cause of the differences in inheritance practices among communities

questions.s: The passage suggests that detecting methane alongside oxygen is significant because
questions.e: Methane 'reacts with oxygen and would soon disappear unless something kept replenishing it,' so finding both implies an ongoing source, which life could supply. The passage says such a combination is 'far harder to explain without life,' not that it proves photosynthesis, so the last choice is too strong. Nothing links methane to retained water, ultraviolet shielding, or the type of star.
o: methane is produced only on planets that have retained most of their original water
methane shields water vapor from the ultraviolet light that would otherwise split it apart
methane cannot be produced on any planet that orbits a small, active star
the presence of methane proves conclusively that the oxygen came from photosynthesis
the persistence of two gases that react with each other implies a continuing source of at least one

questions.s: The passage implies which of the following about a planet whose atmosphere contains abundant oxygen but no methane? Select all that apply.
questions.e: Oxygen 'found alone' is the case the passage treats as explainable without life, for instance by ultraviolet splitting of water and hydrogen escape. Small, active stars only make such buildup 'especially' likely, so 'almost certainly' is unsupported. The passage says 'Few researchers conclude that oxygen is therefore useless as a biosignature.'
o: Its oxygen may have accumulated through a process involving no living things.
It almost certainly orbits a small, active star.
Most researchers would take it as showing that oxygen is useless as a biosignature.

questions.s: The author mentions early buttresses "placed too high to meet the thrust they were meant to resist" primarily in order to
questions.e: The example follows the claim that builders worked from 'proportional rules' rather than a theory of forces: misplaced buttresses survived only thanks to extra-thick walls, so success did not require exact knowledge. The passage says collapse happened 'on occasion,' not to most churches, and it grants that the account of the buttress's structural role 'is not wrong,' which rules out 'no structural purpose.'
o: illustrate that the builders' success did not rest on a precise understanding of the forces involved
show that most of the early Gothic churches built with flying buttresses eventually collapsed
argue that flying buttresses in fact served no structural purpose in Gothic churches
explain why later builders chose to decorate their buttresses with pinnacles and tracery
suggest that thick walls were a later improvement that replaced the flying buttress

questions.s: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
questions.e: The author says the structural account 'is not wrong, but it is incomplete,' then adds two qualifications: builders worked by rule and trial rather than theory, and buttresses also served display ('Nor was the device chosen for utility alone'). Because the account is retained, 'rejected outright' is wrong, and no particular buildings are named.
o: A traditional explanation is rejected outright and replaced by an opposing one.
Two competing theories are described in turn and the evidence for each of them is weighed equally.
A historical puzzle is posed and then explicitly left unresolved by the author.
A familiar explanation is granted partial validity and then supplemented in two respects.
A general principle is stated and then illustrated by a series of named buildings.

questions.s: According to the passage, which of the following have been observed in research on loss aversion? Select all that apply.
questions.e: All three are reported findings: the early experiments required a gain 'roughly twice the potential loss,' and later work found that people accept such bets readily at very small stakes and that the asymmetry 'shrinks or vanishes' with money seen as a gambling budget. The later findings complicate the interpretation but are still observations, which is what the question asks about.
o: Participants refusing even-odds bets unless the possible gain was much larger than the possible loss
A weakening of the asymmetry when the money at stake is regarded as set aside for gambling
Readier acceptance of even-odds bets when the amounts involved are very small

questions.s: The author's evaluation of the view that loss aversion is "real but conditional" is best described as
questions.e: The author credits the view with 'the merit of explaining both the original results and their exceptions' and then adds 'though at the cost of' predictions that depend on hard-to-measure expectations, which is praise with a reservation about testability. The 'wholly favorable' choice ignores that cost, and the passage says the view explains the early results rather than failing to.
o: wholly favorable, because the predictions of the view are easy to confirm
favorable, but qualified by a reservation about how readily the view can be tested
unfavorable, because the view cannot account for the results of the early experiments
neutral, since the author declines to compare the view with any alternative
unfavorable, because the author believes that loss aversion is an artifact of framing

questions.s: The author's main point is that
questions.e: The author grants the sampling biases but rejects the skeptics' inference: 'uncertainty runs in both directions,' and the record supports 'not complacency' but recognition that the global picture is 'largely unmeasured.' Tropical losses 'could exceed' recorded ones, which is a possibility, not a certainty. The author accepts the baseline bias but denies that it shows exaggeration overall, so the skeptics' choice is half right.
o: insect declines in tropical forests are certainly far greater than the declines recorded in Europe and North America
flaws in the evidence make the extent of insect decline uncertain without showing that it is minor
long-term records of insect abundance are too unreliable to be of any scientific use
intensive agriculture and habitat loss are the principal causes of insect decline worldwide
skeptics are right that unusually productive baseline years have inflated the declines

questions.s: Select the sentence in which the author suggests that a bias emphasized by skeptics may be offset by one that they overlook.
questions.e: The sixth sentence concedes the biases in where and when sampling began, then argues that 'uncertainty runs in both directions' because the least-studied regions, tropical forests, may have suffered even greater losses. The sentences about well-studied regions and productive baseline years describe the biases themselves, and 'That inference does not follow' rejects the skeptics' conclusion without yet giving the counterweight.
o: Reports of steep declines in insect abundance have alarmed ecologists, but the evidence is uneven in ways that complicate any global estimate.
Most long-term records come from a handful of well-studied regions, chiefly in Europe and North America, where intensive agriculture and habitat loss are already known to be severe.
Many series also begin in years that happen to have been unusually productive, so that later counts look low partly by comparison with an exceptional baseline.
Skeptics sometimes conclude that the declines have been exaggerated.

Biases in where and when sampling began make the size of the decline uncertain, but uncertainty runs in both directions: the regions least studied include tropical forests, where clearing has been rapid and where losses could exceed anything yet recorded.
What the record supports is not complacency but a recognition that the global picture remains largely unmeasured.

questions.s: The author refers to emblem books primarily in order to
questions.e: The emblem books are introduced as 'textual support' for the vanitas reading, which the next sentence says 'sits awkwardly' with how the paintings were made and sold. The support is suggestive, not proof of what buyers understood, and the author ends by saying the readings 'need not be exclusive,' so the passage does not argue for abandoning the vanitas interpretation.
o: show that still-life painters copied their compositions directly from printed sources
prove that buyers understood still lifes as sermons on the brevity of pleasure
explain why still lifes were often hung beside maps and portraits in Dutch homes
acknowledge evidence for an interpretation that the author goes on to complicate
argue that the vanitas reading of Dutch still lifes ought to be abandoned

questions.s: Which of the following does the author present as sitting awkwardly with a purely moralizing reading of the paintings? Select all that apply.
