Foreign and exotic are synonyms, but they agree with the truth rather than contrast with it, so the "in fact" correction would make no sense. Common fits the sentence, but being numerous is not the opposite of being a newcomer, and common has no partner.

questions.s: The coach praised the team's _____ effort, noting that the players kept running hard even in the final minutes of the match.
questions.e: Players who keep running hard "even in the final minutes" show effort that never lets up: unflagging and untiring. Halfhearted and lukewarm are synonyms meaning lacking enthusiasm, which contradicts the coach's praise. Collective fits a team, but it describes who made the effort, not its persistence, and no other choice shares its meaning.

questions.s: The chemist was _____ by the unexpected result, unable at first to explain how the sample had changed color.
questions.e: Being "unable at first to explain" what happened describes confusion, so the blank means puzzled or baffled. Bored and weary are a near-synonym pair, but an unexpected result is the opposite of tiresome. Alarmed could describe a reaction to a surprise, but it means frightened rather than confused, and it has no partner.

questions.s: Because the assembly instructions were _____, many customers put the bookshelf together incorrectly.
questions.e: Customers making mistakes is the effect, so the instructions must have been hard to follow: vague and unclear. Precise and explicit are synonyms for clearly stated, which would prevent rather than cause the errors. Brief might explain some confusion, but short instructions can still be clear, and nothing else in the list means short.

questions.s: The restaurant's portions were so _____ that most diners took half of their meal home.
questions.e: Taking half the meal home shows that the servings were larger than one person could eat: generous and ample. Meager and skimpy are synonyms for too small, which reverses the result. Rich food might also leave diners full, but rich describes heaviness rather than size and has no partner in the list.

questions.s: The two historians' accounts of the battle are _____: one describes a swift victory, while the other describes a long and costly struggle.
questions.e: The colon introduces two accounts that disagree (a swift victory versus a long struggle), so the blank means contradictory or inconsistent. Identical and matching are synonyms, but they claim the accounts agree, the reverse of the evidence. Detailed could describe both accounts, but it says nothing about their disagreement and has no partner.

questions.s: Though usually _____, the professor spoke at length and with obvious passion whenever the conversation turned to her favorite poet.
questions.e: "Though" contrasts her usual manner with speaking "at length and with obvious passion," so she normally says little: reserved and reticent (inclined to keep quiet). Talkative and chatty are synonyms, but they describe her exception, not her usual habit, and destroy the contrast. Strict can describe a professor, but strictness is not the opposite of speaking at length, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The city's new transit system proved so _____ that average commute times fell by nearly a third within a year.
questions.e: Commute times falling sharply is the result, so the system must work smoothly and quickly: efficient and streamlined (simplified to work better). Sluggish and slow are synonyms, but a slow system would lengthen commutes, not shorten them. Popular fits a successful system, but popularity alone does not cut travel times, and no other choice matches it.

questions.s: Amara's _____ handwriting made her lecture notes nearly impossible for her classmates to read.
questions.e: Notes that are "nearly impossible ... to read" have handwriting that cannot be made out: illegible and indecipherable. Neat and tidy form a synonym pair, but neat writing would be easy to read. Tiny handwriting could also be hard to read, yet tiny describes size rather than readability and has no partner among the choices.

questions.s: The historian argued that the trade agreement was _____ from the start, since neither country ever intended to honor its terms.
questions.e: If neither side meant to keep the terms, the agreement was certain to fail: doomed and ill-fated. Durable and lasting are synonyms, but they predict the opposite outcome. Secret could fit an agreement nobody intended to honor, but it has nothing to do with the cause and effect in the sentence, and no other choice shares its meaning.

questions.s: Unlike his _____ older brother, who saved nearly every coin he earned, Mateo spent his wages as soon as he received them.
questions.e: The brother "saved nearly every coin," and "Unlike" contrasts him with Mateo, who spends at once, so the brother is careful with money: frugal and thrifty. Extravagant and lavish are synonyms describing free spending, which matches Mateo rather than his brother. Serious might describe a saver, but it does not mean careful with money and has no partner.

questions.s: The bridge's design was _____ for its time, and engineers around the world later copied its methods.
questions.e: Engineers everywhere copying the design shows that it introduced new ideas: pathbreaking and revolutionary. Conventional and ordinary are synonyms, but nobody would copy a design that only followed existing practice. Expensive may well describe a famous bridge, yet cost does not explain why others imitated it, and nothing else in the list means costly.

questions.s: After months of _____ negotiations, the two companies finally reached an agreement in a single afternoon.
questions.e: "After months of" and "finally" show that the talks went on for a long time before ending suddenly, so the blank means lengthy or prolonged. Brief and short are a synonym pair, but months of talks cannot be brief. Tense fits difficult negotiations, but it describes their mood rather than their length and has no partner.

questions.s: The speaker's remarks were meant to _____ the audience's fears, but they only made the listeners more anxious.
questions.e: "But they only made the listeners more anxious" contrasts the result with the intention, so the remarks were meant to reduce fear: soothe and ease. Heighten and intensify are synonyms, but they describe what actually happened, not the intention, so the contrast with "but" disappears. Address also fits (the speaker meant to deal with the fears), but it does not say whether the fears would grow or shrink, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The film's ending was so _____ that audience members argued for weeks about what had actually happened to the main character.
questions.e: Viewers arguing for weeks about "what had actually happened" means the ending was hard to interpret: cryptic and enigmatic (mysterious). Straightforward and plain are synonyms, but a plain ending would leave nothing to argue about. Shocking fits a memorable ending, but a shock can be perfectly clear, and no other choice means shocking.

questions.s: Sofia's description of the journey was so _____ that her friends felt almost as if they had traveled with her.
questions.e: Friends feeling "as if they had traveled with her" shows that the description created strong mental pictures: vivid and evocative (bringing images or feelings to mind). Dull and bland are synonyms, but a bland account would not transport listeners. Long fits a travel story, yet length does not create the feeling of being there, and long has no partner.

questions.s: Although the merger was presented as a partnership of equals, the larger firm soon became _____, making nearly every important decision on its own.
questions.e: "Although ... a partnership of equals" and "making nearly every important decision" show that one firm took charge: dominant and controlling. Subordinate and secondary are synonyms, but they describe the smaller partner's role, not the firm making the decisions. Profitable fits a large firm, but it says nothing about power within the partnership and has no partner.

questions.s: The volunteers were _____ in their support for the public library, attending every meeting and donating books each month for years.
questions.e: Attending every meeting and donating "each month for years" shows loyal, consistent support: steadfast and unwavering. Fickle and inconstant are synonyms meaning changeable, the opposite of the evidence. Vocal (outspoken) also fits supporters, but speaking out is not the same as long, steady commitment, and no other choice matches it.

questions.s: The researchers cautioned that their findings were _____, since the trial included only twenty patients, and they called for a much larger study.
questions.e: A small trial and a call for a larger study show that the results are early and uncertain: preliminary and tentative. Conclusive and final are near-synonyms, but researchers would not ask for a bigger study if their results were settled. Surprising findings might also prompt more research, but surprise is not about certainty, and surprising has no partner.

questions.s: The negotiator remained _____ throughout the tense meeting, never raising her voice even when others began to shout.
questions.e: Never raising her voice while others shout shows that she stayed calm under pressure: composed and unflappable (not easily upset). Agitated and flustered are synonyms describing the very loss of calm she avoided. Polite also fits someone who does not shout, but politeness concerns manners rather than self-control under stress, and no other choice shares its meaning.

questions.s: Far from being the _____ figure portrayed in early biographies, the inventor was in fact a shrewd businessman who guarded his patents with great care.
questions.e: "Far from being" sets the biographies' portrait against the truth, a "shrewd businessman," so the blank must mean the opposite of shrewd: naive and unworldly (lacking practical experience of life). Cunning and crafty are a synonym pair that matches the real inventor, so a hurried reader picks them, but they erase the contrast. Reclusive could also be a myth about inventors, yet a recluse can still be shrewd, and no other choice means reclusive.

questions.s: The new policy's benefits proved _____: within a year, most of the initial gains had disappeared.
questions.e: Gains that vanish "within a year" were short-lived, so the blank means ephemeral or transient (lasting only a short time). Enduring and permanent are synonyms, but they flatly contradict the disappearance described after the colon. Modest fits small benefits, but the clue is about how long the gains lasted rather than how large they were, and modest has no partner.

questions.s: Although the reviewer called the memoir _____, she conceded that its plain style suited a story about ordinary farm life.
questions.e: The concession that the "plain style suited" the story implies that the reviewer's main charge was dullness of style: prosaic (commonplace) and uninspired both mean ordinary and unimaginative. Lyrical and poetic are synonyms, but they are the opposite of a plain style, so there would be nothing to concede. Brief could be a reviewer's complaint, yet it does not connect to the remark about style, and no other choice matches it. Litigious means inclined to sue.

questions.s: Hoping to _____ the effects of future floods, the town council funded a network of new drainage channels.
questions.e: Drainage channels are built to lessen flood damage, so the blank means mitigate or alleviate (make less severe). Worsen and compound (here, make worse) are a synonym pair, but no council would pay to increase flood damage. Predict is tempting because the floods are in the future, but drainage channels reduce effects rather than forecast them, and predict has no partner.

questions.s: Kwame's _____ answers in interviews frustrated reporters, who had hoped for long, revealing quotations.
questions.e: Reporters wanted "long, revealing quotations" and were frustrated, so the answers were very short: laconic and terse (using few words). Garrulous and loquacious are synonyms meaning very talkative, which would have pleased the reporters. Rehearsed answers can also frustrate reporters, but they need not be short, and rehearsed has no partner in the list.

questions.s: The archaeologists' claim, though _____, rested on a single pottery fragment, and few colleagues were willing to accept it without further evidence.
questions.e: "Though" concedes a strength before the weakness (one fragment, little support), so the claim was reasonable on its face: plausible and believable. Absurd and preposterous are a synonym pair, but they are weaknesses, not a concession, and they would make the colleagues' caution unremarkable. Bold also fits a claim based on thin evidence, but it does not mean reasonable, and no other choice shares its meaning.

questions.s: Economists were surprised that consumer spending remained _____ during the recession, as they had expected households to cut back sharply.
questions.e: The surprise is that spending did not drop as expected, so it stayed strong: robust and buoyant (staying high). Sluggish and stagnant are synonyms that a hurried reader links with "recession," but weak spending is exactly what economists expected, so there would be no surprise. Unpredictable fits the idea of surprise, yet it does not say whether spending stayed high, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The painter's late works are strikingly _____: after decades of crowded canvases, she began leaving large areas almost empty.
questions.e: Canvases with "large areas almost empty" are plain and uncluttered: stark (bare, severely plain) and minimalist. Ornate and elaborate are synonyms describing her earlier crowded style, not the late works. Dark could describe a late style, but it concerns color or mood rather than emptiness, and no other choice matches it. Punctilious means attentive to fine points of behavior.

questions.s: Rather than _____ the critics who had mocked his early experiments, the chemist simply continued his work and let the results speak for themselves.
questions.e: "Rather than" contrasts the blank with quietly continuing his work, so the blank is the action he declined: answering the critics with arguments, which is what rebut and refute mean. Ignore and disregard are synonyms, but ignoring the critics is exactly what he did, so they cannot be the rejected option. Sue also fits grammatically as a response to mockery, but it means taking legal action rather than arguing back, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The once _____ trade route fell into disuse after the new canal made the overland journey unnecessary.
questions.e: "Once" contrasts the route's past with its later disuse, so it used to be busy and successful: bustling and thriving. Desolate and forsaken are synonyms that describe the route after the canal, not before, so they break the contrast. Dangerous could describe an old overland route, but danger is not the opposite of disuse, and dangerous has no partner.

questions.s: Despite her reputation for _____, the conductor spent an hour patiently explaining a single passage to a nervous young cellist.
questions.e: "Despite" sets her reputation against patient, kind behavior, so she is known for being abrupt and rude: brusqueness and curtness. Tolerance and forbearance (patient self-restraint) are synonyms, but they agree with her behavior and remove the contrast. Perfectionism fits a conductor who works on one passage, yet a perfectionist can be patient, and no other choice means perfectionism.

questions.s: The documentary was criticized as _____, presenting only the evidence that supported its director's view while omitting inconvenient facts.
questions.e: Showing only supporting evidence and leaving out "inconvenient facts" is one-sided presentation: biased and slanted. Impartial and evenhanded are synonyms meaning fair to all sides, the opposite of the criticism. Superficial is a common complaint about documentaries, but it means shallow rather than one-sided, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The botanist's notes, though _____, contain the only surviving record of several plant species that have since vanished from the island.
questions.e: "Though" concedes a weakness before stressing the notes' value, so they must be partial: fragmentary and incomplete. Exhaustive and comprehensive are synonyms, but they name a strength, which would not need "though." Informal could be a weakness of field notes, but it describes style rather than coverage, and nothing else in the list means informal. Gregarious means sociable.

questions.s: The firm's annual report, usually a model of clarity, was uncharacteristically _____ this year, leaving analysts unsure how to interpret the figures.
questions.e: "Uncharacteristically" signals the opposite of its usual clarity, and analysts were "unsure how to interpret" it, so the report was hard to understand: unintelligible and incomprehensible. Lucid and transparent are synonyms meaning clear, which describes the usual report, not this year's. Late could also be uncharacteristic, but lateness would not make the figures hard to interpret, and late has no partner.

questions.s: Initially _____ about the plan, the investors became enthusiastic supporters once they saw the first year's profits.
questions.e: "Initially" and "became enthusiastic" mark a change of attitude, so the investors started out doubtful: skeptical and dubious. Sanguine (confidently hopeful) and optimistic are synonyms, but they leave no change for the profits to cause. Divided fits investors who disagreed among themselves, but it describes disagreement within the group rather than shared doubt, and divided has no partner.

questions.s: The novelist's characters are so _____ that readers often forget they are fictional and write to the author asking what became of them.
questions.e: Readers forgetting the characters are invented means the characters seem like complex real people: rounded and three-dimensional (fully developed, with many sides). Wooden and stiff are synonyms for lifeless characterization, the opposite of the effect described. Likable characters might also prompt letters, but being pleasant is not the same as seeming real, and likable has no partner.

questions.s: What critics dismissed as mere _____ in the composer's later scores was, she insisted, a deliberate decision to let long silences carry as much meaning as sound.
questions.e: She answers the critics by calling the feature "deliberate," so the critics must have seen it as unplanned or careless: carelessness and sloppiness. Diligence and meticulousness are synonyms for careful work, which critics would not "dismiss." Repetition can be a criticism of music, but the defense is about deliberateness, not variety, and repetition has no partner.

questions.s: The scientist's _____ approach, testing every assumption twice before publishing, slowed her output but earned her colleagues' lasting trust.
questions.e: Testing every assumption twice is extremely careful work, so the blank means meticulous or scrupulous (careful about every detail). Slapdash and slipshod are synonyms for careless, which would neither slow her down nor earn trust. Secretive could explain slow publishing, but it does not match double-checking and has no partner.

questions.s: Although the treaty was hailed as a breakthrough, many of its provisions were _____, merely restating commitments both nations had made decades earlier.
questions.e: Provisions that "merely" restate old commitments add nothing, so they are redundant or superfluous (unnecessary). Novel and original are synonyms that echo "breakthrough," but "Although" sets the provisions against that praise, and restated promises are not new. Vague is a plausible flaw in a treaty, but it does not match the clue about repetition, and vague has no partner.

questions.s: Olga's letter was outwardly _____, but anyone who knew her well could detect the anger beneath its polite phrases.
questions.e: "Outwardly" and "but" contrast the surface of the letter with the anger beneath, and the surface is described as "polite phrases": courteous and civil. Hostile and belligerent are synonyms that catch a reader who notices "anger," but the anger is hidden, not on the surface. Typed could describe the letter, but it says nothing about tone, and typed has no partner. Verdant means green with plants.

questions.s: The study's conclusions were seriously _____ by a later analysis showing that the original sample had been far too small.
questions.e: Showing that the sample was too small damages the study's support, so the conclusions were undermined or weakened. Bolstered and reinforced are synonyms meaning strengthened, the reverse of what a sampling flaw does. Overshadowed also fits, since a later analysis could draw attention away from the study, but it does not mean the conclusions lost their support, and overshadowed has no partner.

questions.s: Coastal towns that depend on fishing have proved surprisingly _____, responding to declining catches by developing tourism and fish farming.
questions.e: Towns that answer a decline by building new industries recover well from hardship: resilient and hardy. Vulnerable and fragile are synonyms that a hurried reader links with "declining catches," but "surprisingly" and the successful response point the other way. Prosperous is possible, but adapting to hardship does not prove wealth, and prosperous has no partner. Taciturn means saying little.

questions.s: The historian warned that the merchant's diary was hardly _____, since he had every reason to exaggerate his own successes.
questions.e: A writer with reasons to exaggerate is not neutral, so the diary was "hardly" impartial or disinterested (here, free of personal interest, not "uninterested"). Biased and partial are synonyms, but "hardly biased" would deny the very problem the historian is warning about. Legible fits a comment on an old diary, but readability has nothing to do with exaggeration, and legible has no partner.

questions.s: The startup's early success owed less to its founders' vision than to _____ timing: it launched just as its largest competitor went bankrupt.
questions.e: "Less to ... vision than to" contrasts planning with luck, and a rival's sudden bankruptcy was outside the founders' control, so the timing was fortuitous or serendipitous (happening by lucky chance). Deliberate and calculated are synonyms, but planned timing would be part of the founders' vision, which the sentence downplays. Perfect timing fits the result, but it does not convey luck as opposed to planning, and perfect has no partner. Lugubrious means mournful.

questions.s: Though the museum's new wing drew large crowds, many architects found its design _____, a collection of mismatched styles that never formed a unified whole.
questions.e: The phrase after the comma explains the blank: "mismatched styles that never formed a unified whole" means disjointed and fragmented. Harmonious and cohesive are synonyms meaning unified, which the phrase denies. Ostentatious (showy) is a plausible criticism of a new museum wing, but it does not describe a lack of unity, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The professor's _____ remarks about the assigned textbook surprised her students, who had assumed she chose it because she admired it.
questions.e: Students who assumed she admired the book were surprised, so her remarks must have been critical: disparaging and derogatory (belittling). Laudatory and complimentary are synonyms for praising, which would match the students' assumption and cause no surprise. Offhand (casual) remarks fit grammatically, but casualness would not by itself contradict admiration, and offhand has no partner.

questions.s: Rather than settling the dispute, the mediator's proposal only _____ it, as each side found new grievances in the fine print.
questions.e: "Rather than settling" and "new grievances" show the proposal made the conflict worse: exacerbated and inflamed. Defused and calmed are synonyms that mean nearly the same as settling, so the "rather than" contrast would collapse. Prolonged also fits, since new grievances could extend the dispute, but it means made longer rather than made worse, and it has no partner.

questions.s: The species, once _____ across the continent, now survives only in a few isolated mountain valleys.
questions.e: "Once" contrasts the past with survival in only "a few isolated" valleys, so the species used to be found everywhere: ubiquitous and widespread. Rare and uncommon are synonyms describing its present state, so they destroy the contrast. Hunted is a plausible part of the species' history, but it does not contrast with a narrow present range, and hunted has no partner.

questions.s: The critic's praise was so _____ that the author wondered whether the review had been meant as satire.
questions.e: Only praise that seems excessive would make an author suspect satire, so the blank means effusive or gushing (overflowing with enthusiasm). Lukewarm and tepid are synonyms for half-hearted, which would not look like mockery through exaggeration. Sudden praise might puzzle an author, but it does not suggest over-the-top satire, and sudden has no partner. Ductile means easily shaped.

questions.s: Though Priya claimed to be indifferent to the award, her _____ attendance at every event connected with it suggested otherwise.
questions.e: Attending "every event" connected with the award shows steady, careful effort, which contradicts her claim of indifference: assiduous and diligent. Sporadic and intermittent are synonyms for occasional, which clashes with "every event" and would support her claim instead. Conspicuous attendance also fits, but being noticeable is not the same as persistent, and conspicuous has no partner.

questions.s: The essayist's prose is so _____ that even her most intricate arguments can be followed on a first reading.
questions.e: Intricate arguments that are easy to follow at once require exceptionally clear writing: pellucid and limpid both mean transparently clear. Convoluted and tortuous (full of twists) are synonyms, and they echo "intricate," but twisted prose would make the arguments harder, not easier, to follow. Elegant prose is admirable, but elegance does not guarantee clarity, and elegant has no partner. Querulous means complaining.

questions.s: Though widely dismissed as _____, the explorer's plan to cross the ice sheet on foot was in fact grounded in years of painstaking preparation.
questions.e: "Dismissed" and "in fact grounded in ... preparation" show that people wrongly thought the plan was a fantasy: quixotic (idealistic and impractical) and chimerical (wildly unrealistic). Pragmatic and practical are synonyms that describe the plan as it really was, so they cannot be what critics dismissed it as. Dangerous fits an ice-sheet crossing, but careful preparation does not make a trek safe, so the contrast fails, and dangerous has no partner. Nascent means just beginning.

questions.s: The shareholders' meeting, normally a sedate affair, turned _____ when the board announced the cuts, with investors shouting over one another.
questions.e: Investors "shouting over one another" contrasts with the usual sedate (calm, dignified) tone, so the meeting became noisy and hard to control: obstreperous and unruly. Placid and tranquil are synonyms for the calm mood that the meeting lost. Tense also fits bad news, but tension can be silent, and it does not capture the shouting; tense has no partner. Abstemious means sparing in eating and drinking.

questions.s: Beneath its veneer of praise, the review was distinctly _____, each compliment concealing a barb that attentive readers could not miss.
questions.e: Compliments that hide barbs are mocking in an indirect way: snide (slyly derogatory) and sardonic (scornfully mocking). Eulogistic and encomiastic are synonyms meaning full of praise, but they describe only the "veneer," not what lies beneath it. Lengthy fits a review, but length has nothing to do with hidden barbs, and lengthy has no partner. Sartorial refers to clothing.

questions.s: The scholar's _____ manner in seminars, where she rarely spoke and then only briefly, belied the expansiveness of her published work.
questions.e: The description "rarely spoke and then only briefly" defines the blank: taciturn and uncommunicative (inclined to say little). Voluble (talkative) and prolix (wordy) are near-synonyms that fit her expansive writing, but "belied" (contradicted) requires her manner to differ from that writing. Diffident (shy, lacking confidence) could explain her silence, but it names a cause rather than the silence itself, and no other choice matches it. Salubrious means healthful.

questions.s: Because the evidence for the hypothesis was _____, the reviewers asked the authors to soften the paper's confident claims.
questions.e: Reviewers ask for softer claims when the support is weak, so the evidence was tenuous (very slight) or flimsy. Incontrovertible and irrefutable are synonyms meaning impossible to dispute, which would justify confident claims rather than soften them. Indirect evidence might also call for caution, but indirect evidence can be strong, and indirect has no partner. Sonorous means deep and resonant.

questions.s: Far from being _____, the reforms were introduced over a full decade, each step carefully tested before the next was taken.
questions.e: "Far from being" contrasts the blank with slow, tested, step-by-step change, so it must mean rushed: precipitate (done suddenly and without care; not to be confused with precipitous, steep) and headlong. Incremental and piecemeal (done bit by bit) are synonyms that describe the reforms as they actually were, so they cancel the "far from" contrast. Popular reforms are possible, but popularity is not the opposite of gradual testing, and popular has no partner. Lachrymose means tearful.

questions.s: The ambassador's _____ was legendary: she could decline an invitation so gracefully that the host felt honored by the refusal.
questions.e: Refusing an invitation so gracefully that the host feels honored shows skill in delicate social situations: tact and finesse. Tactlessness and gaucherie (social awkwardness) are synonyms for the opposite quality; a reader who sees the root of "tact" may pick tactlessness by mistake. Popularity might follow from such skill, but it is not what the example demonstrates, and popularity has no partner. Avarice means greed.

questions.s: Initially welcomed as a _____ for the region's economic troubles, the new factory soon proved to create far fewer jobs than its backers had promised.
questions.e: "Welcomed" and the later disappointment show that people expected the factory to solve every problem: panacea and cure-all. Bane and scourge are synonyms for a source of harm, which no one would welcome. Symbol fits the sentence (a factory could be welcomed as a symbol of renewal), but "for the region's troubles" calls for a remedy, and symbol has no partner. A soliloquy is a speech to oneself.

questions.s: The philosopher's argument, though ingenious, is ultimately _____: it assumes the very conclusion it sets out to prove.
questions.e: An argument that "assumes the very conclusion it sets out to prove" is circular, also called question-begging. Cogent and compelling are synonyms that echo "ingenious," but "though" and "ultimately" signal a flaw, and the colon spells out that flaw. Obscure is a possible criticism of a philosopher, but it describes unclear expression rather than faulty logic, and it has no partner. Gustatory relates to taste.

questions.s: Admirers saw her refusal to revise the manuscript as integrity; detractors saw only _____.
questions.e: Detractors give an unflattering name to the same refusal that admirers call integrity, so the blank must mean stubbornness: obstinacy and intransigence (refusal to compromise). Vacillation and indecision are synonyms for wavering, but a firm refusal is the opposite of wavering. Vanity is a plausible negative reading of a refusal to accept edits, but it names a motive rather than the stubbornness itself, and it has no partner. Verisimilitude means the appearance of truth.

questions.s: The novelist's later books abandon the _____ of her early work, replacing its elaborate sentences and dense metaphors with plain, almost clipped prose.
questions.e: What the later books abandon is described as "elaborate sentences and dense metaphors," so the blank names a decorated style: floridity (excessively elaborate style) and ornamentation. Austerity and spareness are synonyms that describe the plain later style, not what was abandoned. Ambition could also be dropped from a novelist's later work, but it does not match the clue about sentences and metaphors, and it has no partner. Perfidy means treachery.

questions.s: Although the treatise's argument is often _____, its occasional moments of startling clarity reward the patient reader.
questions.e: "Although" and "moments of startling clarity" set the usual argument against clarity, and "patient reader" implies difficulty: abstruse and recondite both mean hard to understand. Perspicuous (clearly expressed) and intelligible are synonyms that describe only the rare moments, not the usual argument. Repetitive could test a reader's patience, but repetition is not the opposite of clarity, and it has no partner. Venal means open to bribery.

questions.s: The ambassador's _____ remarks, carefully calibrated to offend neither side, ended up satisfying no one.
questions.e: Remarks "calibrated to offend neither side" are deliberately inoffensive and bland: anodyne and innocuous. Incendiary and inflammatory are synonyms for provocative, the opposite of remarks designed to offend no one. Scripted also fits carefully prepared remarks, but it says only that they were written in advance, not that they were bland, and scripted has no partner. Hirsute means hairy.

questions.s: The biologist's _____ in the field was remarkable: she kept searching through monsoon rains and months of fruitless surveys without once considering abandoning the project.
questions.e: Continuing through rain and "months of fruitless surveys" without thinking of quitting shows persistence: doggedness and tenacity. Lassitude and lethargy are synonyms for weariness and lack of energy, the reverse of the behavior described. Skill is admirable in a field biologist, but fruitless surveys show persistence rather than skill, and skill has no partner. Penury means extreme poverty.

questions.s: The retrospective did not merely confirm the photographer's reputation; it _____ it, revealing a body of work far more varied than anyone had suspected.
questions.e: "Did not merely confirm" signals something beyond confirmation, and revealing unexpected range improves a reputation: burnished (polished, made brighter) and enhanced. Tarnished and sullied are synonyms for damaged, and a reader who sees the metal image of "burnished" may confuse the two, but discovering greater variety is a gain. Complicated also goes beyond confirmation, but it does not say the reputation improved, and it has no partner. Abjured means formally renounced.

questions.s: Her _____ about her own achievements was so complete that colleagues learned of her award only when it was reported in the newspaper.
questions.e: Colleagues hearing of her award only from the newspaper shows she never drew attention to herself: modesty and self-effacement (keeping oneself in the background). Vainglory and boastfulness are synonyms for the opposite habit; a boaster's colleagues would have heard first. Secrecy fits the result as well, but it suggests deliberate hiding rather than humility, so it would change the meaning, and it has no partner. Rapacity means greed.

questions.s: The committee's decision, which seemed _____ to outsiders, followed a clear logic once the budget constraints were explained.
questions.e: The contrast is between how the decision "seemed" and the "clear logic" it actually followed, so outsiders thought it had no reason behind it: capricious and whimsical (driven by passing impulse rather than reason). Judicious and prudent are synonyms for wise and careful, which is what the decision turned out to be, so they remove the contrast. Hasty could be an outsider's impression, but speed is not the opposite of logic, and hasty has no partner. Ebullient means bubbling with enthusiasm.

questions.s: The essay is less an argument than a _____, heaping scorn on the author's rivals while offering little evidence for its own claims.
questions.e: A piece that heaps scorn on rivals instead of arguing is a bitter verbal attack: diatribe and tirade. Panegyric and encomium are synonyms for a speech of high praise, the opposite of scorn. Memoir might also be "less an argument" than personal storytelling, but it does not match "heaping scorn," and it has no partner. A palimpsest is a manuscript written over an erased earlier text.

questions.s: The economist's forecasts, once dismissed as _____, now seem remarkably prescient: nearly every downturn she predicted came to pass.
questions.e: Her forecasts predicted downturns and were "dismissed," so critics thought she exaggerated dangers: alarmist and scaremongering. Panglossian and Pollyannaish are synonyms for unreasonably optimistic, but forecasts of downturns cannot be too rosy. Technical forecasts might be ignored, but technicality is not the opposite of prescient (showing foresight), and technical has no partner. Emollient means soothing.

questions.s: The poet's early verse was largely _____, borrowing freely from the masters she admired; only later did she find a voice unmistakably her own.
questions.e: "Borrowing freely from the masters" and the contrast with a later voice of her own show the early poems copied others: derivative and imitative. Idiosyncratic and singular (peculiar to one person, unique) are synonyms describing her later voice, so they reverse the time contrast. Sentimental is a common flaw of early verse, but it does not mean borrowed, and it has no partner. Pugnacious means eager to fight.

questions.s: Although she was notorious for her _____ in household matters, the philanthropist was remarkably openhanded when it came to funding scientific research.
questions.e: "Although" sets the blank against being "openhanded" (generous), so she was tight with money at home: stinginess and miserliness. Munificence and largesse are synonyms for generosity, which would match rather than contrast with her support for research. Caution is close in spirit, but caution is not the opposite of generosity and need not involve money, so it has no partner. Celerity means speed.

questions.s: The new evidence did not so much refute the theory as _____ it, forcing its proponents to add qualifications that made it far less ambitious.
questions.e: "Not so much refute ... as" calls for a milder effect, and the qualifications that make the theory "far less ambitious" restrict its scope: circumscribe and delimit (set limits on). Corroborate and substantiate are synonyms for support, but supporting evidence would not force proponents to scale back their claims. Complicate fits the added qualifications, but it does not convey the narrowing of scope, and it has no partner. Ingratiate means to bring oneself into favor.

questions.s: To his admirers the critic's verdicts seemed fearlessly honest; to the artists he reviewed, they seemed merely _____.
questions.e: The sentence offers two readings of the same verdicts: "fearlessly honest" from admirers and an unflattering version from the artists, so the verdicts were harsh and the artists saw only bitterness: vitriolic and venomous (bitterly harsh). Sycophantic and obsequious are synonyms for flattering, which no one would call fearless honesty. Predictable is an unflattering label too, but it does not reinterpret harshness, and it has no partner. Diaphanous means thin and translucent.

questions.s: The once _____ debate among astronomers over the planet's composition has largely subsided now that the probe has returned unambiguous data.
questions.e: "Once" and "has largely subsided" imply that the debate used to be intense and bitter: acrimonious and rancorous. Amicable and cordial are synonyms for friendly, and a friendly debate would not need to "subside." Famous fits a prominent scientific dispute, but fame is not what dies down when data arrive, and famous has no partner. Vestigial means remaining as a trace.

questions.s: Though the historian's prose is _____, her research is meticulous, and specialists consult her books despite finding them a chore to read.
questions.e: "Though" sets the prose against meticulous research, and books that are "a chore to read" have heavy, dull writing: ponderous and leaden. Sprightly and lively are synonyms for energetic, which would make the books a pleasure rather than a chore. Archaic (old-fashioned) prose might be hard going too, but it describes period style rather than heaviness, and it has no partner. Bucolic means rural.

questions.s: The manager's _____ in the face of repeated setbacks struck some colleagues as admirable and others as a failure to grasp how serious the situation was.
questions.e: Only calm could be read either as admirable or as not grasping the danger, so the blank means equanimity or imperturbability (steady calmness). Despondency and dejection are synonyms for discouragement, which no one would mistake for failing to see that things are serious. Optimism also allows both readings, but hopefulness differs from calmness, and optimism has no partner. Frugality means thrift.

questions.s: The theory's appeal lies partly in its _____: a single principle accounts for phenomena that earlier models explained only with dozens of separate rules.
questions.e: Explaining with one principle what others needed dozens of rules for is simplicity of explanation: parsimony (in science, using the fewest assumptions) and economy. Intricacy and complexity are synonyms describing the earlier models, not the new theory. Novelty could add to a theory's appeal, but the colon explains the blank with simplicity, not newness, and novelty has no partner. In everyday use parsimony means stinginess, which is why it is easy to miss here.

questions.s: The young composer's _____ was evident in her willingness to challenge the conservatory's most revered teachers in public.
questions.e: Publicly challenging revered teachers shows boldness that may border on rashness: temerity and audacity. Deference and submissiveness are synonyms for yielding to authority, the opposite of challenging it. Talent may well be evident in a young composer, but a willingness to challenge teachers shows nerve, not ability, and talent has no partner. Aridity means dryness.

questions.s: The archive's records are maddeningly _____: some years are documented in minute detail, while others are missing entirely.
questions.e: Records that are detailed for some years and absent for others were kept without a consistent plan: desultory (lacking method, random) and haphazard. Systematic and methodical are synonyms describing the orderly record keeping that the colon clause rules out. Ancient records might also be patchy, but age does not explain the unevenness, and ancient has no partner. Mellifluous means sweet-sounding.

questions.s: Breaking the bad news to the anxious clients called for a _____ approach, so the manager chose every word with great care.
questions.e: Choosing every word with care in a delicate situation describes a 'tactful' approach (sensitive to others' feelings). 'Blunt' and 'casual' are the opposite of careful wording, and 'rigid' says nothing about sensitivity.

questions.s: Within a decade of the digital camera's arrival, the film-developing machines found in most pharmacies had become _____ and were sold for scrap.
questions.e: A new technology replacing the old one, and the machines being sold for scrap, show they were no longer useful: 'obsolete' (out of date, no longer used). 'Indispensable' and 'profitable' machines would not be scrapped.

questions.s: Unlike the polished official biography, the artist's private letters are _____, revealing doubts and quarrels she never mentioned in public.
questions.e: 'Unlike' contrasts the letters with the polished biography, and revealing private doubts shows openness: the letters are 'candid' (frank, honest). 'Guarded' and 'evasive' describe hiding things, the opposite of what the letters do.

questions.s: Planting trees along the riverbank helped _____ the erosion, though it could not stop it completely.
questions.e: 'Though it could not stop it completely' means the trees reduced the erosion without ending it: they helped 'mitigate' it (make it less severe). 'Accelerate' and 'cause' point the wrong way, and 'measure' does not fit the contrast with stopping.

questions.s: The documentary covers a fascinating subject, but its narration is so _____ that many viewers fall asleep within the first half hour.
questions.e: 'But' contrasts the fascinating subject with the narration, and viewers falling asleep shows it is boring: 'tedious'. 'Lively' and 'gripping' would keep viewers awake, and 'informative' or 'accurate' narration is not a reason to fall asleep.

questions.s: The once struggling bakery became so _____ after opening a second shop that its owner repaid all her loans within a year.
questions.e: Repaying all loans quickly requires the business to make a lot of money, so it became 'lucrative' (profitable). 'Unprofitable' describes the struggling past, and 'crowded' or 'famous' shops do not necessarily make enough money to repay debts.

questions.s: The expedition's food supply was _____: each climber received only a handful of rice and some dried fruit per day.
questions.e: The colon introduces evidence of very small rations ('only a handful'), so the supply was 'meager' (scanty, insufficient). 'Plentiful' and 'varied' are the opposite, and nothing suggests the food was spoiled.

questions.s: The coral reef proved surprisingly _____, recovering within a few years from a storm that scientists had expected to destroy it.
questions.e: Recovering from damage that was expected to be fatal shows the reef was 'resilient' (able to recover quickly). 'Fragile' and 'vulnerable' describe what scientists expected, so they cannot be the surprise.

questions.s: Because the advertisement's claims sounded too good to be true, many readers remained _____.
questions.e: Claims that seem too good to be true make people doubt them, so readers remained 'skeptical' (doubtful). 'Convinced' and 'delighted' are the reactions the advertisers wanted, not the result of suspicion. Readers who saw the claims are not 'uninformed'.

questions.s: In a room full of dark business suits, her bright orange coat made her instantly _____.
questions.e: Bright orange against dark suits makes someone stand out, so she was 'conspicuous' (easily noticed). 'Invisible' and 'anonymous' are the opposite, and the coat's color has nothing to do with comfort or timing.

questions.s: The historian treated the diary's claims with caution until letters discovered in an unrelated archive began to _____ them, independently confirming several of its dates and names.
questions.e: 'Independently confirming' defines the blank: the letters 'corroborate' (support with further evidence) the diary. 'Until' shows the caution ended, which a contradiction would not cause; that is why 'contradict' is the trap. 'Embellish' (add decorative detail) is not confirmation.

questions.s: Far from easing the city's traffic problem, the new highway seems to _____ it, drawing even more cars into an already crowded center.
questions.e: 'Far from easing' plus 'drawing even more cars' shows the highway makes the problem worse: it seems to 'exacerbate' it. 'Alleviate' (relieve) and 'resolve' are exactly what 'far from' denies.

questions.s: The editor struck out every _____ phrase in the manuscript, so that the final version was half as long yet said everything the original had said.
questions.e: If the shorter version says everything the original did, the deleted phrases added nothing: they were 'superfluous' (unnecessary). 'Essential' is the opposite. 'Ambiguous' phrases would need clarifying rather than simply deleting, and cutting them would lose some meaning.

questions.s: The novelist has a gift for finding drama in the _____: her best stories concern grocery shopping, commuting, and the washing of dishes.
questions.e: Grocery shopping, commuting and washing dishes are everyday activities, so she finds drama in the 'mundane' (ordinary, routine). The gift is noteworthy precisely because such topics seem undramatic; 'exotic', 'heroic' and 'supernatural' would already be dramatic.

questions.s: Though she had campaigned on bold ideals, the new director proved thoroughly _____ once in office, adopting whatever policies seemed likely to work regardless of where they came from.
questions.e: 'Though ... bold ideals' sets up a contrast, and choosing policies by whether they work defines a 'pragmatic' approach (practical rather than theoretical). 'Idealistic' repeats her campaign stance, and 'dogmatic' (rigidly attached to doctrine) contradicts openness to any source.

questions.s: Once found only in a handful of research laboratories, such sensors have become _____, built into everything from phones to refrigerators.
questions.e: 'Once found only in a handful of labs' contrasts with sensors now 'built into everything', so they have become 'ubiquitous' (present everywhere). 'Rare' and 'specialized' describe their past, not their present.

questions.s: Kwame's feelings about the promotion were _____: he welcomed the higher salary but dreaded the long hours that came with it.
questions.e: Welcoming one part and dreading another means he had mixed feelings: he was 'ambivalent'. 'Unequivocal' (leaving no doubt) and 'ecstatic' capture only the welcome, 'resentful' only the dread. 'Indifferent' (not caring) contradicts having strong feelings both ways.

questions.s: Hoping to end the long dispute, the company's new chief executive adopted a _____ tone with the union, opening her first meeting by acknowledging past mistakes.
questions.e: Wanting to end a dispute and admitting past mistakes describe a 'conciliatory' tone (meant to make peace). 'Belligerent' (hostile, aggressive) and 'defiant' would prolong the dispute, and 'condescending' contradicts the humble admission.

questions.s: The museum's dating of the statue is only _____; curators expect to revise it once the results of the chemical analysis arrive.
questions.e: A date that curators expect to revise is temporary: 'provisional' (arranged for now, subject to change); 'only' supports this. 'Definitive' (final) is the opposite. 'Fraudulent' implies deliberate deception, which nothing suggests.

questions.s: Visitors expecting the lavish decoration typical of the period are often surprised by the merchant's house and its _____ interior: bare white walls, plain wooden benches, and a single small window.
questions.e: Bare walls, plain benches and one window describe a severely simple interior: 'austere'. 'Surprised' contrasts it with 'lavish decoration'. 'Opulent' (luxurious) and 'ornate' are what the visitors expected, so they cannot be the surprise.

questions.s: No appeal, whether to reason, to sentiment, or to self-interest, could move the _____ landlord, who refused even to discuss repairing the building.
questions.e: Someone unmoved by every kind of appeal is stubbornly unyielding: 'obdurate'. 'Pliant' (easily influenced) is the opposite. 'Capricious' (whimsical, changeable) is a trap for readers who see only 'difficult landlord'; a capricious person would be unpredictable, not fixed in refusal.

questions.s: The young lexicographer's _____ attention to detail, checking each citation against its original source, impressed even the dictionary's most demanding editors.
questions.e: Checking every citation against its source shows diligent, persistent care: 'sedulous' (painstaking, assiduous). 'Even the most demanding editors' were impressed, so the blank must be strong praise. 'Cursory' (hasty, superficial) and 'desultory' (unmethodical) are the opposite.

questions.s: Her _____ response to the market crash (she shrugged and went back to her crossword) alarmed colleagues who had spent the morning in a panic.
questions.e: Shrugging and returning to a crossword while others panic is carefree unconcern: 'insouciant'. 'Frantic' and 'apoplectic' (overcome with anger) describe the panicked colleagues, not her. 'Rueful' (regretful) and 'morose' (gloomy) do not fit a shrug.

questions.s: So _____ was the chef that she rejected entire crates of tomatoes over a single bruised fruit.
questions.e: Rejecting a whole crate over one flaw shows extreme attention to quality: she was 'fastidious' (very demanding about detail and standards). 'Slovenly' and 'lackadaisical' (lazily careless) are the opposite. 'Impetuous' (acting rashly) misreads her decision as impulsive rather than exacting.

questions.s: Admirers prized the essayist's _____ criticism, which cut straight to a book's weaknesses in a few incisive sentences.
questions.e: Criticism that cuts straight to weaknesses in incisive sentences is 'trenchant' (sharp, forceful, vigorously effective). 'Anodyne' (bland, inoffensive) and 'sycophantic' (flattering) avoid weaknesses, 'rambling' contradicts 'a few sentences', and 'equivocal' contradicts cutting 'straight' to the point.

questions.s: The exchange of letters, which began politely enough, grew so _____ that both scholars eventually threatened legal action over the insults it contained.
questions.e: Letters full of insults bad enough to prompt legal threats are 'vituperative' (bitterly abusive). 'Began politely enough' signals the change. 'Cordial' and 'decorous' (polite, proper) describe the beginning, not what the letters became; 'esoteric' (obscure) has nothing to do with insults.

questions.s: Thanks to a _____ bequest from a former student, the small college was able to triple its scholarship fund overnight.
questions.e: Tripling a fund overnight requires a very large gift: the bequest was 'munificent' (extremely generous). 'Paltry' (tiny) is the opposite. An 'anonymous' or 'conditional' gift could be of any size, so neither explains the dramatic result.

questions.s: The screenplay relies on _____ devices (the mistaken identity, the last-minute rescue, the villain's lengthy confession) that audiences have seen a thousand times.
questions.e: Devices that audiences have 'seen a thousand times' are overused and unoriginal: 'hackneyed'. 'Innovative' is the opposite, and 'obscure' contradicts their familiarity. 'Subtle' does not describe such stock plot turns.

questions.s: After months of rapid growth, the housing market has turned _____: sales have slowed to a crawl and prices have barely moved since spring.
questions.e: Sales at a crawl and unmoving prices describe a sluggish, inactive market: 'torpid' (lethargic, dormant). 'Buoyant' and 'frenetic' (wildly energetic) fit the earlier rapid growth. 'Volatile' (prone to sudden change) contradicts prices that 'barely moved'.

questions.s: The reviewer was so _____ that she devoted half her review to minor slips of punctuation while saying almost nothing about the book's argument.
questions.e: Fixating on trivial rules of punctuation at the expense of substance is 'pedantic' (overly concerned with minor details and rules). 'Lenient' clashes with nitpicking, and 'perceptive' fails because she missed the main point. 'Effusive' (gushing) and 'laconic' do not describe her misplaced focus.

questions.s: Although the committee had expected the proposal to provoke heated debate, it was approved with a _____ that surprised even its author.
questions.e: 'Although' sets up a contrast with 'heated debate', so the blank needs the opposite of disagreement. 'Unanimity' (complete agreement) is exactly that. 'Hostility' and 'skepticism' describe the debate the committee expected, not a surprising contrast to it, and 'reluctance' still implies division.

questions.s: The new manager was admired for her _____ approach to problems: she gathered the facts, weighed every option, and only then made a decision.
questions.e: The colon tells you the second half restates the blank: gathering facts, weighing options and deciding last describe a 'methodical' (orderly, step-by-step) approach. 'Impulsive' and 'whimsical' are the opposite, and nothing in the sentence concerns secrecy or leniency.

questions.s: Because the bridge's original timber supports had become _____ after decades of exposure to salt water, engineers replaced them with steel.
questions.e: 'Because' signals cause and effect: the supports were replaced, so salt water must have damaged them. 'Deteriorated' (worn down, weakened) gives the reason. 'Durable' and 'waterproof' are traps: they describe timber that would not need replacing.

questions.s: Far from being a minor revision, the second edition of the textbook was a _____ overhaul, with nearly every chapter rewritten.
questions.e: 'Far from being a minor revision' calls for the opposite of minor, and 'nearly every chapter rewritten' confirms it: the overhaul was 'thorough'. 'Cosmetic' and 'partial' describe exactly the minor revision the sentence rules out; 'hasty' has no support.

questions.s: Critics conceded that the novelist's plots were sometimes _____, but they praised the richness and depth of her characters.
questions.e: 'Conceded' and 'but' mark a concession: the critics admit a weakness before praising a strength, so the blank must be negative. 'Contrived' (artificial, forced) is the only criticism among the choices. 'Vivid', 'original' and 'moving' are praise and would not need to be conceded.

questions.s: Unlike her _____ predecessor, who announced every decision at lengthy press conferences, the new mayor rarely spoke to reporters.
questions.e: The predecessor is defined by the clause after the blank: someone who held lengthy press conferences was 'outspoken' (ready to speak openly). 'Unlike' then contrasts this with the quiet new mayor. 'Reclusive' describes the new mayor, not the predecessor, and is the main trap.

questions.s: The museum's new lighting is so _____ that visitors can now see fine brushstrokes that were invisible under the old lamps.
questions.e: The 'so ... that' structure needs a quality of light that would reveal previously invisible detail, and 'intense' (strong, bright) does that. 'Subtle' suggests faint light, the opposite of what is needed, and 'flickering' would make detail harder to see. 'Costly' says nothing about visibility.

questions.s: The researchers' findings proved _____: the same experiment, run independently in three different laboratories, produced nearly identical results.
questions.e: The colon introduces evidence that defines the blank: identical results in three labs mean the findings were 'reproducible' (able to be obtained again). 'Anomalous' (irregular, unexpected) is the opposite, and 'biased' would be undermined, not shown, by independent replication.

questions.s: The economist's forecast was at first dismissed as overly _____, yet the recession she had predicted arrived within a year.
questions.e: She predicted a recession, and 'yet' shows that the people who dismissed her were wrong: they had judged her forecast too gloomy, or 'pessimistic'. 'Cautious' is close but weaker; it does not capture predicting a downturn. 'Detailed', 'technical' and 'popular' are not reasons to dismiss a forecast of recession.

questions.s: Since the letters were written in a regional dialect that few scholars could read, their contents remained _____ for more than a century.
questions.e: 'Since' gives the cause: almost no one could read the letters, so their contents stayed 'obscure' (unknown, not understood). 'Disputed' is a trap; a dispute requires people who can read and argue about the text. 'Celebrated' contradicts the cause.

questions.s: The coach's praise was famously _____; because she rarely complimented anyone, a single word of approval from her meant a great deal.
questions.e: The second clause restates the blank: rarely complimenting anyone means her praise was 'sparing' (given in small amounts). 'Lavish' and 'constant' are the opposite, and 'insincere' would make her approval worth little, not a great deal.

questions.s: While the sequel is _____ in its own right, it lacks the originality that made the first film so memorable.
questions.e: 'While' introduces a concession, so the blank must be a positive quality balanced against the criticism that follows. 'Entertaining' is the only praise. 'Derivative' (copied from earlier work) is the trap: it agrees with 'lacks originality' instead of contrasting with it.

questions.s: The long drought did more than _____ the region's harvest; it destroyed it entirely.
questions.e: 'Did more than X; it destroyed it' needs X to be a milder version of destroying, so 'diminish' (reduce) fits the scale of degree. 'Improve' and 'guarantee' point in the wrong direction, and 'announce' and 'inspect' are not steps toward destruction.

questions.s: The software update was supposed to make the program faster, but it proved so _____ that many users reinstalled the earlier version.
questions.e: 'But' contrasts the update's purpose with its result, and reinstalling the old version shows the result was bad, so 'unreliable' fits. 'Efficient', 'popular' and 'intuitive' are all qualities that would make users keep the update.

questions.s: The essayist's early pieces were notably _____, but her later work became increasingly concise and direct.
questions.e: 'But' contrasts the early pieces with 'concise and direct' later work, so the early pieces must have been wordy: 'verbose' (using more words than needed). 'Succinct' and 'brief' are traps that match the later work, not the contrast.

questions.s: First regarded as a harmless curiosity, the imported water plant soon proved _____ to native species, crowding them out of entire wetlands.
questions.e: The phrase 'crowding them out' shows the plant harmed native species, which contrasts with 'harmless curiosity'. 'Detrimental' (causing harm) fits. 'Beneficial' and 'vital' point the opposite way, and 'indifferent' cannot describe an effect on something.

questions.s: The treaty's wording was deliberately _____, allowing each side to interpret its terms in whatever way best suited its own interests.
questions.e: Wording that lets each side read the terms its own way is 'ambiguous' (open to more than one interpretation). 'Precise' is the opposite. 'Lengthy' and 'formal' wording could still be clear, so they do not explain the freedom to interpret.

questions.s: The firm's profits had been _____ for several quarters, so investors were relieved when the annual report finally showed strong growth.
questions.e: Investors felt relief at growth, so profits before must have been worrying; 'stagnant' (not growing, inactive) fits. 'Soaring' and 'impressive' would leave nothing to be relieved about, and 'audited' and 'published' say nothing about performance.

questions.s: The pianist's performance was not merely competent but _____, keeping the audience on its feet for ten minutes of applause.
questions.e: 'Not merely competent but ...' requires a word well above competent, and the ten-minute ovation confirms it: 'dazzling' (brilliantly impressive). 'Adequate' is the trap; it means about the same as competent, so it fails the step up in degree.

questions.s: Though the survey sample was small, its results were _____ enough to justify a larger follow-up study.
questions.e: 'Though' concedes a weakness, and the results still justified more research, so they must have been encouraging: 'promising'. 'Discouraging' and 'irrelevant' would argue against a follow-up study, not for it.

questions.s: The poet's public persona was jovial and gregarious, but in her private diaries she appears _____ and withdrawn.
questions.e: 'But' contrasts the diaries with the jovial public persona, and the blank is paired with 'withdrawn', so it must mean sad: 'melancholy' (gloomy, sorrowful). 'Cheerful' and 'sociable' repeat the public persona instead of contrasting with it.

questions.s: Because the new tax regulation was so _____, even experienced accountants struggled to explain it to their clients.
questions.e: Experts struggling to explain a rule points to its complexity, so 'convoluted' (extremely complicated, twisting) supplies the cause. 'Straightforward' is the opposite. 'Lenient' and 'temporary' describe the rule's effect or duration, not why it is hard to explain.

questions.s: Unlike most of its relatives, this species of desert lizard is _____: it hunts at night and sleeps through the heat of the day.
questions.e: The colon defines the blank: an animal active at night is 'nocturnal'. The other choices are real animal traits, but nothing after the colon is about venom, water, diet or defending territory.

questions.s: The founder was known for being _____ with money, yet she spent lavishly on any equipment her engineers requested.
questions.e: 'Yet' sets her reputation against spending lavishly, so she must usually be careful and economical: 'frugal'. 'Generous' and 'careless' agree with lavish spending, so there would be no contrast to signal.

questions.s: The historian's account of the dispute is admirably _____: she presents the arguments of both factions without favoring either.
questions.e: Presenting both sides without favoring either is the definition of 'impartial' (fair, unbiased). 'Partisan' (taking one side) is the opposite. 'Exhaustive' (complete) is tempting but describes thoroughness, not fairness.

questions.s: Because all of the evidence for the supplement's benefits came from a single small study, the review panel judged the manufacturer's claims _____.
questions.e: Thin evidence (one small study) leads to the judgment that the claims are 'unsubstantiated' (not supported by proof). 'Proven' is the opposite. 'Harmful' is a different charge that the sentence gives no basis for.

questions.s: The building's exterior is admittedly _____, but its interior spaces are full of light and ingenuity.
questions.e: 'Admittedly ... but' concedes a flaw before praising the interior, so the exterior must be unattractive: 'drab' (dull, colorless). 'Striking', 'elegant' and 'novel' are compliments and would not be admitted as a weakness.

questions.s: The scientists' warnings grew steadily more _____ as each new measurement showed the glacier retreating faster than before.
questions.e: Worse news with each measurement would make warnings more pressing, so 'urgent' fits the rising degree. 'Muted', 'infrequent' and 'optimistic' all move in the opposite direction from the accelerating retreat.

questions.s: Rather than _____ her students' questions as interruptions, the professor welcomed them as signs of genuine engagement.
questions.e: 'Rather than' needs the opposite of welcoming, and 'as interruptions' shows a negative view: 'dismissing' them. 'Encouraging' is close to welcoming, so it gives no contrast, and 'answering' questions is not the opposite of valuing them.

questions.s: The language has been remarkably _____: its spelling and grammar have changed so little over six centuries that modern readers can follow medieval texts with ease.
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: changing very little over centuries means the language has been 'stable'. 'Complex' and 'widespread' may be true of many languages but do not explain why old texts are easy to read today.

questions.s: The telescope's images were so _____ that astronomers could not tell whether the faint spot was a single star or two.
questions.e: Being unable to separate one star from two is the result of unclear images, so 'blurry' completes the 'so ... that' cause. 'Detailed' and 'enlarged' would make the stars easier to tell apart, the opposite of the result described.

questions.s: The restaurant's menu, once famously _____, now offers only a handful of carefully chosen dishes.
questions.e: 'Once' contrasts the past menu with the present 'handful' of dishes, so the old menu must have been large: 'extensive'. 'Limited' is the trap; it describes the menu now, not the change. 'Affordable' and 'exotic' do not oppose a short menu.

questions.s: Children in the study who were _____ by nature, approaching strangers and unfamiliar toys without hesitation, adapted to the new classroom most quickly.
questions.e: The phrase set off by commas defines the blank: approaching new people and things without hesitation describes 'adventurous' children. 'Timid' is the opposite, and 'obedient' and 'restless' describe behavior the sentence never mentions.

questions.s: The composer's late string quartets, though _____ to audiences of his own day, are now considered among his finest works.
questions.e: 'Though' contrasts the original reception with today's high regard, so the first audiences must have reacted poorly: the quartets were 'baffling' (confusing) to them. 'Pleasing' and 'accessible' would agree with the later praise and remove the contrast.

questions.s: The tremor was so _____ that seismographs in the neighboring town barely registered it.
questions.e: Instruments that barely registered the tremor show it was weak, so 'slight' fits. 'Violent' and 'destructive' are the opposite of what the result requires, and 'sudden' or 'prolonged' describe timing, not strength.

questions.s: Although the negotiator appeared _____ throughout the talks, she later admitted that she had been anxious the entire time.
questions.e: 'Although' sets up a contrast with 'anxious', so she must have looked calm: 'composed' (self-controlled, calm). 'Nervous' matches her hidden feeling instead of contrasting with it, and 'hostile' or 'exhausted' are not opposites of anxiety.

questions.s: The witness's account contained so many _____ that the jury decided it could not rely on any part of it.
questions.e: A jury refuses to rely on testimony that contradicts itself, so 'inconsistencies' supplies the cause. 'Details' and 'facts' would normally make testimony more useful, and 'emotions' or 'repetitions' alone would not make every part of the account unreliable.

questions.s: Bamboo is an extraordinarily _____ plant: some species can grow almost a meter in a single day.
questions.e: The colon introduces evidence of very rapid growth, which describes a 'vigorous' (strong, energetic) plant. 'Dormant' (inactive) is the opposite, and 'edible' or 'rare' may be true of some plants but are not what the evidence shows.

questions.s: Early mobile phones were heavy and _____, whereas today's models slip easily into a pocket.
questions.e: 'Whereas' contrasts old phones with pocket-sized modern ones, and the blank is paired with 'heavy', so it must mean awkward to carry: 'cumbersome'. 'Sleek' and 'portable' describe the modern phones, not the early ones.

questions.s: The translation is not always _____ to the original wording, but it captures the spirit of the poem better than any literal version.
questions.e: The contrast with 'literal version' shows the translation sometimes departs from the exact words, so it is not always 'faithful' (closely accurate) to them. 'Superior' and 'inferior' compare quality rather than closeness, and 'not always opposed' makes no sense here.

questions.s: As the cost of imported wheat rose sharply, local bakeries had little choice but to _____ the price of bread.
questions.e: Higher costs for an ingredient cause higher prices for the product, so bakeries had to 'increase' the price. 'Reduce' and 'freeze' run against the cause, and 'advertise' does not follow from 'little choice'.

questions.s: The critic's review of the exhibition was not simply unfavorable but _____, condemning it in the harshest possible terms.
questions.e: 'Not simply unfavorable but ...' calls for something stronger than unfavorable, and 'harshest possible terms' confirms it: 'merciless'. 'Lukewarm' (mildly unenthusiastic) is weaker than unfavorable, so it fails the step up in degree.

questions.s: The village's legal customs were entirely _____: elders passed them on by word of mouth and never wrote them down.
questions.e: The colon defines the blank: customs passed on by word of mouth and never written are 'oral'. 'Ancient' and 'strict' may well be true but are not what the explanation after the colon describes, and nothing suggests the customs were 'secret'.

questions.s: Unlike gold, which resists tarnish for centuries, iron is highly _____ and rusts quickly in damp air.
questions.e: 'Unlike' contrasts iron with gold's resistance to change, and rusting quickly shows iron combines readily with air and water: it is 'reactive'. 'Inert' (chemically inactive) describes gold, not iron. 'Magnetic' is true of iron but has nothing to do with rusting.

questions.s: Because the instructions were entirely _____, every participant completed the task correctly on the first attempt.
questions.e: Everyone succeeding at once suggests instructions that left no room for doubt: 'explicit' (stated clearly and in detail). 'Vague' is the opposite, and 'lengthy' or 'printed' instructions are not necessarily easy to follow.

questions.s: The philosopher's arguments are rigorous, but her prose is so _____ that few readers make it past the first chapter.
questions.e: 'But' and the result (readers give up early) show the prose is hard going: 'dense' (packed and difficult to get through). 'Lively', 'elegant' and 'accessible' would keep readers going, so they contradict the result.

questions.s: Decades of careful irrigation turned the once _____ valley into one of the most productive farming regions in the country.
questions.e: 'Once' and 'turned into' signal a change, and irrigation adds water, so the valley must have been dry before: 'arid'. 'Fertile' is the trap; it describes the valley after the change, not before.

questions.s: The director is notoriously _____; she insists on approving even the smallest decisions herself.
questions.e: The second clause explains the first: insisting on approving every small decision is 'controlling' behavior. 'Indecisive' is tempting, but she is making the decisions, not failing to make them, and 'absent' contradicts her constant involvement.

questions.s: Even the film's harshest critics _____ that its cinematography was stunning.
questions.e: 'Even the harshest critics' signals a concession: people who disliked the film still admitted one strength, so they 'acknowledged' it. 'Denied' and 'doubted' would not need 'even', since harsh critics are expected to disagree.

questions.s: The effect the physicists predicted was so _____ that detecting it required instruments a thousand times more sensitive than any then available.
questions.e: Needing extremely sensitive instruments means the effect was tiny: 'minute' (pronounced my-NOOT, very small). 'Obvious' is the opposite, and 'dangerous' or 'sudden' would not explain the need for greater sensitivity.

questions.s: The northern coast is rugged and sparsely populated, while the southern shore is _____ with resorts and fishing villages.
questions.e: 'While' contrasts the south with the 'sparsely populated' north, and the resorts and villages show many people: the shore is 'crowded'. 'Barren', 'untouched' and 'remote' describe the north, not the contrast.

questions.s: Because the two languages share so much vocabulary, speakers of one often find the other surprisingly _____.
questions.e: Shared vocabulary makes a language easier to understand, so speakers find it 'intelligible' (able to be understood). 'Foreign' and 'difficult' run against the cause, and 'surprisingly' fits only an unexpected ease.

questions.s: Mateo is unusually _____ for a teenager: he saves most of what he earns and plans his purchases months in advance.
questions.e: Saving and planning ahead define a 'prudent' person (careful, sensible about the future). 'Wasteful', 'impatient' and 'carefree' are the opposite of this careful behavior.

questions.s: Once thought to be inherited, the leaf blight is now known to be _____, spreading from tree to tree by wind-borne spores.
questions.e: 'Once thought ... now known' signals a correction, and spreading from tree to tree means the blight is 'contagious' (passed by contact or transmission). 'Genetic' is the trap: it repeats the old belief that it was inherited.

questions.s: The proposal is _____ in theory, but putting it into practice would cost far more than the city can afford.
questions.e: 'But' contrasts the theory with a practical problem, so the theory must be good: 'sound' (well reasoned, reliable). 'Flawed' would leave no contrast, and 'expensive' repeats the cost problem the second clause raises.

questions.s: Her remarks were so _____ that several members of the audience walked out in protest.
questions.e: Walking out 'in protest' is a reaction to something objectionable, so the remarks were 'offensive'. 'Inaudible' might make people leave, but not in protest, and 'humorous' and 'reasonable' would not provoke it.

questions.s: The biography is less a balanced portrait than a _____, praising its subject so uncritically that his failures disappear from view.
questions.e: Uncritical praise describes a 'tribute' (a work honoring someone). 'Critique' is the opposite, and 'parody' mocks rather than praises. 'Sketch' and 'summary' say nothing about the book's admiring tone.

questions.s: Although the region's economy grew rapidly during the decade, wages for most workers remained _____.
questions.e: 'Although' contrasts rapid growth with what happened to wages, so wages must not have grown: they stayed 'flat'. 'Rising' and 'generous' agree with the growth and remove the contrast.

questions.s: The painter worked in a _____ style, reducing each scene to a few bold shapes and blocks of color.
questions.e: Reducing a scene to a few shapes is the mark of a 'minimalist' style (using the fewest possible elements). 'Ornate' (heavily decorated) and 'realistic' are the opposite of stripping a scene down.

questions.s: The town's position where three trade routes met made it _____ to merchants from across the continent.
questions.e: A meeting point of trade routes is good for business, so the town was 'attractive' to merchants. 'Inaccessible' and 'unknown' contradict a location on three routes, and nothing suggests danger or hostility.

questions.s: Though famously _____ in conversation, answering most questions with a single word, the physicist gave lectures that were expansive and richly detailed.
questions.e: The phrase 'answering most questions with a single word' defines the blank, and 'though' contrasts it with expansive lectures: she was 'laconic' (using very few words). 'Garrulous' (excessively talkative) is the trap; it fits the lectures, not her conversation. 'Erudite' (learned) does not explain one-word answers.

questions.s: Far from _____ the controversy, the museum's carefully worded statement only drew more attention to it.
questions.e: 'Far from X, it only drew more attention' means X is what the statement was meant to do but failed at, so X must be calming the controversy: 'defusing' it. 'Inflaming', 'publicizing' and 'prolonging' describe what actually happened, so they cannot follow 'far from'.
